Windows 8.1 or 10?  Don't bother.
From what little I've played, it seems like a great game-- however, due to compatibility issues this game is downright unplayable.  The pathfinding is just broken so that you'll indefinitely run the wrong way and have to click 3 times in arbitrary points to do any interaction, and the game is very prone to softlocking.  This is especially problematic as WHEN (not if) the game softlocks and crashes, it locks your cursor, meaning either restarting your computer or going through Task Manager with Ctrl-Shift-Esc and keyboard controls without looking at the screen will be necessary just to close the game.
I'm definitely glad I got this from a Humble Bundle, otherwise it would have been a huge letdown.  Even then, it's disappointing because these problems stand in the way of what seems to be a genuinely great game.  Go buy it on GOG instead, from what I've read they fixed the problem.  The 1.3 version Steam has is broken on Windows 8 and above, and quite possibly 7 as well, so once again, GOG is the first place you should look for old games.  Accept no substitutes.
On the bright side, the sequel "FF vs. the 3rd Reich" seems to be fine on modern systems, even with the Steam version.  You're still a fool if you buy it on Steam instead of GOG, but hey, you'll be a fool with a working game.

Freedom Force is a fantastic game for any fans of Silver Age comic books. This may be the most authentic representation of that era I've ever seen, presented without becoming a parody. Yes, most every character takes some inspiration from a pre-existing comic book hero or villain, but they're altered enough to work as their own character.
Gameplay is fun with an easy to learn system that. Finding the right character to take on the right enemy is always satisfying, though inevitably any characters I didn't try out or unlock early on ended up useless by the end as I continually upgraded my four or five favorites. Generally this is not at all a game genre I'd be interested in, but the comic book presentation pulled me in and kept my attention.
However, I can't rightly recommend the game without mentioning the Fist Icon Bug. You may turn off the game and later come back to find your icon is permenantly stuck as a fist, making it difficult to move, and making the character Minuteman run off on his own accord. I've seen a lot of suggested fixes, but since my computer upgraded to Windows 10, they don't seem to work anymore.
These fixes, such as lowering the resolution, may work for you, but please consider the risk. If the answer is no, I'd recommend the sequel, Freedom Force vs. the Third Reich, which does not have this problem.

Almost all the negative reviews for this game were written by incompetent kids. Reading other reviews you will hear complaints about achievements, difficulty, and a lack of warning of whats dangerous.
The third complaint listed above is the only reasonable complaint however it can be dismissed with about .5 hours of trial and error. After that time you should have a basic understanding of what is and isnt dangerous.
The most common complaint I have seen is that its too difficult to beat the game. Its a perma death rogue-like shooter. Read the tags before you buy a game it will actually end up saving you money if your not looking for a challenging game. Not to mention that after a little trial and error you find that the game is actually quite easy.
And the final complaint I have seen is about the achievements. The achievements appear harder to get than they are. Its important to note that each achievement asking you to get a certain number of kills or gather a certain amount of ammo is asking you to do it within a single run so if you die you have to restart. You need to have 1000 bullets in the top left corner of your screen to get the achievement. The rest of the achievements are self explanitory.

You may not be familiar with this title if you're younger but Another World is one of those games that everyone should play at least once in their life. Developed by Atari ST and Amiga, Another World came out in 1991 and was really special as a cinematic platformer, setting a high standard for future games in the genre. You may wonder looking at it so many years later what made it special, it's tough to explain as there are lots of things about it I really appreciate. The buddy that helps you along your jounrney (literally named Buddy) is a perfect example of a sidekick, someone that is not constantly offering you hints or interupting the game but rather a small motivator that helps you out of sticky situations, the artstyle is great and even today passes, clever level design and puzzle solving and finally genuine difficulty! As this is an older game, it will most likely feel more difficult and frustrating to younger players but offers a great feeling of satisfaction when you push yourself to complete it. Truly, it is nothing short of a classic and an essential game for any collection.

Anyone who likes to make some mental arithmetic within logical puzzles on the basis of geometric tasks and to spend about between 1 and maximum 10 minutes to find a solution for a specific problem (out of 90), should have a look at the game.

The possibility to use the game surface for writing some calculations is a nice plus factor, and that the pen is quavering makes the result to look quite handwritten as mine on a piece of paper.
I needed 2.7 hours to find all 90 solutions, i.e. a little bit less than 2 minutes for each. I found it worth the money and would have a look at a new version.
Instead of using solution guides, it would be better to have the possibility to get a hint in game (but such coding is more complicated and I personally prefer that the efitor adds more levels than help). But there are some hint giving players in the steam discussion forum replacing such a fonction.

I like the idea of Costume Quest and the first game. It took the idea from that Buffy episode (and Treehouse of Horror, and probably a lot of other examples) where the characters turn into their costumes and use it as the combat mechanics of an rpg staring kids battling candy stealing goblins. It's was a cute idea, that had charm and was pretty funny in a silly Double Fine way. A pretty good if simple game. Along comes Costume Quest 2 and brings in time travel and a insane dentist and it's just not as good as the first game.
It's not as funny this time. The costumes are not as creative, and the novelty of the game has worn off after 1 game and a DLC expansion. The combat is somewhat more involved this time, bit it adds a really anoying mechanics with the removal of post battle healing, forcing you to backtrack to a fountain (or to eat some candy). It doesn't add anything, it doesn't make the game any harder and it just makes the battles anoying.
Overall it's still pretty much the same rpg-lite for kids, but the combat mechanics is still kind of uninteresting and too simple and the storyline is weak, even when you take "it's for kids" into concideration. The first game had charm that made it a pretty good game. This is not bad, but I can't recommend it unless you desperatly need more after playing the first one, and can accept a game that's slightly worse on everything.

I pre-ordered this game ages ago, since I was too late for backing but still wanted to contribute. And I do not regret that decision because it was a very fun game to play!
The story is about a girl named Mina from a small village whose dream it is to become a member of the battlechef brigade, an elite group of chefs who kill monsters for food and keep the world safe. She therefore runs away to the city to join the competition which determines who can join the brigade. You have to face-off against chefs to earn your place. And then there is some other storyline which I will not spoil. The story is fun for the biggest part, not too spectacular, but well executed.
The game is a sort of weird sounding mix between side-scroller brawling and 3-match game for the cooking part. It sounds weird, but it actually works very well. The 3 match is basically match gems of the same color and they promote to a higher level, match 3 of those again to get the highest level. The 3-match has been changed up a bit to make it more interesting, with fragile parts (cannot move to much or they break) poison parts and upgrading of tiles. Besides that there is several interesting cook-ware you can buy to help you with the game and change some stuff around. For instance there are 2-match pans that only work on 1 kind of gem, but there is also 4-match pans that skip to the highest possible gem quality. There is 3 types of gems and each judge in the competition has different tastes in what they want so that's another thing to keep in mind. The battle aspect it not all that hard, there is basically one challenging enemy in it as far as I'm concerned. I didn't mind that it wasn't overly complicated though I liked the focus to be on the cooking part.
The thing that attracted me to this game most was the art. It is beautifully drawn with good character design as well as world design. And the food looks delicious! It is not all extremely detailed but I think that's part of the charm. It just looks colorful and vibrant and i absolutely love it.
The music I think is well done. The main song is constantly hanging around in my head. It fits the atmosphere really well, and sounds kind off heroic during battles.  The sounds during the battle are also well done. Especially the clock when time is running out, very stressful! Voice acting is solid, voices fit the characters well.
Note that none of these are dealbreakers just little things I noticed.
The difficulty spikes in this game are a bit crazy. Basically it is all pretty easy until you encounter the first set of bosses and then it is a lot harder all of a sudden. I would liked it more to have a more gradual increase in difficulty, just each battle a little bit harder instead of this spike. Besides that it goes down again after these 3 bosses and up again with the final one. It is a bit all over the place. And it does not help with learning to get better.
Second thing is that they had decided somewhere along the way to make Thrash (one of the other game characters) playable. And they had to sort of implement that into the storyline. So one of the chapters you are all of a sudden playing as Thrash for no good reason. This chapter felt random and weird. Besides that you had lost all the stuff you bought cause it did not carry over. I am all for more playable characters but it would have been more logical to then make a complete seperate campaign for him. I know that may be to much time consuming and expensive but well I would pay for DLC for new storylines with different characters. Now it just feels rushed.
Besides these two small issues I really enjoyed the game and I may replay it at some point. The art is amazing, gameplay is fun and the food looks delicious. I am a sucker for cooking games but I swear this game is amazing and would really recommend it. I hope they will add more content at some point, I would love a DLC about one of my favorite characters Ziggy!

I do feel the game slightly outstayed its welcome for me. While some are disappointed that the game is short (~8 hours), I actually feel it was too long. Much of the content is repeated. There are also two difficulty spikes that at least one other reviewer mentioned. The first one wasn't too bad, but I had to use one of the guides to beat the final challenge.
Overall, a fun and interesting experience.

Edit: Only a day after I posted this a lot of the issues have already been fixed. Music no longer stops suddenly and polish on just general mechanics have already gone out

I would still recommend the game because you're looking at a pretty fun, and rather extensive, game for the price. A MUST buy JRPG for fans of the 16bit era! These guys have captured what made the SNES RPGs timeless classics! This is the real deal; so many others have tried and even come close but this is the standout and it deserves to be enjoyed by all! Traditional Square-Enix menus and battle commands with fast game play, save anytime, no random encounters, no grind required - but kill what you see to maintain the difficulty, great story, graphics are somewhere between Final Fantasy 4 & 6, excellent soundtrack, characters with personalities that you become attached to and a great price point! Support this game - we need sequels and more game like this that deliver a nostalgic experience while being new at the same time! Sure you will see a lot of influence from Final Fantasy 4-6, Chrono Trigger, Phantasy Star 4, Dragon Quest 6-7 and Breath of Fire 1-2 but it is done respectfully and delivers!
Update - I just finished the game - this is a true masterpiece and I hope it gets ported to consoles so all can enjoy!
A note to the dev team:
My 1st system was the Atari 2600 and I fell in love with Adventure, Riddle of the Sphinx and Raiders of the Lost Ark.
I've finished countless RPGs from The 8bit era to current gen with my fondest memories belonging to the 16bit era.
My 3 favourite RPGs (true RPGs - not Zelda or MetroidVania games or Faxanadu or Diablo - which are also awesome) in a very specific order are Final Fantasy 6, Chronotrigger and Final Fantasy 4.
I have also enjoyed less common/known RPGs that are hidden masterpieces like Septerra Core, Crimson Gem Saga, Albert Odyssey and Symphony of Eternity.
I have been waiting and disappointed time after time even with indie studios with hardcore retro roots.
Finally - THIS - is the game I have been waiting for! You guys clearly understand what made the old school RPGs timeless classics that can be replayed end enjoyed even when you know exactly what to do without a map or walk through.
Thank you for giving me something that really makes me feel nostalgic and yet is a new experience!
I hope you guys get the recognition and success you deserve for creating this future classic that I hope ends up on other platforms and has many sequels - all JRPG lovers should finish this game!
I have no issues buying this again for my home console (if a port gets made) and will be spreading the positive referrals to my friends - and the price point just augments the value even further!
Congratulations and thanks; you guys are awesome and have brought me back to my best time in gaming; which I thought would not be possible playing a new game!

If you like Trese Brothers games and you've been like me and waiting for the fabled Star Traders 2 to hit starport, now's your time to get excited! It's here!
I'm not going to focus on the flaws of the game because, honestly, what can you expect when there's still active development?
Don't let its Early Access status scare you away though, the Trese Brothers are hyper vigiliant in updating content for fixes and bugs and incorporating most requests. They are active and listen to their fans and you're guaranteed nothing but improvements and enhancements. As it stands, for being Early Access this game already has a TON to offer and I'm impressed with the depth of gameplay already. You can easily get lost in the universe as is and enjoy a full gaming experience. The game runs smoothly and I've yet to encounter a glitch. There's a bit of a learning curve if you're new to the Star Traders franchise, but there is a lot in the way of resources here and elsewhere on the webs in with an active player base and the Trese Brothers both being quick to answer questions.
If you're new to the Star Traders franchise I'll try my best to give you an idea of the game. It's a rogue-like sandbox rpg where you are your own star captain in charge of a ship trying to make their way in the galaxy, you can do that however you like, my favorite is to go for spying and or bounty hunting with a dash of exploration. You may just find it better to become a merchant instead. There's really no correct way to play the game except to strive to survive and then strive.
Now, as I said, this is a rogue like game, what that means is that you must be very careful because there is no save point. Your game gets saved when you exit, but if you screw your ship up and have 0 creds and are stranded in the middle of space with a ship about to blow up, you can't simply restore a save point, it's game over. I bring this up because I notice a lot of individuals requesting a save system or complaining that none exists, that's as intended because the game was not meant to play like a game where your actions have limited consequences, and tbh, that detracts from the alure of the game and reduces the imersiveness of the game so, if you are absolutely tied to the hip to save points, maybe this game isn't for you, but maybe you give it a go and realize you enjoy this type of play to :-)

This game is deeper than any screenshot or video can show you.
It's deeper than the impression you get even 5 hours into it.
The only games that come close to building a dynamic, interlinked world simulating economy, strife, and intrigue is the paradox games of EU4/CK2. I'm not going on hyperbole here - the world in this game is alive.
it is a roguelike that will last you a day, a week, a month, or many months depending on success and failure.
it is a roguelike unlike any other game. I honestly cant make an elevator pitch to illustrate what you'd be getting into. the only thing i can say is that it makes Original Star Traders look like a simplified, Mobile hack of this game - and considering Star Traders for mobile was the deepest strategy game ive played on mobile - this is no small praise.
This game is a min/max'ers dream because you can never 'get it' and coast. Every action is not linked to one stat, but 2, or 3, or more. A simple first pass min/max attempt for 'ezwinz' doesnt exist, here. The world is alive and you cannot tame it by doing a middlign effort min-max to get OP status. If you coasted through Divinity Original Sin 1 and 2 in a breeze on highest difficulty - this might be for you. If you loved the complexity of interlink/connectivity of RimWorld but needed a visceral RPG element where you had immediate goals to stay alive - this might be for you. if you are looking for a game unlike any other strategic RPG - this might be for you
It's an open world unlike any other open world.
My biggest issue with open world games is they come in two flavors: amazing combat and theme but lacking a 'real world' at all (See Wasteland2 - amazing game). it's just a series of boss fights and baldurs gates style maps to loot. the world is completely scripted, unmoving, unbreathing, unchanging, and the factions, npcs, events are all disconnected from your actions through it. any second playthrough is lackluster. then there's another open world game type: the Skyrim/Witcher - these games give you large, expansive worlds - but are again stagnant, unmoving. They dont live. Did you spend 10 hours waging war between City B and A for two different nations in Skyrim? nothing happens to affect the that nation or the neighbors. They just feel like chapters you walk through, a world that is at most a haunted house, and by no means alive.
ST is alive. It's just not easy to see in those pictures. It's again not easy to see as you go through the galaxy and see this chaotic spam of events (news) coming at you - but later, when you are no longer getting your sea legs, and you are big enough to understand the game of houses you realize that this is a dynamic, wartorn area and you have to ride the waves of conflict and intrigue to make money and grow. and you can do this in soooooooo many ways. more on that later.
many open world games have the problem of "ok, its big, its grand. but its so non-linear that i am BORED" sandbox games suffer from this - without a direct goal, you kind of lose urgency. in ST just staying alive and succeeding pigeonholes you into succeeding at all costs, through any means you can, to progress or die. Unlike too-open sandboxes, you always have immediate and long term goals. and in achieving those goals the world around you helps you, and hinders you, as it goes about its chaotic game of factions. there are missions (quest like) but that is not what you 'do'. The missions you take from NPCs are but a quarter, or less, of the missions you do for YOURSELF. You know you have to jump 4 sectors - in these 4 jumps you will plan out one way Trades where you pick up from one supply Market, dump to a demand Market, so that you are running cargo for profit just traveling the sector, you will be listening to rumors to take a detour in case there is a conflict or event that triggers rare success in specific mission types, you will hunt down VIP targets like smugglers, you will look for upgrades, and note prices.... in other words, this is a game wher eyou are giving yourself quests dynamically as you do a main quest, or pursue a main goal. This is the next innovation in gaming instead of 'go to npc, get quest, complete quest, collect reward' snooooore. ST gives you a world that is alive and you are a true freelancer - you will do everything, from explore, smuggle, bounty hunt, spy, back parties, and betray parties - all on the same character even. and only 15% of the time will it be because an NPC said to do it. the rest is pure opportunism and greed!

Day 1 Review ~ 4h of gameplay
tldr;
While in need of some polish, a well concerted effort from a small, indie dev who are clearly trying to shoot for the moon.
The long review:
Where the game falls short: audio.
Mechs don't sound heavy. Not enough thunks, and booms. The rest of the audio is a bit more than atmospheric, and while not terrible, doesn't add much either.
Where the game succeeds: Core mechanic.
A fun crafting system that doesn't feel like work. A nice balance of action and exploration where mechs are a tool and not a means for unending material grind.
Combat system could use a little work in terms of creating "impact" which you hit an enemy... but this also isn't a fighting game. It plays a lot more like an isometric ARPG, which isn't a bad thing.
Finally, the dev team is EXTREMELY responsive on the forums. They are currently answering every single question and concern that pops up, which shows a lot of promise for future development. I have confidence that Whalebox will continue to shape this game into a well polished gem.
All in all, it's hard not to recommend this title, despite its flaws. It has so much ambition and heart, I can forgive its first day fuzzies. If you like the concept of this game at all, I'd say it's worth showing your support.

I have been a long time fan of the Touhou series, for the beautiful bullet patterns, cute girls, friendly difficulty and occasionally memorable sound tracks. And of course the shock and awe when you find out that everything is made by one person who drinks too much beer. And now it's finally on Steam for everyone to buy properly.
Just like any other bullet hell game, Touhou Tenkuushou has to have a signature mechanic unique to the game, aside from shooting and spellcards (spellcards are basically bombs in the Touhou universe). This time it's the seasons: certain actions spawn season items, you collect them to gain slightly better firepower, and can also release them as mini-spellcards.
Personally I quite like this mechanic, because it provides me with additional tools to defend myself with, and doesn't require too much of my attention. Traditionally the only way out of crises is to use a spellcard, which is incredibly powerful but you have to pray for refills as they don't come very frequently. In Tenkuushou however, you have a second choice of releasing season power. Sure it is less powerful, but it refills really fast, and you can collect season items blindly just like any other item. As a contrast, some mechanics from other games in the series either require too much attention, or just outright work against me. I'm looking at you, human-youkai gauge from Touhou Eiyashou and UFOs from Touhou Seirensen.
Other than the seasons mechanic, Touhou Tenkuushou doesn't really feel different from previous games. I do find it even more difficult to tell items from bullets, and bullets from the background, but that might be just me.
To those not familiar, please remember that the Touhou series is entirely made by one person, and has never been seriously commercial. It's only natural that they have inferior graphics and sound compared to commercial bullet hell games. However, Touhou does take a slightly different approach, emphasizing the beauty of bullet patterns instead of a sheer overall difficulty. It's also set in a unique fantasy world called Gensokyo, where everyone looks like a maiden. It's definitely worth looking into.
+ Vibrant graphics
+ Lovable characters in a fantasy setting
+ Beautiful bullet patterns
+ Season power
+ Wide span of difficulty
- Mediocre music
- Bullets don't stand out enough
8 out of 10, excellent.

When I first turned on this game I was doubtful if it really was going to be as fun as people had recommended it to be. It looked like something out of an educational children’s game. Despite that and the initial gameplay starting off simple compared to other puzzle games that I've played, it continued to build on the mechanics as the story progressed along and I realized that it was necessary for it to be that way so the players can properly grasp what it was supposed to be towards the end. To someone not sure if this is going to be fun based on the first few minutes of gameplay, I say don't throw in the towel just yet, because even if it takes it's time to start up, it’s definitely going to be something you're going to be hooked on.
The gameplay is split into gathering ingredients and using them to create dishes. These two stages of the game gives it diversity and makes it very much layered, giving you many things to do and think about each time you play. Gathering requires you to platform and hunt monsters with your weapons and magic. The Cooking part of the game requires you to use the ingredients you gathered to puzzle out the best dish you can use with your tools and boosts. The customization involved with the items you choose allow you to decide which weapons and boosts to take into battle, what ingredients to gather, and what tools you use to get the job done. The combat is very smooth and feels clean, the abilities are appropriate for the characters and the combos they pull off, never will gathering feel like a tedious part of the game. The cooking part may get a little confusing at the start, but since it’s a puzzle game one can say figuring it out is the fun of it.
Built on the gameplay is a cast of characters wonderfully voice acted and taken across a story that fleshes out the universe, really getting you invested in the characters and their adventures in their culinary careers.
The only lacking part of the game, I feel, is the lack of things to do post-story mode. Surely the developers are working very hard to add more content and expand to this game. So in the meanwhile it’s very worth playing the story mode a few times to satisfy your urge for another round of hunting, gathering, cooking, and the best part of all, serving your completed dishes, glowing with flavor gems to the judges who give you very high scores for your work.
In conclusion, this is definitely a game that has a little something for everybody. I don’t write reviews for games at all, but I really would like to add one more positive review to this game so that I can make a difference in hopes that a few more people decide to purchase and discover it. People have to buy the game if we’re going to have more of it, and I really do want more, you will too. Check it out.

[DISCLAIMER: I did play the Alpha, before the game was released on Steam (Despite being... Late in that game. Also in this review)]
This game isn't for everyone. Anyone can plainly see that. That being said...
It's a singleplayer, roguelike, sci-fi RPG.
Roguelike, you WILL die, and will die often. You learn from previous mistakes, and make better ones. Try, fail, fail better. Contrary to popular belief as what I've seen, there is Permadeath ONLY on Hard+
The game is constantly updated, and will be updated for quite a while, as has been shown by these devs previously. The UI is being updated, the combat's being updated, RNG rolls are being updated, all in an attempt to make a good game, and the devs are open to any suggestions.
Now, RNG, yes. There is a lot. RNG encounters, RNG for Patrolling, Blockading, Spying... Space is dangerous.
The game is filled with lore, and if you take time to view the Forums, you can read about, and ask about some lore, and yes, the Devs themselves are willing to talk. They have a discord where they are very active as well. There is also a Lore PDF being made, currently, however it's not ready yet. [I will most likely edit this when it's done]
Basically, if you DON'T like: Roguelikes, Difficulty, Space, Singleplayer Only, and RNG, chances are you won't necessarily like the game.
It's a great game for those who think, "Hey, I could do better than *insert your team's GM here*".

Worst part is, I actually posted a few questions about this game in the forum. I asked how to edit a few things, like player ratings, rosters, etc. And guess what? The developers deleted my post.

EDIT: (5/20/2016)
New update, fixed most of the issues. Still some frame rate glitches during special moves, but all in all, much easier to play. Thanks to the devs, who increasd the stack limit of your inventory. Can't wait for more updates!
EDIT: (5/132016)
So the devs were able to patch the game quickly. I've been playing it for about and hour and it hasn't crashed once. Stil, some fine tuning would be appreciated. There is stll some disconnect between strikes and hits. The devs addressed the problem where the player doesnt have any sound effect for attacking, but the sound effect for contact on the enemy is either unsynced or does'nt trigger at all. Also, since I assume that chaining combos among the goliaths in your loadout is a big part of battle, they could make the transitions more fluid control-wise. I have to wait for a combo attack to finish in completion before I can bring up  the submenu for changing goliaths, which breaks the flow of my control inputs, because I'm spamming the LB button (It could just also be my controller, but I've never had this problem with other games). On a more subjective note, I think there should also be a lot more storage space. You have the three chests in your camp, but each hold only 16 slots a piece. Inventory in this game is done so that each item has a cap limit per slot in your inventory, before it takes another slot. I'm used to this game play, its a lot like Diablo of old, but in a crafting game it feels very restricting and, honestly, very stressful playing when I dont remember if I have enough space in my chestas for something while I'm out farming for drops. I could also, just be part of the game difficulty, thats why I lead with stating that the inventory issue was more personal.
All-in-all, Goliath is still really fun to play, but I still feel like the devs need to work on the the technical issues I mentioned above. I would gladly, change my review to positive after. The inventory thing is just something that the devs can think about.

I completed the game in 11 hours (some offline) which included most of the optional end-game sidequests.
The pixel art in this game is fantastic! I often found myself just looking at all the details in the background and couldn’t believe how consistently good-looking it was throughout the entire game. If you’re a fan of (or even open to) pixel art then you’ll be very happy here.
The soundtrack was really good and the devs should consider putting the OST up as well! I found the tracks worked well with the art and complemented the whole experience. The only exception to this was the battle theme became a bit tiring after fighting a few consecutive battles.
This was probably the weakest area for me. I felt the character development was a little soft and relied heavily on the intermittent flashbacks throughout the game to simply establish the character, as opposed to further develop them. The tone of dialogue between characters seemed inconsistent with the overarching plot and almost detached at times from the current context. The story is definitely serviceable, but wasn’t enough to really stand out from the pack.
The battle system is well balanced and the level of difficulty is slightly above something like final fantasy. Enemies are visible on the map and there is no level grinding required. Your characters have a range of skills to work with and there is usually more than one way to win the battle. The puzzles are challenging enough to make you think, but not so much that they become frustrating. It is clear that the devs have really thought about all aspects of the gameplay and it shows.
The best way I can describe this game is honest, it knows exactly what it is and if you’re looking for a retro jrpg then you’re likely to be satisfied.

I wish I had known about this game when they were still in their Kickstarter phase. As it is, I only heard about the game 2 days ago (the day before launch) and am loving every minute of it. Shadows of Adam is truly an homage to the JRPGs of old. If you are a fan of SNES era JRPGs, then I highly recommend Shadows of Adam to you.
Music - the music is amazing, hands down. Each track is unique in its own way, and enhances the mood of the area you are in.
Battle System - the AP system is a new and refreshing take as opposed to an MP based one. Each skill takes a certain percentage of your AP. You regain some each round or for defeating enemies, but it's up to you to ration how you spend it between fights and during bosses. This adds a nice level of strategic thinking to determine how best to approach each fight.
Graphics - the 16bit style that the devs went for harkens back to classic SNES JRPGs for a major nostalgic factor. The backgrounds are wonderfully done, as are character sprites.
Story - I'm just about to start the 3rd major dungeon, so I'm not sure exactly how far along I am. There have been some interesting plot reveals via flashbacks that have a nice pacing so as to not innundate the player with backstory before needed. From speaking with the Devs in Twitch chat the game casually should run between 14 and 16 hours. While there is no New Game + mode, there are bonus dungeons and side quests that add to the story as well that I'm looking forward to.
The Devs have been very active on Social Media and Twitch offering to answer any and all questions about the game, and sharing about their experiences making it - which has been a nice touch in my opinion. Overall I'm extremely pleased that I took a chance on Shadows of Adam - it has been my best and favorite purchase since Stardew Valley. Great job to the guys/gals at Something Classic - you've created an amazing game!

Although I love a lot of things about this game, the short of this review is that the game had a lot of technical issues back in the day, and still does- it's a pain to get running, and it's a pain to get things like the pathing bug resolved.  While one can expect PC users to be problem solvers, I still think it's important to raise the flag with a non-recommendation.
With that (mostly) out of the way:
Freedom force is a top-down squad game with superhero motif and themes and character progression elements.  The shining features of the game are undoubtedly its self-aware corniness, the ability to create your own superhero and fight alongside freedom force with them (Cancerquake did his duty well), and the voice acting.
To my knowledge besides its expansion, Freedom Force is one-of-a-kind, and tries to hit all the theme notes- secret societies, giant bugs, giant robots, aliens, gangsters, communists (in particular nuclear winter's theme song is a thing of greatness)- however it generally involves the same small sets of enemies for a number of levels in a row, and levels get really long with limited healing.  I ripped through it due to a great custom character, and it still took a long time; the game manages to be both erratic and kinda boring simultaeneously.  The giant robot enemies in particular are enormous wads of healthpoints.
The combat is serviceable- but arbitrarily either tough but manageable or an unending onslaught.  One particular issue is when you're forced to bring heroes that are woefully unqualified for their required tasks.  A couple notable examples are El Diablo's early battle with mobsters and freeze soldiers, any map where Minuteman actually needs to hit something, Liberty Lad's levels wherein he needs to survive eight fights when he can barely win three, anything with Eve or Deja Vu, and any part of the last gamut of levels wherein you will inevitably run out of steam many times.  You are going to have to save and load to disarm Nuclear Winter's bomb.  Probably a lot.
The combat is simply not balanced- throwing objects and area attacks are the only reliable ways to deal damage (and the latter don't work against fliers).  Beams miss more often than not, melee is required but most of the good fighters miss often or take forever to swing and get trounced, and healing is a nightmare.
Through this tirade of flaws, the game still manages to be fun with its corniness- but that's sure to be a turn-off for some as well.  There are a few points where maybe a little subtlety might have worked better, but the cheesy narrator and the hilariously sketchy comic-book origins are worth a lot of laughs, as do the alliterative item descriptions.
If you can struggle past the bad and you're not scared of a lot of savescumming and obtuse scenarios, the fighting is strategic to some extent and there's a hell of a lot of customization- as well as mods for traditional superheroes if you know where to look.  Some people are going to love Green Latern helping the freedom force, and it's hard not to see that appeal.
Long of this review is, the game is cheap and novel, but you're probably never going to play it because it's a pain to do so.  I ended up playing it due to a roulette.

This is not a game; there is no clear objective. It's an interactive movie, one about a physicist and an experiment that goes horribly wrong. Everything about the game was revolutionary when it was first released; more than twenty years later, it still feels like a fresh and innovative experience, even when it's influenced almost every video game that was released subsequently.
But yes, you will die. You will die a lot. You will live, walk around for a moment, and die again. The game is unforgiving, but that's what makes it rewarding. If you're interested in the history of gaming, and/or are an aspiring game developer, and/or are simply someone who wishes to see just how powerful the art medium can get, play Another World.

The game's concept is a lot of fun, don the cape of a silver age super hero and fight crime. The graphics are meh but whatever. What annoys me is the controls. Simple enough, right? Nope. Instead of going where you just told your character to go he instead heads off on a B-line in whatever direction he is facing. You then have to left click where you want him to go and then he'll actually go in the right direction. Then there's the matter of path finding/climbing buildings.
The initial protaganist, The Minuteman, has the ability to leap onto roof tops, sometimes. Other times instead of scaling a building to get to the roof he'll bring the roof too him by destroying part of the building. While this show ingenuity on his part it is highly detremental as the citizens of Patriot City aren't so keen on their costumed heroes tearing apart the city while bringing about justice.
From what I understand the issues I've faced are related to the game being incompatible with different operating systems. While that might be a fine explanation I'm not pleased with buying a game and having to dig through tech support forums to make it work. want to like this game, I really do; but unless there is a patch that didn't load for me then it is too finicky to be played.
Steam ought to consider putting notices on game that won't work with modern operating systems.

This game is a roguelike space saga that has great potential even if is still in early access (so expect some bugs/balance changes).
What I like the most is the lore around the factions (chose your own fate as a StarTrader in a galaxy with complex politics and almost constant war/trade bans/spying) and the immersion it provides.
Story wise the game gives the player the opportunity (if he chooses) to affect major events with sometimes high risk high rewards behind it (get some legendary officers/crew combat weapons).
The gameplay is straight forward with high replay ability considering you can choose between 9 factions (each with their own strengths and weaknesses aka traits), 8 major classes (aka Jobs in game e.g. Military Officer, Spy, Pirate, Bounty Hunter, Merchant, Smuggler, Explorer) and some dozen starting ships (which affect what you are good at e.g. patrolling/blockading/spying/ship to ship combat/crew combat etc) and of course your own fully customizable Captain.
Crew management is really fun with the option of promoting officers, recruiting new crew and as the captain your decision making(major emphasis on this)  will shape them as the game progresses. Each crew will gain new traits and abilities as you start to know them better and rely on them in every aspect of handling your ship.
This journey is awesome!

This was awesome fun.  The short of it is, this is part platformer where you battle monsters and collect their parts as ingredients, and part match-3 game where you have up to 3 pots, each representing a different match3- grid where you can combine ingredients (colored gems) in order to transform them into more powerful flavor gems.  Some pots will have restrictions like only being able to match red (fire) gems, others will have special abilities like slowly increasing the potency of your gems.
It really feels like a cooking battle game, and the anime-styled scenes and art remind me strongly of The Legend of Korra (sequel to the Avatar: the Last Airbender series).  I found the story engaging and the characters sympathetic; the voice acting was well done.
Only downside for me was that I found the timed cooking battles rather harrowing, but you can always come back to them, and about 50-70% or so of the game wasn't under a time limit, so the pressure isn't constantly on.  You can always try a match again as well, if you lose, you're asked if you want a rematch.  Explore the stages and examine the ingredients you can get from the monsters, and the way the monsters interact with loose ingredients-- often they will eat them and then create another ingredient, or metamorphose into a form which gives you a new and better ingredient.  Experimenting is crucial to working out better tactics for defeating your enemies!

One of the best hardcore representations of tabletop wargaming i have ever seen in digital form. From the visual dice rolls to the perfect implementation of cards for giving commands to the movement and combat of units everything feels spot on perfect. Even artillery is handled with tabletop excellence with setting up one's target on a different screen before giving the order to fire into enemy trenches or the open battlefield.
Oh and did i mention the very boardgame centric rich visuals of intro screens and gameplay giving one flashbacks of opening freshly purchased wargame boxes with that smell that says minty new.
Music is very well done adding a sense of tension and heroic conflict as one can just imagine infantry rushing the open ground in hopes of not being taken down by a fuselage of enemy fire or a artillery barrage.
COMMAND & COLORS: THE GREAT WAR a exhilarating tabletop experience with the guiding intuitive hand of modern technology as your game master and host. Hexwar Games has truly delivered a priceless masterpiece with the amusing price of what we would probably have paid at a gaming shop.
COMMAND & COLORS: THE GREAT WAR, BUY IT! PLAY IT! and enjoy the rare taste of wargaming excellence.

I expect that my review will change to positive, but for now I can't recommend it - it needs some work.  I'm a long-time Richard Borg fan, have owned and played many of his games including Memoir '44, BattleCry, C&C: Ancients, as well as BattleLore.  Here are a few of my observations, things that need some attention:
- there's a lot of icons on the main screen but no quick / easy way to know what they do.  No mouse-over popup or anything?
- some unique colour coding schemes between Allied and German forces would be beneficial.  More than just tiny icons.
- view scrolling with the keyboard is really slow.
- the cards that the player is presented with at the bottom of the screen could stand to be bigger so you can easily read what they say at a glance.
- if it's in the options it's not set to default : it would be good if the view automatically centered on the units that are taking actions or moving.  It's easy to miss things happening and that kind of sucks.
- it's hard to tell what I'm supposed to be doing and when.  For example, at the end of my turn, there's no UI indicating that it's the end of my turn and I need to click on something.  Some UI clues as to what the player should be doing at any given time would be very useful.
- the cards themselves.  The text is grey on a kind of cream background.  Would be awesome if the text was black - it'd be so much easier to see and read.
- is the audio off?  I adjusted my settings and find that the music isn't balanced well with the sfx.  Music is much louder.
- the dice fly everywhere and sometimes away from what where the player's viewpoint is and the screen doesn't snap to the result.  Why? As mentioned above, the keyboard view movement is slow.
Generally the game feels like it has been focusing on style before substance.  Take a look at Memoir '44 online, that is a great implementation of a Richard Borg game (aside from the P2P approach).  I like the graphics upgrade here but I don't like how the graphics seem to be putting actual gameplay in the backseat.  It feels like so much of the emphasis is on the dice roll, how amazing it looks (and hey, it looks great), but the real beauty of a Richard Borg system shouldn't be the graphics but the gameplay.   And if you want to make it all about the graphics, then throw some realism here - I mean, grass-covered no-mans-land? What?  Trench warefare was known to be a boggy, muddy mess.
Speaking of which, why only trench warfare?  I hope and expect to see some expansions (I don't want to pay more money) where we're seeing some of the many other kinds of battles in WWI - the battle of the Marne, Serbia, Turkey, Russia - there's a lot of opporutnity for some interesting tilesets and challenges that aren't just trenches.
Anyway, I like the game and it has a lot of promise.  The devs seem to be responsive and genuinely interested in making this title better.  I've shared some ideas and I look forward to where this can go, but for now, I can't recommend it - espcially to people who are new to a Richard Borg game or this style of game in general.

This game is a fantastic, budding giant, in the same vein as Templar Battleforce.  You'll definitely need a love for Sci-fi and classic turn-based RPGs, but its multi-layer approach, open world, and card-based randomizer strike a fantastic balance!  You are a ship and crew... not just a single hero, and that functionality either works as a unit, or comes apart at the seams when you forget to pay your crew on time...  >_>
EA Rating:  A-
Blind Rating:  C+    (this is completely ignoring that it's been out for only a month!)
Definitely worth the $15 even if it was released just like this... but I'm confident it's going to age into something magnificent.
Pros:
+ EXTREMELY responsive Dev team
+ Rapidly developing Early Access
+ Solid, enjoyable sandbox construction
+ Multi-layered gameplay
+ Stats are based on your collective crew... not just your hero!
+ Factional system keeps you busy
+ Has died more from my own Poor Life Choices (TM) than any cheesy game mechanics or scripted nonsense
Needs Improvement:
~ Grinding / Monotany needs improvement.  It's not at all terrible!  ^_^  But it'll need some polish before getting to 1.0
~ Graphical distinctions for weapons, armor, etc.  Currently there is a lot of rubber-stamp ships staffed with rubber-stamped characters.
~ UI is in rapid development, but will need more Ease of Use work before it's truly ready
~ While the graphics are passable, they'll need to go just a bit further than they already are in one direction or another.  Either towards the flat Tactical RPG style, or the cell-shade Story RPG style.  Currently dabbles in both (and looks good!) but still needs to level up a bit.
~ Extreme expansion of weapons, armor, and equipment (reluctant to mention this, as it's already planned!)
Negatives:
- Old School design, lacking in any real deep instructions.  (I take this as a positive... but many may not!)
- EA bugs (mostly script / visual / balance, not crashes or glitches)
- Some storylines abruptly end (again, see EA)
Suggestions:
?  Would definitely suggest distinct factional traits, strengths, etc.
?  Desperately needs a proceedurally generated, random loot and equipment system.  A little Diablo or Torchlight would go a LONG ways in a game like this.
?  Ships need to be more empty than they are currently, and rely more on tonnage and less on 'slots'.  This allows more lateral customization and variations of a single design (... but also min-maxing, for better or worse)
?  Consider mod support.  There are players and modders out there that will HAPPILY expand content violently for you, if you make those mods visible and accessible on Steam. (ie. Rimworld)

I've played a lot of indie RPGs over the years and can safely say that Shadows of Adam stands out from the crowd as one of the better ones I've played. Having scripted encounters instead of random encounters makes exploring dungeons far less frustrating than other titles I've played, and boss fights are all well balanced and interesting encounters. The music and animations are really top notch, and the game really feels like a 90s era SNES title at heart. For people like me who enjoy nostalgia RPG experiences, I would highly recommend this game.

If you remember role playing games before Playstation, than this game is for you.
All the elements that make a classic RPG are there for Shadows of Adam. From hidden chest to chasing after annoying monsters that steal your mushrooms. Inn keepers that will give you a room for free, and shop keepers that will literally buy the clothes off your back.
Even the most minute details are handled spectacularly. Many of the maps jump to life from birds flying away to fish jumping out of streams.
Of course, I wouldn’t consider it a fair review without some nitpicking. For instance, there is no explanation to the battle system. A small nuance, but it took a few fights to get the swing of things.
Some of the dialogue windows are difficult to follow, but this is a common factor in these type of games. After you get the hang of character names, it becomes less of an issue. That being said, the game tries hard to catch the player's attention but sometimes leaves you wanting more explanation.
It’s really hard to complain about these things considering all the additional effort that went into the immersion of the player. I look forward to spending many more hours with this title over the weekend.

Shadows of Adam is an 'old-school' traditional RPG created by a team of developers known as Something Classic, and is an intentional throwback to the 'classic' era of 8/16-bit RPGs, drawing liberally from titles from the early nineties.
The game begins with an homage to Final Fantasy VI in a world ravaged by a destructive war that was caused by magic. Seeking to escape the destruction, fearful citizens fled into the wilderness and founded a small town called Adam to hide from the war until the wicked magic-wielding Lodan Empire was destroyed by a great cataclysm.
'Magic' in Shadows of Adam is not merely a cool fantasy power, it is explicitly a force for evil, drawn from the world of the dead, and is a power men should never wield or touch. Nevertheless, this power does still exist in isolated places and individuals, such as a girl named Asrael in the village of Adam. The people of Adam are superstitious and mistrustful, and when an evil force begins infesting the nearby wilderness, the people think Asrael is to blame. Kellan, the son of a local hero, stands up for Asrael and is sent to investigate the disturbance to prove it is not her doing. What Kellan and Asrael discover in the wilderness will send them on a quest in search of Kellan's missing father, who they believe needs their help.
The game's visuals, set-pieces and plot are all drawn from the well of classic RPG tropes and conventions. There's a lot of reasons why someone might want to make an 'old school' RPG and nostalgia is certainly one of the highest on the list. I suspect another reason might be the comparative ease of making one compared to other types of projects, with relatively simple programming and artwork. But to assume design simplicity was a goal for Shadows of Adam might leave you surprised. While decidedly steeped in the design auspices of the 'old School,” Shadows of Adam also brings modern design sensibilities to the table as well.
The game takes the form and shape of a traditional world-spanning 'collect the artifacts' quest where you'll explore towns, fight monsters, enter dungeons and meet a lot of weirdos. Dungeons are a particular winner in this game for me. Eschewing random encounter-filled mazes, dungeons are deliberate, well-paced, and designed with the player's consideration in mind. Encounters are similar to Final Fantasy Mystic Quest; static, non-random, and once fought do not return until you re-enter the dungeon. They are placed judiciously and not overused, so the game is very resistant to forced grinding. More emphasis is placed on study of your environment and interaction with various puzzle set pieces. These puzzles mostly feel organic, clear, intuitive to interact with and solve, and build on mechanics introduced in earlier areas. You won't really see anything you haven't seen done elsewhere, but what's here is nearly perfectly executed, with nothing feeling forced or thrown in.
Combat sequences play out in a fairly typical Dragon Quest or Phantasy Star manner. Each of your four heroes has variety of special abilities they can use by spending AP, which replenishes by a small amount each round. Each hero also has a special ability they can use to restore their own AP as well as grant them some other benefit. You'll have traditional attack and recovery abilities but equipping certain 'Artifacts' can change the way some characters operate, such as granting them more attacks per round or additional AP regeneration. Combat plays out quickly and with satisfying visual and sound effects, experience comes at a quick pace and leveling up has a noticeable effect on your performance. Encounters are challenging but not murderous, but throughout the game your party's HP totals are relatively low compared to the amount of damage enemies can do so while healing abilities come early and are effective you must stay constantly vigilant to stay alive, especially since while most encounters can be seen coming, the occasional scripted ambush does occur.
Finally we'll talk about the characters and story, which is important for me because this is an area where I feel like the 'old school' conceit doesn't work. The depth of the characters feels a bit more akin to a first-generation Dragon Quest game than a modern RPG made in 2017. The game has two protagonists, with Kellan being a typical brave but not-too-bright RPG hero and Asrael being a mysterious, empathetic orphan girl with unexplained powers. The problem is that neither particularly ever grows beyond these very basic RPG tropes to offer us a 'new' take on these characters. There's just not much else to them.
Most of the additional cast is introduced early. Our heroes are quick to make an ally of Curtis, a wandering martial artist who insists he was just passing through but seems a little too invested in what's going on. He definitely has a history, and you'll get to see it before the game is over, but we don't know a lot about Curtis's personality other than that he likes meditating and is a bit of a smartass. The fourth hero, Talon, offers quite a bit more potential. He is an old friend of Kellan and Asrael who was very sickly as a child and was thus always left out by the other children. He has grown up resentful and left Adam to make his own fortune. When we meet him, we learn he is fond of Asrael but deeply dislikes Kellan. Seems like a great opportunity for him to serve as a foil for the group and provoke some conflict and character development. Unfortunately, barring one major exception late in the game, this rarely amounts to anything other than Kellan and Talon calling each other names. The rest of the cast is rounded out by Prince Malvil, a nefarious royal who wants to be Kefka so bad he can taste it, and his duo of comically ineffective but very persistent henchmen.
The game does offer us a lot of context about the characters. We learn a lot of the 'whys' and 'hows.' But we never really get to know these characters or learn 'who' they are, what they care about, where they're going in life.
The game's world-building also leads a lot to be desired. The world clearly has some history but the player isn't given a lot of opportunity to get invested in it or learn what's going on. I think a pretty major problem here might be in the NPCs in most of the towns. Rather than using them as building blocks to introduce lore, flavor text, current events, a lot are just used to indulge in cheap throwaway gags. You learn very little about the war, the evil Lodan Empire, or exactly what became of them. Which is a shame because there was at least one twist that I thought was pretty cool when you eventually make your way to the continent of Lod and find out what's been going on there since the war. Ultimately though I didn't really leave this world feeling any sort of connection to it. The building blocks simply weren't there.
Shadows of Adam has a lot to offer you. But for people who like to indulge in a game's writing and characterization, be aware that this title doesn't offer a lot in the way of it. Whereas with most features of the game, Something Classic took something old and made it feel new, here it still feels old.
One aspect of the game not pulling through for me isn't enough to drag down my impressions too far however, mostly because the other parts of the game are good enough to make up for what I perceive as shortcomings, The game offers some classical and enjoyable dungeon-crawling and RPG combat; the kind of game you might have enjoyed as a kid, with most of the rough edges sanded off. The game is about ten hours long from beginning to end though there is some additional end game quest content to explore as well. If Phantasy Star or Final Fantasy dominated your childhood and you've been searching to recapture those feelings for the past twenty years, Shadows of Adam might be just the game for you.

Nice looking sprites, good music, and charming writing. This is what you can expect out of Shadows of Adam. Every so often I see an indie game in developement and I look out for it for a year or more until it finally comes out. I knew I was in for a treat when I saw Lun Calsari, creator of the RPG maker cult hit "The Way" was doing the writing, and to my understanding, some of the mapping.  I was a huge fan of his work and had played it numerous times. So I played the demo, and boy, was it good. If you have any doubts about the game, or are curious as to how it plays, you can always check out that demo.
Really, a lot of different things sell this game. The gameplay is simple, but there's some thought to be had since MP is a percentage and skills take up a set percent of how much you have. This means you can't just spam skills to win. You need to manage your skills, if only just a little bit. The graphics are nicely shaded, and are reminiscent of games like Final Fantasy V, but have a personality of their own at the same time. The writing is great, and althought I had some serious head turning at some of the things said, since there's a lot of slang exclusive to the world. While made up slang was present in The Way, it felt natural and made sense, like it was something you might hear in the real world somewhere.
Anyhow, if you give the game a chance, I'm sure you'll find something you'll love about it. It's an RPG through and through, and I constantly find myself finding new things to explore, and a bunch of hidden chests and treasures. There are also a lot of references to Lun's older work that I appreciate a bunch as a fan of his game.

Pythagoria:
~~~~~~~~~

Maths is a rather interesting subject; either you like it or you don’t!  And yet, everyone uses maths on a daily basis in one way or another. Now, you lucky devils, it is time for you to put your brain to the test with Pythagoria.
Pythagoria (or Area Maze) is a clever and challenging puzzle game where you have to find the missing value (number) in a specific area which will be identified by a question mark. All puzzles can be resolved with basic mathematics and the answer will always be a whole number, as decimals are not allowed.
The game has three sets of 20 puzzles to resolve (60 puzzles in total) and the difficulty will increase as you go through the sets. What you need to remember playing this game is that the diagrams are not drawn to scale, which will probably throw you off more than once. Well, it certainly did for me!
As I am writing this review, bear in mind that mathematics and I were never really the best of friends. However, I really enjoy this type of challenge. This game prompted me to look at the origins of this type puzzle and I am absolutely amazed to find out that it was created for Japanese school children and has now becoming extremely popular with adults (Area Maze)!
Also, I would like to mention that I really like the soundtrack in that game.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	60 good puzzles
-	Great soundtrack
-	Good price point
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Short game
-	Needs a better tutorial, in my opinion.
Pythagaria is an interesting puzzle game for all ages.

Awesome F2P game. Ignore the bad reviews and try it if you like RTS and/or Moba games or ever played with toy soldiers or table top games.
Players get to command 1 of 3 battalions initially. These are Jeeps x 12, Tanks x 4 or Rocket troops x18. There are 15 battalions in total all of which can be unlocked without spending a cent. You get a crazy amount of customisation options from 6 perk slots with potentially 100 perks to chose from, Special abilities, and even mixing in units from other Battalions you own.
Unlocking the battlions you want is quite quick as F2P. Getting all the perks you really want can be time comsuming as they may be spread through the progression trees of multiple battalions.
I think the large amount of bad reviews must be due to people not understanding the games damage mechanics. Rock,paper, scissors (RPS) forms the basis of how effective your units will be vs other units. The game makes this very clear but it does not stop countless noobs going "TANKS! HELL YEAHS!" and then getting ripped apart by rocket troops, rage quitting and writing a bad review.
Map awareness is crucial to avoiding horrible encounters. That said every unit can be air evacced after a few second delay to your base where your units heal quickly. This has no cool down. You press 'q'. Units depending on their abilities may have other ways to counter bad situations also. The game is played by 2 teams of 5 players (or bots if you have no cahones) which means there will more than likely be someone(s) who you should hunt on the other team and someone(s) you should avoid. Tanks can kill troops, and most troops don't do much to tanks it is just inefficient unless your tanks are flame throwing tanks. Your Attack has an RPS and so does your armour. Many things can help mitigate the RPS like cover, perks, range, shooting the back of tanks, AoE to grouped units etc etc. In other words if used correcttly your rock could defeat somebodies paper.
You don't need to fire a single shot to win the game as there are 3 primary objectives on each map that accumulate points for you if your team hold more than the enemy. There are many secondary objectives providing worthwhile bonuses when controlled also. All maps are very well designed and that is one of the strengths of troop battalions.
When new it can be a good idea to follow somebody who would wreck the enemies you should avoid. This way you can cover each other and both be much more effective in a fire fight.

Hidden Star in Four Seasons may be my new 3rd favourite Touhou game, right behind everybody's darlings Imperishable Night and Perfect Cherry Blossom.
What makes it so good, apart from generally fun and clever pattern design, has to be the release system. Hitting C on the keyboard activates an effect that can be described as a "soft-bomb". This ability needs to be charged, but can help you in a pinch and won't even forfeit a Spell Card capture bonus. Smart combinations of soft-bombs and the more valuable series staple Spell Cards (your "hard-bomb") can get you a long way just through strategy rather than relying only on your full-on dodging skills. Putting your resources to good use feels immensely satisfying, more than e.g. Ten Desire's Trance Mode.
The difficulty of the game is slightly below average among other installments of the franchise, which is not at all a bad thing to me. Some Touhou games have been too tough for me to enjoy as much as this. Hidden Star in Four Seasons was in my eyes a great choice as poster boy for ZUN's Steam debut.

A thoroughly fun and enjoyable throwback to the classic JRPGs of old. Beautiful graphics and soundtrack, an enjoyable battle system, and some silly and self-aware writing.
As can be seen by the screenshots, the game looks gorgeous. It retains that 16-bit SNES style, but modernized for a new age. The environments and backgrounds on the maps are stunning and diverse, without that feeling of everything being the same tiles repeated over and over again. The battle artwork is great as well, with well designed (and dynamic) enemy sprites, more gorgeous background artwork, and quick, stunning attack and spell animations.
The battle system itself is a perfect example of a modern turn-based battle system. Turns and animations are quick, and the AP system used for attacks and abilities is a simple system which doesn't punish the player for doing anything other than basic attacks. As of the point I'm at in the game now, battles have felt challenging, but not punishing. I've found myself having to be slightly tactical in boss battles, and as of yet no abilities seem "useless" as in some JRPGs, with buffs and debuffs actually being useful and helpful.
Storywise, the script has been enjoyable so far. It's very tongue-in-cheek, and aware of the fact that this game has a base in a long running and beloved genre of games. While the self-aware, tongue-in-cheek, and slightly parodied approach of writing isn't for everyone, I found it charming. Like so many other things in this game, it fits in nicely, without being overbearing. The characters are a little silly, the plot isn't out of the ordinary or convoluted, and the wonderful soundtrack really helps tie everything together.
As far as technical things go, I've encountered a few very minor graphical issues, all of which I'm sure are easily fixable. But otherwise, the game is solidly designed and runs quite well.
If you're a fan of the classic JRPG genre, this may be the game you've been looking for. A fun, exciting foray into the days of old, but with a modernized eye for design. The game will tug at your nostalgic heartstrings, in many ways (the music especially reminded me of so many old SNES RPGs), but it does so without relying on the nostalgia as its only selling point. At its core, it remains a solid, simple JRPG, the likes of which are few and far between these days, and I would recommend it to anyone looking to revisit that classic style with a new age twist.

Another World - 20th Anniversary Edition is a rerelease and upgraded version of the original Another World (also known as Out Of This World) released back in 1991 for the first time and became a landmark for videogames at the time. You take the role of Lester Knight Chaykin, a physicist who gets transported to another world, and once there needs to escape it. I first played this years ago when I was still small, and felt some nostalgia seeing it in the store.
Pros:
-Amazing platforming, which still holds up to today. Use of various environmental objects and placements, to the structure of discovering how to progress is captivating and is exactly what a platformer should be
-The simple, 2D polygonal character and art style is beautiful and ties in well with the entire "another world" feeling
-The narrative of the story is presented well through progression of certain events while playing and the flow to cinematic cutscenes
-This edition contains the soundtrack, concept art and technical drafts, and can be found in the Steam directory in which the game was installed
Cons:
-This can be off-putting to some, but the game is incredibly difficult and does not baby-sit you. You will have to try, die, and try again till you discover what to do. (Or find a full speedrun walkthrough on YouTube, as I did if you don't want to struggle)
Overall, this platformer is brilliant and set the standard for future platformers. Worth buying if you love the game, or love a great platformer.
8/10

As an indie game developer myself I am very proud to see the Something classic team complete such an amazing game that captures the polish and soul of the classics that inspired it so well.  If you’re a fan of classic JRPGs of the SNES era, I think you’ll love Shadows of Adam.  And at $15 it’s an absolutely great deal for the quality.  If you’re still on the fence, here’s a more detailed review:
Shadows of Adam (SoA) is a game inspired by classic JRPGs from the SNES era.  The closest game I can think of that resembled SoA would be Final Fantasy: Mystic Quest.
Shadows of Adam has great music, beautiful pixel art, and an interesting a succinct story.   You start off with a warrior named Kellan (male) and a sorceress named Asrael (female).  A darkness called the “Tangle” is taking over the world and has reached your secluded town named “Adam”.  Of course, it’s up to you to stop it!  Later on you’ll get two more human members to your team: a dark-skinned monk named Curtis, and a red-headed thief named Talon.
Shadows of Adam’s controls require either full keyboard or full controller.  I played with an Xbox 360 controller, which required no additional setup and worked perfectly.
You can move in 4 directions similar to classics like Final Fantasy 6.  There’s a run button that you can hold to run, which you pretty much do the entire time as there’s no real reason to walk.  Luckily you can go into the options from the menu and turn on “always run” so you don’t have to be bothered holding the button your entire playthrough.
This is probably my only complaint about Shadows of Adam:  My personal preference is that a game on the PC should be playable with a mouse, though I do understand that a classic game like this really is better with a controller.
Later on you acquire an airship which you can enter and explore similar to Final Fantasy 6.  This of course helps you travel the rest of the world you normally couldn't on foot.
The sprites are beautiful, but in lower resolution to have that classic feeling.  I first started playing Shadows of Adam at full screen on a 1080p monitor, but the lower resolution made the graphics look too muddled.  I switched to windowed mode and felt that it was much easier (and better looking) to play on a lower resolution.
Bosses have multiple forms depending on their current HP percentage.  This adds a nice effect to show you’re near the end of a long fight, and the boss may start to look more angry or more tired.
Spell effects are beautiful and fun to watch even after the 100th time you’ve seen them.
There are no random battles.  Instead, enemies are engaged by bumping into them on the exploration map.  Once you do, you’ll be whisked away to the “battle zone”, which has the enemies and protagonists lined up on opposite sides of each other to combat.  Enemies will respawn when you exit and re-enter the dungeon, which you’ll need to do sometimes to rest in town.
Combat is turned based based on character’s speed stat.  This means you select the actions for all of your characters at the beginning of the round, and then every character, including enemies, take a turn in order based on their speed stat.
Shadows of Adam has replaced the traditional Mana resource for a rechargable AP resource.  All of your skills take a percentage of your AP (e.g. 40%), and then your AP regenerates either by using certain AP regenerating skills or naturally each turn.
Abilities are earned by leveling up through gaining experience in combat.
Note: If a character dies they do not receive EXP.
Equipment is set up into 3 basic slots: Weapon, Armor, Artifact.  Weapon and armor contribute pretty much to what you’d think they would, while artifacts can contribute in different ways depending on the affixed stats.
The stats are simpler than some complex RPGs, but maintain variety.
The level design is very well done.  Each dungeon has its own puzzles that significantly add to the atmosphere and spirit of the scenes.
There are many hidden treasures, making exploration very rewarding and fun.  The treasures range from equipment to items like any good RPG would do.
Also…
Come get a slice, baby!  But watch out; this cake bites back... <3

The game has pop up windows that explain what is going on, but reading the actual rules for the board game helped me figure out all of the changes that it has from the system I'm used to playing.  If you have played any Command and Colors games, you should be able to get started in this game right away and it has some unique mechanis that really help give it a trench warfare feel as you try to manage your hand to get the advantage needed to make a breakthrough while avoiding the attrition from the enemy.

How do you rate your prospects as a Great War general? Find out by playing historical scenarios in Command & Colors : The Great War. Bear in mind that the advantage lies with the defender unless the attacker has superiority of numbers. Read the scenario brief to find out if the attackers gained the objective or had to retreat. Try running the scenario both ways: Allied against German AI and German against Allied AI. You will need to play your cards carefully to gain an edge and beat AI. Pay careful attention to terrain and line of sight. Learn to manage and conserve your resources. The cards and game play are designed to model actual Great War events and tactics to give a sense of realism and historical accuracy. The battle is finished. The war goes on.

Sometimes a friend will ask you how to describe a game in a sentence, and often times it ends up being a challenge. Like how would I describe NieR: Automata to you in one sentence? "A story-driven character action game that also has bullethell and 2D platforming sections; but is also an existential nightmare" might be a little verbose. Battle Chef Brigade is far easier: "Imagine Monster Hunter mixed with Iron Chef." That describes everything you really need to know about BCB.
It is a great little 2D sidescroller which combines combat and puzzle. It has really compelling characters, a fun story, lovely art, great music, and feels like it was crafted with a lot of love. I had minor problems with the game (framerate was wonky with my 1440p screen for some reason, sometimes the combat felt like it wasn't as responsive as I'd liked, etc) but, overall, I feel very strongly that Battle Chef Brigade is worth your time. A ton of fun, and stressful in all the right ways!

Battle Chef Brigade plays like a timed match 3 game, with minor combat and puzzle elements on the side. It has a basic combat system, with a small amount of combos to keep gameplay interesting, although I usually just wound up mashing attack except on the boss monsters like Hydras, Dragons, and that bird thing who's name escapes me. But it wasn't boring, and the combat stays out of the way of the match 3 and score puzzles, which are the game's main draw. Also features a hard mode for advanced players.
The match 3 itself involves you presenting dishes to the judges. Your dish can be made from fire, water, and earth gems, with the amount of lvl 3 gems of one type determining what type your dish predominantly is. There are also poison and bone gems that you must make sure don't make it into your final dish. The judges will always ask for either one type of gem to be dominant, or several types to have equal representation, and failing to grant their wishes loses you points. The judges will also include an ingredient that MUST be in your dish or you will lose points (although you must hunt the ingredient yourself). So basically, this game is iron chef in game format. Complete with "Vive Brigade" instead of "Allez Cuizine" as the 'go' phrase.
The one thing it could use improvement on is some quality of life features. There's no way to check what the combat combos that generate special moves are while in game. At least, not that I've found. I've also never figured out how to get one of the AIs to play a practice match with you (if it's even possible). One QoL feature that is in the game, is that the competitors you face will start to present lower quality dishes to the judges if you lose to them too often. Although, I only noticed this on the final boss, who took me 5 tries to beat.

Kill monsters, collect their organs, cook 'em up in a match-three style mini game, bring it to the judges for a score.
This game is a cross between an RPG, a Brawler, Anime, Tetris, and Iron Chef. And you know what? It's a recipe for success. *Ba da tshhh*
The voice acting sounds like a not-so-good English dubbing in an anime. Not sure if it was intentional or not, but it gives the game some charm.
