I cannot recommend a game that asks 9 to 15 minutes to get into a match, with 3 to six other people. Gameplay has promise, the game itself isn't bad by any means. It's very well done. In fact it reminds me of another well done game that lost it's audience, Hawken. Very very promising well delivered gameplay and content, however the sense of reward isn't there at all. I couldn't care less if the characters were low-poly count and minimalist or as real life and complex as they can be, if the content has a limited sense of feedback the experience falls flat and unfortunately after two matches and four loot boxes, I decided if that's the game it simply won't do. And as a free title, I shake my head questioning how it would make money. It's really just too bad because it's a decent game, it's just a bit flat and confounding for people. I'm not alone having that strange pervasive feeling that something is missing, something that matters a lot, and that lacking sense is a major component of what is wrong with the experience. As a creative person I could come up with 'deeper levels' to the gameplay structure, however they'd break in as entirely new sets of mechanics, tilting the design. So maybe that's part of it too for way more people than just I.
Part of it is, the game goes from clunky to fluid motion so often I'd really like to get rid of or modify HUD effects, screen shake. As with the grenade lobbing medic I'd have liked a reticle that show's a sense of momentum impacting it's trajectory, because it would, or something. So that's a cut in motion and fluidity that people probably feel too. And morever the reticle was very cs:go pachink-like, sort of not-so-random at times firing cones.
Part of it is, huge emphasis on literally VERY SMALL DETAILS that in having no impact whatsoever and consisting of three character customization types. And that too - none of that flat colour swapping, model+ stuff really helps sell characters I'd don't care about. Just like in R6S's case - the entire concept of having characters instead of equipment loadouts is perposterous. Equipment+Technical Training=Proficiancy. And needlessly restrictive content - so more slogans and walking doll-house logo's - can run around selling 'hip hip hooray' emotes and dances HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH THE CORE EXPERIENCE.
I could imagine this would work out well for many people as a console game. A stabalized and sort of pizza-pop-like game experience is exactly why Hawken is still supported on consoles. Which if this game wants to survive at all should probably figure out a purchase plan that makes sense and go free to play. This is a money pit and you should not bother dropping in your $20-$30 it isn't a matter of saving your money its a matter of this gaming having retained less than 1% of it's audience since launch. The developers can still make something of this but it's expense increases and it's audience doesn't.

Touhou returns in a classic yet always fresh take on the well-known format. Bringing with it a selection of 4 playable characters, each with unique bullet patterns, spell cards and other quirks, the player can choose from the classic protagonists Reimu and Marisa or choose from either the ever favourable tengu Aya Shameimaru or Cirno, sporting a glowing tan. The difficulty remains fair yet challenging, with each stage requiring memory, skill and patience to pass successfully. The music is diverse and evocative, and certainly deserves a place among the already revered Touhou soundtracks of the past (most notably the theme for stage 4). The bosses are unique and all equally daunting, but once you being to progress you begin to realise how easily you can surpass each one, despite their spell cards being a worthy hurdle to overcome, and one that you may fall flat on your face over many times.
Overall it's hard to fault yet another stellar entry to the immortal Touhou series, as ZUN continues to put his heart, soul and physical years of his life into his single-handedly crafted masterpieces.
English patches are available through Touhou fan sources so for those who can't read Japanese I would recommend making use of those.
Finally i manage to buy this to support our lord Zun, 7/10 quite better, but i prefer old touhou than this, i hope our lord Zun grant us all touhou collection on steam >.<

It chronicles the journey of two inhabitants of Adam, a remote village, as they travel an expansive world to find their missing father one decade after his disappearance. The story is charming, relatable and strongly supported by mostly intuitive game design and fast gameplay. After talking to just a few NPCs, it is possible to quickly become engrossed in learning about every aspect of the lore that you possibly can to get clues for future events and side quests. Despite being influenced by games designed for older hardware, it spares no resources in presenting itself as a clean and visually and audibly aesthetic title that takes advantage of modern system capabilities. Most importantly,
.
While the game is primarily linear, it certainly has a distinct and pleasant pacing that will keep you interested. Each of the main characters has their own vibrant feel and personality, and the matter-of-fact dialogue that they exchange breaks the monotony that you might expect from a JPRG title. While some NPCs are clearly present for decoration,
have still managed to find a way to make them relevant by having the main characters turning the interaction into a nonchalant and humorous experience.
The puzzles in place to progress through the story are, for the most part, intuitive and fulfilling, and often are designed in a way that make you feel like you are just progressing through the game, rather than solving an abstract problem. My experience has had me particularly stumped on around three of the many mandatory puzzles available, but make no mistake that solving these puzzles made me feel like a
and did not detract too much from how I was progressing and my immersion.
That being said,
replayability is lacking, as of the version at release, outside of trying to uncover and complete every single side-quest. There is currently no
option or the like to keep diehard fans entertained beyond the first completion. However, the need to replay the game is nullified by nature of learning absolutely everything possible about the lore and taking the time to explore the in-game world, which can be done in one very fulfilling run. Given that the average run would probably not take more than 13 hours to complete, it is definitely worth it. For those who wish to explore the world after defeating the final boss, saving to a separate file (of which 15 are allowed) before taking the plunge is
recommended, as you will not be able to leave the final dungeon even after winning this battle.
Speaking of battles, each one is surprisingly fast-paced, and the system, overall, is an intriguing one to master. The battle system is turn-based, with each character performing their actions after issuing a command to the entire party first, and each command is executed
. While there are four distinct characters with their own classes to develop, each one will still start off being able to do a similar amount of damage with their basic attack, making the early game faster than your traditional JRPG. The only hindrance with this fast-paced style is that it is hard to track stat debuffs, such as a decreased attack stat, as these do not have icons or messages that remain on screen after they have been applied. On the other hand, status debuffs, such as burns and poison, do have icons and are easy to track and manage. A majority of the encounters are not random, so in the long run, you will not have any nasty surprises hit your party.
My favourite aspect of the battles in
is that every single character, ally or foe, is overpowered in one way or another. This will lead the player to exploit two main playstyles in the mid to late game: impenetrably defensive or overbearingly offensive. There are no words that can explain the level of elation from the serendipitous discovery of ability combos that enable you to take little to no damage or deal
to an enemy in a single turn.
While these feats are possible, they are truly balanced by the need to properly manage AP, the resource expended to execute the special skills belonging to each character. Therefore, overuse of powerful combos will lead to one using turns trying to ramp AP, leaving them completely open to be on the receiving end of some devastating attacks, and probably resulting in their death. Planning before each battle and choosing the correct Gear will help the strategically-minded player get even more enjoyment from this dynamic battle system.
is supported by incredibly beautiful pixel art and the graphics are animated smoothly.
have combined an authentic old-school JRPG feel with more vibrant colours and greater frame rates (currently, up to 120fps are allowed). In turn, whether you are watching a cut scene or getting lost in battle, an immersion happens where you often forget that you are looking at pixel graphics and merely experience the story, much like a movie.
Essentially, each new skill that you learn actually feels more powerful than the last, and dire moments, such as a cave in, truly show the struggle expressed in the moment in both the environment and character sprites.
For those who really wish to relive the old days, there is an option to render a custom number of scan lines as you play, providing the feeling of playing the game on a CRT screen.
Similarly, while inspired by old classics,
have not held back on sound. Each track is beautifully designed and remains authentic to the JRPGs of old, but do not sound muddy as they once were. Every song is relatively catchy and helps enhance your immersion while playing the game, and some themes are effective in expressing the likeness of particular characters. Ditzy enemies sound like ditzy enemies, and tense moments sound like tense moments. The battle themes are intense and fun, and the sound effects are clear - they make you feel as if you are in trouble when you are attacked and strong when you attack. Graphics aside, even just
to your strongest abilities will make you want to ramp AP to perform those actions again and relive that strong sense of power.
is an immersive, cohesive, and overall, fun experience that takes advantage of fast-paced battles and challenging puzzles, beautiful pixel art and crisp and classic sounds inspired by the JRPGs of old. Despite some negligible shortcomings, I would highly recommend this title to JRPG fans, especially for its fun and customisable battle experience.

Outstanding computer football game to the core. Would recommend to anybody who loves NFL football or any version of American football. Worked great from day one and is easy to play. Loved the way the game engine breaks down the season to create an offseason where you can Hire/Fire Staff members, sign Free Agents,  Draft incoming college players and rework your entire roster. I also like the coaching features where you can adjust your gameplan and even scout your opponent. I do see some minor drawbacks like forcing a team to carry three QB's on the active roster and no 10 man Practice Squad but overall it hits all the major issues that other football sims seem to either ignore or simply do a bad job with.

I have officially played this game long enough to create a dynasty, then watch it fall apart again. A lot of the guys doing reviews on this game have 2k+ hours on record, so my 60+ really aren't impressive in the least bit, but this game deserves as many positive reviews as it can get.
This game is as deep as you personally want it to be. Want to just do the draft, sign free agents, and simulate a few seasons to see how you did? Go ahead. Want to do that, plus set the actual packages and plays your team runs, along with formation specific substitutions? This game will let you do that.
I've played 25 seasons in this game. The progression and regression of players is extremely realistic, and the effects of how good or bad your coaching staff is is very noticable. I've felt the pain of having the first rounder I was gunning for get taken right in front of me, I've felt the nervousness of trading away a ton of future draft picks to move up early in the first for a guy that I thought could be the face of my franchise, and I've felt the triumph of seeing that guy become the face of the entire league over the past 12 seasons.
At some point I want to start a new game, create new stories, start over with the players that are in the league today. I'm far enough to the point that every player in today's NFL are a distant memory, and sometimes I long for the familiarity. With that said, I can't just end my game. These "Fake" players are very real to me. I've seen how rookies I've drafted have panned out over time. I keep tabs on them as they go to other teams, and wonder how I let them slip away. I've seen guys I've drafted make it to the hall of fame, and its just incredible.
If your a fan of the sport, or a fan of management games in general, this is the game for you. Be warned though, this game is very addicting. I haven't even tried an online multiplayer league yet, and I've heard that's the best part of the game. I'm very satisfied with this purchase, and will likely purchase every future installment of this franchise for the rest of my life. I just bought like, 12 games on the steam summer sale, and I honestly have no desire to even touch them because of this game.
10/10

Gameplay: 8.5/10
Now if you live under a tree infested with mutant animals in Chernobyl and dont know what a shmup is, then I guess I'll explain a bit of that too. A shmup (Shoot em' up) is a bullet hell type game where you shoot down enemys coming at you, there is usually some sort of bomb mechanic that can clear a screen and deal massive damage to enemy weakspots. Shmups usually have 5-8 stages but some will have less or more. Touhou 16 Hidden Star in Four Seasons is a shmup with the unique Touhou feel to it, and also a mechanic called a release (*cough* Len'en *cough*) which is pretty much a free, easy to get, weaker bomb. There are 4 different releases in the game all with different mechanics, all of which have their own advantages and disadvantages and I think its a fun mechanic that balances out well (cirno release is best release tho). Touhou games are usually 6 stages long with 1 extra stage if you really wanna bash your head against a wall, and that stays true for this game. As far as characters go there are 4 choices:
Aya: who has a bomb that stays out for a while, giving you long I frames, and a decent damage shot with wide unfocused spread and tight focused spread
Cirno: who has an "OK" bomb that is a big circle on the screen staying out for a bit less than ayas bomb, and who has I think the worst damage in the game, but an alright shot type aiming wise.
Reimu: who is a good starter for beginners to Touhou, she has good basic bomb, and an ok damage shot that homes in on enemys
Marisa: who is the best girl, Marisa has the highest damage and my favourite bomb, which is just a huge friggin laser that wipes out anything in its path, her shot type while dealing the most damage, is probably the most narrowly spread though.
All of those characters can be good for whatever your playstyle is and all their releases can be mixed between characters for whichever character/release combo you want. Now that I've talked about all that, lets get into something pretty important; the difficulty. Touhou 16 is probably the overall easiest Touhou game, probably due to the releases and most of the boss attacks in the game being fairly easy compared to the other games, there are 4 difficultys though, so if your having an easy time with normal mode, move up to hard or even lunatic if your actually crazy, and if your having a hard time, then go down to easy modo, which im sure you wont be made fun of for playing. But those difficulties are only for the base 6 stages, the extra stage only has one difficulty, which I have heard people say that extra stages are usually compared to lunatic mode but I dont get that at all, so lets say that extra mode is more comparable to hard mode but its  1 stage with an extra hard boss at the end.
Overall: 8.5/10
A pretty good Touhou game, but definitely not the best, if your new to Touhou this game would be a good place to start because of how easy it is compared to other Touhous, but after you get the hang of being decent at the game, it would certainly benefit you to look into some of the other games, as I believe most of the PC touhou games are better than this one.

Just going to start off with this because it only being released in Japanese might set some people off from the game, there should be guides around the internet to make your playing experience more enjoyable, and also an English patch.
I'm also going to say that this probably not the best review to go off from because this is from the perspective from someone who, while plays the game quite often, hasn't mastered or even beat it yet. I am not a Touhou fanatic in any shape or form, but I do love the gameplay. What I mostly played is EoSD, a bit of LoLK (of course I reset over 100 times in Pointdevice Mode…), and this. I am also quite a newcomer to the franchise, only really starting to play this year. This is also the first real review I've ever done, so that keep that in mind.
While my current time tracked on Steam is rather... low, I actually started playing this game ever since the game got posted online (of course I was a pirate too), so my time in this game is probably past eight to ten hours or so. I even played this game in the computer lab during school hours with my now broken USB, and well, the ICT teacher didn't care much. This is also the first Touhou game I was really hooked into, my first one was EoSD, but HSiFS was the one that made me love the franchise even more.
But back to the main point, Hidden Star in Four Seasons is the 16th (technically not really the  16th due to the other games that are numbered in-between) official Touhou game, and the first one to be put on Steam. While I'd talk about the series here, I'm not a Touhou historian and there are a million other people who can explain it better than be in the internet. But by the screenshots, it's a game where you dodge bullets while shooting your enemies. There are four difficulties, but I usually stay in the lower half because I'm not the best player in this.
There are four characters, each representing a different season. Their type and range of attacks and speed are different per character, and while it can be fun to use different characters, I personally like using Marisa (representing Winter) the most due to her speed. There are also sub-seasons, which also represent the four seasons (obviously), and can be used to complement a season's strength or add a bit more variety into your play, all with different sub-shots that in a way, represent the respective character for that season's abilities.
If you feel like you're close to being absolutely cornered, you can use a bomb, but you will lose your bonus during a boss' spell card. You can also press C to release the season you collected, effects of course, depending on the sub-season chosen. This will also remove a varying amount of bullets from the screen.
There are four different difficulties, and in my opinion, while some people may think otherwise, choose the one that you are most comfortable with at first. While frustrating at first, once you start getting the hang of it, it's a lot of fun and well, addicting. Sometimes you may end up realizing that you spent more time than you thought playing the game. There are many enemies with different patterns and tricks up their sleeve, and being able to overcome them also, well, brings that good feeling of success.
While sure, not everyone is really a person who wants to try again and again to win, and to be honest, even I am a sore loser. But playing again and again (I'm not really a person to use continues, bombs, or season releases because I guess my mind is just not used to doing so.) and being able to succeed is just so satisfying. I'm more of a person who plays Touhou on and off, so I'm not really a person who plays in the higher difficulties, but I still get that good feeling even in the smallest successes in the game.
And while the character art can be... off putting to some, I personally don't really have a problem with it, and in fact, I kind of like it. The real art here anyway is the art of bullets, and still as gorgeous as ever from what I've seen throughout the series. The music is a charm to listen to, and it really adds more to the fight itself in my opinion, and is really a part what made me love the game even if I really suck at it. Sometimes it just doesn't feel the same at all without hearing the music while playing in the school's computer lab.
To be honest, aside from the frustration of losing and losing and losing all over again, there's nothing I really even dislike about HSiFS. Maybe it's different for those who played more games in the franchise, but coming from someone like me who doesn't play that often, I don't really have anything negative to say about it. Apparently there are bugs left over from the original release, but I have yet to encounter them myself.
Major props to ZUN for the everything, really shows he did so much for the franchise and still is, despite it being since what, the mid-1990's since he started working on Touhou. Many people had to pirate Touhou in the past, and with the public's reaction to HSiFS' Steam release now, hopefully in the future we continue to get more Touhou titles via Steam (maybe even some titles of the past too) in the future, maybe with even more Steam-related features.
So in a nutshell: Hard, yet fun, addicting with great music, will suck away so many hours of your life without even realizing it, but will feel so satisfying to get the hang of it. I definitely recommend you to get it, and while this might not be a game for everyone, it could be one for you… especially when the addiction gets to you. Seriously. Only not recommended for those who aren’t really into it or can’t handle the sheer difficulty.

In 1993, my family got a Macintosh LC III that ran system 7 for its OS. What it also ran was "Another World", or "Out Of This World" as we knew it as here. And what a great time we had playing this fantastic old atmospheric platformer game until we finally passed it, a great deal of time later.
I don't even know how long it took us, maybe even over a year. Looking back that's funny because you can easily pass this game in under 40 minutes if you know what to do.
This version has been given a beautiful modern HD treatment here that is faithful to the original game. Apparently the original polygon engine is what allows for that. But of course this version allows you to toggle between the old and the new sound/graphics, if you want to be reminded of how much worse it originally looked.
The HD update makes it look as amazing to me as I believed it looked in 1993. However I don't know how much the average player would enjoy this game today, if they didn't already have their own personal nostalgia for it to begin with.

Batman: Arkham Asylum reinvented the Caped Crusader in video games. The title spawned a series which has been hugely successful both commercially and critically – the non-Rocksteady-produced Arkham Origins being the exception – and more importantly influenced an entire generation of games.
The gameplay core consists of stealth elements and extremely fluid combat built on a few basic but highly interactive moves. While the overall game design is very linear, most stealth set pieces allow the player to take an individual approach. Combat and investigations can feel repetitive at times, but the game's length – the main story is relatively short – alongside the unexpected Scarecrow levels wrap those elements in enough variation to make it work.
The world building is impressive in scope and quality, especially considering the brevity of the story and the setting. Any additional material found in the game holds up to the high standard established by its main characters and their voice actors and the writing is top notch for even the only optionally found recording tapes. The Riddler might get annoying when he's mocking Batman while the latter is solving his puzzles and hunting for collectibles, most players will find new appreciation for both the character and the voice actor once they take the time to listen to his interrogations. Discovering everything hidden by the Riddler also rewards the completionist with a satisfying conclusion to this optional side plot and makes sure the hunt doesn't feel meaningless after the fact.
Outside the story the challenge mode pits Batman against more hordes of nameless goons in the two core modes the game provides: all-out combat and stealth based room clear. Both work as advertised, getting all medals especially on the harder combat maps defnitely is what the name suggests – challenging.
Overall this is one of the greatest games of its generation, even though that might just be its biggest flaw when played for the first time now, years after its release. Considering I am writing this review in 2017, new players might feel like the gameplay is all too familiar from other titles simply because Arkham Asylum was the game that originally introduced it.
+ Innovative gameplay
+ The Batman we need and deserve
+ Convincing story
+ Compelling atmosphere
+ Great art direction
+ Stunning visuals
+ Flawless voice acting
+ Perfect soundtrack
- Somewhat uninspired final boss
- Hordes of nameless clone goons
- Repetitive segments
Conclusion: Batman: Arkham Asylum is a near perfect game that deserves a 9/10.

TL;DR: A puzzle game about doing trigonometric brain-teasers.
A bold move: create a game based on math. It was an insta-buy for me though.
In
you get to solve geometry and trigonometry problems. In a given puzzle there's a bunch of squares, rectangles, triangles and sometimes even circles. Your task is to find the correct answer to certain length or area.
It's certain that you need some knowledge of math to proceed and whether you like & know math will determine whether you like the game. All the required knowledge should become available to children of age 13-15 in most school systems. It includes calculating areas of triangles, rectangles and circles and using knowledge of (right) angles, trigonometry and Pythagorean theorem to deduce other angles and associated side lengths.
That said, every solution is an integer from 1 to 9. It doesn't mean that no other length or area in the puzzle could have a non-integer solution, but it does mean you could easily
guess all the answers and be done with it. I would argue you'd be missing the point but who am I to judge though?
The problems are nice brain-teasers: some can be solved in a few seconds, others take tens of minutes of intense deduction (if you refrain from guessing). The in-game pen makes it simpler to solve many of the problems.
Some problems look like they were pulled directly from a high-school math book (which is fine and likely) so it might look like a scheme to make you do math.
Bright background is inconvenient when playing in a dim-lit room in the middle of the night, but it seems to be the unfortunately established part of Unity puzzle games. At least it's not completely white, which alleviates it a bit.
Music is the usual forgettable but relaxed tune, though a bit on the groovy side. I think classical orchestrated music would have fit this game better, although the soundtrack was otherwise fine.
Playtime will vary tremendously depending on your knowledge of math, ingenuity and whether you guess. Without guessing I had completed all 60 puzzles in 4.5 hours and rehearsed a bit of my knowledge of trigonometry in the process.
It left me craving for more. Puzzles don't change on playthroughs but as replay value goes, you may come back to practice and try them again after a bit, having forgotten the solutions. However for $2-game I think it had enough content anyway even if you didn't. For the low price it's a nice little game. But probably only if you like geometry and math.

Freedom Force was a fantastic game back in its day (though I didn't play it back then) and has stood up reasonably well over the years. The genre is (still) unique and the game is a lot of fun. The destroyable city environments are especially impressive given the game's age. Now, most of the destruction isn't that USEFUL. It might look cool to pick up a telephone pole and bash someone with it, usually using your super powers makes a lot more sense.
You get a large variety of characters and the game does a decent job of forcing you to play most of them (instead of just picking the 4 you like best and sticking with them for every mission). That said, there were several characters that just didn't see as useful as others. In general melee characters seem underpowered--they take damage at a high rate and keeping them alive is sometime challenging. I found it usually better to try to pack my roster with ranged attacks.
The character builder is pretty amazing but I can't imagine actually spending the time on it. But back in the day, lots of people did, and you can lots of custom skins and characters. I don't feel like the game really rewards you for that effort, especially given that multiplayer is non-existent today (and I don't think it was ever that popular).
Overall, a great game that (provided you get it to run; not every has) is still fun today.

"Costume Quest 2" is a direct sequel to "Costume Quest" and also plays like. Well, most of the time.
In the sequel a grumpy Halloween-hating Dentist threatens to destroy the beloved holiday in order to build a new society where candy and Halloween are illegal. The heroes from the last game - the twin siblings Wren and Reynold - again fight baddies, collect costumes, candy and trading cards but this time also have to use time travel where they take a glance into a bleak future with even North-Korean, communist tendencies (no joke, there are two or three or even more references).
So the story's a bit bigger than last time, although I admit that I prefer the first game also because of the story. It felt like something a child would completely fantasize about (some bullies stealing candy and fighting you, the own mother being the evil witch boss) while the sequel provides a story that's almost nowhere just out of a child's mind. It's a matter of taste but it's still enjoyable. But the first game just spreads that Halloween feeling much better.
The gameplay is almost the same and not hard to learn after a while. However, fighting and handling the menues and trading cards are different. Generally it's not bad but if you played the first game and liked the controls there, you might need time to get used to the new controls. When it comes to fighting, there's a character teaching you moves in tutorials.
The new costumes are sweet for the most part and in some way or others replace the old ones (like the clown replaces the Statue of Liberty...I never thought I would actually say this or write this down...).
The graphics are a little bit better and the music is okay, though, not very memorable.
The puzzles throughout should be easy to solve, yet there are also challenging ones (like getting access to a place or finding necessary items in a city with easy missable corners). And also you can collect achievements for a couple of optional actions (like pimping your costumes which you can but don't have to do).
Overall it still is fun but I like the first "Costume Quest" more. If you haven't played the first game, you might not totally get into the characters or their references to the first story. I generally recommend to play both if you love RPGs and/or Halloween.

Costume Quest 2 is a sequel to the extremely fun and interesting kids' adventure embodied in the original Costume Quest. While the story of Costume Quest 2 is meant to continue on from the first game, and is meant to embody the same style, I would say that this sequel is not quite as strong as the original.
I am an extreme fan for the first game and still really enjoyed this game, but it definitely has some big weaknesses. Note that I played both of the games back-to-back, so certain details stood out even more than they might have for years apart.
An adventure RPG is here for you again, as you continue with the brother and sister from the first game, stuck in a bad world suddenly being taken over by a dentist of all people. You must fight your way through some returning monsters from the first game as well as robots created by the dentist to keep his world in check.
Many of the mechanics of the first game still exist, such as using costume abilities to explore the map, the same player stats, the turn-based RPG battles... However, there are some tweaks here and there. In the first game, the only way to sprint across maps was to use the robot ability, which was a slight grievance to keep changing costumes. This game fixes that with its own designated button, thankfully. Further, in the previous game, most battles were triggered at specific points, with only a few sections having enemies walking along the map. This game now has many sections where enemies will run around on the map and you need to avoid them unless you want battle - and many of them respawn. That change is good for giving the maps more life, but bad in the sense that the game adds in some grinding.
Other bigger changes are to the battle style. In the previous game, you mainly performed normal attacks and used the special powers when available. This game adds in a few changes to that: First, you can now run away from battles if you do not want to have them. Second, the developers removed Battle Stamps and you now find Treat Cards which allow for special attacks or powers in battle. You can equip 3 cards at a time and any character can use them. They can only be used once per battle, and each card has a different time limit before it can be reused (i.e., you must complete X number of battles). Third, when you perform attacks, you must now hit the attack button at an exact timing to perform more damage, which is much tougher than in the original game.
Some of those battle changes make the game stronger, some make it weaker. One thing I particularly noticed is that the majority of battles take a lot longer than they did in the first game. The developers seemed to make enemies a lot stronger and you a lot weaker. (As a note, I did have one of my characters being the Candy Corn costume the whole game!)
Besides the above, the rest of the game is pretty much the same, but this time not as fun. You explore the maps, use costumes to get around, and perform trick-or-treating a lot while also solving some side quests... While the first game was quite nice to do that exploration, it now became somewhat of a chore. The story of the game is not as well-done as the first, for many of the main characters only show up occasionally, and the game has a significantly smaller amount of conversations and funny dialog. Further, while the places of exploration are still nice in style, that lack of characters and events makes some of them particularly boring.
If you enjoyed the first Costume Quest, you might still enjoy Costume Quest 2 to some ends, as I still did. But I definitely think that the developers fell behind on keeping the game consistent. The feeling of heart and charm that I had for the first game only happens sporadically for this one.

Anyone who has played Star Traders RPG will not be disappointed by Star Traders: Frontiers, especially once it is complete. The game has some bugs but they are very minor and barely affect gameplay; crashes will rarely, if ever, result in you losing progress. They also don't stick around long, with new fixes and updates coming almost every other day.
Despite RNG controlling almost every part of the game, the game still treats the player fairly most of the time.
The problems I've noticed, or things that I believe are problems:
-Some ship upgrades (such as the deflector arrays, sig dampeners, sensor array, and boarding assault system) lack an adequate description of their effects.
-Enemies very rarely or never suffer morale breaks in crew combat at minimum morale.
-The AI is pretty bad at crew combat. Every AI ship appears to have only four fighters in its crew, which it uses fairly well and is capable of putting up a fight with. The rest of the crew is a bunch of pilots/engineers/etc. which it often puts in bad  positions regardless of health, placing crew members with snipers and rifles (which can only be used from the back) in the front, and those with snubbers or swords (which can only be used from the front) in the back.
-The danger rating of a wilderness and the level of black market access appear to have little affect on the actual risks of exploring or accessing the black market.
-Occasionally a rifle appears as a sniper or snubber in combat or when equipping crew members. This issue only appears to affect rifles; snubbers always appear as snubbers, snipers as snipers, pistols as pistols, and swords as swords.
-The "Naval Veteran" award considers all encounters to be ship battles
Some suggestions I have:
-Allow players to see what talents are and aren't on cooldown when deciding what to do during an encounter. (Knowing whether a talent like evasive maneuvers is ready or not would be very useful)
-The ability to see what the trade law of a planet was the last time you visited it could also be useful, though is not essential since you can write that down.
-Alter the date format at the top of the screen to include the day
-Would be nice to have the option to completely exclude the story missions from a game.
-Should probably make it so that a planet doesn't have as high of a demand for a product from another planet in the same system.
I am unsure what to say about the card system. Sometimes I like knowing what I might encounter and having the ability to knowingly influence the outcome, sometimes I think I'd prefer RPG's blind rolls, not knowing what you may encounter on this expedition or patrol once you click the button or exactly how your stats and abilities affect your odds.

Battle Chef Brigade shows the marvelous and creative things small developers can do. This is a game that supports its story with its mechanics. While the story it has to tell is full of tropes it is still very enjoyable.
TL;DR
- Playtime: ~8 hours
- Competent 2D Combat
- Deceptively complex Matching Puzzles
- Replayability: At least 2 times (once for Normal, once for Hard)
- Story: Good enough that I'd have watched
- It's only 20 USD
Current Negatives:
- Limited Keyboard support (fixes for that should be coming with the first major patch)
- No versus mode for a "cook-off" game
- No freeplay mode
You may see the following in other reviews: Sidescroller, Match 3, Anime... and rightly wonder why reviewers are gushing over this fairly short game with seemingly very little replay value. To which I'd suggest
any capable reviewer or player doing one cook-off. Like any good dish, if you just look at the ingredients you may question if it will be any good.
It is important to understand how all the systems mesh together to really understand what's going on. The first major components is the Time Limit. Time managment is constant pressure that impact performance in the other two aspects of play.
2D Combat: Is competent. I'd leave it at that. It can sometimes feel a bit unresponsive, however that also feels like over zealous button mashing error. When you play it at a more techincal level it works just fine. This is where
pressure will start in on you. Being too hasty can lock you into combos, or cause you to miss some platforming. If you wouldn't likey make as many errors.
when you can say "this feels like my mistake, and I can do better at this."
Puzzling: Deceptive. 5 main "Gem" types, rotate 4 at a time. Combine 3 to "level" them up for better score. Now limit the grid to 8x8. Add required" pieces from the "Theme Ingredient." Limit the amount of "stirring" with Cracked Gems. Effects from different Cookware. Needing to balance making upwards of 3 different dishes at once. It can get very demanding fairly quickly. The "stirring" mechanic captures, in game form, the basic mechancial task of cooking. If you are not a fast "Match 3" puzzler, this aspect of the game may be too much for you. If do not come into the cook-off with a plan it is easy to get overwhelmed with everything you need to track. Fortunately there are ways of playing that can reduce your need to be a swift puzzler.
That could BCB's catch phrase. Did you have a plan to your hunting? Did you have plan a for you dishes. Now this is slightly thwarted by not being allowed to see the details of a Cook-Off before going into it, but only slightly. If If you
a match you can either Rematch
Return to Town and re-gear. There is no campaign penalty for doing either.
This is where BCB can start having its replay value. Even after you complete the campaign on Hard you may not have gotten all the Steam Achievements, if you are of that inclination. You may even want to go through it again, using different cookware and with a different "plan" to your culinary combat.
Who knew cooking could be this fun?

The original Costume Quest was a great game and the sequel doesn't disappoint either.
Costume Quest 2 is, plainly, an RPG about kids trick or treating.  On the surface, that's all it is.  However, it's Tim Schafer at the helm with all his inherent crazyness making it absolutely hilarious.  The battle system is quite nice and nods to classics such as Super Mario RPG with its timing mechanisms and job system (well, costume system in this case) of Final Fantasy 5, but put in a very light way so people of all ages can enjoy it.
So yes, it's a turn-based RPG with timing mechanics based on trick-or-treating that is absolutely hilarious and charming...just like the last one...except this one revolves around a time travelling plot.  Pretty fun stuff overall.

This game is much more than what its individual genres look like together on paper!
- Unique genre mash that flows together surprisingly well
- Character and world design are great
- Story is good and satisfying to finish
- Equipment and trinkets allow for a lot of different focuses and playstyles, and makes multiple playthroughs more considerable
- Daily challenges help even more with longevity
- Lots of unique food art
- The stage that you collect ingredients from in chef battles rotates to different places with different monsters occasionally, to a total of 3 different areas; each encourage different strategies and learning the layouts
- Soundtrack isn't a standout, but it isn't annoying either
- Voicework isn't bad, but some people have notably different microphone qualities
- Story is relatively short (seems to range around 8 to 10 hours on average)
- Enemy chefs' food seems to be random or picked from a batch of outcomes; I had a few rounds with a chef I was having trouble with where his point total at the end of the match was drastically different one time compared to another
- You only play a different character once in the story, and there is no actual moveset customization, just move tweaking with equipment
- Difficulty spikes occur seemingly out of nowhere sometimes during certain jobs, particularly the Puzzle job
Overall, the game's really solid. Problems I had during chef battles mostly felt like they were my fault for not being skilled enough to pull off what I was trying to do. The characters are charming and funny, and the gameplay stands out incredibly well. There's a lot of replay value here, as well. I'd say it's definitely worth full price, and one of the few games where I actually hope they announce DLC soon!

This is the football sim that I've been looking for. Growing up I would play madden, but I rarely ever played any actual games (never felt like it was real football). The only aspect I liked was franchise mode.
Pros
- Very accurate sim stats
- Real life rosters (and the ability to edit team names)
- Simulation only takes seconds for an entire season (one of my only issues with OOTP 16, the long sim times)
Cons
- As other reviewers have stated, the UI from this game looks like it was made in the 90s.
- I'm not a fan of the way coaches are handled. (coach drafts every season, I'm not sure if there's a way around this and I missed it)
Overall, I would recommend this to anybody that wants an accurate NFL sim. The UI may be poor, but it doesn't hinder the experience too much. That being said, it will be frustrating to play until you get used to it. If you're willing to overlook the flaws there is much to like.

Another World is a pretty well known piece, so in a way it may not even need my review at all.
In my defense, I've never played it until recently, at least until the end that is, since I have never finished it completely and hadn't a pleasure of getting all the achievements. But I enjoyed many of the hours I've put into this game, admittedly looking up a few solutions to the complex puzzles I've encountered in the game. And while the game is not that long, it didn't take quite a lot of time to finish it, upon completing it I still felt some sort of personal achievement and pat myself on the back (the two guards by the bottomless pit really got on my nerves). The renewed graphics feel fresh, but still bear the same old school 2D feeling, for those with some nostalgic attitude I'm pretty sure the old pixelated textures can be turned on, but the whole gameplay doesn't change one bit. As mentioned above the game is a classic and need not be renewed or rebooted in any way.
I would recommend this one for any and all sidescroller fans, as I think it's still a rather popular genre even in recent titles, but the whole atmoshphere of Another World really is a unique and yet ever so pleasant experience, full of truly distant world environments, which remain still so close to real life imagery.

Definitely a game for someone who really can stick with a good puzzle and has at least some skill with basic algebra and geometry. If you enjoy brainteasing geoemtry puzzles then this is for you. It's not too tough and can actually be very enjoyable, assuming you're not the type of person who despises the sight of a triangle. The music and visuals are nice, the math is all simple enough to do in your head, with no fractions or decimals ever being required to come to a solution, and the puzzles can be truly headscratching at times. There's even a built in drawing tool to facilitate working out the numbers, which I found extremely handy. Calculators or any algebra past the Pythagorean Theroem are unncessary. Just remember that like in Geometry work, the visuals are usually not to scale.
If you get stuck, the answers are few enough to just brute force an answer, and there are two different Steam guides that provide answers and explanations for your benefit.
At this price, take the plunge! I actually find the music and visuals along with the unlimited time make it a great game to relax to.

There's a lot to take in at once, and the in-game help briefly touches on several things, but doesn't really HELP you figure things out.
At the start, the game gives you a 3 units to use, the first being a Crusader tank, which appears to be a medium tank with modest firepower. The game doesn't really tell you that, nor does it also say "Hey, this tank also fires special rounds that will slow an enemies movement speed.
The second unit is called a Dune Runner, which appears to be a heavy scout unit. Now, the game says that it's effective at taking out infantry, but apparently slightly effective, as it seems most infantry are meant for taking out vehicles.
The last free unit they give you is something called an enforcer, and here's where I kind of began to dislike the game. The enforcer unit gives you about 12 infantry in a match, which is nice, BUT their rockets IGNORE armor on all vehicular units. They can keep up with most units, and are entirely capable of surrounding and decimating the heaviest of tanks.
Now, there's several different kinds of units, but they are expensive to buy, each one costing 10,000 in game currancy. All of them. From the 'skirmisher' infantry, meant to take out other infantry, to the 'juggernaut', the heaviest of tanks. This wouldn't be a problem, since most pvp matches earn you about 800 coins (I don't think they have a name for their in game money), but starting out and unlocking skills and perks for your units, you're going to want to spend that money, since the perks are mostly helpful. For example, if you're trying to become better with the Crusader, your first skill is a movement booster, which boosts anyone's movement speed that steps into the skill area. The second, which is one you'll unlock through spending experiance and money, is a machinegun straff, which in name sounds useful to you for taking out those pesky infantry, but after spending the money you'll find it's not entirely useful, and here's another problem.
The game doesn't really give you any stats to go on, at least from what I could see. The game will say things like "This rocket barrage ability will do 450 points of damage to units every .5 seconds, ignoring armor (there's another 'ignore armor' perk). Now, this sounds useful, right? "That sounds like it might deal some pretty good damage." But you don't have anything to compare it to. From what I understand, Crusader tanks have 3,000+ health, and that's all I can tell you about their stats. There's just not much to go on nothing to really help you out.
Now, for those who are still reading, I really want to go on, but there's too much to type out at once. There's too much to warn you about. The bad tutorials, the confusing game play, how the game is both fun and disappointing. All I can do is advice you to move on. There's better things to try and play.

Obviously, a lot of people have been having trouble with this game. I haven't but I think I'm in the minority, so that alone might be pause for consideration before forking out on the pack. if you can get it to run though, Freedom Force is a lot of fun. I purchased the pack for convenience as I still have the boxed version gathering dust from back when FF first came out and its nice to be able to run the game at a higher resolution that the older version allowed. That said, FF avoids looking too dated as it uses a comic style for its design that, while simplistic by todays standards, looks more indie than archaic. The whole game has a tongue in cheek silver age Marvel aesthetic that honors the genre while lovingly pointing out just how silly it often is. It a delicate ballance that FF pulls off well with numerous superheros, archvillians and plotlines that made the game stick happily in my memory more than a great many other contenders.
In gameplay, where FF excells imo, is in the ballance between challenging and frustrating. You can usually find a way to complete a level relatively swiftly but you can't just stroll in and expect to win. The levels themselves have enough variety to avoid repetition and invite you to play around a bit until you solve them. The game mechanics work well but begin to show the cracks in a potentially great game: Certain abilities are of more use than others to the point that using half the roster simply makes the game inherently more difficult and the xp awards add to this. XP is too limited, increasingly limiting the usability of most characters in the roster as you focus on the better ones. In other cases, the XP is insufficent to max out some toons; Eve being the obvious example, with her top tier abilities inacessible with the amount of XP provided from her addition to the roster. The 'create your own heros' option is limited too, leaving such characters outside the xp generation pocess and highly expensive to purchase (and grossly overpowered if you pay attention to the weaknesses of enemies).
In short then yes, Freedom Force is flawred, it has issues but Great Scott, it is fun when you get into it.

Even though I recieved this game for free and it is developed by a close friend of mine I still hope you will take the time to read my honost opinion of the game.
Castle Explorer is a basically board game for pc, and what makes board games good? The experience you get when playing with friends so if you don't have any friends to play this game with and you have to play with only the AI, I wouldn't recommend this game.
In Castle Explorer the RNG reign supreme, and even though that might be frustrating to some (especially competitive) people, I have found it quite amusing that you could end up dead on your first turn due to bad luck on the roulette or a bad choice when picking which tile to pick up and place.
Speaking of luck, your heroes do have different stats which actually matter a bit when planning your run. If you have high luck for instance you have a much higher chance of surviving in the castle even after the dragon has awakened thereby giving you a better chance of collecting more gold before you run for the exit. If you have a big HP pool you have a higher chance of surviving the centipede or awakening the dragon which can deliver a ton of damage. If you have high strength you don't need to worry too much about that porticulus that has closed between you and the exit etc.
Theese little things are what sets the heroes apart, but just like life castle explorer is like a box of chocolates and you never know what you are going to get and might NEVER get a chance to exploit your heroes strenght or face his/her greatest weakness.
If you think you would enjoy this kind of randomness, and have a few friends you think would feel the same way about it and who could enjoy dying on turn one and still have fun as they try and force/taunt you to take risks again and again so they don't end up being the only one who doesn't make it out (not likely to happen even if they don't taunt you) buy the game and make sure your friends does so as well, or at least play it singleplayer for a bit untill you are sure that you and your friends would enjoy it before buying it for them/asking them to buy it.

The game is beautiful. Every character, even the ones you see for a very short time are full of personality, in the way they talk as well as the way they are dressed and posed. Their designs are all unique and interesting, making each character feel like they are their own individual, with a proper back story. The background and levels are on the same level as the characters, and my only complaint would be that they are so small that I'm sitting there wishing I could dive in and explore more. The animation is fluid and full of energy. You can really see how much care went into the animation and design when you look at the way the monsters move and attack. Everything makes sense, and all their attacks are well telegraphed. It really adds to their personality as well.
The voice acting is outstanding. Everyone has so much personality when speaking with you. I especially love the people you serve in the restaurant. Their little comments when you serve them always got me laughing and smiling. Everyone's voice and accent really fit their character as well. There was only one time where I thought the voice didn't really add up with the character and that was cause I thought the character was a girl, but the voice was... pretty deep. Who knows, maybe the character was a girl with a deep voice.
The music is beautiful. There were so many times while playing where I just got lost in the music that was playing, especially in the city. The music is so uplifting, it brings a cheerful mood to the game that otherwise wouldn't be there if absent. I feel like people forget how important music is, and only focus on the visuals, but I argue that music is just as important as the visuals, sometimes more. Think about how many games you know the theme songs to, or how easy it is for a melody to bring you back to a specific moment in a specific game. While there may not be any songs in this game that I would consider Legend of Zelda memorable, they are great nonetheless.
The story is cute. It's a world where people of different cultures and races bond over food and other culinary persuits, and you play as a girl who dreams of joining the Battle Chef Brigade, a organization that leads in the study of the culinary arts. No crazy nonsense drama. Just a feel good experience.
The gameplay is really nothing like I have ever played. Which is weird because the game has elements from a lot of games that I have played. But putting them together creates a whole new experience. You fight monsters in a side scrolling combat style in order to get their meat and other parts for cooking. Then it becomes a puzzle game, like a cross between tetris and  bejeweled, where you try to match up the same items to create a more powerful type of that element. And if that sounds boring, trust me, it is not. Time management is a factor cause you got a certain amount of time till you need to present your dish to the judges. And then there are minigames that I didn't even realize were minigames at first because they are surrounded by their own charming little story. Everything just works well.
There is only one thing that I dislike about this game, and that is the length of it. This is not because I feel cheated out of my money. I definitely feel like I have gotten my money's worth. Especially now when full priced games from AAA companies really leave you feeling disappointed and cheated when finished with them. The reason why I dislike the length of the game is that I absolutely want to keep playing. I want to see more the world, and explore the dishes you can make. It felt like the story was just getting started for the main character, and all of the sudden the game is done. And I can't say that this is a bad thing. A game that leaves you wanting more is a game worth playing.
Thanks for the great experience Trinket Studio.

I really like this game.   But I have stopped playing it for now.
This game is a rogue-like space adventure.  As soon as you start you have to make decisions about character creation.   You can boost your stats up OR you can go with lower stats and a mid-game ship plus other goodies at start.
Basic gameplay is doing missions for people.   This increases rep and then opens doors to better rewards and more missions.   Your basic RPG style.   You can choose just to trade, smuggle, or be a pirate if you like too.   But you will have the chance to do all these things when completing the missions.   So why not make a little extra?
You upgrade your character as you level up by earning XP.   You use money to upgrade your ship and pay your crew.   And that's where this game really shines to me.   Crew Management.
Crew management means that along with your Captain Character, your crew will level up as well.   Your captain and your officers can have three jobs.  All other crew have can only have one job.   Jobs open access to special use skills for combat, mini games (smuggling, exploring, spying, etc. are all minigames), and back ups in the event of failed saving throws.  Jobs also provide stats that help when making those saving throws and with weapon accuracy during combat.  Upgrading your ship gives you access to more crew and officers.
It's a great game but the reason I am going to set it aside for awhile is that it's not complete.   However, the devs have a plan and are very rapidly implementing features from their roadmap.   I just don't want to burn myself out before more of these features are put into the game.  Fortunely, I don't think I will have to wait very long.

Castle Explorer is a virtual board game which centers around the idea of finding a key to escape from a dangerous castle and with more gold in tow than every other dugeoneer locked in there with you.
It works like this: it's your turn, you choose a square to move to, if it has already been revealed you'll just day an event card. If the square is unknown you select a random floor tile and place it and then draw a card.
Many floor tiles feature different types of rooms, some have traps, others have enemies, others will lock you in or dowse your torch. This is where the challenge is, depending on the obstacles you face in that room you'll frequently need to spin a virtual wheel to decide if you live or die. This is a bit over simplified for time but that's the jist, your success relies quite heavily on random chance. Both in terms of the types of room tiles you 'draw' as well as the traps and enemies you encounter.
If you are lucky, the RNG gods smile down upon you and you reach the center room with the dragon, grab as much gold as you can and a key and then make your way back out before the dragon wakes and starts filling the castle with fire.
If you get out, you win. But it's pretty rare that anyone will actually make it out of the castle without dying providing you play the game on it's default settings. Most will perish in the castle, often quite unfairly, to traps and enemies.
While the game plays best with other people and does have an online lobby, you can also play solo and it's a fairly challenging dungeon crawling experience and easily provides a couple hours of entertainment if you can stomach the inherent unfairness of RNG mechanics.
Watch this video for a better understanding on how the game is played and my thoughts on it:

You have no non-trivial choices to make as a player, other than your choice of character.  There's nothing here but watching what the RNG does to you.  Also, no progression of any kind, unlike many similar boardgames.  Great sound and the controls are obvious, but they forgot the gameplay.  There are many better choices on Steam.

A cute little digital board game that pays tribute to some of the forgotten classics of yesteryear.
If you like board games where you get to choose from a cast of heroes with different strengths and weaknesses, but you want the added feature of brutal difficulty that makes every turn tense and potentially lethal, well... it's that.
The rules are simple enough that the game practically teaches itself, the basics can be easily mastered in the first 20 minutes of play. You enter a room, draw a card, pray it's not a big stabby ogre that wants to hurt you, and spin some wheels against your stats when the situation calls for it. Turns rarely last more than 2 minutes and are often just around 15 seconds, so the pacing is good.
Production value is middling, it certainly lacks polish in places but succeeds in setting the mood and conveys gameplay information fairly well. It's about right for it's price tag imho, although that is of course highly subjective. No bugs or glitches from what I've seen so far.

FOF7 is a fantastic simulator. It's probably the most realistic and immersive game of its kind, far exceeding the realism of Football Manager series (it's soccer, but there are no other football simulators so bear with me here). Everything from setting up your starting line-up to play calling is completely realistic. Player stats are completely within an acceptable range; you don't see QB's who throw for 7000 yards or RBs running for 3000. Even things out of the realm of football (like the population of cities, differing fan preferences, franchise values etc.) are simulated extremely realistically. The game has unending replay value; just pick a different team (or the same team, as stats and future development of players are "random" within a pre-determined range) and call different plays. The players coming out of the draft also add to the playability because the talent pool never seems to drop and you can have a career that spans for more than a century! The best part is that the game doesn't experience any lags, even after 100 seasons.
Of course there are a few negatives: The "graphics" are primitive. Actually, there are no graphics to start with. It's a completely text-based simulator so if you are looking for a 3D interface like in FM, tough luck. Other than that the play calling, while very extensive, lacks a few crucial ones such as trick plays where a WR or RB passes the ball. You can still go for fake punts or kicks, but I found it weird that the developer overlooked trick plays during regular downs.
I highly recommend FOF7 to all American football fans who were dismayed by Madden's franchise mode. What's lacking in graphics is made up by the extreme realism of this game.

I'm a bit up in the air about this game. I'll give it a thumbs down, because it's not worth the money I spent on it, and it's a huge pain to be able to play the game the way I want to play it.
Positives:
- It's a good simulator, if you want to play with current NFL players.
- The preseason draft option is fun, again, if you play with the current NFL players
Negatives:
- Trying to play with randomly created players. When creating a draft for these players, there are normally 2-3 good quarterbacks to chose from (rated 75-95), another 3-4 decent ones (rated 55-74), and the rest are completely worthless (Sometimes, the best rated qb is in the low 60s). Unless you get the first few picks in the draft (you can't chose what pick you will get), you won't get a good quarterback, and if you don't have a pick in the top 15, you are screwed, and your team will struggle to win any games because your quarterback is so terrible (we're talking backup NFL material here). The poor quarterback ratings don't seem to affect the computer-owned teams much, but a poor qb certainly affects you plenty.
- The "Preference Draft" idea sounds like a good one (you can chose to allow the computer to draft for you, based on your weighted preferences on each team unit), but it doesn't work correctly. You'll likely end up with 4 RDEs and 0 LDEs, and if you try to move a RDE to LDE, he becomes worthless (his ratings go down tremendously). Even switching a RDT to LDT, or a RG to LG (both of which should have little to no effect), makes the even the best player on the team a mediocre one. If you could trade to even up your roster, that might help, but teams won't trade after the draft (I don't know how long this lasts...it's at least half a season).
- Trading is difficult. If you can find a player that another team will actually let go of, they want way too much for him.
- Searching for kick returners and punt returners in the game is a pain. Basically, you have to open up the profiles of all the running backs, receivers and defensive backs to see if they can fill that role. A search for roles would be extremely helpful in the draft (you can search in this manner after the draft). It would also be helpful for the long-snapping role. I hate wasting a roster spot on a guy who is nothing but a long snapper. Centers should also show long-snapping ability in their profiles...only the rookies do.
The "Full X-Factor" option seems to do nothing at all. It certainlky doesn't do what it says it should.
I give this game a 6 out of 10. It is a good game if you want to play with real NFL players, but personally, I have more fun with computer-created players, and this game just destroys that aspect of the game with it's many flaws. It's also a inferior product for the price I paid for it.

A fun game that marries cooking and hunting into a delightful package!
Needless to say, the art for the food and ingredients are absolutely appetizing.
The character artwork is simple but expertly done. The characters have an abundant number of poses and expressions. The characters' personalities reflect well in how they carry themselves in both the artwork and the dialogue; it's been fun learning more about the characters in those regards!
I was a bit iffy about the gameplay at the beginning... but after playing for a while, it makes sense! You add and mix the elements in the platform as you would add and mix ingredients in a cooking pot. The mechanics are well-integrated into the story as well with regards to "carefully preparing" the dishes.
Personally, the time limit for duels are a bit too short for me to amply prepare. I would say it's enough to keep things challenging for me, but it might push some more anxious and less experienced players away. Maybe adding an easier mode where time limits are a lot more forgiving and hunts are less punishing would be good.
I echo another review's sentiment about cooking loadouts. It makes more sense to me to be able to prepare your tools
knowing the stipulations of the challenge. There's a bit of frustration in knowing that you have the perfect tool for this particular challenge that you just missed the opportunity to use. If there were some context clues prior to the duels that can tip the players in on which loadout might be optimal, I think this could turn into a fun little guessing game of sorts.
Let me preface this by saying that I love going into the Practice Kitchen. Casually hunting (or practicing hunting) for the ingredients and cooking at my own pace, turning the dish into a delicious monstrosity for the history books... that's a very relaxing thing for me.
If it hasn't been done already, I would love the opportunity to be able utilize a mode like the Practice Kitchen and be able to choose the hunting location as well. And to add to that, a journal of sorts where you can record your best culinary creations I think would be a very cool feature.
If you're a cooking game fan, if you're a hunting game fan... heck, if you're a cooking game
hunting game fan, and if you like beautiful 2d visuals to boot, Battle Chef Brigade is right up your alley!

Battle Chef Brigade is a charming yet quirky hybrid of about 20% 2D platformer action game and 80% match 3 puzzle gem cooking battle. This game was far more story driven than I had originally expected, yet I found myself pleasantly surprised. The characters were genuine and there is meaningful dialogue and the story is well paced. The best part of the game is the cooking battles. It's an episode of Chopped mixed with an intricate match three puzzle game that slowly builds on mechanics as you progress through the story.
Other notes: I hope at some point they implement a multiplayer mode where you can compete in teams. I think that the concept has lots of potential and the execution is rather decent. As it current stands the game is rather short so take it or leave it whether or not you feel $19.99 is  worth it.
Price aside this is a solid 8.8 / 10 for me.

To keep things short and simple, this marks the first time Touhou has seen a release on Steam (and I want to say a Western release, but I don't think this is teachnically true).
Touhou games at their core are fairly basic shoot-em-ups, but in play, you'll find yourself practicing over and over again trying to beat the games absolutely dazzling spectacles of a boss fight without a single bullet hitting your hitbox.
This game is really not for those without any sense of patience or any desire to put hours into a game just to learn the ins and outs of a level, the patterns of attacks in every boss, and so forth. But to those looking for a challenge, this is a game for you.
Asides from its gameplay though, you will find yourself accompanied by some really spectacular jams as you fly through levels and sweat bullets trying not to die. So there's that too.
Art wise, ZUN could probably do with a sit in at one of Betty Edwards "Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain" lessons they usually do worldwide. Or just read the book.
In any case, I am absolutely excited to see this game on Steam and hope to see more Touhou, either ZUN's or from the doujin community at large, soon

This game is text based. If you're in to that sort of thing and have imagination then you can have a great time with this game. You're the president of a team. You choose where your team is located, the name, the coaches, the players, the training staff, roster moves, draft decisions, trades, gameplan, ticket prices, stadium construction, and essentially anything else that a team president would generally control.
Some of the things that i'm able to control I really don't want to control such as the gameplan for the team. That's something the coach that I hired should control. I don't want to guess how much to charge for tickets so that is also delegated. For me the fun is in putting the team together. Deciding on my coaches, players, free agency, and the draft. The key to success in this game is drafting well and being smart with your contracts. The scouting information you receive is dependent on how well your scouting staff evaluates talent. Then there are curveballs thrown in such as player volatility. Many factors go in to scouting information and the accurracy of that information.
In some cases your scouts can be dead wrong about a player such as in the real NFL. In some cases players may not be committed and you will see your prized first round pick with tons of potential not really develop. Or in some cases he may even begin to regress. This accurracy of information can be adjusted. By default it's set at 50. I have left it on 50 because it does seem like a good balance. I would imagine that on 0 you just couldn't depend on any information your scouts give you and set on 100 the information would be 100% accurrate.
This game is a lot like Head Coach 2009. That is a game that I loved because the draft was very exciting. Front Office Football gives a similar excitement. Though the drafts are not accompanied by Schefter talking about the prospects you are not limited to just 15 seasons like in HC09. I think i'm currently in year 2132 of my franchise. I should have been dead long ago. :)
You have to consider things like leadership, how players mesh together, conflicts between players, and players with a bad attitude. All of these things are done very well in this game. I'm not a young man anymore and played Madden since the first one. Franchise mode was what I used to love to play because it felt like you were in control of your favorite team. Head Coach was similar. However, I think that FOF7 does a much better job of giving you control and a realistic feeling of managing a team.
I'm so thankful that I found this game. I didn't know it existed until it arrived on steam. I was still playing Head Coach 09 even though I had memorized all of the players names and how good they were. Then when I got this game I just fell in love. Not at first but once I got into it a little deeper. FOF7 is a game that has infinite replayability. The drafts are completely random. The names and stats are randomly generated so you'll never run into that problem that I had with Head Coach.
It's hard to describe a text based game but I can say that this game is a ton of fun. It's challenging, rewarding, and something that you can play without getting bored of it.
That being said it isn't perfect - but it's close. There are some little ergonomic issues like with mouse wheel scrolling in certain menus and things. Nothing major and it's just more of an annoyance that adds an extra click to your menu diving. That's really the only complaint. I'm not sure how many hours i've played but i have never had a single crash in all my hours. Everything runs perfect.
This is truly the greatest football management game ever. It's certainly worth it's pricetag if you're someone like me. I will probably play this for the rest of my life and not get tired of it. I love it.

A quick review: after 13 years, it's still the most complete title so far. 24 hours full cycle, smart AI, variable weather, a full series story and championships. A true study-case for the modern SIM-racing producers (actually most of them only hot lap simulators) learn how to do the stuff.

I had this game on disc back in the day and spent thousands of hours learning how to sim-race on it. It wasn't my first sim racing title but it was the one I used the most when I got my first wheel and also where I learned to drive a manual.
Sadly, this Steam version of the game came about after a lengthy lawsuit in which Simbin lost the rights to have certain car manufacturers in the game anymore. Thus, this title does not grant you the ability to drive several vehicles (if I recall, Ferrari, Porsche and Lamborghini are no longer present but I could be wrong). To make matters even worse, not only can you NOT drive them but the AI still do; so when you are racing there will be literally dozens of cars with all black textures which completely and utterly kills any sense of immersion or realism.
There is a workaround to get those cars back but requires some more "advanced" steps that the simplified gamer may not be capable of following. In my opinion, there are other more modern sim racers out there that provide ALMOST the level of satisfying modern GT racing that this game brought to the table so go check out something else.
The ONLY reason why you should still buy this and why I am still willing to rate this title up is because you can acquire a FANTASTIC mod called the "Power & Glory" mod which essentially replaced GT Legends and even expands upon it.
Aside from Automobilista this is arguably the best title built atop the rFactor engine and unlike Automobilista this is actually the most feature rich, including night racing, full dynamic wet weather and allows up to 24 hours of racing in one event with dynamic weather and time enabled.
You can enjoy this terrific rFactor engine at its finest with the terrific "Power & Glory" mod as you should.

GTR2 is one of the most well known and beloved racing sims for good reason. It is a game that got just about everything right and still holds up, 11 years since its release. It delivers on everything a fanatical GT racing fan like myself would want out of a racing game.
Sense of speed is great, car models, interiors and sounds are spot on, physics are excellent and the game has full wheel support with lots of options. It also has mod support as well.
The Steam version of this game does have some drawbacks. While I really like being able to own this game once more and being able to play it in 1900x1200 resolution with my G27, buyers should know that Ferrari and Porsche models are not accessible without mods, most likely to licensing issues at the time the game came out on Steam. Also, if you do not run Steam as an administrator and make sure to double click the game from your library and choose "Play Game", your playtime will not be recorded and you won't have access to the Steam overlay. It is a minor issue but it is quite annoying. This issue was also present in GT Legends.
Minor laws aside, this game is absolutely brilliant and I highly recommend it if you are a fan of GT and Endurance racing.
