Yes. Get this game. Learn what mind blowing graphics were in 1991, remember a time when a hacker, a vision, and way too much time in front of an assembler is all it took to put a game to market. Sparce in music, no hint system, just you, your Buddy, and your blaster that always seems to go out at just the wrong time vs an entire world of aliens.
This game, it's hard. Brutally hard. This was a time when progress was the reward for those who took the time to master the game, because storage constraints meant the game had to fit and ship on 2 or 3 floppy disks. You will die, you will die a lot, and you will die brutally. This is the game the wise elder geeks cut their teeth on, this is why they complain about today's modern games that spoonfeed you hints and story without subtext. Despite everything that would be a game's deathknel in today's modern game scene, it works. You piece the story together by interacting with the world. The deaths are unfair, and unapologeticly so; as this alien world is not fair, the odds are stacked against you to survive. If you died doing a thing, you learn not to do that thing, and try something else. Remember as you see the password scene though, that you will be back at the puzzle in seconds due to your fast gee wiz machine, back in '91 your mistake would earn you 30/40 seconds of loading time to ponder just where you went wrong. Press on, because every obstacle can be overcome. You can get through in about an afternoon of determined play.

Another World is a milestone in computer gaming evolution. For younger gamers it might be not clear why, because in comparison to modern titles AW is of course ascetic and visually poor, but at the time of it's release in early 90's it was a little revolution in platform type of games, further continued by Flashback and many others, mostly because of animation and movement of a character, but also due to diversity of adventure and puzzles - every level is something different, you're not doing boring stuff here.
As regards remastered version, the most important thing is that, unlike new version of Flashback (which is a bit dissapointment by the way), it doesn't change the game design and mechanics except adding optional higher resolution (you can switch it during play by pressing "p" key) and levels of difficulty.
Before i started to play, after more than 20 years, i had thought that it was going to be just a little nostalgic return to Amiga times, but this game "still got it" and it took me for a couple of hours again - i just had to finish it once more and i hope i'll be able to do this again at it's 50th anniversary ;)

The game is great, but you're most likely to encounter a game breaking bug in the game. This is how to fix it. Credit to cajun for this fix. But look after that
1) Find the executable "fforce.exe" in C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common\Freedom Force
2) Right-click on it and open the Properties
3) Click the Compatibility tab
4) Click the checkbox for "Run this program in compatibility mode for:", and select "Windows 98/Windows ME"
5) Click the checkbox for "Disable visual themes"
6) Click the checkbox for "Disable desktop composition"
7) Click "Apply" and click "OK"
8) Double-click the "fforce.exe" file to run the game directly, rather than going through Steam

HOWEVER, each time you exit the game, it goes back to it's old status. You must verify your files each time you play again. This is teidious, but if you love the game, you'll bear it. If you get past the bug, you'll get the excellent game.

The 16th numbered game, 25th in the series, and first of them on Steam, Touhou: Hidden Star in Four Seasons is a top down, vertical-scrolling bullet hell shooter, much like Mushihimesama or the Danmaku Unlimited series.
While I can't say for certain whether or not this is the easiest of the bunch, I can say it is a good starting point to jump into, given some of the mechanics.  You can not only practice stages you've reached (as opposed to having to clear the stage first, as in previous games), you can even practice against specific spell cards (ie, the big moves done by the various bosses of the game), making it easier to learn That One Attack that keeps screwin' you over.
Another nice thing is the sub-season item pick-ups, which can act as a mini-bomb, either helping you escape a tight spot, or get you a nice bonus to your score.  But unlike bombs, you can use them during an enemy's spell card and still capture it (netting you a nice bonus, which can get you more lives).
I've yet to beat this game, but I've enjoyed it, and I hope to see more of the series come over this way.  With any luck, so will the soundtracks.

(EDIT as of August 11th, 2017: A while back, a version on
was released which evidently fixed many of the issues the Steam version has with compatability. While I can't speak from experience and would recommend doing research, I would highly advise checking that version out if this game interests you.)
I first got this game several years ago, played a ton of it, and was pleased to find it was on Steam along with its sequel (which I unfortunately haven't played as of yet). It's an enjoyable real-time pause-based strategy game set in a 40s-50s era metropolis filled with superheroes and villians.
Overall, the main appeal this game has (at least for me) is how much like a comic book it actually is. The writing is fun and incredibly campy (and revels in it), and very cartoonish, but it has its more serious moments too. The characters are all knockoffs of actual comic book superheroes and villians (though I didn't catch some of the parallels. Granted, I'm not well-versed in comics), but each has his or her own twist, and I found them all enjoyable, and while fairly cliché, they worked well. Personally I found the game to be hilarious, but I do enjoy some campiness now and then.
The gameplay itself, as I mentioned, is a mix between real-time and turn-based gameplay, with events happening in real time, and the issuing of commands done while the game is paused, though you can still issue some commands (such as a certain attack or movement) in real time as well. Sometimes the pathfinding is a bit clunky, but it works, and any little quirks can usually be fixed with a quick pause or micromanagement. The game also features many destructible objects (including buildings) for you to knock down, pick up, wield as clubs, throw, blow up, etc., all the better to dispatch the enemy henchmen with. Enemy variety and the simple aesthetic of the game make this all the more enjoyable. Something that also pleasantly surprised me (although I could just be bad) is that the game is fairly challenging, and a few moves can mean the difference between failure and success. It's not particularly brutal or anything, but it's not exactly a breeze, which is nice.
The game is structured in different missions (complete with a comic book cover loading screen, but with modern systems you might not have time to appreciate them), with several usually spanning a certain villian, before their inevitable demise. Between these missions, you have several different options to upgrade your heroes using experience you accumulate during the missions, as well as hire new heroes with a 'currency' called prestige which you gain from completing objectives. The most enjoyable part about this is that the game also includes a hero editor, wherein you can create your own superhero, and you may then hire them using prestige to play them in your campaign, though this isn't necessary to complete the game by any means.
As for the Steam version, I did have a bug when I attempted to play the game, in which the default left click action is set to attack and cannot be changed (on the forums this is sometimes called the 'Fist Bug' if you need help), meaning you can't click to move (though you may still move and use other actions using the right click command interface). For me, this was fixed by verifying the cache, but this may not work for everyone. (EDIT: If this did work and you have the issue once again, I found you need to verify the cache each time you launch the game. It's a bit annoying, but it only takes a few seconds. However, I personally need to redownload a 24 KB file (though this does happen automatically and quickly after hitting the Verify Game Cache button in the preferences), so if constant internet connectivity is a problem, be warned.) Keep in mind this game is over ten years old now, and you will likely have some compatability issues. From the sound of it, most can be fixed, but do be warned.
Overall, I found it a fun little romp through a comic book world, and I highly recommend it if it sounds remotely interesting. You can pick up both this game and its sequel in a bundle for the same price as one, so why not try both? (EDIT January 1st, 2016: During this winter sale, it appears the bundle with both games is now about 40 cents more (unsure of other regions). Still, it's incredibly close.)
EDIT: If this isn't enough, John "TotalBiscuit" Bain recently called this game "f***ing great" on the December 17th episode of the Co-Optional Podcast.

This version of the game is EXTREMELY buggy for me. It's because of Windows 7 Professional.
I had to do the following.
Find the FF.exe file in the game folder, right click it, go to properties, compatibility tab,
1. check the box that says "run in compatability mode" , in the pull down menu select "Win95"
2. check to box to disable visual desktop
3. check to box to disable desktop composition
4. check run as administrator (!!!)
5. click the OK button
6. Now right click on the STEAM shortcut on your desktop that launches STEAM (not the game shortcut.
7. right click it, go to properties, compatibility tab.
8. check the box that says
"run in compatability mode" , in the pull down menu select "XP service pack 3".
9. click the OK button
*IMPORTANT*. EXIT steam, make sure you right click close steam thats is still running on your system tray or the changes won't take affect.
Now when you launch steam it will be in xp compatibilty mode, which will allow you to launch freedom force in win 95 mode to play the game without the fist bug on newer video cards / newer OSes.

The main reason I cannot recommend this game is that the Steam version is buggy.  It took me a long time to find a partial solution to the cursor (fist) bug.  The solution I found does not work all the time; when the Steam client is open, the cursor bug comes back.  Lauching the game frequently automatically launches the Steam client, something I have not been able to prevent.  Perhaps I am wrong about the cause of the bug, but the point is that after hours of reading and experimenting with solutions, it still takes several game re-starts to get the game working without the cursor bug.
The character editing tool that comes with the game just flat out does not work on the Steam version.  Again I have read extensively for fixes and tried many things, but nothing works.  The game is playable without the character editing tool.  However, part of the appeal of a game like this is making one's own characters for campaign play, and that is a part of the game I cannot experience because the character editing tool does not work.
The bugs are a shame, because it seems like a fun game.  The gameplay and mechanics were well-done, and the interface is easy to learn.  I do have one major complaint with the camera, in that it is hard to control the camera rotation feature.  That makes some maps frustrating to play, when I need the camera at a different angle to get a clear view of what I want to see.
Since I have already bought the game, I intend to try to finish the campaign mode, so I will probably play it a bit more.  However, had I known about the bugs, I would not have bought it even at the sale price.  (Or perhaps I would have researched to find whether I could buy a more functional version elsewhere.)  Hopefully the sequel game (Freedom Force v. the Third Reich) will be more functional.

Yes, I recommend this game, but that comes with a whole lot of small font at the bottom of the page. I think that should be brought out immediately to avoid any dissapointment, which is why I'll start by giving the cons of this game. Of course, it's a short piece of work, so there isn't exactly a list for pros vs cons.
But first, to describe what this game is. Another World is a cinematic platformer along the lines of Abe's Oddysee, though not as long and with a much different structure. The game constantly switches between cutscenes and gameplay, and perhaps mixes the two frequently.
The number one problem with this game is, sadly, the gameplay. The controls are the main frustration. I kind of wish that they'd polished them for this edition. And admittedly, they kind of did. Before I found out this was on steam, I was going to try this on an emulator. The controls were so screwed over there that you couldn't jump as long as you were holding down the action key and the left. They fixed that here, but it can still get finnicky. Even for a DOS game, I find it unreasonable that there be one general action button for both running and attacking. This means that if you have to kill an enemy on the run, you have to flat out stop running (and be sure that you stop by letting go of the direction key, not the action key, or else you won't shoot immediately.
However, even with the control polished up, there's also the puzzle design. There's combat too, but I see it as a puzzle in of itself, since, typically, a puzzle will inolve the player dying over and over again. This is usually the result of guards practically being in every other room. Some will even shoot you the second you step inside. This is counter-acted with check points that are basically fifty yards apart. And here's a tip; if a check point seems to be sending you back a considerable distance, then that probably means you missed something that creates a path further down the very short line. It might seem at first that there are multiple ways you can reach your goal, but trust me, you'll have to visit every screen at least once. And you figure out why through trial and error. Not that trial and error is always bad, but it goes a little to far here. The player character does different actions based on what situation he's in. Pressing down while running won't make you combat roll anywhere besides that one patch of ground where your gun falls that one time. This made me feel that I was missing a specific action in one segment where I was stuck for over an hour before having to look at a walkthrough, which always makes me personally feel ashamed bad design or not. Which leads me to tip number two: don't overthink it.
But if you can handle frustration as if you have the ability to smash bricks with your head, then there are things to enjoy about this classic. Mainly the plot, which is completely told through imagery and gameplay, as frustrating as it is. I mentioned cutscenes earlier, but they're mostly so quick and abrupt that they are practically seemless. And the pacing is spot on. The alien place you end up in seems to go from barren wasteland to chaotic warzone over the entire course of your visit. And the graphics, especially the remastered scenery, are breathtaking.
The reason I'm recommending this game is the same reason I'd recommend a classic novel like, say, Don Quixote. It's a great story, but there is just so many dated phrases and lengthy tangents that it's hard to get through, the same as how Another World is an excellent interactive story littered with old fashioned DOS clunk. But if you're fine with that, then I say you should give this a go.

This is a game about solving two dimensional geometry problems. I've played the first two of three problem sets; so far the problems have required knowledge of basic geometry, but nothing beyond that (ie, no trig).
Some of the problems could be a little more clear (it's sometimes difficult to know what you can assume), but I've had a lot of fun solving these. If you don't want to solve math problems for fun, this isn't a good game for you. If, for some reason, you hate solving math problems that involve fractions, this isn't a good game for you. But if you enjoy a good mental workout, then this might be a good game for you.

I wish I could give this game an "in between" rating, instead of just yes/no. I like the concept of the game, that is, the general idea. It's a fun idea. I love geometry, and while I'm by far no "expert" in general math overall, geometry math is usually my personal forté when it comes to math. I have a deep and strong love for anything to do with geometry on any scale - 2D, 3D - or even stretching into the more theoretical dimensions beyond those.
That said, maybe it's my computer monitor... Or maybe I need to brush up... but it seems that some of the puzzles are wrong, in my eyes. Judging by what my eyes are seeing, and then choosing what I'm "pretty sure" is the right answer, but then being told it's wrong, I'm thinking that either 1.) my computer monitor is stretching the diagrams creating an illusion as to what the actual answer should be, or 2.) I'm just wrong (I will admit, that is still a remote possibility, and I'm okay with making that suggestion), or 3.) The puzzles are wrong, and need to be fixed.
In any case, to be fair, I like the concept of this game. And I really hate that there's no way to give an "in between" rating (because I would prefer to do that). In all honesty, I don't want to say completely "no". But rather, I hope that the developer can find ways to improve on this game, which is, in all respects, a fun concept in general that could be improved with work.

Interesting game and the whole Arkham series overall with a really smart combat, similar to the Devil May Cry series' combat which basically means the better the player the better the combat becomes.
You can pull off insane moves varying from stealth knockouts, to explosion takeouts or to thug group wipes using your fists.
For me this combat is a solid 10/10 even though I was not particularly skilled at it, but to experience the full depth of it you have to see the videos in youtube
.
This is not so much an "action only combat" like for example in Kindoms of Amalur:Reckoning, but rather "smart play" and in a way "inventing" your own combos and follow-ups. It also combines in a lot of Stealth.
Mentioning Stealth it's time to list my problems with this series and why I didn't finish them and instead casually enjoyed  watching them from the above linked youtube videos. This game requires a ton of Stealth, a ton of patience and a lot of investigating and searching. You have to constantly repeat "avoid detection" missions, find hidden clues and entrances and complete fights without using brute force. As I said... smart play
You also have to constantly open your Navigator (unless you are the dude playing in these videos) to find out where you have to go and all these things make playing this game REALLY taxing after work. For me at least, this was not the game to enjoy at night after 8 hours of work... but rather the opposite, it made me feel like I was back at work.
So yes in the end, I do recommend playing this game and the whole series, but if just like me you find them more exhausting than enjoyable, then by all means watch the video-series here
and enjoy them from a literally "robot" like flawless player.

But, and there's a big but here. The fact that the game is fun to play, feeling like a kind of simulated game of the pen and paper game, Rogue Trader. With complex, but accessible systems. Makes that recommendation go from a shakey, "If you like watching games develop," recommendation. To a, "Buy this game, the price point is right for an Early Access game, and has good core gameplay, and has active developers,"
Overall, my only complaints are thus,
The UI needs a usability pass.
-Things in the character creation that make no sense. If attributes start at an amount and you cannot lower them below that amount, why does the bar start mid way through?
-Why not use those bars on the skills screen instead to unify the aesthetic.
-The Contacts screen could be clearer on what exactly each contact does, maybe a seperate panel on the right side of the screen giving you a breakdown of each thing a contact offers when you click on them.
I could go on and if I continue to play this game, I just might go on, but in a seperate forum thread. But the long of it is above and the short of it.
Super fun, super accessibly complex, lots of variety in gameplay, lots of choices to make, shakey UI, with a dev team that is amazing so far. I may update this review in the future. Again if I keep playing this game. Which I might, because it scratches an itch very few games manage to scratch.

Full disclosure, I am a backer at the basic tier of $25 USD.
With that said, I'm proud to be a backer (for once)!  To be honest, while I backed it because it looked very interesting, I wasn't sure how much I'd enjoy it personally.  I've never been great at sidescrolling fighters like Dust, and while I do enjoy puzzle games I wasn't sure how it would work with the actual cooking, but I was pleasantly surprised.
Neither aspect is especially challenging, at least not in my opinion.  Hard enough that caution and skill is warranted, but easy enough as to not be inaccessible to most players.  It took me a couple fights to get the hang of the combat system, but I quickly got into the flow and was moving with a great deal more grace than expected.  Similarly, how the cooking works also takes a couple battles to get used to, but is intuitive once you get into it.
The cooking really comes into its own later on, as new gem types are introduced and careful planning of the variety of cookware, using multiple pieces of cookware at once, and adding ingredients at the right time becomes highly rewarding.  It makes the daily cooking challenges an actual test of skill.
Unfortunately, the combat never really evolves beyond its starting point.  There are three stages, each with a dozen or so monsters and a few harvestable ingredients, and they spawn in the same place every time.  The game tries to make combat more challenging later on, but it doesn't really succeed, so if you're looking for a good fighting challenge you aught to look elsewhere.
The soundtrack is definitely a treat to listen to; it's clear that great care went into it to make the audio fit both the mood of your task and the feel of the scene.  My favorite is The Chef's Resolve.  That said, there's not much of it; there are 30 songs, a good deal falling under 1 minute and 50 seconds.  Taking out the 30-seconds-or-less fanfares and jingles, there's about 55 minutes of audio there.  I can't recommend buying the soundtrack unheard; play the game and see if you like it first, or wait for it to go on.
As for the writing, I was amazed.  I hadn't closely been following the updates, so I expected "Story Mode" to be a basic premise to frame you fighting seven random people followed by a boss, but the game is significantly deeper than that.  There's complex intrigue, drama, and heartwarming moments, and they all feel natural in how they come about.  The tone expertly mixes a bit of silliness (expect a lot of food puns) and grandiose characters with a serious world with real problems.  In a lesser game, the tone would clash and detract from the other.  However, befitting a game about combat and expert cooking, the two blend together to make a compelling world that feels neither dreary nor absurd.
Finally, I do a couple other issues.  It'd be really nice if we could have a "Quick Battle" feature, where you can choose your loadout.  Possibly the judge(s), location, and/or theme ingredient, too.  As it stands, when you finish the game, you're stuck replaying the very challenging final fight or starting a new game from scratch.  Alternatively, there's the daily cooking battles, but everything in there is pre-set; there's no real way to hone your skills or just have a casual battle for fun.  It would also be nice if we could use the non-competition practice mode to practice in all the stages, not just the first one.

By far the game most often played in my library. You will start your first season with your favorite team. You will probably play 10-15 seasons learning the ropes, and then you will either start over with your team or a new one. Then you will start a new game with a fantasy draft. Eventually you will find the historical roster and draft files at the front office football community. Finally, you will work up the nerve to join a multi-player league.
My point here is that if you are a football fan and love the idea of running a team, this game will suck you in. there are numbers to crunch everywhere, and options galore. On top of that, there is a community that has been around for close to 15 years standing by to help you.

I'd played this game for many years before it migrated to Steam. It's a game designed for the consummate geek: a text-based simulation that gives you the ability to micromanage a football team. There are no graphics to speak up and, beware, the interface and looks are kind of ugly. A true geek, however, doesn't care about any of that, and you'll find that the game engine is very deep and impossible to quite figure out, as the interplay of elements is so mysteriously woven with chance and there are so very many of them in the first place. FOF is an art as much as a science.
At first the game is fascinating in SP, but eventually you will find your way to MP because it's really the only way to play. The SP game-engine is challenging but only to a certain degree. An MP league, however, gives you a shot at a deeply immersive experience along with regular yet powerful doses of excitement. Imagine simulating an entire season over the course of three months, at a leisurely pace of one stage a day -less during the regular season: maybe just two or three games a week (different leagues follow different rhythms, simming as fast as one season a week, and you can join as many as you can handle). Imagine a live draft -thanks to Wheels' third party browser app- with hard time limits and all the excitement of the blockbuster trades and the pick-by-pick analysis of the local Mayocks in the chat room -a little hangout not unlike watching NFL network. The suspense of training camp as you wait for the verdict on the players you drafted, the development of young players, and the decline of veterans. The chess game of game-planning against human players during the regular season. The drama of the playoffs. The fun team reports written by dedicated owners and posted in the web forums. And all in a friendly atmosphere of camaraderie. There is no bullying in MP leagues, and shy owners can keep a low profile if they wish. A bit of banter, sure, but well within the limits of good taste (I suspect there's a very healthy age distribution among GMs). Besides, there is no such a thing as a player who always wins so the best players know better than to be arrogant.
As to the details of game play, well, you can sign coaches, franchise players, renegotiate contracts, sign free agents, change positions and weight, training camp emphasis, choose formations, coverages, defensive fronts, blitzes (and who and how many you send), tendencies (run/pass), pass-protection schemes, depth of routes, personnel by formation, make adjustments to tendencies by score and time remaining, define playing time, and so on, and in SP you can also call the plays if you wish. And of course, you can study as many stats as you can handle. However, there are elements to watching the games “live” that you will not find in the scoreboard -the equivalent of watching film- so that's a must for the dedicated GM. Finally, the cap is a serious issue in the latest version, so you will have to be very careful with the team finances. If you like, you can focus only on either roster building or game-planning and let the AI handle the rest.
There you have it. In conclusion, I'd say this is one of those cult games: either you hate it or you love it forever. And hopefully after reading this review you'll be closer to knowing which.

Though I can't decide on a title, I'm sure Pythagoras would be rolling over in his grave if he knew of the abuse of his principles here. I would argue with the maths, but you can't argue with someone who keeps changing the rules. The puzzles are inconsistent, incongruent, and irreverant. >:-[ It's like playing cards with some one who is making up the rules as you go. Of course many of the inconsistencies are intentional, like with the incorrect dimensions. Then there are the errors sprinkled in like salt, the fact that you can accurately assume the answer to many with no math, and the puzzles which contradict the designer's own rules. Oh, and what about the one with no question? 3.7 has no unknown to solve. [/]
I will concur that the puzzles are intended to be "recreational maths." They are also deliberately represented by incorrect dimensions in drawing, presumably to force you to use the numbers. It doesn't always work, as in the case of 3.17, which is pretty obvious in a way that violates the game's design rules. And, 3.18 has glaring inconsistencies.  [/]
In defense of the designer, the game appears to be incomplete. I think he is still trying to "polish it up" a bit, from what I read in his answers on the forum. But, IMHO, that would be a bit like rearranging chairs on a ship that's sinking. My suggestion would be to come up with a way to represent the math without the shapes being drawn incorrectly, for one. But, then again, the answers are multiple choice and you are bound to get it right. [/]
Though it's an easy 100% game I can't recommend it. I mean, there are better puzzles out there... and better designers who would take this great subject matter and make it work. But, hey... kudos for the great idea! [/]
***Update:
I had a second look at the game, afterwhat appears to be an update. I did not see any of the problems I mentioned changed in any way. My opinion of the game itself remains unchanged. I really do love Math puzzlers. And, I can recommend Two Digits, Three Digits, (which I'm still trying to beat) and Energy Balance if you're looking for great Math Puzzles.
But, I noticed recently that cards were added, and I have to add that the artwork is great. The backgrounds are great Math art and I'm using one on my profile now. If you are just looking for some neat Math art... here it is! The cards and emoticons are geometry shapes. But, the backgrounds are neat patterns and Math equations with a blackboard look. The profile badges have images of famous Greek Mathemations. If you're into art the cards are for you.

Starting this game I was immediately skeptical. The first Costume Quest held a special place in my heart. It's sequel had a lot to live up to.
From the get-go I was not impressed. The game's storyline seemed loaded, time-travel - really? Despite the graphics retaining their similarity with the original there was a lot of added 'detail', it felt cluttered. To top it all off the fighting mechanics had changed. From playing the original to this in a short span of time, the altered fighting style was jarring and uncomfortable.
But the costumed kids had provided me such joy in the past, I gave the game the benefit of the doubt and stuck with it.
After some groaning and grousing. Some frowning and some grumbling. The storyline began to unfold. Familiar faces resurfaced and a smile was gracing my lips. The world you explored had deepened, the hidden bonuses for exploring were genuinely rewarding. The battle system, especially as it expanded became just as enjoyable, if not more enjoyable than the original.
By the end I was thoroughly satisfied! The antagonist was a great blend of bizarre and entertaining and entirely appropriate for the game's Halloween-themed setting and the cotumes were, as always, fantastic to see in battle-form. (Of particular note was Jefferson's 'Declaration of Destruction.') The strengths and weaknesses mechanic was also a nice detail and the ability to upgrade your costumes, which in turn, changed their appearance, was kind of awesome.
Unfortunately, the game felt much easier this time around. Much more forgiving, especially later on in the game. The water fountains were never an issue, as you could eat candy on-the-go to keep your health in check. I didn't use the cards a single time, only after I had finished the game to farm the achievement. The only tedium I found was exploring the little overworld's your character's traverse, as the maps were almost entirely useless and a few secrets and a hiding kid or two drove my patience to it's limit.
Nevertheless, I would highly suggest this game for it's charm, maybe not at full price, mine was bought at a discount, but for the original I shelled out the full price, here and on my old ps3. It provided me with quite a few hours of enjoyment, it is an exceptional sequel and I would definitely buy another installment. I've always had a soft spot for Halloween. :)

The game isn't polished in any area, but it has potential.  Trese Brothers has a long history of updating their games well after release, so I fully expect they will continue to work on it until that potential has been realized.
If you rage at rogue-like games where a couple bad decisions or random events could cause a death-spiral, then this is probably also not the game for you.  (Save-scumming is possible with a little technical know-how, but there's no manual saving as I write this.)
There are legitimate complaints that there can be an annoying mixture of hidden complexity, purely random outcomes, and a lack of options/control.  (Complaints that the developer actively listens to and  engages in fruitful discussions.)
But if you're looking for a single-player, moderately open-world, turn-based space adventure game, you're in luck.  If you'd like to help influence the development of such a game, now would be the time to get it and join in.
The original Star Traders on Android was my first and deepest experience with Trese Brothers.  I've bought every game of theirs since, either on Google Play or Steam.  I did it because I believe they needed rewarded for the sheer commitment they show to their games.  That original Star Traders game?  It's
getting updates, even years later as they work on the sequel.
Unfortunately, Trese Brothers games were in a sort of awkward place for me--too involved to be a "play it for 10 minutes every other week" mobile game, but not involving enough to compete with "real games" on the PC.
ST:F changes that for me.  Even in this early version, I see the game as a worthy addition to my Steam list and it's rapidly climbing my game list in terms of time spent playing.
Just create a character and go.  You start out with a ship (including crew) and get introduced to the game's storyline.  Run with that story or completely ignore it and go do whatever you want to do.  You can be a simple trader, a privateer, a hired gun, a military officer, an explorer, a spy, or any mixture of the above.
Just be prepared:  Probably at least 1/3 of the galaxy will end up hating you.  Most missions are going to be against a faction (who aren't going to appreciate it).  Selling goods could cause someone to hate you.    Hell, just passing by a ship can cause you to lose a little bit of reputation.
You are not alone in flying through space.  Your ship has a crew and officers.  Your crew level up as you do things and can gain "talents" which are special abilities such as saves for certain bad conditions, special attacks, and the like.  Each crewmember has their own traits and morale.  Too many bad things happening at once or just continued neglect (such as not paying them) may cause a crewmember leave--or, if enough of the crew becomes demoralized, you could literally have a mutiny on your hands.
The overworld portion is definitely the highlight for now:  Flying through space (with the game tossing dice in the background to see if you pass skill checks).  Landing on planets.  Managing your ship/crew.  Maybe a little trading.  Talking to contacts to get services and missions.
Contacts are a key addition over the original mobile game.  They are your interface with a given faction.  If you don't have a contact with an associated faction, you can't get missions, get ranks/permits, or even pay to absolve your transgressions.  Getting in good with a contact generally gets you better/more of what they offer.
There are a few different mission types, but most are the usual fetch/carry quest or kill/capture something quest.  There are some special-purpose quests like "spy on someone" or "explore this unpopulated area/planet".  Again, usually a mission will gain you reputation with the issuing faction (as well as the contact), but at the cost of reputation of another.
Missions lead to what is probably the weaker elements of the game at this early stage.
Exploring, patrolling, and spying all use "cards".  You're shown five result cards.  You press a button and four cards slowly disappear.  The remaining card is your result.  The result may trigger a battle or a save roll.  Some crew talents let you modify the cards before pressing the button, but that's it really.  The process has all the strategy of pulling the arm of a slot machine.
Ship battles offer a little more in the area of strategy.  Each turn you can decide if you want to advance/retreat, then what weapons to use, and finally if you want to activate any crew talents.  Both sides execute their selected actions.  Rinse and repeat until one ship escapes or is destroyed/disabled.  The only variation is the ability to send a boarding crew, which takes us to crew combat…
If you've played Darkest Dungeon, you know the basics of crew combat--4v4 turn-based battles where individuals have special abilities, usually tied to party position.  It's the most strategic of the "doing stuff" part of the game.  It could use some more depth, but it is the most interactive component in the game at the moment.
So, the game isn't the best thing ever made, but it also was just released in Early Access.  It's also being actively worked on by a pair of guys who are personally invested in every one of their games and listen to their customers.  I paid double the current asking price in the Kickstarter and I feel I've already gotten my money's worth.

A critical look at my "first" impressions of my new favorite game: Battle Chef Brigade
It's not often any more that I will become so engrossed in a game that I will skip a full hour and a half over my bed time without realizing what time it is. The blend of action combat, clever puzzle design, and engrossing time management brought me fully into the world of the Battle Chefs. It's a frequent problem with game designers that they cannot stop analyzing a game, and they start to lose the raw passion they had for playing games that made them want to enter the field in the first place. With this game, I enjoy it so much my inner critic is over shouted by raw exhilaration.
That being said, Now that I've stepped back, had a night's rest (and a quick round of Battle Chef Brigade before work...) I want to actually take a step back and do that analysis. So, cards on the table, I played the hell out of the beta when they released it, so my impressions weren't completely blind going into the full version.
In Battle Chef Brigade, you're making anywhere from 1 to 3 dishes for judges with different tastes and desires out of monsters you murder out in the arena in the back of the kitchen, all in a time limit dictated by how many dishes you have to make. Your character gets different cookware with different abilities, new combat equipment, and cooking powers that give you special ways to complete your dishes.
First, the easy part- the hunting. Combat feels very fluid in this game, with just a ton of combos and abilities that your character brings to the field. I'm playing the game on hard mode, and combat definitely feels like a challenge. Each enemy has different attack patterns, strategies, and rewards for taking them on, so you get a good mix of opponents in each round. The field also has interesting interactions, like birds picking up food items you leave around and turning them into eggs you can pick up. The combat does a great job of feeling fluid and natural, and the hand drawn animations are gorgeous.
That being said, I do have some minor complaints about combat. Enemies, if they telegraph at all, give only a few frames to react to the attack that's about to barrel down on you. That's fine if you're fighting the smaller beasties, but fighting the dragon, for example, just feels unfair. Luckily they could fix this pretty easy by lengthening the animation juuuust a smidge between wind up and attack. Also, Mina’s Backstab ability lets you teleport behind enemies, but sometimes this is a little unpredictable- I’ve teleported up like thirty feet to hit an enemy three platforms above me before. Overall, the combat flaws I see in the game feel like minor nitpicks in an otherwise incredible system.
Now, onto the puzzle mechanics. The only things that genuinely annoyed me about the game came from the puzzle system, although these were dramatically overshadowed by how amazing the system was over all. It centers around a rotation match 3 puzzle system, where you rotate a square of four gems to get a line of 3, which condenses into an upgraded gem. There are also fascinating “breakable” gem mechanics, ovens that slowly upgrade or duplicate gems automatically over time, poison mechanics, and wildcard mechanics. They do a lot to innovate over traditional match 3 puzzle games, including, essentially, building the puzzle yourself out of the monster parts you hunt down. The system is a lot of fun to play with, and the cookware offers interesting variations that let you build your own strategy.
Now, the downsides- Some of the cookware have limitations that are not well explained. Take the poison mechanic- in the regular old dull pan, you can match three poisons together to safely remove them from your dish without harming your other ingredients. There’s also a dwarven pan that lets you match four of the same gem to promote it straight to level 3, but it doesn’t tell you that it doesn’t match poison gems at all. There are some of those finicky edge cases that the game just doesn’t have, which feel unfair the first time you run across it. Ultimately though, you roll your eyes, add that quirk to your understanding of the game, and then it’s not a problem any more.
Also, you can totally screw yourself over with lack of care when it comes to picking your cookware, but resetting/rematching a game does not let you re-pick your equipment. To avoid this, just make sure you have the dull pan or the combo pan on you at all times until you fully understand how the tools work. Also, a practice mode can help you smooth out the edges in how the tools work.
Despite the minor troubles I had with those edge cases, though, I enjoyed this match three game more than I ever thought I would. It’s been the only game like it that I’ve loved, spare only Puzzle Quest 1. If you’re not a puzzle game enthusiast, don’t let that deter you from trying this game out.
The concept is a fascinating one, but funny enough, it’s kind of hard to sell people on with just an elevator pitch. I find myself saying “Trust me, it’s a million times better than the concept suggests.” more frequently than I thought I would. The timing of making your dish is definitely what ties this whole concept together, and elements of both the puzzle and combat system play nicely into creating a rich and unified game, which was way more complimentary than it has any right to be.
The monster and veggie respawn rate is set perfectly so that you never lack for something to fight. At the same time, you can’t just hunt the same monster for two minutes straight, you have to wait for the proper respawns. In cooking, the different ovens allow you to do some minor puzzling, and set it to bake for a while, incentivizing a blend of both hunting and cooking over time, rather than just doing all the hunting and then all the cooking. I was worried it would be very easy to figure out the fastest route to any particular dish, but the design’s combination of its hunting and cooking makes each variety a challenge.
Overall, this game is a fantastic title, and despite a few flaws here and there, it might well be my favorite game in recent memory. For $20 on Steam and Switch, it’s worth the price and more. Anyway, thanks for reading!

I'm relatively new to this game in that I've logged maybe 50 single player seasons and I'm just starting my first season on my first multiplayer league.  That is still noob status, as many of the people in the community have been playing for over 10 years and have simmed literally thousands of seasons.  The depth of detail in this game is incredible, and the amount of data mining the community performs in order to understand the ins and outs of player development and play calling is astounding.  If you are interested in this game do yourself a favor and look up a site called Front Office Football Central.  Browsing there will give you a hint as to what you're getting with this game.  It's definitely not a casual sports sim.  For a comparison Madden is to Front Office Football what Call of Duty is to ArmA.  If you're looking for a game that lets you pretend to be your favorite player and rack up 5,000 receiving yards in a season look elsewhere.  If you're looking for a game that forces you to debate signing veterans vs. getting rookies playing time and whether you should build a smashmouth defense oriented team or a spread offense high flying powerhouse, this might be the game for you.  You'll never get to watch your players make acrobatic leaps, but you will get to watch them develop as players and have to deal with how they form friendships and animosity between their teammates and the fans.  If you've ever had the urge to study film on your favorite team's offensive line you'll fit right in here.

PROS:
+ It's a neat idea.
+ It has VR support (which is nice if you own a VR setup)
+ It's cheap.
CONS:
- Will often start in VR mode (even if you told the game you wanted to play in non-VR mode), which leaves you completely unable to do anything, even exit the game unless you ALT F4. This isn't consistent, however, so non-VR mode might load properly once or even twice, but after that, you'll never see it again.
- The controls are a complete mess. Nothing makes sense at all. For instance, you can't go backwards or change your elevation, you can only go forward (with "W") and steer with the mouse. "D" is apparently night vision, "A" lets you land on objects, but doesn't work, and "E" is a camera that does nothing.
- There are no settings or options menu (other than choosing VR mode or non-VR mode, but that doesn't usually work either and automatically loads VR mode), so you can't change the graphics or audio at all.
- The tutorial is an empty room with the controls displayed in front of you. Basically, it's the "controls list" of a normal game's options menu. An actual tutorial, that teaches you the basics of the game doesn't exist.
- As far as I can tell, there is no way to save mid-mission, not that it really matters considering the game is practically unplayable.
VERDICT: This isn't a game, it's a cruel practical joke. As a commercial product sold on Steam, it's complete garbage. The game doesn't do a single thing right.
I dont care how cheap it is, it wouldn't be worth it if it were free. In fact, if Microspy weren't as cheap as it is, I'd request a refund, but for under $3 there's really no point.
So stay far away and never buy it unless you're a masochist or hate the person you're sending it to as a gift.

Umbrella Corps started as Capcom’s attempt at creating a competitive squad-based online shooter, and it ended up as a cheap-looking, repetitive, and desolate mess.
For a game that was supposed to rival Overwatch at its launch, Umbrella Corps manages to impress us only with its spectacular list of failures.
It is a third-person shooter with the world’s lowest field of view; a 2016 game where the animations and textures look like some indie project from 2002; and a competitive game with barely over half dozen maps (all smaller than many 2-player deathmatch arenas in Quake 1).
The list could go in infinitely, but it would be moot anyway, since the online portion of Umbrella Corps on PC died two weeks after launch.
As for the single-player part, it is a series of 24 challenges, spread across the seven available maps. These are just barebones horde mode with some flavour text, a predetermined loadout, and a mixture of three possible objectives. We can hunt for samples by killing enemies, collect five briefcases from all over the map, or hold designated spots for 10 seconds before moving along. Calling this repetitive is a mild understatement. It is boring, lazy, and can be even frustrating: ammo is often scarce by design, and some challenges want us to complete three different objectives in a row, where failing one puts us back to the very start.
Admittedly, Umbrella Corps is not the world’s worst third-person shooter, but it ranks high up there. It is now a symbol of how low Resident Evil can sink, but maybe it also represents the rock bottom the series can never reach again.

This is an extremely promising game, and even in its early access state it can suck you in. The game is somewhere between a space sim and a sandbox RPG/roguelike, and has a great deal of depth if you are willing to scratch beneath the surface.
For example; your contacts (who provide missions, equipment, etc) all have both a faction allegiance and an influence score within their faction. This means that by aiding them you can increase their influence, allowing you to become a sort of kingmaker. This level of detail is given to many of the game's features, with the result being a universe that feels much more alive than that of similar games.
Some people may be put off by the Early Access tag (understandably), but the developers are extremely active, with consistent weekly or even bi-weekly updates. They are also receptive to feedback through the discussion page, and it is very likely that the finished product will meet all the expectations of the playerbase.
In short: good game already, potential to be great, excellent developers.

Although old GTR2 is still one of the best racing sims out there.
GTR2 is based on the 2003/2004 seasons of the FIA GT Championship, and its base content includes 25 cars & 15 track locations used in those seasons. The game has nice graphics, good sounds, handling of cars is very good, precise & intuitive, controller support is good, and there's lots of mod content available.
Graphics can be slightly better than rFactor depending on the mod/track used, and replays generally look better than rFactor. The game only requires 512MB of video memory when run on the highest settings, so even if you have an old PC you should be able to get good graphics in this game.
Controller support for Xbox360 controller is pretty good, the default controller settings work well, require precise inputs without being frustrating.
Gameplay is very good, there's driving school, 24hr races, championships, or you can simply create custom race weekends with cars & track of your choice, being able to restrict AI to use only specific cars instead of allowing all base cars can make races more interesting imo. There's also weather & time change in all tracks, both of which increase the challenge and make races even more interesting.
Base content might seem kind of slim with only 25 cars & 15 track locations, but mods more than make up for it. GTR2 has a lot of mod content (not as much as rFactor, though), there's lots of tracks & cars that can be found on the internet, and the large amount of mod content combined with the excellent gameplay can provide lots of replay value.
I bought Race 07 before buying GTR 2 thinking Race 07 might be better than GTR 2 because of the larger amount of base content. Race 07 is a great game imo, but I think overall GTR2 is better, better gameplay, better car handling & controller support, more mod content, more replay value. Even if you already have Race 07 GTR2 is still worth buying.
GTR2 imo is a must have for fans of sim racing, great gameplay, low price, lots of mods, and it can run fine even on old PCs. Highly recommended.

After training camp you find out he cant throw the ball over 20 yards without hitting a defender, change the coach's scheme to play the short game. Dump off passes will go to your RB more often, learning your RB has stone hands become evident. It all snowballs based off your little designs.
You have the chance to truly find gems in the draft. Snagging a DE and successfully converting him to a 3-4 OLB is a very nice feeling. Injuries are only as accurate as what your staff tells you. If your strength coach is a "special" guy, he may green light a minor injury that costs a player his leg. I've had a guy listed on the injury report for optomology (sp?), the amount of detail the guy put in to making this game is more vast than anything we collectively could have imagined.
The true beauty of this game is finding a multiplier league that has a good commissioner. I just completed my first 32 team draft this morning and I was glued to the damn computer. Anxiously waiting to see if the guy I really wanted would fall to me or not. Thinking you found a gem and having someone else pick them before you. I can't stop playing this game. This game is probably the best Football(American Football) sim I've come across, but it does come with some flaws as well.
If you don't know what you're getting yourself into, it's a text based game that is focused on statistics(and does this game ever track them).
The good parts of this game is that is when I've ran statistical sims without giving much attention to rosters for testing purposes, the game does provide pretty accurate data that corrensponds with the players rating, the teams rating and other factors such as personality, coaching etc.  This exceeded my expectations on how the game would compile stats.  The game doesn't allow for too many lopsided trades to load teams up(note you also have a salary cap to deal with), but if you really try hard you can fleece the AI(but what fun is that?).  Aside from being the General Manager, you are able to coach your team, set your depth charts, and run 100's of different plays.  It's not too complex, and it's very enjoyable(remember, this is a text based sports sim, not Madden).
My biggest gripe is the user interface.  The UI is so outdated(it's something you'd expect out of a game created 20 years ago).  It makes navigating really difficult, and it's unsightly compared to other sports sims.  Back to the navigation, is that it's very clunky, the menus aren't well organized(I attribute this to the clunky feeling of the UI).  If the UI was ever improved, this game would be a hit amongst sim enthusiats.  The UI also makes this game very unfriendly to new players, not just to this game, but those making this their first sim they've tried.  There is no tutorial, there is no glossary for stat abbreviations (or the reason they're tracked).
I'm a little harsh on the negative aspect, but once you get used the UI and if you have prior knowledge of Football, the game is quite a bit of fun.  While it's not a 10/10, I'd give the game a solid 8/10, and I recommend it with a little caution as there is a bit of a learning curve.

This game is so deep!  If you have ever wanted to sit in the drivers seat of an NFL franchise, this is your chance.  FOF7 is franchise mode in Madden - on steroids. The only knock is that the interface looks dated.  In future versions, if the interface catches up to the level of gameplay FOF will be a 10 out of 10.
For now, I'd rate it a solid 8.

I am one of those who love and played this game back in the 90's. What I remember is that this game was very ahead of its time in certain ways. It was totally unique, though the graphics were somewhat outdated, the type of cynamatic quality it had made it totally interesting. I highly recommend that if you have purchased this game, you check out the bonus video that goes into a bit of interview of how this game was created. I enjoyed the insight and the history behind the game which helped me appreciate it even more.
The game play is designed for a much older system at the time (Amiga if I remember correctly), though it seemed to port well to dos and many gaming systems at the time. The original I believe was designed around a joystick and two buttons which really limited the type of actions you could do. This game like many others has you depend on timing and pattern recognition. It can make the game difficult at times, but I would say the remake is actually much easier than the original. The original was more arcade style, where you were not able to save or automatically keep track of points in the game. Everytime you died that game would give you a code that would be a save marker to that point in the game. Also like many games in the 90's, you could expect to die a lot. It is mostly trial and error which can really frustrate people. Battle is all about timing your shots and shielding right, while also memorizing how your enemies attacked from the last time you died. Its tricky, but also provides a lot of personal satisfaction when done right.
I kept my game with the remake graphics and sounds just to see and experience the new touch. Everything seems to feel the same, especially when using a gamepad. Switching back to classic is fun too. But the remake does make things feel a bit new. I also have not experienced any crashing like some others have mentioned. My first session of the game I was able to accomplish 3/4th of the game in one sitting. I got tired or I would have finished it without a single crash. This also was a sign to me that things felt original and it didnt take me too long to get right back in to the rhythm of the game. I had to relearn many things but overall I could remember the basic points. The game is not all that long once you know what your doing.
I recommend this game if you are familiar with this type of retro gameplay style. It probably isnt for everyone, but this game is definitely significant to my life and childhood. Nice to have it in my steam library.

is an okay puzzle game that I seem to remember being free on Newgrounds at some point. Which is where it belongs, really, seeing how it's so short that you'll complete a non-Nightmare playthrough in less than an hour.
I think some people will appreciate the surreal aesthetics of the game. I, unfortunately, don't; I think that as a straightforward Twin Peaks/Dali/Magritte/M. C. Escher knock-off,
lacks any semblance of creativity. It's not even heavily inspired, it just plainly throws apples, bowler hats, backwards speech, and liquid clocks your way. Just llifting someone else's ideas may not necessarily be illegal, but it definitely is distasteful.
The puzzles are too few, and they underutilize the game's mechanics. Only a few of them use the impossible architecture; only one forced you to kill the sleeper at least once. For the most part the game feels like a tutorial that ends as soon as things become interesting.
Still, it does have a bunch of interesting ideas. You have to use both tactical thinking and speed, since the sleeper walks in real time, and some puzzles require sleuth of hand. There's a number of different ways to deal with enemies. And the core mechanic—the sleeper always turning clockwise when he collides with something—strongly reinforces the game's core themes (the feeling of being hypnotized and time passing).
I gave
a thumbs up as a gesture of appreciation: the developer was kind enough to give it away for free to promote their new game. And I did get 10-15 minutes of fun from its more intricate puzzles.
But do be warned that 10-15 minutes is all the fun it has.

This is a decent follow up to the first Costume Quest that I would recommend to anyone who loved the first one, although it doesn't add a
to the game. So I would play this game with the "Hardcorn Mode" achievement in mind, because the last game did somewhat better at not just favoring the player in most battles.
Pros:
Graphics are slightly better. "Hardcorn Mode" achievement is a genuine challenge. Level depth seems better. Power up attacks and counter attacks (learned later in game) are welcome additions.  Variety among costumes, their abilities, focuses, and purchaseable upgrades. Candy wasn't so plentiful like the first game that I naturally had enough candy by the end to buy all creepy treats - A welcome challenge.  Maps are nice, and their counters for costume pieces & secrets are very helpful tips.
Cons:
New additions to the game make it way easier outside of Hardcorn Mode. Time travel story is a little more convoluted than the story from the first game.  Creepy treats are now special attacks, and they're either consumables or attacks you can reuse after a certain number of battles (can't spell "Con" without convoluted).  Maps cost way less than creepy treats.  A faint dark translucent horizontal line appeared on most levels throughout the game when navigating on foot - Does not appear in any other game of mine.  Battles almost always feel in favor of player unless playing "hardcorn mode" but that feels like forced balancing.
10/10, lots of fun, a worthy sequel to the original.

Ever wonder what it would have been like if Hitler perfected his saucer technology and withdrew his forces to the moon? Me neither, but I was pleasantly surprised by this game. First, I'd like to say that I got a copy for only $1.99 using a coupon I received in the Steam Market. Second, upon getting a copy I learned that the game coincides with the movie "Iron Sky". I watched the movie before beginning the game in order to get a better understanding of the plot. The first few minutes were kind of bad, but once I realized it was a comedy more than anything, I was sold. So I went into the game understanding that the plot was meant to be a joke. That aside, the flight mechanics are really good (I played using a Dual Shock 4) other than my ship got stuck on the hulls of much larger ships from time to time, but only if I actually impacted the ship, and it wasn't hard to break out of. The music gets a little repetitive as there aren't that many tracks, but I tended not to notice that too much. The game's weakest point is by far the sub-par acting of the foreign diplomats during the live-action cut-scenes (again watching the movie helps). On the other hand, the game's strongest point is assaulting the space Zeppelins and other capital ships. All-in-all if you like flight simulators, killing Nazis, and can get a copy of this on sale, then it's probably worth your time.

is a Halloween-themed role-playing game made by Double Fine in 2014.  Once on a Halloween night, there were two kids named Reynold (Ren) and Wren who were brother and sister of parents, Everett and Lucy. A dentist named Dr. White believed that all the kids in the community were telling lies to others in the true meaning of Halloween. All of us should recall, Halloween was once a holiday that was pure, holy and upright. It was a holiday that was carried out through the Roman Catholic church and the Celt tradition of Celt festivals carried out each year that is still celebrated today.
However, today, we celebrate Halloween externally as a holiday in which others dress up in costumes, some cute, others scary and yet others overly gruesome and gory. In fact, one other type of costume that has not been popularized as much is the bunny costume in which females try to dress provocatively with bunny ears, usually consisting of a low-cut top and hot pants. We also know by tradition, in popular culture, horror; zombie movies, games are appropriated to media outlets every single year.
The people that play these horror and zombie games year-round celebrate the basis behind what Halloween has been shaped into. That is, an occult holiday that serves Satan and not Christ. This is filled with irrational behaviors such as people egging others houses, the old stink bomb out of the car prank and obliterating pumpkins outside on their neighbor's porches. A very long time ago, Halloween was not celebrated this way. Instead, trick-or-treating got its start following the Catholic tradition of praying for the dearly departed once a year that was seen in purgatory, the transitional state between redemption, purification, and grace from one's final eternal state. It was pure that never included the occult.

overall is a cute game where Dr. White forces kids to give up their candy and wants to stop the tradition of Halloween. You pair up with your sister, and, your friends to try to stop Dr. White before he gains the talisman to the past. The talisman unlocks portals of time that function as a time machine, time holes that can transition you from the past to the future and, the future back towards the past.

The Repugians are monsters that were unlocked from the future that are trying to go to the past, then the present to stop Halloween. You see these Monsters at the start of the game's story. Then, the other enemy type we have, the ones you see most often within the Bayou and French Quarter are called Dr. White's Krony's. These are pointed hat, short creatures that have a dark shadow cast over them with a time clock in the center of their chest. His Krony's have taken over the city of Auburn Pines within the future. We can even call this the future-past.
Since the time transition occurred in the future that now effects the present, however, what is occurring in the present seems to change the past. That is why this categorization of it works perfectly to describe the time manipulation mechanic. That is not all, however. The main overlord behind these Krony's is a supreme overlord, Kronoculus. He has two or three forms and controls time in the game because he is Dr. White's master.
The chain of order in command of the enemies with power is Kronoculus, Dr. White, the Krony's and finally, the Repugains which are small, green monsters. That is all I can reveal for the story, enemy and character aspects to avoid any potential spoilers.

The gameplay is characterized by battles when you are trick-or-treating from house to house. Some will be adults that put candy in your bag, while many of the residents are actual Krony's. Before the combat menu pulls up, one of your characters in your party will have a cutscene; it is only a power-up animation such as in a cheap superhero movie of some sort. Now, we undergo combat. You can select which enemies you want to attack first. Thankfully, the combat is not turn-based but rather a direct line of attack. Each attack is one-on-one in other words.
Each character costume has different strengths and weaknesses. Some are weaker against the mechanic type of enemies, but more effective against monsters. Others are more vulnerable to monster attacks but effective at fighting against technical enemies, technological.

The sound is surround sound with small details that are most appreciated such as crickets chirping and animal noises in the Bayou. The battles are like
combined with
when the power up animation begins. When powering up, it shows a comic-strip narration with small catch phrases. These catch phrases reveal to you the timing and accuracy of your attacks, relative to how well your impact damage is which is factored in by the timing of the ' attack reticule' like an online game of darts hitting a bulls-eye.  You can easily dodge attacks by the timing of your resistance to impact which is also guided by this reticle feature.

Quests show costume patterns, which costume designs have been unlocked and have slots underneath; this is for when we gather new materials which only come when we have collected a full set of three material pieces that contribute to the final byproduct and creation of our new costume. Our materials are located on the left-hand side of our notebook. Costume Information, in contrast, is on the right-side. The costume information corresponds from left-to-right in our notebook to the costumes on the previous page (The left side looking from the right-hand side). In addition, vivid inscriptions have been added such as the ' candy corn.'
The candy corn is " a dollop of sugar, corn syrup and wax shaped to look like a piece of corn.” “Focus: Inaction
Combat Special: None, but looks delicious, so draws attention."
This shows us that the candy corn costume is the only one in the game that has no offensive attacks. It makes your character passive throughout every battle. Finally, our status tab shows our level; experience points (current and amount until next level), our health and our total candy we currently have.

Creepy Treat Cards are power-ups in the form of cool playing cards in the game that can increase your overall experience and rewards at the end of a battle, double your damage done to enemies, give you an extra turn and other positives and negatives for each. Some of the names on the cards are very satirical while others are more formal names that are more appropriate for the game. I find it very amusing, as a result, it is one of the few times in this game that I have smiled out in the open and laughed inside myself.

Graphics are lifelike, characters are animated, environments are well-lit. The most impressive feature of the beautiful graphics is when you go door to door trick-or-treating. Candles down the walkway to the front door light up until you leave from house to house. This instance of the candles was one of the other times I smiled and found solace in my heart knowing that Double Fine has made this Halloween memorable for me, despite my review being, only days before Halloween. The presentation rather makes the battles repetitive knowing how many Krony's you must duel and the animations do get old after a while over longer periods of time.

This gun shoots lasers and grenades. You are swarmed with hundreds of robots. Shoot them all while collecting orbs. Green orbs restore your health while red orbs give you grenades. The entire environment is destroyable too! Blow through walls with grenades and such. I do have to give bonus points to the fact that you have a body in first person. I know its a dumb thing to like in a game about mechanics but this is a highly immersive feature that even in a game like this helps and is sadly overlooked in most AAA industries. The last thing I want to mention is this game is hard. Only a few hits will kill you. This makes it so you are always moving. No time to stand still when ninja robots are hounding your♥♥♥♥♥ This is also partly where the destroyable environment comes in. It really encourages quick thinking. Get cornered? Make an escape! The game is surprisingly well optomized too. I am running around at 120 FPS at the maximum settings. With the destroyable environment and the amount of enemies on screen this is an amazing feat. The only downsides or things that I would change would be to add a proper main menu, change the hud around a bit to look more futuristic, right now the hud is kind of ugly and lastly reduce the amount of cinematic slow-mo that happens when you kill enemies. There is just way too much of it.
Would I recommend this game? Absolutely! if you are a fan of fast paced shooters and need something new this game will fill that gap. Its cheap, fun and well put together.

I completed the campaign dealing with 2 persistent issues.  Your workaround may need to differ, but for me playing on Win-7 64bit.
(1) Fist icon that won't change to move or interact:  In STEAM I deleted the local files through the LIBRARY-> GAMES menu and then reinstalled them using STEAM.  I had to do this every time before I played the game again.  "Deleting the local files" does not delete your saved games.  This worked 100% of the time...although I guess I did have to delete the game...reinstall the game...restart Windows twice.
(2) The missing NEXT prompt on the hero exp screen:  This issue was a bit more irritating.  You need to do one of two things depending on where you're at in the campaign.  In the mission summary screen there will ALWAYS be a NEXT button.  On that screen you either:   (a) save the game  (b)exit the campaign (c) load the save you just saved
OR
press NEXT and go to the exp with a NEXT button.

Great game, but needs a little configuration to get it to work in Windows 7 64-bit.
1) Find the executable "fforce.exe" in C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common\Freedom Force
2) Right-click on it and open the Properties
3) Click the Compatibility tab
4) Click the checkbox for "Run this program in compatibility mode for:", and select "Windows 98/Windows ME"
5) Click the checkbox for "Disable visual themes"
6) Click the checkbox for "Disable desktop composition"
7) Click "Apply" and click "OK"
8) Double-click the "fforce.exe" file to run the game directly, rather than going through Steam

I've never been a big fan of beat em ups or puzzle games, but everything about this one just felt... right somehow. All the soundtracks and voice acting are on point, and it has a distinct, colorful artstyle. Game mechanics are slowly introduced into the game, which was paced well.
The fighting mechanics are easy to understand and not too complex, while the cooking part, while also simple to understand, is much more challenging.
My only complaints are that this game clearly lacks a control scheme intended for mouse and keyboard, which took a while to get used to. That, and that the story, which I really enjoyed the writing and humor of, felt short. (10~ hours length)
Some people say that the combat is too easy, but I feel that extremely challenging combat was not the intention of the game design, as the point of hunting the monsters is not to defeat them, but to defeat them as quickly as possible to harvest ingredients and return to the cooking station.
Thus, eventually you'll be able to defeat all the monsters on the map quickly. The penalty for being defeated in combat seem minimal, you drop all the ingredients you're carrying and get sent back to the cooking station. This gives the illusion that the combat is too easy. However, the game integrates both the fighting and the cooking into the "duel". Being defeated costs you precious seconds of time running back to where you were to get your ingredients back, and trust me, you will need every single second you can get during a duel.
So much fun. While somewhat short, the Daily Challenges will keep your busy for a long time.

I work for a math education company, but we don't sell anything that competes with this game, so take this as an unbiased review by someone who teaches and uses math on a daily basis.
Note that my first "Pro" bullet isn't, "Can teach you something."  You will learn very little geometry or algebra or whatever doing these puzzles.  At best, you'll practice your multiplication and division skills a lot, but that's elementary.  Well, elementary school level.  So what do I mean by the game can make you smarter?
When most people think of math, they think of boring drills where they plugged numbers into formulas and and other numbers.  It's mindless busywork because the students are just grinding through procedures like an automaton.  There's little need to be creative or think on their feet.  Take a look at Problem 1.1 in the screenshots.  If a student saw this on a standardized test, they'd probably start by finding the width of the area 10 rectangle.  But, oh gawd!, now they have a fraction.  Then they have to add 2, then divide 16 by the resulting fraction.  That sounds tedious in the extreme, and I have an engineering PhD, so it's not like fractions scare me.
Now look at the solution given in the screenshots: by filling in the missing rectangle, we observe that we have two rectangles of equal size.  This is just one big rectangle cut in half, so the unknown height must equal the height of the other half.  No adding or dividing by fractions!  Rather than follow the obvious path, by being creative and considering alternative approaches (something modern math education doesn't do very well, sadly), we find a far less painful, more elegant solution.  What these puzzles do is make you better at solving problems: we have some information, and we have a problem we want to solve.  Someone with good problem solving skills can get there more quickly and easily.
That said, allow me to critique the problems in this game: Take a look at Problem 1.16 in the screenshots.  We fill in the missing rectangle as before.  We notice there are two rectangles of area 28 and 56, so right one is 2 times the width of the left, and we're done.  Now take a look at Problem 2.5 in the screenshots.  Again, the key is finding the area of hidden rectangles and looking at the ratio of areas.  A lot of puzzles in the game involving rectangles are like this, though you still have to be canny and figure out which areas and what ratios.  But there were only maybe a dozen puzzles that made me stop and say, "Ooh, that's new.  What's the best way to deal with that?"  I could have used more of those moments.
Even worse, there a couple puzzles where the solution is the unimaginative tedious method of figuring out all of the side lengths.  I'm looking at you Problems 1.18 and 2.18.  You're well past the initial training exercises and have no excuse.
Leaving the puzzles using rectangles, there are puzzles using triangles and circles, like 3.2 in the screenshots.  But they have to keep it simple since pi and geometric theorems are off-limits, so I found these problems to be pretty trivial compared to the rectangles.  Though there were a few problems where I resorted to algebra or using properties of similar triangles, which seems to violate the premise that these are puzzles that can be solved without math more sophisticated than areas and ratios.
While we're on the subject, the whole conceit of these puzzles is that there are ways to solve them without using fractions.  What we could do with Problem 1.1 is to put it in the copier and enlarge it by a factor of 3: the area 10 rectangle now has height 9 and area 90.  Now it's width is no longer a fraction.  In fact, we can now solve this puzzle the humdrum way without running into any fractions.  We could do this to every rectangle problem in the game, making them tedious but trivial to compute.
Don't do that though.  Despite my complaints that I wish there were a greater variety of ideas and fewer straightforward problems, the times when the game did make me say, "Ah!  I see!  So now this is twice that, and these two are equal, and we're done.  Cool!" was worth the $2.  These moments only happen if we accept the no fraction rule and are forced to get creative.

.
