Inquisitor is, despite the whiny reviews, an excellent game. There is some truth to the negative reviews -- it's complex, it can be difficult, it doesn't have flashy or high tech or polygonal graphics. And for all of these things it should be celebrated. It looks amazing, like a much more detailed, hand-crafted Diablo, with a beautiful and mysterious world that is fully immersive, aided by the great writing and plot.
Its difficulty is nothing severe, and when compared to a game like Baldur's Gate or Beyond Divinity is not indimidating. It is a game that rewards exploration, patience, curiosity, and most of all, an adult's attention span and reading comprehension. The gaming community is short on these qualities, so if you find that they don't describe you, you won't like this game. Nor will you like it if you've only started gaming in the last 5-10 years and expect all your games to hold your hand and to have demanding graphical qualities. This game's look is spectacular. It plays smoothly and only gets better as you progress. It recreates a medieval fantasy world with more character and beauty and intrigue than any of its peers, past and present. It carefully balances realism with the fantastical and mythical, and slowly unravels to the player a detailed, fully realized world of occult mythology and evil, with greater depth than what you'll find in Diablo, and with a more serious and immersive tone than what you'll encounter in the masterful Baldur's Gate.
The story is superior to most other isometric RPGs, and most games in general, blending a mysterious inquisitor/investigator framing around a medieval fantasy adventure that's thoughtful and compelling, putting the player in a position to drive the story and to make choices that affect how things unfold. This is one of the few gaming experiences in which one will be genuinely curious to see how the story progresses.
I've seen complaints that there's too much text in Inquisitor. This is a complaint from a generation that needs voice acting and cinematic cut scenes to convey a story, from children who can't read a book. If you can read a book this game won't seem like much. If you can't, look away.
I've also seen remarks that the game is all combat and nothing else. This is false. My first 10+ hours of the game was spent exploring, speaking with NPCs, learning history, discovering secrets, solving mysteries, trying to obtain better equipment, and fighting only when I couldn't avoid it. I in fact HUNGERED for more combat. And later, it was delivered to me. But not in some mighty, terrifying abundance like some imply.
The only way this game can be "purely combat" is if one intentionally disregards all of the NPCs and does not interact with anyone but merchants or priests, does the minimal amount of exploration needed to find a passageway or a new location, and spends all their time fighting. The thing about a good RPG is that it is largely what the player makes of it. If you are a boring, uncurious, careless gamer, you will have a bad experience with a game that doesn't guide you along a linear path and a door-to-door story.
Everything this game does it does well, despite a few imperfections or elements that could afford to be fixed. But it's in a higher class than games it is unfavorably compared to, like Diablo or Torchlight. It's an RPG for those who want a real, immersive, deep, substantial, and involved experience.

Promising and deep space-trade-combat game. Enjoyed playing it so far but for me there's a few downsides that prevent me from starting over at the moment. Part of it might be it takes time to master a game like this but I am not sure. I compare this game to Battle Brothers a few times, one of my favorite games. There are similarities.
-->  Not really a reward for all the (crew-) micromanagement.
It takes time to build your ship and especially your crew. It's not unusual to have a crew of 30+ you need to level up constantly, especially in the beginning). Since they die quickly or lose morale after a fight and quit (even if they win)  I did not grew attached to them like in Battle brothers. They are too generic at the moment. It might work with a smaller crew and a different, less harsh, morale system. The whole skill system is based on a larger crew though.
--> No sense of control
Even if you are careful not to over extend and get in difficult fights / quests early you might get a few bad fights / failed quests and lose it all very quicly. I did not feel to have any control over these circumstances (RNG). Just to make sure: I played Battle Brothers for countless hours because I always felt my actions and choices mattered despite the RNG elements.
Since it's early access I hope some of these issues are tackled. I will not go into the the Pro's at the moment but they are plenty. Definitely one of the more interesting games I played recently and look forward to the new updates. Especially the one where you have a chance to get some nice loot after crew combat ;)

Bot Colony is an ambitious title, maybe even too ambitious for what it's worth. So far, playing it is more of a struggle than entertainment...

I've said it. Natural language understanding is just not ready to be implemented in a game. It wil get you right about one time out of ten. Other then that you'll get replies like "I don't know what you mean".
Leaving Natural language understanding aside, the game is also full of bugs and glitches. Most players will give up on Bot Colony during the tutorial. Without any doubt it had some promising perspectives and with a lot of more work, time and money it could've moved the adventure genre to a whole new level, but i'm afraid that's all what's gonna be left of it since the developers already pulled the plug on Bot Colony and the servers will be dead on March 15, leaving the game unplayable.

This game was extremely ambitious in scope and had it been able to continue I'm sure it could have been really cool.  As it currently stands, the game is more of a testament to what it could be rather than anything.  Basically, the idea is that you are required to interact with robots in order to perform some rudimentary tasks like rearranging furninture.  You do this by talking to them via a microphone.
Unfortunately if you don't have a good quality mic, the voice recognition suffers.  It also takes a good bit of training to get it to really recognize your voice.  This is probably more than any normal gamer is going to want to be bothered with, however if you DO persevere, it's somewhat fascinating.  The only other game that seems to have attempted this was a game on the Dreamcast called "Seaman".
This game lacks the whimsical charm of Seaman and it's a lot more serious.  You also seem to have a lot more freedom in the way you can teach the bots to interact with you.  That's right, the bots actually learn from you.  It starts out with just a few basic commands for movement, item manipulation, and other things, and when you issue a command the bot doesn't understand, you have the option to teach it how to perform the command using a series of steps from the commands he already knows.
I think this could have been the real hook to this game.  The "plot" to the story would be a side-quest compared to just trying to teach your bot to do things with a series of basic commands. Still, at times I felt like I was wrestling with the bot to get it to perform an action, not because the bot had a lack of understanding but because the voice recognition was stubbornly refusing to hear a certain word.   For example, I'd say cushion, the game would hear "question".
As with most forms of voice recognition, it works best with the commands it expects to hear.  If you say "what is this" and click on something it invariably works.  If you have to be more detailed in your command, expect a word or two to be misheard.  Thankfully if you can't get it to understand at all, you can always type the command in directly.

Tl;dr - game has still plenty of bugs and serious balance issues, and seems to be abandoned by devs.
Oafmatch is a match 3 rpg, very similar to Puzzle Quest series. You fight by making matches which deal damage and grant mana, which is spent on various special abilities. In Oafmatch you have party of 4 characters, each of them has one special passive ability, one strong and one medium skill out of 6, which correspond to 6 gem colors, they also have two slots for equipment, which make for skills in this game.
What is good about Oafmatch is the number of available heroes and skills, there is plenty of variety, so you can experiment with various builds.
And that's mostly the end of strong points of the game.
The game offers two modes:campaign and so called roguelike mode. Campaign is pretty barebone, you just move from one dot (battle) to another on the map, sometimes you have choice to select battles or to skip some of them. There is also an arena on each map, in which you fight infinite waves of enemies, which get harder over time. Compared to Puzzle Quest or Galactrix this is very basic, because in campaigns of those games not only there was much more freedom in map movement, but also there was something to do between battles, like mining resources, gathering blueprints and crafting things in Galactrix, or capturing monsters and cities in PQ. Story is very poor even for a game which doesn't takes it's story very seriously, especially the ending is very shallow.
Second mode, which also has it's variation which you can play after the campaign is so called roguelike mode, which again is very basic - you are present with tow different battles with different rewards, and you just have to select one of them - and so until the end of game. It really could be at least a little more complicated.
The game also has massive amount of bugs and balance/design problems, and it's obvious that it neither was tested at all, or only "tested" by some streamers or tubers, to which devs gave some keys hoping they will get more sales that way, tubers recorded some videos getting their attention and money from views or when they thought the game is not interesting just probably put the testing key on everybody's favourite key site to earn few bucks anyway, and so everyone is happy and no one cares for bugs, except the people who actually paid money for this. I have played this game mostly on 1.03 version (and each of three patches have large bug lists), and I still have encountered about dozen of bugs, varying from graphic and text bugs to gamebreaking stuff like for example blank tiles on board, some equipment not dropping properly, or heroes joining fully upgraded when they are not supposed to do so. This game should still be in beta or more probably in so popular those days early access.
There are also heavy problems with balance near the end game. There is hard cap for level of your characters, which leaves you somewhere in late 2/3 of the game in situation in which you have tons of now useless gold and where enemies, especially in the arenas have higher level than you. It maybe wouldn't be so bad, but there are also another issues. Enemies come in two types, heroes which are identical to the ones you get and who can use same equipment as you and also can make matches, and a lesser type of enemies, let's call them minions, which can't make matches and have in most cases only one fixed ability, but to compensate that, they have passive mana gain every turn. They also gain additional benefits - even when you have about 20 levels more than them, they the same or higher HP as your characters, and actually higher stats than you, so when they sometimes manage to make matches thanks to their special gems, they are quite strong. In around the middle of game, a problem arises with the power of you matches - they seem to be getting weaker as the game progress, instead of being the same or stronger, and you need a lot of even 5-matches to kill single minion. So later you will be doing majority of damage with the skills, and like other reviewers say, equipment comes in ranks, and the jump from one rank to another in damage done is in many cases quite insane. Damage done by cheap 6 mana skill rank 5 skill compared to damage done by two matches needed to gather that mana is laughable. Other issue is that later enemies get very powerful skill gems, which not only sometimes can oneshot your heroes or have additional effects like long stun, they also have low mana requirements and low activation times. What is even worse is that in many cases there will two or three of the same monsters, so they will gain more mana of their colour, and they will sometimes placing their gems every turn, so the board will very quickly run out of gems of that colour, which will leave you defenseless unless you have some skill to destroy them. And some of those gems have additional lives, forcing you to match them twice or more to make things worse. Placing gems by AI takes much time, it is especially infuriating when they will gain enough mana to place something like half of dozen of them, it is faster to alt-tab the game, kill it process and to restart it and the fight that to wait for animation to end! There is also lack of balance in regards what characters game gives to you in campaign, it gives you many heroes with purple and white as their primary colour, but doesn't gives you second character with primary yellow until few fights near the end of the game. Some of heroes have also much better passive skills that others, which pretty much makes some of them mandatory. It is quite similar with items/active skills, so there is not that much actual variety.
After initial waves of patches, devs went quiet and the game seems to be abandoned, and before that they wrote that they are unable to reproduce and patch some of mentioned bugs. Game is not recommend unless you played every Puzzle Quest clone in existence and you still want more. If you didn't already, it is better to play original Puzzle Quest or some other, better of it clones.

Me at purchase time: Match-three games are so dumb. I'm only getting this because so-and-so recommended this for some dumb reason and its on sale. *grumblegrumblegrumble*
...aaaand two days later it's the most played non-multiplayer game in my Steam library.
This game is stupidly addictive. Yes, match-three games are still really lame, but this one is worth it for the dumb-yet-funny plot and the RPG stats that require actual strategy.
Only downsides for me were that it is Windows-only (which limits me to my main gaming desktop at home instead of my portable MacBook which I use everywhere), and it was actually so addictive I literally had to force myself to stop playing for a few days so I would actually do work.

On the surface this may seem like just another Match3pg, and it is. What sets this apart and above the others, though, are a few things worth mentioning.
The campaign is long and pretty fun. There is a great deal of humour here, and while I appreciate humour is subjective, to me, some of the dialogue was pretty hilarious.
It may  seem like a simple RPG-Lite, but, if you dig a bit under the surface and unlock more options you realize there is a tonne of tactical depth here. Anywhere from your team party to their equipment and potions. You can set up a lot of builds, good for those who like to tinker around to maximize their damage output or for those who just like a lot of variety.
The music is quirky and engaging enough, sometimes it sounds like something straight from a Saturday morning cartoon. Unfortunately some tunes get stuck in your head, but in an obnoxious way, like an advert jingle. The graphics are cute. Nothing amazing here but well done and fit the game. The character design is pretty good, albeit a bit generic at times. One thing I would have really liked to see is more and better special effects when you use different attacks. At most it's just a vague damage splash with -HP indicator. That hurts a bit.
Where the meat of game lies is in the Rogue-Like mode. While the campaign is fun and pretty engaging, the rogue-like mode is what gives you that replayability and that "One more game" itch.
Overall if you like Match 3 games, you'll love this as the core mechanics are simple enough to enjoy and if you like Match 3 games but love RPG games with strategic builds and/or Roguelike games, you'll love this.
Overall: I went into this thinking it'd be an okay time waster but found there was much more lurking under the surface. I'd definitely recommend this. Oh, as a bonus, or maybe I should say testimonial, darkgod of Tales of Maj E'yal fame (or infamy ;) ) is one of the creators of this game along with another guy who was a player/content creator of TOME. And some other guy I don't know.
PS: Don't judge my time played as I've been playing the DRM free mode and just recently rebought the Steam version.
Edit: What honestly baffles me is why there is no multiplayer mode. Maybe out of budget? Either way, for the massive amount of party set ups you can have, it seems it would be tailor made for PvP. It would most likely need balancing and other things, but even a decent MP mode I think would have brought in a larger consumer base.

Normally I would stay away from first-impressions, but until some major content is added in (as well as tweaks to annoying mechanics) I can't recommend you buy this game even at its low price. With some improvements and additional content, SHOWTIME could become the addicting arcade hybrid of Painkiller and Pac-Man it wants to be.
I know Unity has been heavily criticized for a lot of schlock on Steam when it's not the engine's fault. Nor am I implying that any game that uses bought assets can never make something interesting. However, and this is only speculation, the game does feel like an asset-flipped game. (For example, the cyberpunk enemies combined with the other assets like the spheres and dancing girls.)
That is the quality I would describe SHOWTIME 2073 overall. Outside of the weird sphere visuals with the rest of the game's visuals, this thought occurred to me when I booted up the game. Also it had a Unity styled launcher with settings like "Graphics: Good, Beautiful, Fantastic."
For a $1 game that focuses more on its novelty, I don't think the visuals are an issue. My problem is that it doesn't do enough with its gimmick to make something that should otherwise be addicting.
The game's general description is that it's Pac-Man with guns. That description is misleading because the game is missing many core mechanics that appeal to those types of gamers.
The biggest missing feature from Pac-Man is a scoring system. Nor are there extra lives, time-bonuses, or overpowered bonuses to one-up the enemy. Without those arcade-style features, the game feels like dull with its five same levels.
Including a scoring-system, even a basic one, would go a long way to make the gameplay more intresting. For example, if the game went for something like Bulletstorm where it focuses on flashy combination of kills it would demand more skill of the player to round up enemies for a massive score. Or if the game took a cue from Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball with its arcade style mode that gave you power-ups--and one life--it would make dying more of a punishment and the score-system more valuable.
SHOWTIME doesn't need to take all its inspiration from Pac-Man. Challenge modes with specific challenges (like with the Binding of Isaac) would also give the game immense replay value. Or maybe the game needs more than one objective to spice it up.
That aspect of the game is just one area for improvement. The other aspect, an "old school styled FPS", could also use a little more effort too.
Perhaps I'm mistaken that the game is  going for a hybrid of Pac-Man and an old-school FPS, but if the gameplay took a lot more inspiration from old-school FPS conventions it'd make the combat provide a lot more tactical options. The old-school vibe comes from having to pick up health and ammo from the ground like Wolfenstein 3D as well as how you sprint very fast and can jump quite high.
If the game wasn't going for that route, then it's not a farfetched suggestion to consider for improvement. The tactics/mechanics found in old-school FPSs for health and weapons could be applied here.
For example, you can launch yourself into the air with rockets--or when enemies hit you--but the health lost is way too high to make that viable. You can't "bunny-hop" to gain momentum to avoid some encounters but you can certainly leap over walls and enemies. Weirdly, the white-orbs do not provide any health bonuses--something I think should be added (only about 1 - 5%) to balance enemies dealing 20% damage with each hit--which would otherwise make them more important to collect.
It also goes without saying that this game could use a LOT more enemy and weapon variety. But these weapons should be gameplay changers that require a different approach with each weapon (i.e. a shotgun should be used differently than an assault rifle). Enemies should be balanced to suit these new weapons, and maybe various ammo types could be added to make sure players don't spam rockets.
The developer has stated he will be adding in more content in two week intervals. Although this game is not labeled Early Access, many of the suggestions listed on the "future updates" page and the bare-bone gameplay we have now ultimately make the game feel like you're playing one. Perhaps I'm too optimistic but I think this game will improve down the line.
As a reminder, a lot of these ideas in this review are suggestions for improvement, They are critical about what the game fails to do with its novelty: A Pac-Man FPS or an objective-based old-school shooter. Unlike some other Survival Crafting #30457 Early Access game, the core gameplay is a solid foundation and it has potential (if it's used properly).

I've never made it past the first town in Inquisitor, though I've got incredibly close on my last try: it's brutal combat and need to scoff health potions in ridiculous amounts after every single fight make it at times a grind. But having begun to play it again, I realized why I made it that far in the first place. The terrifying, austere soundtrack of a medieval world drenched in Biblical themes, coupled with the grim graphics and amazing writing which sells the world, puts you into the shoes of an Inquisitor, a person who needs to root out all forms of heresy in a world that is quickly filling up with them.
An isometric RPG, Inquisitor offers a combat system where you just click on the enemy you want to attack and it will happen. You just point, click and select dialogue options, walking around the towns and wildernesses that you encounter. Heading deep within dungeons and ancient cemeteries is easy, though the combat is not. The combat is the biggest hurdle to cross in the game, and you also need to make sure your character is specced well for the trials ahead. Be sure to check out the Guides in the Steam Community section for this game; they offer some excellent tips that the game doesn't provide to you.
An excellent story, coupled together with memorable sidequests, none of which I want to spoil. You are, or were, a criminal who escaped judgement only through becoming an Inquisitor, a member of the Church who are ruthless in their tactics. They hunt out heretics and demons wherever they might hide, and most are suspicious of everybody. Anyone you don't know could be a heretic, a sinner or harbouring a demon. There is a lengthy amount of text to get through in this game, but the way it is written means it doesn't feel like a slog at all, instead you find yourself almost reading a novel. The writing in this game is amazing, but fair warning: there's a lot of it.
Graphics are serviceable isometric RPG stuff: they carry with them the right amount of grim, medieval themes, and make you feel as though you are being drawn into the world.
Atmosphere, then, is excellent, due to the quality of the writing, graphics and lore of the world. The Biblical themes used give it a unique spin, one that I hadn't seen at the forefront of an RPG before, so I am enjoying the themes of the world used so far. It really does pull me into it.
The soundtrack often sounds as though it has just been pulled from church, or sometimes from Hell. It is a powerful soundtrack that is filled with ominous stings and thunderous organs, which is perfect for the dark themes of the game.
If you are willing to stomach some tinkering, sometimes annoying combat, drinking a lot of health potions, and a lot of reading, then you are in for an amazing journey, one I plan to continue for some time.

Battle Chef Brigade is a fusion of multiple genres, it’s a side-scrolling action game crossed with a Match 3 puzzle game and some light RPG elements. This gameplay combination works quite well; the action segments where you hunt monsters for ingredients controls smoothly and are fun and the Match 3 parts where you cook your ingredients are good too. Though fair warning if you can’t do Match 3 at a swift clip you might run into some trouble towards endgame of the campaign, I barely managed to squeak by the final boss on Normal so I don’t ever plan on playing Hard.  I’ve only run into one annoying bug, an audio bug that persisted throughout most of a match. I had to mute the game, but it corrected itself once I won the match.
The writing is quite good, mainly in that the characters are charming and they are bolstered by some real quality voice-acting. The game also has a conclusive ending too. The atmosphere is also great, it’s lively and colorful. The game’s art design is reminiscent of Miyazaki or Wakfu and it has that painting-like quality to it. The character design is quite good too, ranging from a young girl with a teapot robot, an undead necromancer with his ghost slime buddy, and a few different kinds of orc.
Battle Chef Brigade is a unique game with a lot of heart that’s definitely worth checking out.

This game is a diamond in the rough.
Do you like those games where you go from point A to point B, engaging in trade? This is a good one of those. It has more challenges than other trade-based games, which is nice, but it also lacks some of the interface (in the rough, as mentioned).
Do you like games where you can engage in piracy and the like? You can go around intimidating and killing merchants and others, but it's not going to be easy - people will go down fighting.
Do you want to be an adventurer going to wild planets and looking for resources you can't sell anywhere because they're totally illegal? Go unleash your inner Indiana Jones (and get caught in a planet-wide lightning storm that leaves half your crew demoralized).
Do you want to stealthily help out your faction win a conflict through espionage? Yup, you can do that too.
In short, there's a lot of options. However, as mentioned, this is a diamond *in the rough*. There's still a lot of improvements to be done, but it still feels like a complete game at this point - it can just become an even better game with more love and care from the devs.

This title is new to steam but to those of us who have been in sim racing for a number of years this is a true gem and classic. GTR2 is the second title from SimBin to represent the FIA GT Championship. The actual real world series that this title is based on ended in 2009 to be replaced by the FIA GT1 World Championship, which has also come to a very quick end during the 2012 racing season.
This title though harkens back to the glory days of FIA GT racing when you would have an entire field made up of a variety of super cars, such as Jaguar, Porsche, Maseratti, Lamborghini, BMW, Lister, Saleen, and many more. All racing on the track for about 3 hours at a time. This encluded driver changes, which can be done in game, plus the Proxima 24 Hours of Spa-Francorchamps! This race can even be run for the full race distance of 24 hours in game!!!
Don't think of this as a console type game, it's not. I've spent way too many hours racing here and in the various mods to even bother thinking about the Arcade mode which is available as well. Get a steering wheel and get ready for some serious racing competition.
Does the idea of racing at Circuit de Le Sarthe (more commonly know as Le Mans) for 24 hours get you going? Or would you rather race on the Daytona road course, or at Sebring, or Dubai, or Silverstone, or any number of other tracks which can be added to this title. Add to that there is a very active online raceing community still with this title and if that is your thing then this is the one for you!!!
p.s. It might be a little early for anything on steam to be up and running so you might have to look outside of the steeam community for on line racing.

I love this game. It's such a wonderful starship captain RPG game. This isn't a twitch game. All of the combat is turn-based, somewhat JRPG style. There's a lot traveling around and micro management of your ship and crew. It's a bit like Sid Meier's Pirates, but in space.
In my current save, I'm an Explorer/Spy. My ship is quite small, and I'm skilled for stealth and escape. So I'm not looking for a stand-up fights. I'm in it to prosper around the edges: gather intel, court contacts, look under rocks.
I'm having a blast with the game, even though it has some rough edges. Because it's early access, that is to be expected. But let's talk about early access here as well since, at this point, many people have likely been burned by abandoned early access projects: these devs are in the forums responding to the players, they're on a discord server responding to players, they're updating the game frequently. In short, they're awesome.
Pros:
Choose your officers and recruit a crew. Want more options in a space fight? Grab a bunch of pilots and gunners. Want a more military crew for boarding? Recruit more soldiers. Want none of that? Hire exo-scouts, merchants or spies. Your officers and crewmembers all contribute to the type of options you have at your disposal in any given situation.
A lot of character customization options for you and your officers / crew. You can choose the appearance, gender and name of every crew member. They've got their own traits, And as they level up they'll gain various talents and job skills (21 different jobs). Is one of your crew members in possession of exemplary skills and talent? Get rid of your greedy, disloyal quartermaster and promote that crewmember to officer instead!
Play it like a sandbox, or play scripted missions. If you want to run cargo back and forth to make some money, you can. If you want to explore wilderness planets or spy on a faction, you can. Of course if you want to patrol around spoiling for a fight, you can do that too. But if those things get a bit repetitive, talk to your contacts and get some quests.
There is a web of politics and intrigue to navigate as you try to earn enough to keep your crew happy and ship in one piece. When one faction likes you, the others probably don't. You're going to need places to fuel up and repair though, so managing faction relations is a major component of the game.
Procedural universe creation, in case you want a different sandbox to play in!
Cons:
It's early access, so there are some bugs. I've not encountered any crashes yet, however.
The UI isn't always friendly, but they're working on it!
There's no manual at the moment, so it may take a game or two to understand the mechanics (I just figured out what the little dots under the combat talents meant after 10 hours played...).
Neutral:
The game can be difficult at first. Playing on "Normal" is quite challenging. I haven't tried anything harder than that.
I don't see the difficulty as a pro or con as long as each player can find a level that is challenging without being excessively punishing.
Who should get this game:
Anyone who wants to run a starship around and cobble together a trusty core of officers and full crew. Anyone who likes bouncing from planet to planet, trading, doing missions, levelling up skills, random encounters, exploring, and micromanaging their ship/crew/faction relations.
Anyone like me :)

So ... I'm on the negative side of neutral here, but Binary Thumb Choice is Binary.
I genuinely had a lot of fun working through the mechanics and figuring things out - lots of
kinds of moments, and getting more competant at things for new runs had a kind of wonder for me.
At this point I think I've figured out at least 80-90% of the mechanics of this game (not mastering, just ... I know what they are), but as things are now I sadly don't think it will hold my interest. I mean, I want it to, but ...
This is one of those titles that stitches a bigger game out of a variety of smaller minigames, a method that brings
to mind for me at least, though there's no further comparison between the two titles to be made after that. In this game, it basically boils down to 5 RNG-driven minigames that you'll be rotating through to varying degrees as you progress: space travel, ship combat, crew combat, missions, and ... card flipping stuff.
I'll start on that last one - as you can see in the trailer, there's a bit where you're presented with a semi-random selection of 5 cards. You press a button and RNG decides which cards flip over and dissipate and you're left with one card that gives you a bad thing or a good thing or some combat opportunity or whatever. That's the extent of player interaction here, though: you press one button, and some cards flip over. You can try to stack this in your favor through the occasional crew ability ('remove a negative card before flipping') and (I
) maybe stack the RNG more in your favor by stacking up crew attributes, though the mechanics of such aren't clear right now (early access and all).
But even after all that: button, cards. That's the gameplay here.
And this mechanic is used
. Patrol shipping lanes? Flip some cards. Blockade a planet? Flip cards. Explore wilderness? Flip. Spy on a planet's networks? Cards. Gain access to black market? Flip some more cards.
The crew combat feels like a JRPG-lite where each character has ... one ability. You just spam attacks until things die, and the opponent does the same, and it's a spam race to see who can make the enemy dead first. To be fair, I think I'm probably missing the finer points of this system, but honestly - this stuff is
.
Ship combat is more enjoyable by far, though still fairly simplistic. You have a variety of abilities (given by your crew) that you can use per move, and you assign weapons to fire, and there's some range mechanic of sorts that determines weapon/tactic availability ... but just about all of this again comes down to RNG.
Missions, which I am straining to define as a minigame here (though I had to strain equally as much to call the card thing a 'game') boils down to basically one text choice followed by some dice rolling to determine if your choice failed or had some benefit ... maybe some ship combat or something similar happens as a result of this.
The overworld/space travel mechanic, to which I'll also tie the inter-world trading mechanics, is a mess of RNG stuff happening all at once; and once you figure out what you're supposed to be doing to manage your fuel and crew and all that, it eventually becomes a very tedious affair of repetitive clicking and decision making.
"Oh, I've traveled from point A to to point B. I land on this planet. *click* I need to buy fuel, because there is literally no reason why I would not want to do this *click click*; now I will pay my crew to prevent them murdering me *click* *click* *click* and send them on some shore leave *click* *click* oh wait I need to click like 15 times to make sure all of them do it I guess *click* *click* *click* *click* *click* *click*; some of them got sick, so I need to go to the doctor tab *click* and heal them all *click*. In the meantime, all this pay and shore leave made my guys level up, so I need to go the status tab *click* and then the crew submenu *click* and filter my crew to show leveling ones only *click* *click* and then click through every single one of them to assign new job levels and assign tasks, even for the junior crew that have a singular job path *click* *click* *click* *click* *click* *click* *click* *click* *click* ........
And when you travel from point B to point C, get ready to do that whoooole thing over again. It's weird, with all the automated RNG in this game already, that I'm wishing they'd automate this stuff more at this point.
As for Trade, in a game called Star Traders, this mechanic feels very disadvantageous, at least at the early stages with the stuff you can trade in. You can fill your trade ship with some sort of commodity at an A+ price, and sell it off at an A+ price on a nearby planet, and feel good about yourself for making a cool $1K in profits - until you realize that the fuel cost you $600, your crew are demanding about $800 in wages, and demanding shore leave to the tune of $200 more. And you can't really trade in more profitable stuff until you buy very, very expensive licenses - in this manner, Star Traders basically funnels you away from trade and into doing the missions. Why travel from point A to B to try and pull off $1000 profit of trade (that gets swallowed by expenses), when I can travel the same distance for a mission that will give me a $22,000 reward? This is probably the most disappointing part for me, because I was keen to try my hand at some trading. I mean, it's in the title ...
At the end of all this, I can only feel that this title is really not geared towards someone like me, and more towards someone with a heavy background in D&D-like games who love them some dice rolling and RNG. If that's you, well, give it a shot.

Ghost of a tale is a fun to play and a really gorgeous looking game. Stealth mechanics work great, but if you just want to quickly backtrack from point A to point B the game won't punish you too hard for alerting one or multiple guards to your presence, as you can easily find a hiding place to wait them out. Yes, there is some backtracking, but is made far less irritating than in most titles through game's single, continuous environment and multiple paths you can take from one location to another. Speaking of that environment, it feels truly filled, lush, alive and immersive. Being underground feels like you really are underground and in contrast forest really looks and feels like a forest, which is something I find a lot of game struggle with and tend to feel unfinished. Ghost of a Tale actually IS unfinished, but it already feels incredibly rich.
Gameplay is very straight-forward for a stealth game. You can sneak, hide, knock your opponents out or distract them. All of these work well, are fun to do and I've not run into any issues with them during my playthrough. Minor bugs aside, I've not ran into anything game-breaking or quest-breaking, or really any kind of bug or glitch that interferred with my gameplay. If these were present in earlier versions, they have been fixed.
The main character, Tilo, is quite compelling with his adorable appearance, poignant backstory and clear motivations. You are also given some, admittedly very limited, choice with his personality when picking dialogue options during NPC conversations.
Although the story has been described by the developer as linear, there are a few choices to make during the game, most of which unfortunately we do not yet get to see the result of (like what you decided to do with the spyglass). Some quests also give you multiple options on how to complete them and some quests are not all that easily discovered, thus giving you a reason to thoroughly explore this wonderfully crafted world. Expositional text is simple and yet effective in conveying the world of the game to the player. It is sometimes serious and sad, and other times funny, even occasionally dipping into black comedy. Besides telling you about the world, it might also reveal things about Tilo and other NPCs.
On the more biased note; this game will most definitely appeal to the fans of Redwall, Mouse Guard, Beyond the Western Deep and similar works. I thoroughly recommend Ghost of a Tale to those whose stylistic predilections are already aligned with the game, those who enjoy stelath games and those who just enjoy a colorful and well defined fantasy worlds. It’s already worth your time and money in its early access state.

The game, so far (nearly six hours played) is one of the most charming and fun games I've ever played. IT IS NOT a small game. Takes hours to solve some quests, lot's of dialogues -all of them very good written, by the way- and not just a bit of persistence. I don't think I expected that much of this game, but it is one of the greatest promises of the game-world this days. If they don't make it a small game, as it shouldn't be, and make use of the potential of this game to became a medium or large game experience, I do not doubt it'll become so good as the biggest names of the RPG catalogue.
To talk about the developing situation, I must say game is enjoyable so far. I've played quite a long time now and I'm not done with it. There are, nevertheless, some things I'd say could be better. The greatest one is difficulty. I think the trick and joy of the game is in exploring, stealth and solving puzzles. That's an undeniable truth, and difficulty is fine BY ME. But I don't ignore that there could be some players that expect quite more of a challenge, regarding the enemys, I mean. It comes a point where it's just running, knowing that none of them will be able to catch you. I'd put a mark on this point.
Graphics are just fine; beautiful designs on every place of the game, also. Sometimes the change that is produced on the brightness of the screen when passing from a dark area to a clear one -from the jail to the courtyard, lets say- it's to abrupt. Sounds like a silly thing, but it kills me sometimes. Just a minor detail.
I thought I had a problem with finding a key. I saw in a forum discussion that the key of certain door was not yet introduced, and that, therefore, didn't exist. That was sad, since it was relevant to complete a quite important quest, and I thought the quest was impossible to complete then. Took me a day checking the whole world for the key, seeing tutorials and discussions, until I opened my own discussion on the forum. Didn't take more than a night for one of the developers itself awnser kindly my questions, and solve my problems. That's just great, knowing the developers are aware of our issues and there to help us when the time comes. After all the stress of not finding this annoying key, I ended up even more happy with the game, knowing that neither the players nor the game itself are overlooked by the developers.
Anyway, excellent, beautiful and almost perfect game so far! I'm looking forward to the final release; worth every penny. I think it could be one of the prettier games I've played, and it's not like I've played just a few. Thank you! And sorry for my poor english.

Note that I am not here reviewing a completed game, but the early-access version.  Keep that in mind.  Even at this early stage, the game is incredibly fun.  It's a first-person roguelike set in an effectively infinite procedurally generated world.  Although the world is not regenerated every time you play, the fact is that the size of the world means that you'll never run out of unique lands and dugneons to explore.  Gameplay is actually relatively simple.  But because there's no tutorial, and a lot is left to the player to figure out for himself, it can be frustrating until some things 'click'.
The game doesn't have any true classes, but you'll differentiate yourself based on how you kill monsters, and the spells that you cast,  the traps that you disarm, as well as, by your gear.
At this stage, the game only has a few different kinds of monsters, a few different kinds of quests, 2 kinds of dungeon themes a couple of minigames (one for removing traps, another for gambling at the tavern) and a number of different facilities in towns you'll visit (including shops, temples, a fighters guild, mages guild and Thieve's guild and two different kinds of fast transports.
In spite of the incomplete nature of the game, and a few bugs (including some stability issues), the game is very fun to play.  I find myself wanting to just see if I can get to the next level, clear out al of the monsters on my current dungeon floor, or kill just one more goblin or imp in order to complete a quest.  So I do recommend it.  But keep in mind (as I said) there are issues.

I just beat the game on Pur mode, so I think I can write a helpful review (as opposed to playing for 5 min then sounding off because it's too hard).
Yes, the game is very challenging at first.  Just like old NES games, you're dropped into a world with little explanation about anything.  The enemies move faster than you, they do a lot of damage, and not all the terrain is friendly to your robot at first.  I can imagine getting frustrated and quitting because of this.
If you actually take the time to learn the enemy movement and the terrain, you can use this to your advantage.  Careful positioning of your robot is key (it's all about the angles).  If you run and gun, you'll die.  Once you kill a few enemies though, you'll get enough money to buy upgrades, which allows you to kill enemies easier, which allows you to purchase more upgrades...and the cycle continues.  By the end, you can successfully run and gun because of you're boss equipment.

Bot Colony appeared rather promising when it released on Steam as part of the Early Access programme last year. It aimed to be the first game where you truly interacted with the characters through holding conversations with them. But it wasn’t until this month that the potential of this system was was hinted at through an update that introduced a need to pry information out of one of the characters .
The task was to gain access to 14 recorded videos in an attempt to piece together the events of the last 48 hours in the home of a Nakagawa Robot Corp. employee. To do this required talking to Jimmy, a robot servant left in the house. And when I say talking, I actually mean talking. Either through speech recognition with a microphone or typing, Jimmy was capable of responding to questions posed in naturally flowing English.
This certainly makes a refreshing change to only selecting from predefined dialogue options. And had the potential of revolutionizing interaction with game characters. Unfortunately, Bot Colony will cease to be playable in mid March. The result of not enough units being sold to cover the cost of running the server that processes the speech input, let alone paying for further development.
There was a lot of promise in Bot Colony, and anyone interested in seeing that should check the store page on Steam. While no longer purchasable, one of the videos does cover the story as it would have unfolded. It is a shame that Bot Colony slipped under the radar, a likely victim of Steam’s increasing release schedule and lack of promotion. Had it done well it could have been a hit. When the game shuts down, I’m going to miss my conversations with Jimmy.

I am happy that a lot of people like this game and that its creators seem to be doing well, as I'm an avid board gamer and want digital board games to do well on Steam. However, Gremlins is not an "intense strategy board game" as its tagline claims. "If Monopoly and Mario Party had a Steampunk Baby" from the Review blurbs is a more accurate description: long, chaotic, almost entirely decided by luck, and full of decisions that are either trivial or pointless.
I've played serious strategy board games as my primary hobby since 2004. I've played a lot of, and am quite good at, games such as Agricola, Age of Steam, Through the Ages, Scythe, Mage Knight, Terra Mystica, and many others. Gremlins has the trappings of a strategy board game: resources, victory points, a complicated-looking board, complex mechanics, unique player powers, and so on. Unfortunately, it feels like a strategy board game designed by someone who wanted to make a strategy board game but didn't actually know anything about what strategy board games are supposed to be like.
As a longtime fan and player of actual strategy board games, I really wanted to like Gremlins and was bitterly disappointed. The game is chaotic. Long-term planning is impossible and short-term options are limited. If you play without a turn limit, the game lasts forever because bad things inevitably keep happening to you. There is nothing you can do to prevent your hand from being wiped out and/or your character being hauled to jail in the blink of an eye. Your money, votes, and even victory points can disappear at astonishing speeds through no fault of your own. Of course, all this bad stuff happens to your opponents too, so the game feels interminable, with rounds dragging on and on and nobody making any real progress.
Another problem with the game is the lack of escalation. Cards that provide persistent effects are difficult to acquire and very limited in power ("Whenever someone does a thing that no one is ever likely to do, get a trivial amount of money"). As a result, a player's power is entirely a consequence of where they are on the board and how many resources they have -- all of which can change in an instant. As a result, you feel no more accomplished or advanced in the game on turn 30 than you did on turn 1.
As an experience, I don't deny that Gremlins can be fun, as the numerous favorable reviews would suggest. I, however, was not looking for an "experience." I was looking for a strategy board game, and as that, Gremlins quite simply sucks. It is long, luck-filled, chaotic, and entirely lacking in escalation -- all violations of the very most basic principles of strategy board game design. If you want a good digital board game, try Armello or any of the various free-to-play CCGs. Otherwise, get Bluestacks and play any of the excellent board game ports out there (Through the Ages, Splendor, Agricola, and Lords of Waterdeep are among my favorites), or wait for board game ports to start coming to Steam (there is a little momentum in this area, with games like Twilight Struggle already here and titles such as as Scythe promised on the horizon in 2018).
Avoid Gremlins. The strategy board game it claims to be is nowhere near the reality of what it is.

More into a video review. I have you covered.  This video is a first impression look.

The Match-3 genre is one of the most basic and straightforward ones. You have colored icons and it's your job to match three or more of them together to clear them out and gain points. Many games have taken to adding a little spice to the genre, however, bringing in other genre elements that are supported by the core gameplay of Match-3. Oafmatch follows the common trend of blending Match-3 with RPG elements, much in the way the Puzzle Quest series did. There are things that Oafmatch does better than its peers, and things it falls short on. So the question is, is the overall product worth your time and money?
!
Oafmatch aspires to be a humorous take on the RPG genre and it's tropes. While the jokes are clear, they didn't get more than the occasional grin out of me. Humor is often subjective, so your mileage will vary with the humor of Oafmatch. You follow an oaf named Knuckles, who is on a punching quest of punching. Along the way other heroes cross paths with the oaf, and for one reason or another, find cause to follow Knuckles and help take down bandits and dragons, and help themselves to the loot.
At its core, Oafmatch plays like a standard Match-3 game. It has an 8x8 grid (64 total gems) and you swap adjacent gems to create matches of 3 or more. Matching gems gives you mana of the same color. You spend mana on the spells and abilities you equip through the various weapons and accessories you pick up along the way. Making matches, too, deals direct damage to the enemy team. Which character attacks after a specific color is matched is based on their individual stats. If this sounds familiar, it should - it's almost a beat for beat replica of the Puzzle Quest system. However, Oafmatch does a lot of things that help to expand the strategies you'll be using in each fight.
For one, you do not use just one hero. Instead, you battle with 4 heroes, from a selection of up to 30 different choices! That's a lot of adventurers. Each character has two slots for gear, and each slot has a color denotation, restricting what gear they can equip. With 30 characters, 60 items, and each character having a different primary and secondary color combination, there's a ton of variety in how you can build your team.
This variety is amazing, though seems to come in sacrifice of variety in other areas. For one, enemy diversity. Most enemies you fight are jobber monsters and bandits. The stronger types, the ones that can actually make a match of gems like you can, use the same exact character models as the heroes. You don't notice it at first, but as soon as you accumulate more heroes, you realize that you've just been fighting dopplegangers. With such diverse and interesting character designs, to see them re-used so blatantly is incredibly disappointing.
One aspect I didn't like was the social media component. Perhaps I'm just too paranoid, but it rubbed me the wrong way. It's nothing major, at least. The game tells you that there's a community spell that can be used every so often in your game. This spell is determined by other players playing the game. You can only access this spell (as well as the feature of being able to talk to other players while you play) if you sign up on their website. Many players, I'm sure, will find this feature cute and fun, and they likely aren't wrong. However, when a game locks a solo-play feature behind signing up for something, downloading something, etc., I'm suspicious and won't partake.
As mentioned before, the art style of the game is incredibly charming. It blends a style of cute and cool that fits with its (attempts at) humor and sometimes dark situations (like cannibalism). Every character is unique in their appearance, even if those same designs are re-used for the enemies. The simple graphics mean the game can perform well on most set-ups, and plays without issue when minimized as you watch a stream or work on something else between turns.
The sounds are servicable, but nothing enticing. No points can really be taken off for it, but no points can really be given, either. No one should have any issues with the audio of this game.
Oafmatch, like its hero Knuckles the Oaf, is simple in its appearance, but there is more depth there than people would give it credit for. Though lacking in subtlety and grace, there is an experience that is expected when playing a Match-3 game, and Oafmatch succeeds in providing the player with that experience. It's diversity of equipment and heroes is surprising, and refreshing, showing that a game from a casual genre doesn't need to do just the basics to get by. However, it still finds obvious ways to cut corners, and the social element is at best misguided, and at worst exploitative. At the very least, it's suspicious. Any time a game asks you to unlock content by doing something outside of the game it should be met with scrutiny.
For $6, there's a lot of hours of playtime to be had with Oafmatch. While there are other titles that mix the genres of RPG and Match-3 better, all of them have so far been more expensive and lacking in depth for some of the shared features. Oafmatch is a worthwhile experience, for the price of admission.

As a long time player of Rumble Fighter (Since 07) here is my opinion on the game.

-Rumble Fighter offers plenty of different game modes, to keep the gameplay always fresh.
Rumble Fighter like any other game has it's flaws, some far more substantial than others.

Majority of the players that play are over the top toxic. They think they are demiGods and will freak out if you are more skilled then them.
With that being said though, there are plenty of great players to play with that log into the game daily to have a good mellow time, and enjoy everyones company.
If more people were to bring a positive influence to the community, the toxicity would be countered.
Another concern that is voiced by many, is the micro transactions.
Do I think you need to spend your hard earned cash on micro transactions in this game? No. The people that are misguided by this just simply did not take the time to learn the game.
ALTHOUGH, with that being said, microtransactions in free to play games are always a quicker way to the top. Are you at an advantage to a free to play character who just started? Yes. Are you at an advantage to a free to play player who took time to learn the game? No.
People will go out and purchase $60-$80 titles and not bat an eye, but they log onto a free to play game and get upset when they see microtransactions? How do you think Free to Play titles run their services? On rainbows and unicorns, straight out of your hopes and dreams? No, they need money to supply you with the service. So yes, micro transactions exist. You'll go out and spend $10 on a burger, and the burger will be gone in seconds, yet struggle to spend $10 on an ingame item that is yours to keep, to use over and over. That's where I struggle to understand how people playing Free to Play can get upset by this.
There is nothing wrong with supporting a great unique game. Although I do agree, the community needs a wake up call, they need to leave room for a positive attitude for new to the game players.
If you are considering trying this game, understand that it is not as bad as people make it out to be. It can be a great game, filled with hilarious moments, rich gameplay and great conversation. Unfortunately, much like any other online game in 2017, it will be littered with bitter people. It's all how you look at it.
I would rate this game 9/10 all day long. There is nothing like it on the market.

After long pondering and discussions with my coop partner, I decided to
Tristoy based on some interesting game mechanics. However, please note several things: First, Tristoy is coop-only game. For the price you get two copies of it, so you can gift one to a friend (and press him for his share later). Coop modes available are local with split-screen and online through Steamworks. I think if you start a game with one friend online then you can’t continue with a different friend later. Second, the game isn’t Metroidvania as advertised; it is only (decent) coop platformer. Lastly, I bought the game in a 75% sale, so you have a good chance it will run again and you can grab it cheaper. List of pros and cons follows:
+ Original art style
+ Bleak atmosphere
+ Well-made coop
+ “Dialogue between characters” feature
+ Quite hard
+ Voice acting
+ Bosses
-  Short
- Animations and sounds could be better
- Rather buggy
- Choices do not have big impact later on
As Tristoy is a coop game, I decided to make a sort of “coop” review and let my coop partner, Firaas, voice his opinions about the game. We played it each on his own computer but in the same room.
Story and setting
Tristoy takes place in an island prison of the same name. The protagonists are Prince Freedan) and Steyn the Wizard Freedan is imprisoned in Tristoy and with help of Steyn he tries to escape and save Princess Freya who has been imprisoned there as well. There is also plenty of, sadly unused, story background about war, evil king and such so the atmosphere is pretty bleak.
Gameplay
Freedan (played by me) and Steyn (played by Firaas) need to cooperate as each of them has unique skills. Freedan is more agile and can do a double jump and in the beginning is the only one who can fight monsters. Steyn can use “gyromancy” magic which turns gears (Firaas: Turns, but too slowly!) to operate machinery and in the beginning he is invincible, but can only stun enemies. Later he gets a millstone to break walls and monster heads with. The screen automatically splits if one character wanders off too far from the other. This happens even in online multiplayer (Firaas: I hated this. Often good part of the screen which we needed to see got lost in the split. Does not help performance, either).
The game consists of mostly linear sequence of rooms (there is a little backtracking here and there) which contain platforming puzzles and monster fights. The characters, especially Freedan, do not endure much and in our playthrough we died often. The game uses lives system. If even one of the characters dies, you lose a live and are returned to checkpoint (monsters will not respawn). Lose them all and you return to last visited savegame statue, with monsters respawned. Lives are replenished with energy gained by killing monsters and opening chests.
Unusual (at least for a platformer) game mechanic of Tristoy is the dialogue system. At certain plot points or levels a dialogue between Freedan, Steyn and possibly somebody else is triggered and both players can input different choices that (in theory) affect the story. Truth is, the game is very short (took us about three hours to finish it, with plenty of dying and with reading most of the dialogues) and when you see “XY will remember this”, there is no guarantee that him recalling your action will actually fit into the span of the game and often you won’t see the result of your choice.
For a game this short, Tristoy contains quite a number of boss fights which are great not only in quantity, but in my opinion also in quality and graphical design.
Graphics, sound, controls
I liked the overall graphical style and animations (Firaas: Myself, not so much. The characters were not very detailed and the animations were choppy.). Although the game is 2D, you can in certain parts go to a “layer” closer to or farther from the screen. This however leads to situations where you can’t recognize if the destination of your jump is the same layer and you can fall to your death. Music was not very memorable. Weird thing with the combat is that if you hit a monster, a piano sound plays. On the other hand, the voice acting for all characters is excellent (Firaas: Except for death screams. These are horrible and annoying.).
Tristoy can be controlled by keyboard (can’t be remapped, but 2 schemes are offered, 1 for each local player or either one for online players), controller (didn’t try) and surprisingly also by a smart device using an app (might try later and update this review). We found the controls sluggish, especially jumping. Lots of lives were lost when one of us (usually Firaas with Steyn, who is slow and his jump is long only just about enough for most gaps) didn’t perform intended jump despite pressing the key and fell to his death. I should mention that had we not been playing in the same room, we would probably think that the other one is fooling around, rage quit and never complete the game.
Performance
Tristoy runs on the Unity engine. Me and Firaas both played on our notebooks and despite Tristoy being a 2D game, we weren’t able to max out the graphical settings without framerate drops. Setting one level below max ran fine, however.
Now for the biggest flaw of Tristoy: the bugs. I already mentioned the jumping issues. Several others, partly game-breaking, happened to us during otherwise great boss fight or boss chases. At one time, you are required to run and jump over platforms that fall when you step on them. One thing is, the falling is scripted according to the faster character so if you fall behind with Steyn, it is certain death. You must let him ahead of Freedan to make it. Worse thing happened to us: once, after death, one platform didn’t respawn or something and when we jumped where it should be we fell. A couple of times Freedan died after only entering this room. At different boss, we were close to deliver killing blow when I as Freedan died. To our surprise, Steyn respawned before the boss whereas Freedan at the checkpoint after it, as if the boss was killed. We missed out on part of the plot because of this. The hitboxes of certain hazards are questionable as well, but I think the game is also challenging by conventional means.
Misc, verdict
Tristoy has achievements and Steam cards if you are looking for these. The achievements are also buggy though. I was awarded completely undeserved one for not dying once during the game and missed out on another which should have been awarded. I would also like to note that the achievement goals are weird in some cases: One is for dying in smelting room (How is dying an achievement, by definition of it), another is for dying 50 times in trap room (same thing, also where am I supposed to get that many lives?). Another thing is, the game is so short I got only one card drop after finishing it.
To sum it up, Tristoy as a game had potential but was held back by technical issues and short length. I would rate it 6 out of 10.

So I can see why Costume Quest 2 is considered not as good as the first. So here is what they did right Vs. What they did wrong.
The right
1. They kept it cute and charming.
2. The story is interesting.
3. The time travel mechanic was done well.
4. Seeing the characters from past to future was clever.
5. The new and old enemy designs are cool.
6. The new costumes were innovative and well thought out.
7. Using Creepy Treat Cards for a benefit in battle was a good change of pace.
8. Certain enemies are stronger or weaker to different costumes.
The Wrong
1. The change in battle style was unnecessary and was many times just difficult to use.
2. The ending basically ret·cons everything you do. Making what happened in the first one not even matter.
3. Only 3 of the Creepy treat cards are useful from my point of view.
What they should have done.
If they changed the fight style the way it is with certain enemies being stronger or weaker to certain types of costumes. Then to balance it with the annoying combat style they should have made it to where you use a turn in the middle of battle to swap your costume. Similar to switching a party member in certain RPGs.
Still this game took me about 9 hours to complete, it's not that expensive. Granted mine was a gift, and it's fun enough to replay. I give it 3.5 out 5

Oafwatch follows the likes of Puzzle Quest by merging the concept of Match 3 with RPG statistics. At the core, it is essentially match your coloured gems, make big combos and get a shiny gold star for completing the objective. Each gem stacks against weapons - special attacks - that you have to use strategically to win. The enemy is constantly placing their own special moves on the board, which pressures you into making intelligent choices rather than just going for damage.
This makes it a very different style of gameplay to the last Match 3 / RPG hybrids I reviewed, such as '1000000' and 'You Must Build a Boat' which were very much speedrunners. In Oafmatch, you can take as long as you want to find the perfect move.
There are a lot of unlockable party members, and party management involves levelling, equipment and potions. These can be switched around for each fight if necessary, and you will definitely need to put somne thought into that at the higher difficulty levels. One of the downsides is the game can be quite grindy with the usual dollop of RNG luck in there; if you can't complete a level and aren't getting lucky with your gem combos, you will need to grind earlier stages to upgrade your stats to continue.
There are two (and a half) modes; campaign and roguelike. Campaign follows a simple quest where you roam around the map defeating things with violence and unlocking new stages, members and items. Each stage can be completed on three difficulty levels; with a blue star for completion and the shiny covetted gold star for perfect (no party member dies). Getting three gold stars on some of the maps is pretty challenging, and I had to grind, switch up and go back at a few stages. There is also a campaign + where you have your progression unlocked from the beginning, but the fights are harder again.
Roguelike is exactly as it sounds; extremely hard and sometimes unfair, but a real challenge with unlockables that carry over and this adds some real replayability to the game. Replaying the campaign after getting your gold shinies would be boring - but roguelike adds an extra layer of RNG and challenge that means this game contains a lot of playable hours for the price.
Overall Oafwatch has an absolute ton of content, although with the limited scope of Match 3 games it can get repetitive and grindy. This has been alleviated somewhat with an extensive array of choices, characters and items - but ultimately with this sort of game, you're not seeing a massive amount of variation so can feel grindy. It is still a casual game - you can add all the depth in the world to a Match 3 game and ultimately it's still a simple game at the core, and will only appeal to those who find this genre enjoyable.
P.S. The name is pretty dumb though!

Overall, I enjoy this game.  Sandboxes are a big draw for me, but it's very easy to get them wrong.  Thankfully, this one tackles the challenges of building a sandbox, while also providing a well-written story and lore that seems to be optional to partake in.
Cons:
Micromanagement!  This is by far the biggest con, and if you don't like to handle details such as the skills your crew chooses as they level up, this may not be the game for you.
Over-your-head depth:  Ordinarily I enjoy a simulation that eludes my complete understanding, as it can provide interesting surprises here or there.  Unfortunately, this proves to be an obstacle more often than not, and it's a pretty difficult game to get right the first time around.
Difficulty:  Even the third difficulty up is fairly hard to get far before you run into one fail state or another.  The class you choose at the beginning is important to ensuring your survival.  Leave flavor classes for the lowest of difficulties.
Pros:
Customization:  From the ship elements that provide many different kinds of weapons and utilities, to your officers' jobs, skills, talents, and even names/appearances, it's not too difficult to establish a load-out that suits your playstyle.
Procedural generation:  The settings you set for whatever map you create can have a great impact on how the sandbox experience plays out.  How far systems/sectors/planets are from each other, and how dangerous various regions of space can be.
Story:  The story is well written.  Of all the things I like about this game, this is unexpectedly the biggest selling point for me
(For someone who likes sandboxes, story is often optional).  If you don't mind reading a lot of text, this alone will entertain you to no end.  There are various dialogue trees that give you many options to learn more about the lore, and affect choices you make at various points.  The story is very choice-centric, a vital rpg feature.
Difficulty:  While this is something that gets in the way for me, someone more skilled may find the harsher simulation to be a welcome addition to the game.  It's not always easy to make money, for instance, the lifeblood of your ship and crew.  If you run out of money or ways to make money, it's as good as game over.  The amount of failstates can make for an entertaining game, though, I'll admit, and it isn't too much of a drag to start a new game.
Overall, I enjoy this game, and can see myself playing more of it in the weeks to come.

At eight hours I just beat this game and I have to say that was the most fun eight hours I've had in a long time. Battle Chef Brigade is best described as Monster Hunter meets Iron Chef meets Combo-based side scrolling.
In the game you play as Mina Han, a talented chef and fighter who is skilled with wind magic, who dreams of becoming a Battle Chef. A battle chef is basically a chef that uses their skills not only to fight dangerous monsters but to either research their ingredents or use it to cook with.
The story is well made with a full cast of colorful characters that each make the world feel alive and gives it a sort of charm. From the side characters like Master hunter Thorn or the cat-obsessed scientist Belchoir to the main cast like the brave Orc warrior Thrash and the intelligent Kirin, each one makes the world feel unique and fun to experience.
Now onto the game itself, it's pretty story heavy which is a huge plus in my opinion but the mechanics are pretty simple. During matches you need to hunt down monsters in specific areas to harvest the ingredents you need to finish a dish, this is where the Iron Chef part comes in. The matches are judged by a panel of 1-3 judges and each have a specific element or mixture of elements they want and they have a theme ingredent.
The voice acting can feel a bit amateurish at times but overall it was really well down for an indie game, I kinda let that one slide because again, it's an indie game.
Mechanics of the game are extremely solid and it is really fun to play around with.
My one complaint is that the game is a little on the short side but I'm hopeful that we'll see more from Trinket Studios as this game is truely a gem.
I highly recommend this game, again it is the most fun I've had in months and I think I will come back to replay this a lot of times.

Being a party game, it's best to play this with friends, otherwise you'll be playing against bots which definitely gets boring. There are single-player challenges, though best played with two players.
Overall, it's a great game if you're going to play with friends. Alone, however, you may want to watch some gameplay and see if it's what you want to be doing for an hour

TL;DR: Great game held back a bit by technical difficulties. Still HIGHLY recommended though for fans of co-op.
Pros: Well excecuted co-op mechanics and split screen, interesting story (though voice acting is amateur), fun to play in local co-op
Cons: Split screen is frustrating in boss battles limiting your view of the boss, poor optimization (had to edit resolution way down to get it to run well), online co-op does not work well
Tristoy is an interesting experiment, co-op side scrolling adventure games have either never been done before or are very rare. Clearly a lot of thought went into how to use two adventurers in interesting ways. No spoilers but every area has a new way for the two players to interact with the world. It helps that the story is interesting and the fact that each player selects from a seperate dialogue tree really keeps things lively.
What holds back Tristoy most though is it's functionality. Throughout the game there were mulitiple glitches, poor optimization for my resolution, and several times where my controller was either responsive during cut scenes (killing me) or didn't work resulting in my death. This was frustrating but did not detract from my overall enjoyment of the game. At times the accidental deaths even made myself and my buddy laugh out loud.
Going forward I hope that the developers spend some time squashing bugs and optimizing their game. If they can smooth out some of the rougher edges I can call the game a true classic original. If you're into co-op games and have someone to play locally with I can't recommend Tristoy highly enough. You won't be disappionted by the total game but will be annoyed with some bugs.
Fantastic artwork, great story, wonderful use of interactive dialogue elements. The crippling factor is the iffy platforming detection and buggy gameplay. Still, it's definitely worth experiencing.

After completing Costume Quest 1 earlier this year, I was looking forward to playing 2 and grabbed it in the Halloween sale. If you want to know about that one, I suggest you go read my review on it as a lot is similar.
Just like the first game, this is a wonderfully quirky game with so many jokes that I was frequently laughing out loud. In particular, the Candy Corn costume always made me giggle, despite reading the joke 50+ times. There was less meta-humour in this one than the first, but it was never boring.
The combat is very similar to the first, but improved overall. There is now only a single form of attack (compared to various QTE-styles in the first game), but they've added additional mechanics like countering that add another dimension to combat. They also added 'actor types' which are a basic form of strengths and weaknesses split between 3 classes; it sounds odd, but it's easy to understand and it adds a tactical edge.
Like with CQ1, however, I did tend to stick to the first costume you get and swap out the third as I went (the second was always Candy Corn for the achievement), but as the visuals are interesting and the cutscene moves are now skippable, that isn't too big an issue.
One issue I should mention is this game was very easy. I only failed perhaps two fights (and one was because of a glitch), but I did do some grinding in places for XP and candy (in-game currency). The boss fights were very straight forward and fit SO MUCH better into the flow of the game compared to the almost puzzle-like ones in CQ1.
The story is clever and moves on from the first with just enough nods and references to 1 to induce nostalgia. They would, however, go over the heads of anyone who hasn't played 1, so definitely play that before this. It is a sequel in every sense.
This was a fantastic game that kept all the good feelings I had for 1 and added to them, creating its own individual experience that fits beautifully into the Costume Quest universe.
Well worth your time, money and laughter.
