It's with a heavy heart that I cannot ultimately recommend this game. It's got a good concept backed by good music and pretty decent artwork, and the basics of the action combat are kind of neat, too. But only the basics.
Things go a bit south when you have to switch spells, which with these keyboard/mouse controls are done with the same hand as your movement. I can't tell you how many times I accidentally selected the wrong spell because I couldn't stop moving(or enemies would swarm me) while I did it. And that's before adding summons to the mix, which require you to control even more things at once. I only have two hands, and controlling my pets while casting the right spells, all while moving - because you really can't afford to stop moving in combat - is just not happening. At least, not happening very well.
On top of that, regular spells are weak. The game is set up so that you really have to rely on your summoned creatures - which, again, are hard to control - if only to keep enemies from swarming you as you wait for your mana to recharge. You have an attack that'll recharge some mana for you, but it requires you to get dangerously close to the enemies you should be avoiding at all costs. This makes combat drag on a bit since enemies won't go down fast.
Then there's the weird spawning system. The points are pretty close together, and the same group can and will spawn multiple times without you even having to leave the area. This makes thorough exploration of any area more of a chore than it should be. I got to a point where my spells were weak, enemies were strong, and my summons were taking a huge beating from a single group. Accidentally triggering an additional group while running was a death sentence. Not fun.
I want to like it. I really do. But the controls are too awkward, with too much to keep up with in the midst of an active battle situation when you only have two hands. And the encounter balance is very much not in your favor. It honestly just ended up being an exercise in frustration.

I thought I'd take a risk on this. There's currently a bug where there's no tooltips on Linux - but I watched a few "Let's Play" videos and thought I'd be able to manage without for the time being. I have to say I was rewarded with a really deep and fun game.
Though it's in early access, this is a surprisingly complete, functional and playable game already.
I've had no crashes so far (~17hrs play), and other than a couple of bugs in the early scripted storylines (which I think are being worked on) it's been a solid experience. There was a bit of learning curve at first - some of the UI needs a bit of work (especially without tooltips!) but once I watched/read a bit to clarify a few things, I had a great time with it.
There's something of the old Sid Meier's Pirates about it - missions, trade, reputation with different factions etc - though there's a whole extra level of personal reputations and depth to the crew, who can each be upgraded, customised and outfitted.
Additionally, it looks like they've been working hard at fixing and improving everything, and the game designers appear to have good form in long-lasting support and development - so I'm really looking forward to see what this is like a few months down the line.
[edit] Just to add, after having a small bug in my game, I posted a bug report - then got a message back 5 minutes later from the devs saying it had been fixed, and offering to repair my save file if I wanted. That's some seriously impressive service. I think that helps to indicate how friendly and committed these guys are, and how much they care about the game they're working on.

This is my first review so bear with me.
Ghost of a Tale is about a small mouse who was wrongfully imprisoned by a king and was seperated from his wife in the process.  The goal is to help the poor guy escape and determine the whereabouts of his wife.  A very simple story that, quite frankly, I'm okay with.  However, the lore behind this game is far from simple yet the game easily feeds it to you in bite sized chunks that are easy and enjoyable to digest.  The graphics are amazing, far beyond anything that I thought I'd ever see from a team consisting of only five people (one of which worked on 90% of the game by himself).  Gameplay wise this game is amazing and very easy to pick up.  Performance wise it handles like a dream even on my budget desktop.  Honestly the only bad thing I can say about this game are the very few bugs I've come across in my play time and even then the developers are definitely ironing those out at a reasonable pace.  Of course, the game is far from finished given that it is still in early access, but I will say wholeheartedly that I do not regret one bit the $20 I paid for the game as my time with it, however small that might be at the time of this review, was not wasted.  I can't recommend this game enough and I hope to see this game finished in the future.

Among Ripples is pretty much a "Create your own eco-system" game on a smaller scale. Think of Niche, but not as advanced or customizable. ....Or cool. Or Snazzy. Or- Ya know what? This game isn't a slew of things but I'll give it props for being relaxing eventhough that relaxing feeling would be cut off buy me flopping around trying to figure out exactly what the hell I was doing and weather or not I was doing it right.  Honestly, half the time I had not the slightest clue if I was hurting or helping my little creatures. Do they need more oxygen in the water? Dunno. Do they need less oxygen in the water? Dunno. Do we need more clams in the pond? Dunno. This game gives you little to no indication of weather the actions you are making are good or bad. And there's no in game way to tell anything. No gauge, nothing. It's really just a game of "click it and hope and pray it works". Now, you may be saying, "christ almighty, is there anything good about this game?" My response? Otter. literally the only thing I liked about the game besides it nice little tutorial. That being said, I don't hate the game. Not by any means. It's still a nice way  to waste time with graphics pretty enough to give your inner aesthetic seeking critic an ♥♥♥♥♥♥. This is a good, but oddly overlooked puzzle fighter. Beyond the basic rules of putting three units of the same colour in a line to launch an attack or build defensive walls, there's a decent amount of strategy involved. Each of the 40-odd units in the game has a different attack power, special ability, and takes a different amount of time to prepare their attack - during which your opponent can try to defend or counter it. You can also power up your attacks by setting them to launch on the same turn or stacking one right on top of another. And of course, this wouldn't be a Heroes game if you weren't playing a hero, with their own, potentially game-changing ability.
The single-player campaign is quite long, and offers a mild progression and resource management element (as in, you'll have to buy special units if you get them killed in combat) in addition to unique boss encounters. There's also a story, of course, somehow related to Heroes 5, but cartoony so kids might like it, maybe? I don't know, I've lost interest in HoMM around 3, and in cartoons around 12.
The multiplayer component works reasonably well, but you'll have to provide your own opponents - bring a friend or two. And the DLC allows you to play not just as one of the heroes from the campaign, but also the bosses, who can function quite differently.
So, if you're at all into puzzle fighters, give this one a go. It's good, even if you just play the campaign. Maybe play a round or two against your friends.

I don't know how to proceed with this review, I will make it short and simple.
I started playing it with my friend, first, we both played with keyboards online, BIG mistake, even if we're separated phisically, we have to use the defined layout controls (In example: WASD for 1st player, arrow keys for the 2nd) that was a big nono. My friend uses a keyboard without numpad, so it was impossible to him to do any action except move, since he couldn't bind any key at all. We had to swap to controllers.
I must say, we did not perceive any lag at all, which was definitely great! I took a step further and started downloading at 80% of my bandwith speed ( 800kb/s in a maximun of 1024kb/s ) lag was almost unnoticiable, even with a ping of over 400ms. No input lag, no screen tearing, that's pretty good! But let's go back to what playing the game is like;
We didn't play much, we reached the 2nd boss and after trying for the 3rd time stopped playing:
-The mechanic to kill most enemies is; 2nd player uses white fireball to knock them out/open their "shell", depending on the enemy they may spit fireballs that kill you instantly no matter what, or simply stay KO on the ground without moving. This is definitely boring, I will say that 90% of the times we lost, was because of the stupid fireballs and the horrible "double jump" mechanic(You can double jump with 1st character, but you can't double jump if you stood in the air for half a second more after doing the first jump) Basically, you miss every attack to 80% of the enemies, and you're in need of your partner.
-The first boss is stupidly easy, yet hard. I'll relate the fight:
You go into a room, and you find yourself with a giant bat with flying thingies around it, the only way to kill it? 2nd character's fireball to knock it out, then it goes to the ground, then you keep attacking. Repeat 4 or 5 times. Everytime it gets up, it spits fireballs that kill you instantly, and due to the slow movement, doublejump, etc, of the characters, it makes it hard.
But, here comes the 2nd boss. basically you reach a room where a sarcophage revives and starts spitting lightning everywhere, if you get hit you die, and you have to go left, pass a room where pillars come from the top if you step on the wrong one (Which you can tell by the 2nd character lightning up the rune of the pillar that is a trap), which is difficult even if you know which pillars are traps, because of the horribly movement/double jump.
After that, you reach a room with rounded pillars, and a save-game/restore life statue on the left behind a pillar that you can't pass. The boss comes, it blocks the way you came to the room, and you're stuck in a small place to fight it. But you can't come close to it because it instantly kills you, and 2nd player fireballs can't do anything(Or so it seemed the 2 times we repeated it), this is the point where we stopped playing.
-I have to say that the way the conversations progress is delightful, you have some choices of answers and you decide what to say/do, for example, 2nd character needs to feed itself, being the 1st character, you decide if resist or let him suck your life out, and he decides how many years of 1st char's will take, and every character you talk to will remember your decissions.
-The bugs. 1 hour of gameplay, 5 bugs that killed my character.
There's a place where 2nd character has to use his power to move a circle with 2 rounded pillars inside, so he moved the first pillar, I stood on it , he moved it a bit down and I instantly died. Okay, maybe I can't stand in a place when my partner is moving it. So we repeat the stage, and he completes moving everything, the pass is created, and we can proceed peacefully. WRONG. I died on one pillar for NO reason.
Another bug, when 1st character is on a fence hanging up, and 2nd character moves it(Which is the correct way to do it in the puzzle), sometimes 1st character falls for no reason, and if you have no reflexes or your hands are off your controller (Since it's a part for the 2nd character and you're stuck doing nothing for 20 seconds) you will fall to your dead,
Meh, I can keep going, but basically I don't recommend this game, it feels slow, it's one of those games where you don't feel you'll jump and let a character in the place you want, and it's stressing.

First of all, I love this game. My friend and I had a blast playing through this. Even so, this is objectively a bad game. Let's start with the asking price: It's daylight robbery, especially in Europe, even though from what I've heard you get two copies of the game (I got mine for free). The Co-Op is obligatory, so there's no way to play this alone (unless you have very limber feet..).
The controls feel like a swamp; jumps are floaty and attacks feel neither satisfactory nor fluid; there is a lot of animation lag , so even if you want to quickly jump away after attacking you can`t.
The sound design is a mixed bag. There are only a hand full (literally; I counted less than five) different tunes, though I really like the first exploration theme and the boss theme. On the other hand there is this piano tune every time you hit the enemy which, while distinctive enough to tell you if you've done damage, is not to everybody's liking, though I didn't mind.
The game, however, is NOT a Metroid-Vania. There is little to no exploration; you progress through the game in a mostly linear fashion from room to room, complete with a world map, even though you can backtrack once or twice to get optional objectives. There is no real level system either; You do have an experience bar which fills from killing enemies, but all you get upon leveling up is extra lifes. You restart the current room as long as you have extra lifes; if you don't you are thrown back to the last save point. However, there is a huge problem with this: When you save your game you also save your current number of lifes, which means that if you go game over you respawn with the same number of lifes you saved your game. Even worse, due to a bug if you die in the same room the save point is in you respawn at the save point and immediately save after. What this does mean if you go game over in a save room you respawn with ZERO extra lives, no matter how many you had when you first touched the save point, since your lives are always decreased by one.
Speaking of bugs, this game is riddled with it. Platforms don't work for one player while playing over the internet, hit boxes of fireballs, and spikes are seemingly arbitrary, which is especially bad with spinning platforms which sometimes decide to kill you outright even though you only touched the side without spikes. Even worse, sometimes when you die your partner dies immediately after even though he was in a safe spot, which means you lose two lifes even though you only died once. I even got the local co-op trophy despite only playing online...
The voice acting in this game is fair, and I found myself really getting interested in the story. There is a branching story system which, while really simply, is pretty engaging: You chose your own backstory for the game by your dialogue choices: The princess is either your sister or your betrothed, though most of this is fluff. If you can't get engaged in the dialogues this game won't be for you. I found the characters to be interesting enough to continue, though most of your choices don't matter much - though I'm really curious if you could have saved XXXXX by not mentioning her to YYYYY... You and your playing partner make choices for your characters, and at the very end of the game there is a pretty big choice which I won't spoil.
Sadly, though, you can not continue the game with a different partner when you're playing online - at least I didn't find a way to.
Again, most of you won't like this game, this is why I think you will be better off with not playing it. For myself, I will continue, even though I hope the very buggy last boss battle will be patched soon so my buddy and I can finish soon...

TL;DR: If you'rel looking for an ASCII Rogue-like, look elsewhere.  If you're looking for a fun action game, check this one out.
While this game is pretty fun and fantastic, don't mistake it for the classic ASCII games of yore (ZZT, ADOM, etc).  This game plays out way more like a twin-stick arcade game that's been run through AALIB.  It's a cool idea, but the whole thing just feels too fluid and real-time for an ASCII-style game.
Is it worth it? Absolutely.  The game is fun, there's a lot fun.  Basically imagine it as DOOM, but re-created as an arcade game and rendered entirely as an ASCII map.
I wish there was more variation in monsters - so far everything is just the letter M in various colours.  There isn't even any indication on what each monster is... I guess you can use your imagination more there.

d) The game consistently gives you cards with *exactly* the amount of movement points you already have. I had a game where I was given 3 movement cards for a total of 14 turns in a row. WTF MAN. ZERO CHOICES!?
e) The game gives you a criminal card right before you would play a card on a spot you took 3-6 turns to get to. Of course you didn't get any before this specific last turn before you would play it. Of course now you get sniped by other players letting you show your cards, which wouldn't have been bad at all if you wouldn't consistently get this criminal card right before your play.
f) The game gives you a hard time with negative misfortunes (a bad event spot right before certain places on the map) that are bad *for your very specific* situation. Which makes it odd since there are over 40 different misfortunes or so.
So the chance of the one very specific misfortune which is bad for you is not that big.
g) The game gives player X a steamroller experience by handing out
1) good follow-up cards so they can play a really good card (or even several) nearly every turn. Meanwhile you get low to mid useful cards.
2) misfortunes that even help the player with his cards. In one round one guy was teleporting around with them (some misfortunes move you on the map) which combined with (1) gave him half of the win in two turns.
How the **** are you supposed to play against that?
- - - - - - -
So yes, the overall experience is fun. Just don't expect your skill with playing the cards to really have a reproducable impact on how you progress vs the other players.
I posted a similar critique in the forums and the devs response was "lol it's like poker, if you don't suck you will win anyway."
Yeah sure. When RNG hands me crap in 6/10 games, ok in 3/10games, and good in 1/10 games. Then it is my fault when I don't win. BWAHAHAHAHHAHAHAHHAHHAHAHA
[Insert flame here.]
If you do happen to have a game where people get similarly good cards and bad events by the RNG then it gets really interesting and fun though, because then you can actually play out your skill vs other people.
Those matches with fair RNG are *RARE* though. Like 1/20 or even less.
- - - - - - -
Conclusion: If can deal with being f****** by RNG, this is a must buy.
And believe me, you will get f***** by it. Hard.
If you can't, don't buy it or wait for a sale.
Your skill won't matter that much so it'll make you rage while the devs laugh at you for "sucking" even though you can't help with what the game hands you ;) Yay!
- - - - - - -

Thumbs up for that.

Game's promises are fulfilled. However, expect...
- Badly scaled monsters, due to monster difficulty being decided by your current area and your level rather than spawn location (you can kill monsters by running back to outside the town gates and then just blocking all monster hits)
- Long load times (There's a music jingle that plays if you enter a town... only once it actually ends you can play again... the jingle is about 30 seconds long, I think)
- More loading (overworld is divided into 20x20 grid sections. Or 25x25. Whenever you enter a new section... the game has to load. So when you're travelling from A to B, or just exploring, you'll constantly be pulled out of your immersion)
- Bad graphics ("you might have to tweak them to get a good result" = don't buy unless your monitor's native resolution is 1024x768 or 1440x900 - because otherwise, game will look bad. Especially trees.)
- Bad viewrange (~20 tiles, or about 100 meters). You know how there's towers and castles in this game? Yeah, well, you can 't see them until they're in a section next to your section. Meaning that if a castle takes up most of a section, you can't see it until you're 25-30 tiles away from it (about 125 meters). So when you cross a section border, POOF castle.
- NO in-game tutorial. There's one on the menu, but it's easily missed as it's at the bottom of the screen, far away from "continue game" and "new game". What do the gems mean? You don't know, nobody tells you and without knowing that you will DIE. Red = secret area, green = monster, purple = "important object". Which is a town, a dungeon, or a trap. Oh yeah. To exit a dungeon, step off the exit tile, look at it from an adjacent tile, AND CLICK THE LADDER/TRAPDOOR. Again, this had to be looked up online, after I fled from a monster, and found out that I'd easily have been able to escape, but because I was now pinned to the exit tile, I couldn't. Because my character can't stick his arms straight up to pull a ladder down.
In short:
- You don't get much information
- The game is hard because you don't get much information, not because of there actually being things you have to overcome.
However, if you don't find the above listed issues a problem, then this could be a game for you. Because of the game does deliver on the things it promises.

Looking at screenshots and promo video I was hoping for a bizarre mindblowing surrealistic puzzle game like from pictures of M. C. Escher.
But in Back to Bed the power of surrealism is unexploited, which was a huge disappointment for me. There are elements of it like stairs that make the character to stand at a wall, but sadly there are not many of them. Levels' desing is very good and some players will surely find them challenging, albeit they are not difficult and not much different than in other productions of puzzle genre. Still they are very enjoyable.
Developers took more care of surrealism while creating the environment. Graphically the game is absolutely magnificent and it really feels that it was inspired with pictures of masters like Dali and Escher. Due to omnipresent eyes and other strange beings Back to Bed can be creepy, but from the other side, detailed surrounding with a warm light make it cosy.
The main characters - Bob and ucanny looking Subob are very likeable and it was fun for me to help them.
Even though Back to Bed is not much different than the other classic puzzle games if it comes to the gameplay, it is worth  playing due to its amazing atmosphere.

Note that this isn't a proper review, as I only played for 40 minutes, and I wasn't likely even to the half-way point.
Being that the game is free, there's not much reason NOT to try this, but if you do, you might find Back to Bed to be quite lacking.
Put briefly, this game offers some trippy visuals and an interesting concept that drives the game play, but the puzzles aren't very difficult or interesting (at least as far as I made it), there's really nothing in the way of a plot to keep you motivated, and the game changes little as you progress.
Ultimately I quit simply because Back to Bed is boring; it suffers from a lack of variety or intrigue, and simply couldn't be asked to proceed any further. Maybe a true puzzle enthusiast will enjoy it more than I did, but I feel that such a person would feel the game is too easy anyways.

Oafmatch is a great match three interpretation of classic RPGs, and an easy recommendation for the genre.

A match-3 puzzler with RPG elements, much in the vein of Puzzle Quest.
In short, it's a great iteration of the formula - fun and with well-thought-out mechanics. You've got a campaign mode with a goofy story and a sprawling set of characters and locations, and you can also go into a rogue-like mode where you go through consecutive encounters that whittle you down until you die... and then you start again.
It's great if you like this sort of thing. If you don't know if you like this sort of thing, well, think Bejewelled with an extra layer of RPG mechanics on top.
That out of the way, let's get into more detail:
You have an ever-growing cast of characters, each one with their own special ability, and a primary and a secondary stat (out of four). These primary and secondary stats determine the equipment they can, uh, equip. There's no experience, but you can spend gold to level up all of your characters at the same time.
You can take four people into battle, and while in the map you can swap them in or out or change their equipment as you wish. All battles give you gold, and sometimes treasures; in the campaign you automatically heal, and there are no consequences to losing a battle; not so in the roguelike mode.
The tiles on the battles represent each one of the stats (Wisdom is purple, Dexterity is Yellow, and so on) - damage done by matches is affected by the highest stat of that color from among all of your characters. So if your thief dies and no one else has a good Dexterity stat, matching yellow gems from then on is going cause very little damage. There are also "terrain" tiles, and when you gather ten of those a terrain effect that varies per battle comes into effect. This can be something like hitting all enemies for a sizeable amount of damage, or giving you some sort of boost.
After you make a move, then it's your opponent's turn. Enemies come in two main types - the basic mobs, which don't "act" but gather mana each turn. Once they have enough mana, they change a tile to an "attack" tile of the same color; this has a counter that goes down by one every turn, and when it reaches 0 it activates and (usually) takes a chunk of health from one or more characters.
Then there's more powerful enemies, marked by a red outline. They make matches of their own on their turn (never more than one move, at least to the point I played). So they gather Mana and have abilities much the same as your characters.
There are a lot more wrinkles and details - for example, when one of your characters is killed, they turn into a tile on the board; include that tile in a match, and they resurrect, although at a fraction of their health.
The campaign mode is pretty much what you'd expect out of a Puzzle Quest clone: a map of nodes, each one a battle or a town where you can get quests and buy stuff. Many of the nodes have little vignettes attached, and that's where the plot happens. At least it doesn't take itself seriously; it never quite made me laugh out loud, but it's charming, well-written and funny enough. As far as I got, all the battles are the same - there's no equivalent to the crafting or creature taming puzzles of Puzzle Quest.
The Rogue-like mode is... not for the faint of heart. I don't expect to spend too much time with it, but it's very rich. You're presented with a choice of two battles, with the reward an enemies for each clearly visible. Characters that end the battle dead stay dead, and any health loss is not healed in between battles. Building a good party, and changing it effectively as characters die, seems to be vital.
A word on randomness - it's pretty dialled down here; I never got the feeling that it cheated, the way Puzzle Quest seemed to cheat. The only exception is extra turns, I've haven't worked out how they happen yet and it can be annoying in that you can't plan around them except for very specific circumstances.
Anyhow, I think I've gone on long enough. I hope this helps you get a better idea of what the game plays like. There's precious few Puzzle Quest clones around that are worthwhile, and there's a reason I keep bringing that one up, and not any of its follow-ups. Oafmach, though, is definitely a keeper.

Great implementation of a puzzle-based RPG. As someone who likes puzzle-based RPGs, this is the game that I didn't realize I was waiting for.
Personally, I find the plot and characters amusing, but the real selling point is the strong mechanics and the sheer amount of content in a $5 game. (I would happily have bought the game at twice the price!) I have played a lot of Puzzlequest and Gems of War in the past -- and they are both excellent games -- but I like the gameplay of oafmatch significantly better than either of those games.
Oafmatch offers a wide variety of strategic decisions in selecting and equipping your party, as well a strong match-3 gameplay that rewards you for thinking ahead, but also throws in some interesting surprises. (Like when a ressurrect gem for a dead party-member appears in exactly the wrong spot on your board! <grin>) Also, I like the wide variety of effects available on equipable weapons ... many of which reward you for managing the board effectively. (E.g., the putrid ham that deals damage to an enemy each turn equal to the number of green gems on the board)
Ultimately, I think that a key selling point is the rogue-lite gameplay mode. I haven't made it far in that mode (still using the campaign to explore the gameplay mechanics) but the rogue-lite repeated runs at a randomized dungeon to unlock more content in a puzzle-based RPG is an awesome idea!

When I first saw that Monsterland, formerly Dead Colony in its lesser version (on Desura), was released a little over a month ago I was more than a little surprised. Don’t get me wrong I understand that there has been a revival of classic era-style gaming. Atari recently announced that they were bringing back 100 of their classic games in the spring with multiplayer support to Steam in the northern hemisphere Spring and Sanctuary RPG has been relatively successful on Steam as an ASCII adventure but a text shooter? How was that going to work? Surprisingly well and very playable as it turns out.
The concept of Monsterland is quite simple. You begin in a prison and your task is to get the hell out of there. You’re going to come across a lot of monsters that need to be destroyed before they kill you. Before you can contemplate killing them you’re going to have to find weapons and ammunition in which to kill them withg. You’ll also need to find health (H) so you can heal yourself, key cards in which to unlock doors and you’ll also need to learn how to use the environment of each level to your advantage (or your own death). All of this works surprisingly well. The text doesn’t limit immersion either. In fact, I would suggest that it had the opposite effect on me. It made me trigger my imagination quite a lot more than other games would.
If I was to pinpoint the biggest flaw in the game it would be the AI. When I played I discovered that the tracking that the enemy monsters employed to get to me was far too easy to understand and it became far too easy to pick them off. Other minor issues that I came across was that there isn’t a lot of ammunition spread out across the maps. This, however, can be argued as a positive as it makes you consciously aware of when and how to use the weapons that you have at your disposal and in many ways serves to counteract the issue with the AI. In stark contrast to the lack of ammunition is the at times absurd amount of ‘H’ or health spread across the map. I may have precious little ammunition but until I am overpowered by enemies my trusty little scrap gun will suffice.
I’ve seen other players compare the game to DOOM. Despite the obvious differences in artistic styles it’s an apt comparison due to the way in which you progress throughout the game and in the way you regenerate your health.  It’s a smart design choice as it always gives the player something to do – something to find, something to hunt down. It’s one of the strengths of the game. There’s always something to do which fits in well with the quick pace of the game.
Monsterland is a quick three hour long action game that is a helluva lot of fun to play. If you’re an action fan then you’ll want to at least try it.

SHOWTIME 2073
Platform: PC
MSRP: $0.99
Link to Lair Gaming's video review:
Welcome to the Lair Gaming review of PACMAN: RELOADED! Wait, no, that's not right. Oh, yeah - SHOWTIME 2073.
Showtime 2073 without a doubt draws inspiration from the aforementioned yellow dot-gobbler. Armed with what almost feels like a fully automatic version of the flak cannon from Unreal Tournament - you are tasked with collecting a number of round orbs from a maze-like map while assaulted from all angles by robots highly trained in martial arts. Has this caught your interest? It probably should.
Gameplay in Showtime 2073 not only looks like Unreal Tournament - it lives and breathes like it too. Running is a little floaty - and the fact that sprinting isn't a persistent feature leaves you constantly having to press and hold shift after each shot or jump. This sounds really nitpicky, but I honestly don't remember a circumstance where I didn't want to be sprinting - so having the default movement speed at sprint level would have been nice here. In addition, jumping was a frustrating affair on occasion. I would find myself trying to jump over portions of wall and getting stuck atop while enemies piled up on either side below. The engine was somehow unable to handle me riding the top of the wall and eventually would choose a direction to roll me off. In addition to some complaints regarding movement - I also wish there was some kind of impact sound or hit marker to show that you landed shots on your targets - but with the hectic movement and need to "spray and pray" to survive, I understand that there isn't really room for this nitpick to be completely satisfied. Lastly, I wish there was an option to disable the frequent slow-mo that comes when you kill enemies in quick succession. After a while, I did get used to it - and there were even some times I felt thankful for it when I was surrounded by enemies.
In my almost 3 hours with SHOWTIME 2073 to date, I've managed to get to level 5 a couple of times - but I've yet to finish it. The difficulty really ramps up when you hit level 4 and the game doesn't save your progress when you close the application (which is done by pressing the escape key - I learned accidentally). Luckily, deaths only take you back to the beginning of the current level rather than the beginning of the game.
SHOWTIME's soundtrack is wild. It's just a nonstop, body-shakingly loud bass attack throughout. I never got tired of it, but this just isn't music I'd be listening to in my spare time. That said, when my heart was racing - the heavy beat became the perfect track.
Visually, you're not going to feel like you're playing a game you paid sub-$1.00 for. The visuals are crisp and remind me of all of my favorite arena shooters. There aren't a ton of assets used in total. Weapon fire always looks the same and environments don't vary all that much. Still, where it counts, SHOWTIME 2073 delivers. Enemy variety is an excellent way that the developer knew his audience. I counted 5 total enemy types. It doesn't seem like much, but for the price - I honestly expected a single enemy type for every level.
SHOWTIME 2073 did make me want to go back and play Unreal Tournament 2004 again - but most importantly, it made me want to put that off a little while longer so I could stay in the task at hand. This game is so much fun - and I wholly recommend it when you have a spare dollar in your Steam account from selling old trading cards in the market. OK, maybe that's just the story of me finding this hidden gem.
Gameplay - 78
Visuals/Art Style - 73
Audio - 72
Content-to-cost at $0.99 - 90
For what it's worth, I give SHOWTIME 2073 on PC a: 78/100.

Star Traders is a rpg-strategy hybrid game where you take on the role of a space captain and explore a randomly generated map for fame and fortune.
As with all hybrid games it's hard to classify the game. Playing this reminds me of Sid Meier's Pirates! which I enjoyed a long time ago.
Some key features of the game:
0) You travel in a spaceship in a universe of systems connected with jumpgates. Each system contain planets you can visit. You experience random encounters in travel and take up missions and make decisions on the planets you visit.
1) Combat is turned based
2) Missions is card based
3) Both Missions and Combat is affected by jobs (classes) and traits (abilities)
4) Your Captain and Officers and Crews all play an important part in the mix of Jobs and Traits you get and this will heavily impact the outcome of the missions and actions you take
5) You have a very large range of Jobs you can take.
6) There are different ships and modules you can upgrade, you can also equip your crews with different weapons for Land combat
The Pros:
1) The developers have an excellent track for completing and launching their games. I bought this game based off the pleasurable time I had with Templar Battleforce. They are extremely responsive to suggestions on improvements to the game and have issued 4 patches with of bug fixes and improvements in under 2 weeks since EA! Expect a lot of development activity in EA!
2) The game right now is deep enough to have fun with the still evolving gameplay. In EA, it contains enough content and working game systems to shame some indie fully released games.
3) Support them early. Success is the best motivation to a good team in EA! There's a discount that's ending soon =).
Cons:
1) As it's in EA, the documentation is a bit thin. Most of the information is in the forum. The WIKI is still lacking in detailed explainations of some game systems.
2) The game is still evolving and content is still to be fully fleshed out. So expect an uneven experience. You milage may vary, but some may find the free roam + make my own adventure structure of the game off-putting.
3) There's still bugs to be ironed out and UI to be enhanced.
It's a really good EA title. And the developers are hard at work on this judging from the frequency of the patches.
Recommended!

Let me try to explain the nostalgia value of this: Back then around 1990 on Amiga, the processor ran at 7.16 MHz, we had 512 or 1024 KB of memory, harddisks were still an exception, there were 4 sound hardware channels to simultaneously play samples on, 320×256 pixel graphics (4096 possible colors, but without tricks max. 32 of those simultaneously) etc. - quite limited times, but with great programming (the absolute best example of which: "Turrican II" omfg what a feast that was), the boundaries could be overcome, and we constantly kept experiencing more retreat of these boundaries.
The demo scene kept bringing new exciting tech to our screens, one of which was 3D vector graphics. While "Another World" is not 3D, it partly uses vector graphics to tell its story e.g. for the player avatar and shots/explosions. The big difference between baked images/animations and actual vector graphics is that with the latter, a developer can directly manifest their will on screen. They can just change a number to draw everything a bit bigger or to rotate stuff. Vector graphics also allow all kinds of shape shifts (see e.g. walk animation), because not every stage of the animation needs to exist as an image (none actually). It also allows much more cinematic use of graphics, which this game shows right away at the beginning. A movie - told with the in-game graphics engine instead of being a brutally compressed low res movie as we were used to (if we had a movie clip at all).
Not only was it great to see this in action, it also made clear to us
. Nowadays, we
what can be. It has become completely normal today to have this in
dimensions, with textures and elaborate material effects, and in super high res (1920x1080 is >25 times the amount of pixels as 320x256, 4K resolution even >100 times as much). We were there back then when this began, and Another World was the first game (that I know of) that had filled 2D vector animations.

Tristoy is a great achievement, considering its developed by a rather small indie studio.
It delivers on all levels, with nice hand-drawn visuals, great story-telling and a unique gameplay experience.
The game is designed for coop. That said, if you don't have a friend to play with, or if you prefer competitive games, Tristoy might not be up your alley. However, if you are a fan of the genre you'll find some great innovation in this game.
Tristoy may be the first game which supports a dialogue system tailored to two players. The dialogue options between the two characters can influence the story, as well as some gameplay elements. The dynamic split screen is another neat innovation to the genre, which makes splitting up and reuniting with your partner a real atmospheric event.
The only downside of the game is the high difficulty. The platforming aspects of the game can become quite frustrating if you are not prepared to playing the same passage multiple times.
Still, I'd prefer that any day over a game that's too easy and beaten in a couple of hours.
If you are not speed-running through the game, and take your time to listen to the dialogues, I'd say you'll get at least 5 hours out of Tristoy.
tl;dr
If you like a story-rich coop experience and can tolerate some difficult platforming, definitevly give this a go.
8/10

I don't care what anyone says, this game is amazing. Yes, it has a lot of dialogue and text. Yes, the combat is sort of like an early Diablo game and not ultra strategic, tactical or hardcore. Yes, you'll also be drinking a lot of potions (probably, if you don't built a great character your first go around.) But, the game itself is way, way more than the sum of its parts and very engrossing.
Inquisitor features a medieval setting where everything you read about Christianity and the Book of Revelations is coming true. There are tales of demons running amok, succubuses stealing the bodies of others, demonic super storms with howling souls like winds and all sorts of mayhem going on related to religion. At least, it sure seems that way. What i mean is, that is something the game does very well - it is sort of like an investigative RPG. You are never quite sure what is fact and what is fiction, who is telling the truth and who is lying, who's a real person or a demon in disguise. It strikes an oppressive, eerie and always-interesting atmosphere and quite frankly it's a bit freaky and scary at times. The exploration is very rewarding as only those old-school-style CRPGs can be, as everything is hand-placed and there are intrigue, mystery, secrets and things to find around every corner.
The combat is simple in most ways as it resembles a sort of Diablo 1/Diablo 2 kind of real-time combat. You can recruit unique party members who will join you and have quests and stories of their own, but you can't really pause the game like similar CRPGs such as Pillars of Eternity or Baldur's Gate. Still, the combat is challenging and it is rewarding to overcome the often-difficult boss encounters. I find the combat to be just fine, as not every RPG needs to be turn-based or have advanced tactical control, although this game does give you a bit of control as well, such as commands you can give your party members in real-time. The exploration is tied to the combat in such a way that it is a joy to defeat the enemies to see the next part of the dungeon, or whatever the strange creature you fought was guarding.
There are also other unique elements in the game, like the whole being an Inquisitor angle. You are sniffing out heretics among the townspeople and have the opportunity to sentence them to death, after you interrogate them, of course, and make sure you have the right person. It's really interesting stuff as you have to use your brain and piece together clues and subtle hints to discover the truth. There is a lot of talking, especially at first, and this may initially turn some off from the game as it in turn creates a bit of a slow start. But once you start getting clues, exploring the surrounding areas and figuring out what's going on it really picks up steam. It also really rewards you when things come together and you figure things out on your own, and there are plenty of curveballs and crazy surprises along the way.
This is one of those RPGs that will go down in history as a very overlooked classic. It may take more years for that to happen, but the game is so unique and engrossing that it is bound to happen eventually. If you like the sound of a unique, immersive medieval setting that really plays on the myths and legends of religion, with an eerie atmosphere, excellent exploration, lots of well-written dialogue and the investigative aspects of being an Inquisitor, buy it now. If you like old-school-style CRPGs like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Konung 2 or Planescape: Torment, you should buy it now, but just expect it isn't quite the same as those but still retains a lot of their core ideas and old-school philosophy. You won't regret it, unless of course a demon slaughters you and Satan himself steals your soul.

This is an excellent digital version of an excellent board game. It's an enjoyable reproduction of a tabletop game that's well executed with one glaring exception- the payment model. You can freely play two maps, but the vast majority of the game requires an in game currency that, apart from some granted when you start playing, can only be acquired by spending real money. There is no option to unlock certain maps or simply buy a full version. If you want to play again and again, which you will, you have to keep paying money.
I would happily give the developers a handful of my hard earned cash for unlimited play. I'd even pay more if they add new maps. I can't justify paying for each game I play- what if I get interrupted or get matched with a lousy opponent? More importantly, why should I keep paying after I've paid a fair price? If the developers want more of my money, make some cool new content. I'll even pay more than I probably should for it.
Even if money is no object for you, don't buy this game- supporting this payment model ruins it for the rest of us.

The Good;
- INSANELY deep gameplay for an early access $11 game. Like seriously, it's ♥♥♥♥ing insane, like, I cannot even start to list all the traits, contacts, reputation etc etc for every single planet / faction in this game. It's utterly insane.
- Tons of different play styles you can go after (ship to ship combat, trade, spying, ground combat etc)
- Nice art style with customizable visual appearence for each crew member along with heavy customization of crew talents / professions and ship gear.
- Did I mention this game is INSANELY deep?
The Bad;
- Learning curve is basically a vertical asymptote. There is NOTHING that explains to you what in the ♥♥♥♥ any of these stats, attributes, debuffs etc mean. Even when designing your captain, there's pretty much zero explanation of what anything is, so you're essentially flying blind through most of the game through trial and error figuring out what crew does what, why you need them etc
- So theres about like 7+ mini games between ship to ship, ground, spy, patrol, MUDD style quests etc. but once again, you have no idea what the rules are or how anything works, so you'll find yourself getting demolished in one of these game modes and you have no idea what you're doing wrong or what you should even try to do to not suck.
- Although the game is insanely deep, none of that complexity really DOES anything. You basically just fly around progressively longer distances having the same random events occur where you either choose to fight the ship or just run away. And there's like almost no reason to fight the ships because you lose reputation and will rack up hefty repair bills, have crew die etc. So the game becomes really boring as you click from warp-gate to warp-gate, having to stop every so often to refuel and pay your crew on a planet somewhere.
- Unrelated to the above, the story elements that do exist are pretty weak and the script for the text base conversations is pretty painfully bad, you will skip all every single time.
- RNG for losing crew and stuff is probably a little *too* steep as it stands now. I had high levels crew leave because I didn't land intime to pay them because I was doing whatever, and after like spending the entire game on my ship they bounce. Worst part is there's no like progress bar for when you have to pay your crew, so you're just blindly stopping at planets trying to pay them everytime you can. Plus the game CONSTANTLY auto rolls anytime your ship is moving for bad♥♥♥♥♥♥to happen to you and your crews skills / talents are the only thing that stop it, but bad♥♥♥♥♥♥will still happen because of RNG. I think it'd be a bit nicer if you had a chance of some beneficial RNG to happen to mix it up instead of just wondering when there's gonna be some sort of electronics explosion or w/e that mames half your crew while you're running for you life from a pirate.
IN CONCLUSION / TL:DR
Game is undeniabley INSANELY complex, with a learning curve that more akin to a brick wall. After spending 7-8 hours messing around, I can say the game has a TON of potential moving forward. But as it stands now it needs a LOT of tweaking to make it live up to that potential.
Things it needs before I'd recommend someone buying it;
- A decent tutorial for the different game modes to explain the basic rules so you don't keep losing crew b/c you don't understand wtf is happening
- MOTHER ♥♥♥♥ING TOOLTIPS for stats etc to give you an idea of what % increase or decrease in whatever it provides
- Tweaking gameplay to involve less fetch / deliver and more ground / space combat / spying etc. It's incorperated to the story based missions but like 75% of the auto generated missions are fetch quests.
- Did I say some decent ♥♥♥♥ing tutorials and some tool tip explanations?
I'm having a lot of fun with this game so far. Highly Recommended

Compared to other Touhou games? My first was PCB and this gives me a lot of the same vibes, but it doesn't have quite the same level of visual spectacle (admittedly I'm mostly thinking of the final bosses). It's a good middle ground difficulty-wise, and the mechanics are fairly easy to understand for scoring. I do find the spellcards a bit...lacking visually (they don't really match their themes if that makes sense) but it feels like there's a bit more variety within the game in terms of ...play style? That said so far I find this one's a bit messier visually even with the English patch's transparency fix, and the backgrounds are a little busy in places so it can be disorienting at times. It also stretches really weirdly on the highest resolution setting, and I'd recommend picking the middle one instead (the patched menu is especially unreadable stretched for some reason).
At the end of the day though this whole review is horribly biased because I love Touhou. If you didn't like other Touhou games this one will not change your mind.

I knew it was good, but I didn't realise it was that good!
Mechanically the game has been polished to a shine and the ninja feels wonderful to control. The controls are responsive and it ties in wonderfully with the smooth animations. Traversing the levels is quite easy, but with a respectable skill ceiling to work towards. By the end if you're good enough you'll glide through the levels like some sort of parkour superhero.
So far it seems like every level you can
- be a master of stealth by not killing anyone, or even startling/confusing any guard
- be a homicidal maniac and kill everyone in the most imaginative ways possible
- be a pshycopath and scare guards out of their minds with the bodies of their friends, and then kill them!
- mix and match as you want or as is needed to get the level achievements
What is nice about the level achievements is that once you get them, they've been unlocked for good. So in subsequent runs of the level (eg to look for secrets that you missed) you can choose any playstyle you want. The score you earn each level unlocks new items, skins and abilities which you can use to create the perfect character for a certain playstyle. Eg. a character that doesn't have any weapons, but can sprint in complete silence.
Any negatives? Well apart from the fact that it ends, I don't like that all passage ways are revealed on the map. It makes secret hunting too easy. Though I still managed to miss some regardless.

Ever since Ubisoft picked up the rights to the Might & Magic franchise after 3DO went bankrupt and took New World Computing down with it, their work as a publisher for the franchise has been...hit or miss. And usually a buggy, ill provided mess. Clash of Heroes is not such a story; it is the single most polished game to come out of the franchise since the aquisition, helped by its gorgeous art style that immediately evokes Avatar: The Last Airbender, but actually makes me think back to Heroes of Might & Magic 2, with its simple graphics still being the best in the franchise due to just a timeless style. The only thing holding Clash of Heroes back from being an out and out classic is its schizophrenic difficulty curve, and an ending sequence barely any better than a series of title cards with plain letter text.
But it's an incredibly solid puzzle game, and, while the unit recruiting/resource mechanic is a bit tacked on, the artifact and unit tier mechanics are definitely good additions. And, god damn, what sells this game the most, for me, is the total tongue in cheek nature of its story and characters. Like, after Heroes V took itself way too seriously and was just frustratingly stupid, and Dark Messiah took itself way too seriously and was just hilariously stupid, Clash of Heroes almost went and took the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the Ashan universe, which, coupled with Might & Magic X's actually good storyline, gave me hope for this revival of the franchise.

This game is joyous and bursting with charm. It had such an effect on me that I literally started cooking again. There are some rough edges -- framerate issues at full rez, some awkward bugs, little side content and no head-to-head multiplayer -- but none of them are enough to make the experience anything other than solidly worthwhile. I normally stay away from early access because I prefer a "finished" game.  Something about this caught my attention and I am glad I took a chance on it.  The game still needs to flesh out the content and improve some quality of life issues but it is already in better shape than some "finished" games I have played in the past and updates have been common since I started playing.  This is a fairly straight forward turn based game where you create a ship captain as an avatar but includes both ships officers and crew.  The officers and crew offer different options in various situations and need to be managed and levelled to make the most effective team while the size of the team is dictated by your current ship.  Game play includes various missions that have a large RNG outcome (5 different outcomes selected randomly based on the mission that you see before choosing to proceed in what I have seen so far) that can be influenced by captain, officer, and crew skills and combat that consists of ship to ship and 4 on 4 crew battles.  Where the game offers some great twists is the Captain template character creator and the faction/contact mechanic.  The Captain template allows you to trade off different aspects of your starting character by requiring you to rank different categories which dictates the available pool you get to invest in that category so some tradeoffs are required.  If you want the best possible starting ship you need to sacrifice somewhere else.  The faction/contact mechanic dictates which missions are available, upgrades and bonuses, and some services that are available in star ports.  The contacts have both personal interactions and faction interactions that can change during the game and through your actions which provides some added consequence to many of the random encounters and missions throughout the game.  Overall I am very pleased with the game so far and if you enjoy turn based RPG’s with consequences to your actions then give this a try.

I've been playing Malevolence since the Kickstarter release and loving every minute of
it. I'm a great fan of RPG's and roguelikes and Malevolence definately scratches both
itches. I also love when games are unpredictable and you don't know what to expect on
each playthrough.
The game is very old school with some innovative modern touches, the world all
the players play in is truly infinte with each player adventuring in the same version
of the world but discovering areas other players haven't been to yet. When players
discover new areas with online functionality it's possible to claim locations so if other players adventure to the same place it will say who claimed the location. Other online functions are planned and the game has a great community sharing gameplay experiences and finds.
All the loot, quests, dungeons and the world are procedurally generated but the dungeons and world are the same for everyone once an area as been discovered so if players find really cool/difficult dungeons they can share the coordinates and challenge others to clear the dungeon.
Travel in such a vast world is by Griffon and once players have enough gold they can leave the starting area and explore freely going to places far away that have not been discovered by anyone else.
Something else I love about the game is the emergent nature, things just seem to happen to throw spanners in the works and problem solving is often required to complete a quest or dungeon.
The best way to play is permadeath with the gamma turned to zero so the dungeons are truly very dark and torches are essential. With the lights down low exploring can be very intense and I find myself getting drawn into the game. Permadeath also means your name is entered onto the leaderboard so others can see how your adventures are going.
Finally I have to mention the dev team who are the icing on an already delicious cake, updates come frequently and the forums are a hotbed of ideas and player posted challenges which will only grow as the games audience widens. I've seen the game progress from a basic dungeon crawl to something very special indeed and if you value fantastic gameplay and love retro rpg graphics and enjoyed the golden age of RPG gaming then perhaps Malevolence is for you.
I certainly recommend it and wish it all the luck in the world as it goes live on Steam.

Having been a long-time follower of Malevolence and one of the first backers on Kickstarter, I am very excited to finally see this game take it's place on Steam.
Malevolence is a blend of old-school RPG-style difficulty blended with modern systems; for example the various online elements. While you will never see another person in the game with you, if you are online while playing the game you will be able to interact with other players in a number of ways, for example the permadeath ladder where you can compete against other permadeath players, the claiming system where each major part of the world (Such as cities, dungeons and so on) can be claimed, and upon other players visiting that spot, they will see that you were there first.
Some online functionality is even a bit more secretive and should be discovered in-game.
The combat is turn based and gives the player the option of using melee, bows or spells, or mixing them to make a more balanced character.
The equipment is procedurally generated, not just the looks of weapons but also effects and values of armor, weapons and spells.
Aside from that there is an array of quest types (The quest system is still being expanded upon), special epic loot for those that brave the deepest of dungeons and take on the dungeon boss, various guilds to join and much else.

Monsterland feels in some ways like it was based on DoomRL... which is kind of funny, given that DoomRL was, as the name indicates, a roguelike based off of Doom, a first-person shooter. Monsterland takes that back to the Doom formula in terms of having six handmade levels and being a fast-paced action game. It's less solid than DoomRL, but DoomRL is one of the more interesting free roguelikes out there, so I'm not going to fault it too much for that.
Monsterland is honestly a pretty amusing action game, but it also gets rather frustrating at times. When the developer says "Game can be saved and loaded at any time. Because sometimes, you just eat a rocket to the face." it's ... pretty accurate, though suddenly running into chaingunners (teal Ms) or the few NRG-8000 enemies (bright yellow Ms) was just as bad. Dying or taking excessive damage from opening a door or blasting through a fragile wall into a pile of BS that you didn't expect is unfortunately common, but you can save at any point, so it's easy to just reload and come through with the appropriate weapon in hand and strategy in mind. I don't mind saving frequently for that, but if it seems like it would make you mad, this might not be the game for you unless you're better than I am. :)
As far as the weapons go, I found them nicely balanced, with the exception of the range shotgun, which is pretty useless except for destroying barrels and picking off single red enemies without wasting ammo. Most weapons were useful at different times, though the chaingun is pretty much completely replaced by the minigun once you get it - but you don't get the minigun until near the end of the game, so that's fair enough.
In sum, Monsterland is a pretty solid game for its $1 asking price. It has about three to four hours of content, as mentioned by the developer, and while it's on the simple side, the controls are responsive and the level design is generally pretty solid.

Not the first of its kind but certainly an entertaining one. The dialogues between the characters that you meet throughout the campaign are very amusing. This could only be topped by having a bunch of good voice actors, to voice all 30 of them. But a little imagination works well, too.
I'd recommend playing on 3 star difficulty as much as you can, you will get more gold, and therefore can buy more levelups. If you can't beat an encounter, you can always go down a star or two, but not the other way around. I don't think the balancing works well in this regard.
I've often felt that the mana cost for a lot of items is too high to be useful. Once you have enough mana through making matches, the battles are often over and you wouldn't have needed the item ability in the first place. This worsens further as after each wave (on multi-wave encounters), your mana is reset to zero. Making me question if this concept is working well or not.
The campaign drags on for quite a while, and you get little pieces of the story only when you beat an encounter, to further the campaign. So it's not surprising that you can spend 30+ hours on it. But it had me captivated for several hours straight, and I'm sure I will enjoy the campaign in more moderate amounts in the future, here and there.
A lot of the encounters feel like they have a theme, which is reflected in the music track that will be played. I felt like it varies often enough so that it's not repetitive, and they're well picked.
Every map area also has an arena challenge with 20 waves, where you can earn/loot additional items. And then of course there's the Roguelite game mode that you can spend time with, an interesting spin on dungeon crawling.
The strategic element of picking a party of 4 and equipping them with items, opens up different play styles. Which includes carefully picking your target priority. The creatures you encounter all have similar, yet different abilities, some of which your party might handle better, or worse.
I'm probably a little biased, and I did have a positive attitude towards the game from the get-go, on account of having received a preview copy. But I'd still say you're getting a solid Match-3 hybrid that is fun to play.

Oafmatch is a bejeweled-RPG hybrid, heavy on the RPG elements. Match 3 jewels of the same color to deal damage to enemies based off your character's stats, and use spells and abilities to deal extra damage, buff/debuff, heal, alter the board, etc. If you've played Puzzle Quest or any of its innumerable clones you know what to expect here.
The graphics and sounds are amateur but not offensive. The music sounds like it might be from some sort of license-free music library and doesn't fit the game at all. None of these things are that important in a game like this, but it gives the game an unpolished feel. For $5, though, it's about what you'd expect.
The main problem I have with Oafmatch is in the gameplay. Stats, levels and equipment (of both your party and the enemy) have a disproportionately large influence on the outcome of a match. No amount of smart or lucky play will allow you to beat an enemy team that has spells that deal 150% of your party's HP in one hit. You simply need to grind up or lower the difficulty until your numbers are large enough that you can steamroll the encounter.
I read that this game has a 30-hour long campaign, but it's hard to imagine sticking with something this simple and grindy for longer than a few hours. The writing is not going to keep you clicking, either. Every character has one trope to their name (dumb strong guy, cowardly guy, thief who likes to loot, etc, etc, etc) and they all have the same dry/sarcastic sense of humor. It reminds me a lot of early 2000's webcomics.
Anyway. I'd like this a lot more if the numbers were all flattened a great deal, and increasing the difficulty required smarter play, or put a time limit on your moves, or asked anything of you but more of your IRL time grinding. As of now (May 19th 2017) this game is largely forgettable. Good luck to the dev in future games or perhaps in modifying this one to be a bit more interesting.
I recommend this game if you like Match-3 games. It adds RPG elements to make things interesting. 9/10

In my opinion, Megamagic: Wizards of the Neon Age is a fantastic game. It has an 80's retro feel aesthetically to it, but it is extremely responsive and fun to play.  You are able to summon creatures to fight alongside of you and have your friends or family members use controllers to help you battle. The combat is really fun action combat (instead of any boring tab target crap which I hate) where you have to aim your skills to hit the enemy creatures. I'm only on chapter three so far, but the game has a really nice story and tons of dialog that I'm actually interested in reading. As of yet I haven't run into any bugs or glitches at all, which makes me feel as if the creators put a lot of work into testing and polishing the game for release. Also, based on what I've seen so far in the spell book and summoning menus, there seem to be a lot of unique spells and summons in the game. The gameplay reminds me heavily of diablo 2 except there are a few puzzles mixed in and you have the ability to control your summons by yourself or with help of a friend.
The only real negative in my opinion is that you can't go online to battle others, although for someone who plays single player games or enjoys sitting in the same room as someone they are playing with, this game makes for a suprisingly good ARPG. The other small complaint I have is that pressing enter to go through the dialog makes me take my hand off the mouse frequently, (I'd almost rather spacebar serve as a skip dialog button) but it's not a major drawback as the game gives you plenty of time to put your hand back on the mouse before any fight sequences take place.
Overall I'd say I very much enjoy playing it and would recommend it to others.

Developed and published by BeautiFun Games, Megamagic: Wizards of the Neon Age combines fantasy elements such as the use of magic with post-apocalyptic locations and some neo-noir inspiration from Blade Runner’s own neon-lit urban sprawl. This is the dev team’s second game on Steam and they have shown clear signs that they’re capable of delivering a quality game.

Megamagic: Wizards of the Neon Age features a very complex combat system focusing on five magical schools with many spells and disciplines to master. It wouldn’t be an RPG without a set of skills so that is also provided. I found the RTS style of combat to be far better than a TBS form found in the Shadowrun series, for example. Plenty of tactical opportunities that require careful planning. The boss fights can be challenging but that is not a bad thing at all. The game has no leveling system but this novel aspect wasn’t really an issue since you still have real progression through skills and spells. Despite being an open world, the story has no side quests and the linearity of it all, did bother me enough to consider it a con. This beautiful  game world really needs more activities and quests to blend in with the many easter eggs and pop culture references already present. The fact that we have a multiplayer option in the form of local co-op can be the saving grace for those that find SP playthroughs too tedious.

The graphical details in Megamagic are top quality. As far as 2D sprites go, you can’t have them any better than this. The lighting, the particle effects and shading diversity, all scream 2016. The areas and NPCs have been very well polished and I haven’t seen many texture glitches either. So you have a beautiful game in isometric projection which emulates classic RPGs from the past with a modern twist.

The soundtrack is provided by composer Mitch Murder, of Hotline Miami 2 and Kung Fury fame. Someone who composed for those two gems, can’t go wrong with a 3rd ‘80s spinoff title, can he? The game’s sounds and music score is brilliant and fits well within the setting and story. Definitely no complaints here.

Costume Quest 2 is the second game in this series developed by Double Fine Productions.  You play the role of two twin siblings, Reynold and Wren.  The game follows on from the original game in the story and offers much of the same game play elements.  The game has been released on PS3, 360, PS4, Xbox One, WiiU and all of the PC platforms.
Like I said, the gameplay is very much the same as the first game, you travel around in your party exploring the world and encounter enemies, which you battle in a turn based fight scene. These fight scenes have an essence of QTEs in them, so if you hit the button at exactly the right time, you'll either do more damage, or block more damage. As you venture throughout the game, you will discover new and interesting costumes to wear - each costume has its own special ability and unique style of play.  There is some real interesting costumes to find, my favorite is the Clown costume, which acts as your early game healer, but you also have tanky classes and damage dealing classes like in other RPG games.
Graphically, Costume Quest 2 is identical to the original. The art style is beautiful though, I loved the stylized world that you are put in and all of the characters just look gorgeous.  The animation in cut scenes and in the game are second to none too.  The game is so well optimized that pretty much any rig can play this in its full glory.
The plot is similar to the first game too; you are out to stop Dr. Orel White who has taken over the world and aims to bring an end to the holiday, Halloween! Obviously being the candy loving kids we all are, we can't let that happen and you must stop him.  With an element of time travel to be seen, there is some very interesting plot points throughout the game, and this comes with the inclusion of some brilliantly comical moments along the way too.
Sadly the game is not voice acted - for me I was hoping it would be given how popular the first game was, but this doesn't take away any of the charm the game has. You can pretty much imagine how each of the characters in the game would sound, and the animation of them all with the facial expressions aids this ten fold too.
Costume Quest 2 has moments of difficulty; some of the quests are not easily figured out and you have to put a bit of thought into them, or working out where to go next in order to progress the game. Not to mention the boss battles can also get quite intensive too; I actually had to spend a fair amount of time grinding my characters up a few levels just so they were on par with the difficulty of the bosses I was facing. This is by no means a bad thing as with each fight you win, you also get the chance to win a card, which will have a unique effect that you can use in a battle, such as avoiding attacks, doing double damage, or sometimes actually out right killing an enemy no questions asked!
That brings me onto the level design, every single level in Costume Quest has absolutely tons of areas to explore and items to find. You have to destroy typical game world items in order to find the games currency, candy. The candy can the be spent at the vendors which are scattered around the world to purchase costume upgrades, or the above mentioned special effect cards. Each level also has a handful of side quests which you can complete, granting further experience points and candy as rewards. I would recommend people actually focus on the side quests before progressing in the main quest just so you keep up at the right level compared to the enemies. Some of the side quests are linked to the main quest; but a lot can be skipped over if you really want to.
A full playthrough with completing the majority of the side quests at a leisurely pace took me just under nine hours to complete which is actually a bit of a jump in length compared to the original which only took me five hours to finish. Again though, there is no reason at all to play through Costume Quest 2 for a second time apart from maybe mopping up a few achievements if that's your jam. Much like the first, I would really of liked to have seen a "New Game+" mode just to squeeze a couple more hours out of it, and maybe introducing local co-op too, that would be an almost perfect addition given that you play as twins the whole way through the game.
I had virtually no technical issues in my run through. I was able to play at 4K resolution with a steady 60 FPS the whole time. I did run into a few bugs where you could actually walk through some walls when interacting with items on the other side of the wall such as ladders and chests, but there are no real game breaking bugs to be found. I played the game with a controller given the amount of QTEs in the game, I felt that would be a better option, but this can just as easily be played with keyboard and mouse too.
To sum up, I think Costume Quest 2 does exactly the same as the Costume Quest just bigger and better. I can only hope that there is going to be a third game in this series as it just gets better and better with each release. I will go as far to say this is one of my favorite games I have played this year so it gets a strong recommendation from me!

5) This is a must play

When I first read about this game it was a dream come true. A Co-op Metroidvania style game! Almost never done before! To my dismay this game did not live up to its promise as such a game. It only took the very core-aspects of that style of game and made it real.
Story:
The story follows two males who are trapped on "Tristoy" a prison island mean't for those who are traitors to the Iron King. They are forced to work together to secure their escape from Tristoy.
For better or for worst the story was actually quite interesting and the voice acting was absoulutely perfect! The interaction between the two main characters was hilarious. I was however disappointed at how little you get to know about the rest of the world.
This game is fairly short with me and my friend finishing it in about 2 hours so obviously it was a short story too.
Gameplay:
The gameplay was declared to be similar to Metroidvania style but to be honest, its more akin to Trine style. You are a co-op team that must stick together to solve a variety of puzzles to progess through the levels. It is a linear progression throughout the game, I actually thought from the art in the background you would end up going down the Tower and then back up again! But this was untrue. Combat is short and is a not too in depth either.
At the beginning of the game there are a few decisions that can effect the amount of health divided amongst the two main characters. Honestly this made little to no difference considering all it allows is one character to take 1 or 2 more hits, almost every monster can 1-hit KO.
The conversational choices had NO impact on the story what so ever even though it you would presume so. I encountered many bugs within the game and especially in the end with such errors as "[story path not found]".
HOWEVER
Me and my friend did have fun even though we felt 10 quid for this unpolished game was outright robbery, if not huge kick in the teeth. I do respect though only a handful of developers were on this game in comparison to others.
Graphics/sounds:
I LOVE the art-work and the music, they suited the mood very well and gave the game its own personal feel.
Overall:
If the developers had added more content, more exploration and just maybe the ability to separate into different rooms, this could of been one of the most successful games around. Already pumping out a game with no single-player can be quite a risk in doing.
Unfortunately this game in its current state cannot be recommended due to it being 15 quid retail when this is something that could of probably better off benefited from being in early access. It is worth more along 5 - 8 quid in my opinion for the level of effort put into this game and the amount of bugs it has inherited.

Memoir '44 Online is a "free to play" video game reproduction of the actual Board Game Memoir '44.  Worked on Win 10 , looked ok, played ok, sounded ok.  It amounts to more as a Pay to Play than Free to Play game.  Does help diehard fans of this boardgame to find opponents online.  You really need to like playing the boardgame Memoir'44 to like this game.
You can spend from your steam wallet: 5 dollar for 125 gold, 15 dollar for 400 gold, or 30 dollar for 1,000 gold and Expert Mode.  You start off with 50 free gold.  The game is turn-based on hex map that is divided into three sections Right Flank, Center and Left Flank.  You have two kinds of cards that give your units orders, Command and Tactics.  You randomly draw cards but get to pick one of two drawn.  You have to pay 2 or 3 gold per play of a scenario ( didn't see any for 1 ).
You can play Solo vs AI or against another online player.  There is a tuturial video but it didn't help teach the game much, you need to read the manual and seek out more clearer help.  The AI is effective as an opponent.
At the time of this review, i saw like 30 players online, so you can find someone to play, with plenty of invites to play from other online players.  It has a lobby chatroom and uses languages of English or French. You can play with your Steam account or the Days of Wonder account.  Has Steam Achievements.
CONS:
- Has business model of charging you gold for each play of a scenario.
- The online tutorial video have a lot of loading lag.
- There are Only 2 Scenarios (Pegasus Bridge and Juno Beach) that are truly Free.
- Expert mode is currently in Developement.
- Very annoying flicking of rainbow colors as a highlighting feature.
Try it, only if you like wargame board games.  Don't expect to play this game for free for long.
