Christ, where do I start. Ok, here goes, so, im not really an anime/manga type of person. Theres some good animes, and theres some good mangas, just not really my thing.  Then theres Higurashi. See i started by trying out Doki doki Literature Club, right? Next thing i know steam wants me to know about every visual novel available on the platform, almost kind of annoying, as i only played one, and so many more of other games. Why is this important? Shut it, im getting there. Over the holidays i was doing the que thing and getting the trading cards, then this "game" popped up. I read most of the store page, some reviews, and decided for a 2 bucks, at worst i could refund it if i wasnt interested. 14 hours later I was purchasing the chapter 2, i currently own all 5. I guess my point here is, you dont need to be a weeb to get into this.
Lets cover something first while were in the middle, this game has a preset difficulty thats mentioned when you first start. One may wonder, "why does this book have a difficulty?", and the answer is simple, How hard did you try to understand and figure out what was going on. Thats the game, understanding.
So lets cover some pros
Amazing story, i mean its nuts.
Character depth is phenominal, each person in the story has their own unique personality and traits.
The music is fairly catchy
easy to pick up and put down as neccessary
of course theres some downsides
Its written kind of like a book, so at times it can be ahrd to tell whos saying what, but not overly so
the ui kind of sucks
the orignal backgrounds look funny
the original artwork is absolute hot garbage, thank god for the updates
Overall, after reading all 5 available on steam, Im eager to read the rest (i think 14 in the whole story), The story has been enthralling thus far. youll laugh, maybe cry (dont be a weenie), be shocked, confused, anxious, and downright angry a times. maybe youll get those shivers and chills down your spine, goosebumps like i did as the story starts to develop. As I had Solarix and DeVoid already in my library I received PAC for free like everyone who already owned one of the games - a nice present from the developers. This new game is a combination of the stories of the two previous games in a walking simulator without combat or stealth sections.
You can explore the levels, take in the vistas and read and listen to logs of the colony crew at your own pace as your character is in no danger to die. This will be not everybody's bag of tea but I liked it enough to keep me interested.
The first part telling the Solarix story from the perspective of Walter Terrace can be frustrating as due to the dark color palette it's easy to overlook an item like a key card you'll need to progress.
DeVoid's story told from Elizabeth Woolgather's perspective looks in comparison like day to night with brighter colors and overall crisper, cleaner textures. I also like the soundtrack in the DeVoid part better.
If you, like me, love SciFi themed games and/or walking sims you should definitely take this game into consideration.
I played through the Solarix part and have still to finish the DeVoid story and spent around 8 hours due to some backtracking. You'll get your money's worth out of Planet Ancyra Chronicles even if you're more observant than me.
With trading cards, achievements and controller support there's the whole package a Steam user could want at a fair price. I can recommend PAC if you want to play a SciFi walking sim.

Another World is the original title for several adaptations of the game in the 90's. The most popular being Out of This World for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. Originally designed for the Amiga and Atari ST computers, the game was an advancement in technology where previously games would use sprites, or text based graphics, this game would use rotoscoping animations and real-time cutscenes. The game, developed by Eric Chahi with music composed by Jean-François Freitas, went on to have critical and commercial success. It's engaging storyline and original gameplay inspired many other games such as Flashback, Ico, and Metal Gear Solid.
You play as Lester Knight Chaykin, a physicist with a penchant for fast cars and faster scientific results. One night, our hero enters his laboratory with the sole purpose of reconstructing the big bang using a particle accelerator. He enters a new formula, starts the accelerator, enjoys a soft drink and waits.
Disaster! A lightning storm brews outside and with a the will of Mother Nature the accelerator is hit and causes a chain reaction sending Lester to Another World.

When it comes to Out of this World (Or Another World, whichever you prefer), it seems as though the majority of people who've played it consider it to be a video game masterpeice.
And then there's IGN who gave it a 4/10. But they suck. So let's talk about my opinion.
I enjoyed it. I wouldn't consider it as great as some other people made it out to be, but I think it was a unique video game experience that I'll definitely play again in the future.
Another World follows a professor working on some experiments late at night, when a thunderstorm breaks out, and you're stranded in another dimention... another world, as the title implies. You first attempt to survive, but then you're captured by the ruling government in the area, and you make your new friend... Mike Aruba. Game Grumps fans know what I'm talking about.
The game is relatively simple. You can run, jump, stomp, and shoot and the challenges stick primarily to those abilities, save for some exceptions here and there. But I enjoy Another World for it's difficulty being enough of a ramp that you can still grasp what you have to do.
But there are points where Another World is just being f***ing unfair.
There are certain portions where you have to have enough foresight from dying earlier, that you know what to do. Sometimes you don't even need that. You need so much foresight, that in the context of Another World's story, it seems a little odd that the professor knows that he needs to open up a tunnel for water to flow, hit a cave wall to fill up the cave water (even though that clearly is only visible to the player), and that he needs to pull a gun on one guard, and then let one guard throw four grenades before killing him. It doesn't make me hate the game, but these odd choices for solving puzzles did take me out of the experience here and there.
Really these are my complaints, because the experience of Another World is actually... pretty damned enjoyable. You feel contained, alone, and nervous until you meet your alien friend who helps you in many dire situations, and you silently bond with him and you help him through situations, and he does the same for you. It's a truly video game story mechanic that I love seeing played out.
The art style is also pretty great. I like the 20th anniversary blocky textures (having seen the very pixelated graphics of 1991), and the hand-drawn backgrounds that go with them, though sometimes they don't always match up (Like when the professor walks through the uneven terrain of the cave like it's a normal floor). The lighting and color palette are also varied enough that you don't feel like you're going through the same place the whole time. It feels like you're making progress, like you're moving ahead and acheiving something.
Another World is, what I'd consider, a video game must for people who want to play "classic retro" games that actually don't bog themselves down with samey Mario-esque conventions, and want to immerse you in a story. I'm actually surprised I didn't find Another World under the "video games as art" page on Wikipedea. I think it deserves to be on that list. Good on Eric Chahi for making this game pretty much by himself.
Another World is a good game. I like the simple storytelling, the platforming, and the relationship between you and the big alien friend. I wasn't a massive fan of the puzzles here and there, and a few achievements were too easy to get (I snatched all the achievements in my 2 hours playtime. Seriously). I'm giving Another World a recommendation, along with a solid score of 8/10.

I played this game on the Amiga back in like 1993 but I never finished it. Mainly because it was so hard and back then we couldn't just search online for a guide. It's great to be able to go back and finish it now, with the help of a couple of YouTube videos.
I think the final stages would of been amazing to see as a child. It's a really cool game but there is one part, about a third of the way through, that is almost impossible to figure out. So much so, that people online thought it was a glitch, until somebody figured it out and posted about it.
Anyway, I always remembered the unique art style over the years (especialy the part during the opening sequence on Earth). In this version you can switch between the original and some fancy new updated graphics, by pressing a button on your controller. I think the updated graphics would of blown our minds back in 1993, haha.The game also looks great in high resolution and sounds great too.
The game is quite short by today's standards, I finished it and got all the Steam acheivements in around 3.5 hours. You can also access chapters from the main menu as you progress. Which makes the acheivements easier to complete and revisiting specific sections for nostalgia easier too. There's also some extra features which include a making of documentary video.
I would totally recommend buying this game on Steam, especially if you remember it from back in the 90's. It's presented really nicely here, it's hard and you're gonna die alot but it's worth it. With the help of some future online internet technologies you can actually figure out how to finish it in 2016.

The aesthetic of it is so pleasingly dark, not deppressingly or overwhelmingly so, but very dull green, light brown; beautiful in a dreary sort of way. It's got the feel that Diablo 2 had for me back in the day. In fact that's not a bad comparison. It's like a literary Diablo 2, taking more cues from historical events (like, say, the Inquisition)  than high fantasy.
One criticism I might level at it is that tooltips could be more prevalant. I like complicated systems in my games, but I also like to know how to use them. A developer shouldnt play the game for you, but they should at least throw you an instruction manual. But that's it. Even the display issues are given a pass by me, because it's so damn cool.
I might feel compelled to change my opinion once I've played further, but as of now, I've got a thorough erection for this game.

tl;dr - Many glitches, lack of options, not much for free users, not friendly to new-players.
I've played this game for a long while before it came to steam, and have thoroughly enjoyed my time spent with it. Having met some of my best friends here, it would be hard to let go of this game for good. The asthetic is simple but interesting which can also be said about the gameplay. I've even written an absurdly long guide for anyone that doesn't want to play the game to see if they might enjoy it (Dunno why you wouldn't, it's a short download and free to play).
THAT BEING SAID, I cannot recommend this game to most people. Sure it's gameplay is simplistic, akin to Virtua Fighter in that you have a button for punch, one for kick, and another for guard, but the game is heavily overshadowed by many bad things. You have a community that, for the most part, could rival League of Legends, very common program synergy issues, gamebreaking glitches that come with every update (Seriously, we've gone about 8-9 updates, each bringing a new bug that has to be hotfixed the same day because of how bad it is), and a rather neglected market for free-to-play users.
I say the community is bad, but that's just the majority. There are a few good people that actually care about the people they meet (Someone actually paid off a hacker just to get my account back for me). It's hard to pinpoint any one place where the community is the worst, but the majority of it takes place in Guild Wars.
Since Rumble Fighter is on such a dinosaur of an engine, it's very easily manipulated and quite picky about what programs you may have running. There's quite a lot of programs that, if running in your background, will cause RuF to think you're hacking, make the game run very choppy, or just close the game altogether. Most of these programs are ones that try to target RuF as an application for recording. Things like OBS, Plays.tv, and Fraps (who still uses that?). As I said, RuF is also easily manipulated. This isn't entirely a bad thing, but hackers are common, though they typically keep to themselves. People also like to mod the soundFX for the game, which I'm guilty of myself. Honestly, it's just another way to enjoy the game having music from other games and better voices to override those VERY awful current voices.
Aforementioned, RuF has gone through many updates that you'd think are simple, but somehow bring glitches to the game you wouldn't have even thought about. Say an update is supposed to bring a new ExoCore and tweak a scroll released the update beforehand. Well, somehow after the update, even though it wasn't even talked about being changed, an ExoCore from 2 years ago now disconnects everyone in a room if someone uses it (Yes, I'm talking about Blade Spirit). Though, that was a long time ago, I'm just using it as an example.
And now for something heavily debated: The free-to-play market. Some people say there's not enough items for f2p users, others say there's plenty. There IS, in fact, much more content for those willing to pay real money. The thing about RuF, which is something that's desperately needed (and is also a hot topic) is that there's no trade system. People have compromised by using the in-game gifting system to trade, though that raises many trust issues. So to combat that, people have put a thread on the forums of all the trusted traders and the known scammers. My issue with this is that, for the longest time, there's been an in-game tip message that acknowledges that people use the gift system for trading, and it says, "Only trade with trusted players to avoid being scammed." If the developers know there's trading happening, and they are 'concerned' about players being scammed, then why not implement a trading system instead of putting into place a 5day waiting period between when you friend someone and when you can gift them? It's something that's peeved me for so long and I'd love some insight on it. Of course from a company standpoint, that's just more money for them because the player would get scammed, and have to spend more money on the game to get back what they missed out on for being ripped off.
Another big problem with the game is the skill gap. Any new player going into the game would probably quit within the first hour because there's no real matchmaking or ranking system in place. Sure, you start off in the "Amateur" channel, but there's a very well-known glitch that can demote any player into the Amateur channel. Though, I will say that most people in the FGC were big arcade players back in the day, so they're used to learning quickly (Because they played with money). So unless you're in the FGC and you're used to learning through hardship, there's not much fun to be had here.

tl;dr: Try the game yourself, prep for the worst.
Pros:
+ A unique fighting game using a 'rock-paper-scissor' style of fighting.
+ Offers modes for all styles of players, some unique and overlooked.
+ Free to an extent.
+ A growing meta-game that tests a player's ability in given situations.
+ Fairly easy to pick-up and learn immediately, but has a huge learning curve.
+ A PvE aspect that combines platforming and battling AI.
+ The integration of community-made items exemplifies the positive involvement in the community.
Neutural:
~ The learning curve is immense and difficult to master, could possibly turn players off.
~ Events are centered around microtransactions, attendance/log-ins and tournaments. Ever-so rarely do they offer a new type of event to encourage players to explore the game further.
~ Events centered around purchases typically reward the player for making said purchases. (Buying has a positive tradeoff, resulting in more exocores, scrolls, rare equips, etc.)
~ A smaller community which makes learning the game both easy and difficult.
~ A fairly developed
competitve scene within the game that might appeal to seasoned players.
~ Might not be visually appealing to all players.
Cons:
- Glitches that players, on occasion, abuse.
- Terrible free2play market.
- Despite having a PvE aspect, it's fairly underdeveloped. Glitchy platforms, sub-par voice acting, etc.
- Lack luster updates and "new" content. A lot of recycled ideas, concepts and items.
- Like most free2play games, it's pay2win. Scrolls and Exocores give players advantages in the game, most of the "better" scrolls have to be paid for.
- A toxic community plauged with excessive drama and trash talk.
- There's minimal GM involvement which results to the above bullet. A few examples would be players DDoS-ing each other, posting other player's IP in a global chat for all players to see; GMs provide little-to-no action.
- Atrocious interface, SFX, and BGM.
- Lag is prominent and sometimes unavoidable. Rumble Fighter utilizes a peer to peer connection as opposed to dedicated servers.
I've seen this game grow, I've seen it peak, and I've seen it's decline. The community and it's involvement is the worst aspect of this game. Having played this game on and off for 8-9 years, I am indifferent on recommending this game. If you manage to avoid the drama and 'toxic-ness', the game at it's core is admittingly fun.

Costume Quest 2 is the sequel to the original turn-based soft RPG made by Double Fine around 2012. It continues the story of the two twins Reynold and Wren exactly where the last DLC for the first title ended: after managing to return to their own time, they must resort to time travel to stop the evil plan of Dr. Orel White, a dentist bent on destroying Halloween for good and rule the whole world.
Gameplay-wise, Costume Quest 2 doesn't differ that much from the first game's formula, but manages to tweak several elements along the way. The combat is the feature that recived the greatest overhaul: while the whole turn-based RPG fare with QTEs for extra damage is still there, now the health of the characters doesn't refill itself after combat (forcing you to visit fountains scatterd in the areas or consume a stock of candy to heal up), your attacks can either be nice or amazing and dish out damage accordingly regarding when precisely you press the attack button, you can defend yourself and try to counterattack via QTEs, chains of attacks are available and enemies tend to hurt a bit more and some will respawn to free roam the streets again. The sequel also introduces three classes for enemies and costumes alike, Tech, Wizard and Monster: there is a little weakness/resistance system going on between each to put some emphasis on gear and target choice. Finally, this time around  you can actually buy upgrades for your costume, which either empower the character's attacks or add some useful side effects. While these novelties make the first encounters you'll face very challenging and requiring some demanding good timing, as you progress through Costume Quest 2 and gain the roughly ten levels there are to get you'll become more and more powerful and get used to the QTEs general flow, to the point of making most of the battles trivial (the bosses in this game are especially disappointing because, unlike the first game, they don't display any unique gimmick and all boil down to a very easy dps race).
Aside from the combat, eveything you left in Costume Quest returns in the sequel as you'd expect: in the roughly three main areas you'll visit in the second game there a lot of doors to knock on for trick or treating, obstacles to overcome with the right costume, collectable cards that give you a pletora of effects in combat and a huge crowd of NPCs to interact with. The writing is still funny and charming as you remembered.
In short, Costume Quests 2 is a fairly good attempt as a sequel and feel free to buy it if you enjoyed the first game

This game is one of those ambitious titles that seeks to be a little of everything, it's a lot like a mash up of Darkest Dungeons,  Sunless Sea (in space) and possibly Stardew Valley in the sense of combining so many elements. The core mechanics of the game itself seem largely stable and could progress into becoming a sensationally good game. The devs are constantly at work to update, balance, fix or add new content based on gamer feedback.
Pros: Music is nice, writing is pretty good, game is mostly stable with very few bugs encountered. Large amount of depth, clearly the game is designed to be very expansive in what the final product will deliver an example would be the trading system which takes politics into account, house and faction trade bans which will affect your rep and so on.
Things in the middle: Graphics, given that it's definitely an indie style game one isn't expecting great works of art but the things they do have could use some definite polish.
Edit: The character models have been improved and general graphics are now in the realms of good.
Cons: The mini game mechanics for a lot of the ingame missions or quests could do with a lot of work. You're constintently stuck with 'dice rolls' where you have no ability to influence the outcome which has led to 25 mission failures on a storyline mission for which my captain is supposed to be a specialist in their field. This is really the part that makes me want to go away and come back in a few months to see if it's better, this design makes it constantly an unsatisfying grind to achieve anything. Also as you fly through space you are bombarded with skill checks which don't show why there was a skill check, failing intimidation every time you go past a planet and not knowing what exactly that means or how it affects your ship and crew gets old quite quickly.
Edit: A lot of these complaints in the cons are either improved or fixed, the mini games are still quite simplistic with little interaction involved but that in itself has a certain charm and the fail rate for storylines has been largely fixed it seems. About the only big con for me personally is the lack of a save game option because maybe just maybe you don't feel like restarting your level 20 captain who was doing really well until that set of unfortunate occurences deep in hostile space...

As someone who absolutely loves games in all their forms, it's hard to be so harsh on Koihime Enbu. It offers up a combination of buxom young women and ancient Chinese literature that I'm certain would have never been made in the west. However, content is light and as such, the characters don't shine as much as they could without prior knowledge of their personality and mannerisms. Koihime Enbu is a fun purchase if you're a big time fighting game fanatic, but it's hard to recommend it to the average consumer.
Featuring 13 fighters and 7 assist characters, I quickly got a strong vibe of Nitro + Blasterz as soon as I booted the game up. The visual flare is also strikingly similar. In a world where new fighting games are dropping left and right, it takes something to truly stand out in the genre. Koihime seems to want their bullet point to be simplicity. The game features a four-button setup, with three attacks: light, medium, and heavy, and one dedicated throw button.
There is no tutorial, something most fighting games these days seem to be lacking, but once I started digging I found out why. Every character in the game has exactly the same moveset. Every special move is pulled off with the same combination of moves, and even the finishing attacks are all the same layout. It is designed so that players can jump back and forth between characters without worrying about memorizing a long string of inputs. It’s brilliant, but sadly never advertised, and being only on PC in the states doesn’t help either.
Cons of this game
The game features three playable modes: Arcade Mode, Versus Mode, and Training Mode. This brings up another portion of the game that I found frustrating, though. Some of the modes that are supposed to be multiplayer did not allow my friend and I to play together locally. I was trying to play on my Xbox controller while she played on the keyboard, but there was something strange happening that did not allow for us to play that way. Perhaps for certain modes you can only play with two controllers or both on keyboard, but either way this seemed strange to me and the game provided no indication either way. We were only able to play on versus mode in the end.
One other thing that Koihime shakes up is that pretty much all characters have the exact same super move and desperation inputs, and many of the specials also adhere to these same principles. They won’t result in the same attacks, of course, but the command inputs are standard across the board, so it’s less likely for players dabbling with multiple characters to suddenly forget how to pull off super moves at inopportune moments. Even so, the characters all feel reasonably unique—a similar control scheme doesn’t lead to everyone feeling the same.
Conclusion
Koihime Enbu’s a decent little brawler, though it doesn’t do enough to stand out from the crowd apart from its all-female cast. As such, it comes moderately recommended for fighting game enthusiasts who want to jump into something new, but it’s a much harder sell to a more casual demographic.

For 40$ you want to have at least a competent fighting game. Enbu gives you about 80% of that and to it's credit, that is a pretty good percentage from a relatively no-name series/dev team.
The problem with Koihime Enbu is that last 20% is the biggest problem in the game: the AI.
The AI of this game is terrible. It's input-reading laziness that you can either trick or get countered depending on trial and error. Without fail, I have triggered an AI to jump for a single attack 100 times. Without fail, I used a certain attack and got hard countered 100 times.
There is no variance. There is simply the programming of "do this move and win, do this move and lose".
That makes for an ultimately boring game.
So this game is indeed overpriced and underperforming.
I would talk on the balance issues and how there are just clearly better options for characters and assist-characters, but that's all redundant to simple things like input-reading AI.

Very good fighting game, really does as advertised, in terms of ease of playability for varying skill levels.  Fatal Counter system is deadly, but punishable, as it leaves opponents in a crumple state if it lands, but is minus on block, and therefore extremely punishable.  Fatal Counters are universal, and require the same inputs for each character, which are the following; 3B, 3C, 6B, & 6C, and some characters have an extra Fatal Counter input.  Cast doesn't vary in terms of the inputs you need to learn, so learning a character can be quick.  However, assists in this game are locked to certain characters, 2 for each row, so until we get the arcade version, steam players are stuck with only having 2 assists.  All in all, very fun game, whether you be a competitive player looking for your next fix, or a casual looking for something fun to play with friends.

is a mix of two genres: roguelike and hack & slash. From roguelikes, it takes the  dungeon crawling, turn-based gameplay, tile-based graphics, and permanent death of the player character (at least, if you play on hardcore mode). Since
is also very much a loot-driven game that requires nothing more of the player than him fighting his way through area after area of non-procedurally generated hordes of monsters, it's also reminiscent of the hack & slash genre.
So I'm sure the publisher of the game was quite drunk when he wrote the game's description for the Steam Store page, and advertizes
as an RPG, which it's most definitely not. Both the roguelike and the hack & slash genres may initially have been derived from the RPG genre, which explains why a game like
would get tagged 'RPG', but describing this game's genre as "RPG - full stop" is just plain misleading.
When you start a new game, you need to choose which two attributes you'd like some extra points in to begin the game with, but there is no character customization beyond that. You can't even pick a name for your avatar. After that, you find yourself in your typical starting town with two merchant NPCs, two quest NPCs and your storage chest. So one minute later, you're off into your first dungeon.
Combat consists of you holding down one of the four movement keys, the one that would move you onto the tile the opponent is currently occupying, until that opponent is defeated. At that point, you can actually move onto the previously occupied tile and take whatever loot the opponent dropped there.
To keep it short, I'll sum up the rest of the noteworthy gameplay elements in a bullet point list:
The graphics are 'new old school graphics'. You know, the kind that look like nicely polished and upgraded graphics from the 1990's 32-bit consoles. I think
's graphics look nice and vibrant but also a bit basic and repetitive.
One small detail that bothered me a bit is the fact that the game doesn't even have its own sprite for the mouse pointer. You just get your Windows mouse pointer. Come on, computer games in the late 1980s had their own mouse pointer sprites! This comes across as lazy.
At the start of the game, your character gets a knife. No matter what weapon you equip after that, you'll always see him holding a knife. Your character's look doesn't change when you don different armor, either. Again, this seems a bit lazy.
In the town, the music consists of one guy playing the acoustic guitar. The tunes he plays don't fit the game or the setting at all, causing the music to sound very intrusive. The guitar gets too loud from time to time, too, and the music gets repetitive fast, so I was happy to see I could change the music volume in the game's menu, or even switch it off completely.
In dungeons, the music changes to a bit more fitting synthesized music. However, again you only hear one instrument playing, so it gets old fast, but at least the music fits the intended atmosphere a bit better than it does in the town. In the forest, the 'music' consists of birds chirping. Fitting and atmospheric but not what I'd consider music.
Sound effects are non-existent outside of combat. You walk around in the town, you talk to NPCs and get quests from them or browse their inventory, you open and close your storage chest, ... without even a peep. Not one single sound effect. During combat, there are some sound effects but again, they come across as lazy. For example, when you hit something you hear the sound of metal hitting metal, even when you hit an animal with a wooden club. Getting a status effect like 'poisoned' is accompanied by the sound of one bang on a drum. So there are sound effects but they often have nothing to do with what's actually happening in the game and they seem to be there only for the sake of at least having
sound effects.
I cannot recommend
. It's not the worst game ever but it's too 'basic'. It seems like a very nice start for a roguelike hack & slash game, but after playing for a short while you feel like asking the developers when they're going to add the rest: more fitting and more varied music, more random details to the decor, more equipment types, more types of interactible objects, a few more NPCs in the town, more combat styles to play (ranged/magic) and most importantly: a more engaging combat system instead of 'press and hold a button until opponent is dead'. But then you realize you're playing a finished product, and you know there are plenty better games like it, so
disappears in a dark corner of your games library.
has 11 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 6 while running the game.
The 61 Steam Achievements are pretty standard stuff for a game like this: "Kill x monsters", "Open x treasure chests", "Loot x unique items", "Touch x obelisks", "Collect x gold", and so on. But that's fine because they're achievements that fit the game and even complement them. So they add an additional layer of fun, which
desperately needs. Also, you can monitor your progress for each achievement by looking at the progress bars in the achievements overview page, which is always nice.

tldr: Everything is great except some longer load times, "free" content that practically requires spending money to avoid a massive grind and some minor concerns with griefers/cheaters online.
Full Version:
If you don't know what GTA is or need a review of the game to decide, you've probably been living under a rock. In short, third person action game with driving, flying, boating and on foot mechanics. Plenty of good here and the environment is expertly crafted with tons of stuff to do. Graphics are solid, story is solid, gameplay is solid. It's a bit of a beast to run, but well worth it.
If you are interested in the single player experience, buy it. It's worth it.
If you are interested in the multiplayer experience, well... here's the good, the bad and the ugly.
The Good:
Between online free roam, heists, missions and races, there's something for everyone and the game is tons of fun with a few buddies. The stories that will come out of your online shenanigans are endless.
The Bad:
Griefing and cheating is fairly common. They've implemented many controls to help cut down on it, but in the end, you'll likely find someone in free roam doing something you don't like. It's not hard to avoid, but if you are the kind of person that likes to just fool around and enjoy things, you might run into some issues. Especially since much of the newer gameplay content requires you to be in public sessions (though you can generally get around that too).
The Ugly:
The game price is pretty standard fair. The extra content costs are not. Most newer cars and features have in game GTA$ costs. These costs are basically all 6 figures on up, though most are over a million GTA$. Even on sale at $85 for GTA$8,000,000 which is your best deal, that means for ONE new vehicle, it will cost you $10.63. Yes, you can earn GTA$ playing the game and there are numerous guides and tutorials for how to make money "fast". Yes, you can find people to hack and give you money (or you can do it yourself) all at the risk of being banned. But for the casual player who doesn't have time to dump hours into grinding boring cargo deliveries or repetitive content, the game makes it unfun and unreasonable to get any newer content. Most games will release DLC packs and new content and charge anywhere from $10-$30 for it. Rockstar has gone to a scheme that amounts to pay to win and made it near impossible for most people to enjoy the online game anymore without shelling out extra cash or resorting to cheats/hacking. The latest content? An orbital laser similar to the Command and Conquer GDI Ion Cannon that costs GTA$900,000 up front and at least GTA$500,000 to fire. Understandable that you want to limit its use to mitigate griefing, but that amounts to $9.56 to purchase the item and $5.31 each time you fire it. Again, yes you can earn money in game and not pay real cash to get there. Yes you want to limit griefing so you don't want someone spamming the ion cannon. However, there are better ways to do that without resorting to such a blatant cash grab. I'd gladly shell out a few bucks for a season pass or a DLC pack, but I'm not dropping $100 to pick up what amounts to basically 1-2 planes/cars. That's unreasonable. This is why I cannot recommend the game anymore.

So Creepy . . .  From the M.C. Escher level designs, the constantly watching eyeballs and even the deep, heavily accented, sleepy narrator the whole game has a creepy, surreal atmosphere, and yet it's hard to pull away from.  The levels are well plotted out, the graphics and animations are polished and even the movement (I used a controller) was spot on.
The game is a puzzle-platformer-lemmingesque style but is surprisingly forgiving for this genre.  When the sleeper falls off of a ledge the whole level isn't reset, only the sleeper (and enemies) gets reset allowing the player to keep things in position.  This means that even though the levels get harder and harder, the player doesn't get as frustrated and has time to really think things through on how to interact with the environment in order to complete the level.
If you are looking for a pleasant brain-teaser, this game is a great way to spend an afternoon.

I have played the NDS version of this game for more than 200 hours. When compared to the NDS version, the only thing improves on the PC is the graphics. Game mechanics wise, the game is completely gutted and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ised. In the NDS version, there are many interesting creature abilities, and many interesting faction specific artefacts which can boost these abilities even more. When these two combines, there are so many tatics to explore and so much fun to enjoy. Now they are completely gone. Just to name a few, druid from Sylvan is now trash with his ability shortened by one round and his artefact gutted. This unit is now a joke. Maybe still usable, but no longer fun to beat an opponent who is stronger than you. Djinn suffered the same fate, artefact gutted and ability itself neutered. Rashasa is a mediocre Champion, but with his artefact on the NDS, which gives him 25% PWR boost and 1 round charge reduction, he becomes an formiddable foe. On PC? sorry it is spayed and the Rakshasa's artefact now is a joke. Rashasa also received an PWR punish and now this unit looks like a joke. There are many more, I won't cover them in detail. Anyone who enjoyed the NDS version will know this better.
It may seem to stem from the balancing point of view, but this game is basically dead online, and you would probably only play with your friends. And if that is the case, the NDS version with more fun is clearly a superior choice. Instead of fixing some of the weaker units/artefacts/heroes on the NDS, the developer decided to gut anything that is outstandingly fun and watch this game burn.

Let me start out by saying that I love the gameplay in this game. The hunting is straightforward but you get fun mods to use and it's really important to do it efficiently due to the timer on the cooking part. The cooking puzzle game is fun and you can really feel yourself getting better the more you play. They also do a great job of introducing new mechanics over time that throw a wrench into the formula and shake up the way you have to think about the puzzles.
HOWEVER there is one thing that is honestly ruining my enjoyment of the game so far. You get a ton of interesting themed cookware that could be useful in the right situation. But they don't let you change your loadout after knowing the theme of the battle! What's the point of all this cool stuff, I just have to use the red/blue/green pots every time because I have no idea what I'm going to be cooking. As far as I can tell there's no way to manually save either so you can't even enter battle and reload. I'm hoping they do something to patch this soon because there are so many interesting strategies you could try if you just knew when to try them.

Please note that I got this game very cheaply as part of a bundle.
The game it set in 3 different hospitals (a series - though the graphics and mechanics are identical in each) with 4 'episodes' in each - in other words, 12 missions. They have tried to implement a story as a way of introducing each mission but this is actually one of the biggest let downs of the game. I'm a story fan but this is truly awful; the attempt at humor is terrible!
That's not to say the game isn't funny - the diseases, the animations etc are all funny and well done but I think they should have just left it at that and removed the story element altogether.
There's a lot wrong with the game. In each mission you have a scenario that you start with and a set of objectives to complete and you can spend your time re-arranging the hospital, improving the decor, training up the staff and getting things running well only to have it all reset at the start of the next mission. This is particularly jarring within a series where each episode is supposed to just be the next shift at the hospital. Still, once you get used to it you won't keep making that mistake again.
There's also some annoyances such as not being able to properly rotate the screen when you get to the edge of the hospital which makes it difficult to place items in those corners. Also the information screens are sorely lacking - it would be nice to see the laziness rating of the staff on the staff summary screen rather than having to click on every individual staff member one by one. And where's the financial info? Absolutely no financial data on profits / expenses etc which is odd.
But despite all of those negatives I'm actually going to give this game a thumbs up because in the end, I enjoyed playing it and it gave me about 12 hours of entertainment which is all that matters. However, I wouldn't pay full price for it.
I would say that if you are looking specifically for a hospital game and can pick it up cheaply then do so but if you're looking for a sim / tycoon / management game in general and don't mind the genre then give it a miss as there are much better ones out there.

This was actually a surprisingly good adventure game. Not great, but good enough to recommend for fans of Myst style adventure games. This review covers both parts in the series, because although the first game is nowhere near as good as the second, I feel that they are still probably best played one after the other for the story if nothing else.
Firstly, a point of warning - the second game had all sorts of graphical glitches on my GeForce Go 7900 GS making it unplayable. I ended up streaming it from my Mac Air which played it with no problems. I couldn't find any other reports of the issue I was running into - in fact, most people seemed to indicate that they could run the second game fine, but had issues with the first (which worked fine for me), so YMMV.
I picked up both in the series from a recent Indie Gala bundle and after finishing the first one I considdered it to be a fairly average adventure game with forgettable characters, a lack of any meaningful story and a pretty lame ending - but I still had a fairly good time with it, and it was short enough that it didn't overstay it's welcome. Fortunately, the second part redeemed it as the story picked up and the characters instantly felt like they had a lot more depth.
You play as Mina who was trying to set a new world record, but wound up shipwrecked on the shore of a Mysterious Island. Your phone's battery is dead and you can't contact anyone. You want to know the story of the first game? That's pretty much it. You get to explore and see some of the sights described in Jules Verne's novel "The Mysterious Island" trying to find a way to recharge your phone and bring down the shield that surrounds the island, but since I have not actually read the novel I can't comment on how much is a reference to it and how much is new.
In your adventure you find an adorable monkey you adopt and name Jep. In the first game Jep basically becomes a tool to reach high objects, but in the second game you actually spend a good part of the game playing as Jep, since he can go places that Mina can't and can talk to other Monkeys on the island to make friends... and some enemies.
Graphics wise they remind me a lot of the Myst series - particularly Myst III as they use the same technique of fully pre-rendering the scenes from every position you can stand in (and in the second game from two perspectives since you can visit each location as Jep who is much shorter than Mina) and allowing you to freely rotate the camera in any direction. That was a nice trick used at the time to give the game stunning graphics (by the standards of the day) without having to render it all in real-time.
Like most adventure games you find plenty of things to pick up, but here it actually feels a bit over done - both games even give you multiple tabs of inventory (around 8 or so) to organise it because there is just so much stuff. Items can be combined in the inventory to produce new items or tools, and many of those tools can be broken apart again to recover the items used to construct them, which is often necessary to do (particularly in the first game), as the components often need to be used again elsewhere, whereas most of the constructed tools only have a single one-off use.
The first game has much more emphasis on combining items than the second - to the point where working out what items go together actually forms the vast majority it's puzzles. While the combinations do tend to make sense (and there are notes on the more complex combinations), the sheer number of items you find can make it hard to keep track of everything to work out what might go together - it was so overwhelming I often ended up just doing a whole bunch of trial and error to see what could be combined as the resulting tool might give me a clue as to what I might use it with. Eventually you get access to an encyclopedia to provide hints on the items, but by the point you manage to do that you have are near the end and have already solved the hardest combination in the game to get the encyclopedia.
The second game does a lot better in this regard - there is far less emphasis on combining objects and when objects do need to be combined the descriptions often provide clues or the recipe will be in a notebook you find fairly early in the game. Because of this, I didn't really find the need to waste time trying different combinations, and attempting trial and error didn't have much success anyway.
One redeeming factor of the first game - and something I actually quite liked, was that there are almost always multiple solutions to each problem (and you get bonus points for any progress towards the alternate solutions). In some cases you needed to collect a bunch food and the extra solution was simply that there was way more food than you needed if you looked hard enough, but in other cases there were two different items you could constuct to achieve some goal - like two types of batteries that could be constructed out of completely different materials (I still have no idea where the silver was for the other type), or at least three types of projectile weapons. I didn't see this as much in the second game - there's still an excess of food, but I didn't see any obvious alternative solutions to puzzles like the first.
Interestingly, the first game had some conditions where you could destroy an item, and it's the first game I've played where I was concerned that I might accidentally waste or destroy an important item that would prevent me from winning the game later on. I'm not certain if that is possible or not - especially considdering all the alternative solutions. The thing is - one item that can be destroyed is the knife blade, which was the single most used item in the game - I'm a bit curious to replay it at some point and see if there are enough alternative solutions to still win if you destroy the knife at the start of the game... The second game actively seemed to prevent you from wasting inventory items you might need later ("I could use that to start a fire! But, it would be a shame to burn the xxx"), so I was never worried about losing anything important in it.
Besides item puzzles, the first game has a bunch of nearly identical code puzzles and a guess the item quiz - and that's about it. The second game has a lot more variation to it's puzzles (yay, only one code puzzle this time), though I did have to resort to a walkthrough once or twice when I couldn't quite work out what I was supposed to do (usually because I was overcomplicating things, like the puzzle where you pretty clearly need to use trigonometry since you're given elevations at certain points and the distances between them - only it turns out that the angles are all 0 degrees which completely eliminates the math and makes the distances irrelevant... overthinking it...) - I noticed that some of the puzzles had an "easy" mode which you could use at the cost of "pride points", but the puzzles I got stuck on didn't have that option, so I never tried it.
In both games I did often find myself walking around with no real idea of what I was supposed to be doing - the second game was a bit better in that regards as it had objectives, but the objectives still tended to be vague goals rather than specific things that needed to be done. I did feel that the games could have done a slightly better job of dropping hints (Maybe instead of "I think I forgot something" it could have said "The grindstone isn't secure"). The first game was small enough that I never had to resort to a walkthrough (I almost did at one point, but just as I was about to give up and hit shift+tab my mouse finally passed over the saltpeter I was looking for), but I admit that I did have to use a walkthrough a couple of times in the second.
Overall, a good adventure game that I'd recommend to Myst fans. Maybe wait for a sale though.

This is a fine example of branding gone horribly wrong.  Like taking a brand that is a good, cozy brand that you grew up with and has always been a friend and a mark of reliable quality, a brand of trust, and doing something bizarre with it.   Like if Campbells Soup went into manufacturing diesel motors.   Even if the motors they make are good, they shouldn't do it.  Stahp.
We all know Might and Magic as the franchise of addictive 4X games with simplistic tactical combat, classical fantasy units like orcs, knights, vampires and dragons.  Build your cities and outposts, capture resources, cast magic spells and win!
Not with this game.  They put Legend of Zelda, a teenaged american nerd who thinks he can draw anime, tetris and plants vs zombies into a blender, crushed what came out and stamped "Might and Magic: No Really!" on it.    It's a weak puzzle game with a strange anime type veneer on the front.  They threw away all the classical features of Might and Magic, leaving a poor competitor to Bejewlled in place.
Graphics: Limited but works okay in 4K.  Artwork is "american anime", which doesn't work with Might & Magic.  There should be none of this kind of thing.
Gameplay:  Very bad.   You go in expecting you're playing Might & Magic and you're playing plants vs Zombies turned 90 degrees.   You dump your soldiers randomly onto the field like a game of tetris, then build them into stacks or rows so they can do something.   Thematically it's weird.  In terms of gameplay it just doesn't make any sense.
Technical: Not really a 3D game.  Stable and functional, but very simplistic.
Might & Magic is a good solid franchise.  It's not the best and far from the worst.  This game might even be worth a recommendation but the failed branding and sense of betrayal, combined with being far, far below par for a game in this franchise, with such weak gameplay, leaves me with no choice but the thumbs down.   There are better Might & Magic games. There are better puzzle games.  This one has no place to go but down, like pizza flavoured beer, some combinations just don't work.

Early access review after four or five hours play.
A deep and complex top down sandbox sci-fi RPG involving many dice rolls and card based events, with lots of influences from the likes of Firefly, Dune and WH40K, slightly troubled by garish design and an occasionally weak or irritating interface.  If you like the genre and like supporting indie devs there's tons of gaming value to be had here.
I suspect I'll be sinking a good few hours into this title, I haven't even scratched the surface yet.
+ Complex and engaging RPG design with multiple characters (you, officers, crew), each with multiple classes, skills / perks and levels.
+ Lots of design choices when it comes to upgrading your ships and character loadouts.
+ Free form play with plenty of avenues to explore and exploit - trading, piracy, smuggling, spying, going off the beaten track to explore and so on.
+ What looks to be an interesting and engaging main plot arc (that I haven't got very far into yet), with the promise from the devs of lots more to come.
+ Interesting reputation and faction systems to navigage.
+ Even the low difficulty levels are challenging.
+ A very helpful community, particularly on Discord with responsive devs who obviously care passionately about their game.  As an example I pointed out a bit of friction in the GUI and one of the devs came back five minutes later and said "just changed the code, it will be fixed in the next patch".  In some ways quite minor, but that responsiveness to something that will eliminate hundreds of unecessary mouse clicks from any one game playthrough impressed me.
- The depth and complexity isn't always matched by an interface that makes things accessible.  Most of it can be figured out but you need to work at it (having to work at an interface means, imho, that something's not right).  Some of this may be caused by the fact that the game has been designed for multiple platforms.  Still, as noted above, the devs are aware of some of the criticism here and very responsive to ideas about how to improve things.
- I think I'll get my head around most of the gui quirks, eventually, but in a perfect world I wouldn't have to.
- Occasional opacity or lack of feedback eg I buy commodity X on a planet for n% less than the galactic average and take it to a planet where demand should be high, but can only sell at a loss.  There may be many reasons for this, but I haven't found a way to find out what they are.
- Obviously a personal opinion but I find the bright colours used everywhere to be too garish for my tastes.
- Similarly I'm not a huge fan of the cartoonish nature of the art but a) I can see past that and b) we're talking about an indie studio so expecting Star Wars Battlefront II levels of prettiness would be ridiculous.
I was tempted to check the "received this product for free" box as it reflects my experience with these games for the past 10 years.

i'll admit, i bootlegged this game way back when it first released. i had such an amazing time with it, i decided it was only fair to support the developers.
the feeling i got when i first played mark of the ninja, was that same euphoria i've experienced long ago when i played legend of zelda: ocarina of time. granted, it's two very different games, but they were both so well made, and so immersive, and games of this ilk are very rare indeed.
mark of the ninja is a very well crafted stealth game, and in my personal opinion, one of the best stealth games ever made. while it is essentially a 2d platformer, as opposed to many other stealth games such as splinter cell, or tenchu, the mechanics work very well, and keeps you on your toes as you navigate through the map, strategizing at every turn, sneaking past or avoiding enemies, or attempting to stealthily take them out instead.
the graphics may look simplistic, but there's a lot of details put into everything, from the characters to the backgrounds to the animations. the subtle sound cues and music also really helps drive home that feeling of suspense or tension as and when it arises.
and holding it all together, is a fairly deep story about a ninja clan, in a modern world; a story about old believes and values vs modernization, and more importantly, about the player's role in it. with great power bestowed upon the player, at the cost of his mind over time, how does one sort through fact from fiction? reality or insanity? and it all rises to a climactic end.
all in all, a very well made game, and personally, one of the best gaming experiences i've had in many a years. even having replayed it again recently, it still feels like a game that could very well stand the test of time.
VERY highly recommended!

Star Traders is a complicated space faring sandbox that proved addictive despite some tedium and weak UI.
In a fractured galaxy, the player character has inherited the writs to authorize him/her to become a star trader, an independent explorer/trader/pirate/privateer. Then the game pretty much lets you go. You are given an initial mission to begin the narrative, but you are free to ignore it if you'd rather just explore.
Both ground and space combat is similar to Darkest Dungeon, except not quite as pretty or intricate. Exploration and misc orbital activites are resolved through a card draw. Skill and talent checks (such as diplomatic actions) are resolved by dice rolls. Every action is influenced by the skills of your captain, officers, and crew. The development of this crew and their impact on your adventures was one of my favorite aspects. Crew skills are constantly being checked to influence events and actions. This selection and development of your large crew allows for some emergent gameplay.
My complaints would be the occaisonally weak UI and time consuming maintenance. The game doesn't elaborate on why there are constant skill checks or what the consequences are. Tooltips are sparse at best. Your ship and crew require frequent maintenance that you must authorize manually. I would love to see the UI given some love and options for automated maintenance to be added, at least for the easier difficulties.
Overall, Star Traders is an ambitiuos game that doesn't always hit it's mark, but is close enough to provide (presumably many) hours of playable space drama.

Star Traders RPG Elite was the first mobile game I ever purchased.  6 years, and just as many phones later, it is still a game I go back to time and time again.  To this day the developer still adds content on a weekly basis.  They're like that for every title they have released.  For that alone the purchase of this game was a no brainer.
I don't think 2017 was a great year for gaming.  Big publishers have been releasing disappointing over hyped game after disappointing game.  Games 5 years in development are released barely playable, and some companies cram loot boxes into everything they can trying to squeeze just a bit more money from their players.
Despite that there have been many small developers putting out absolutely amazing titles with a fraction of the resources.  This is one of those developers and this is one of those titles.
If you liked what you read in the description buy this game.  Even as early access you're getting a great value.

(Reviewed for EA Version 2.0.7)
Do I recommend this game? By all the fun gods: Yes!
Star Trader is essentially a space sim that neatly falls between the two typical lines of the genre, that is:
1) Hand-held, berates you for even thinking about deviating from the safety zone until you've traded hours of your soul away for the scrap tier fighter.
2) No direction, but you better grind tedium if you want any hope to live.
Star Trader gives you every option a captain could want without forcing you onto one path.  Heck you could even do many things at once, for while the game does recommend trading goods - you can right out the gate get stuck into mischief, profitting from the misfortune of your rival factions - or even independents - while cozying up with your faction of preference.  There is risk, but that's half the fun!
^ Edit2: Just for the record: Entirely possible on Brutal difficulty - one from the hardest - Ironman. :3
Synopsis is as follows; bear in mind this isn't a comprehensive list:
PROS
1. Absolute Freedom of Style - Fighting things early game? Is profitable and fun!
2. Neat Artwork Style (Though some models do look mutated or way too smug, hmm...)
3. Engaging Combat System, made better by a delightful OST as well.
4. Intriguing storyline that does a good job of easing you into the game-world, both as tutorial and lore guide, and avoids being overly patronizing on either count.
5. Very Active Dev Support - this cannot be overstated enough, most OP postive really. :)
QUIRKS - May be CONS
1. Worse morale than the Imperial Guard; your crew *will* desert you until you have enough Commander skilled officers to keep them in line.  This can seriously impair your early game fighting ability, with enough bad rolls it can end a run prematurely. For whatever reason, spice does little to stem the pain either, how dare they be clean.  Also the Captain has the worst morale recovery ever, period.
2. Spontaneous Major Health Fail RNG.  Could just be bad rolls, but are the full health crew playing with scalpels and baking in radiation while we're travelling? Those hospital trips aren't cheap!
X (Reviewer Derp). Trading - This segment has proven slanderous to the name of Shalun.  Redacted; spice is also off the menu tonight, bad reviewer. :P
CONS
1. Possessive Rename UI.  If you ever want to rename your crew into a more easily trackable roster, be prepared to spend 20 minutes wrestling with the game.  This is not an exaggeration.
2. No quick map references when taking contracts, having to exit the planet and everything eats a small amount of fuel, no big loss but it is annoying when all you want to do is check if you're heading 29 AU west, or north.  If there is a way already, it's not easily identifable.
3. Hotkey tooltips could stand for some display speed improvement, maybe even a config list.
See! Even when bad-mouthed this game doesn't come off so bad.  Still, ultimately the choice is up to you gamers if this is your cup of spice coffee.  Shalun favours the brave!

Mark of the Ninja has got to be one of my favorite games I've ever played! Why? Because I actually felt like a ninja playing it!  Most games that feature "ninjas" are too combat heavy for my taste. I've always felt a ninja game should focus more on stealth, and this is exactly what this game does. While still keeping the gruesome reality that you are, in fact, an assassin.
The art style is unique and fluid, the gameplay being just as much so, and the storyline is interesting and mysterious.
I never really had a hard time with the controls at all, even when using the keyboard (which I hate to use). Gameplay usually felt fair and fun. And, a plus in my opinion, is the fact that the game greatly encouraged staying hidden and not being seen. Something I've always thought a ninja should be about. The game requires a lot of thinking and quick reflexes, but I feel is easy to get the hang of.
If you are like me, and love ninjas and just want a game that portrays them in a more traditional and steathly way, this is definitely the game for you! Even if you aren't all about that, I would still recommend this game simply because it's a great game that deserves a sequel!

I played this game on my Commodore Amiga 500 back in 1990. It was very difficult but also a great game back then with hours and hours of fun and hard efforts to understand the puzzles and ways to kill or divert the enemies.
Yesterday I bought it for PC on sale for 2.50€. This is a remastered 20th anniversary edition with tons of extra stuff including:
- Remastered graphics (but you can play the original low res)
- Remastered sounds (but you can play the original low fi)
- The original game soundtrack with 13 tracks in wav format
- 17 minutes making of video with interview from creator Éric Chahi
- The original artwork sketches and drawings from Éric Chahi
- The original hand writing game code from Éric Chahi
If you played this game in the 90's, then you will probably love it today. It's amazing to remember everything from back then while playing it. The hours and hours of fun from the 90's are presented today with better graphics and remastered sound.
Another nice feature is the ability for choosing the difficult level options, something not available in the 90's. The Steam achievements are also nice.
However this in not an ordinary game. You need to understand the concept to like it. In fact this is not a game... this is a legendary piece of pioneer software with millions of fans worldwide.

I took a long look at some of the negative reviews and if you have read those there are some things you should consider. First off there is quite the learning curve to this game so if somone has less than 40 hours played I wouldn't trust their positive or negative review.
When I first got this game I spent about 20 hours starting, then stopping, then picking it up again. I restarted several times (an ARP curse of mine) finally, nearly, beating the first act with the thieft on hard difficulty. I reformatted my computer shortly after, lost my save file and hadn't played the game in almost a year. About two weeks ago I started a paladin on Normal difficulty and am about half way through the second act and going strong.
This game presents one of the most mysterious, yet compelling stories out of any game I've ever played. This is its biggest pro in my opinion. Once understood and givin proper time, the combat is okay. Not great, but not bad. I'll give a list of pro's and con's:
Pros:
-Story is deep, mysterious and as you uncover more secrets extremely rewarding.
-Well written and well thought out.
-Unique Spells that serve you in interesting ways.
-Unique and well written music.
-If you actually read the novel length dialogue, characters are MOSTLY interesting.
Cons:
-Loot system is on the con side of things. Pretty generic and seems, so far, that there are things to look for and things to ignore.
-If they are going to leave the potion system the way it is, please, just please, let me stack them.
-Duribility on gear is poorly designed and should be revisited imo.
-Buggy. Nothing game breaking but enough to force you to save and restart the game a few times during a session.
Conclusion:
If your looking for a unique story, good music, and decent gameplay arpg give this a shot. If you can be patient through the learning curve you'll be happy you gave this game a shot. It offers many hours of gameplay. I would guess im about half way through (could be off there) and I'm about 45 hours in. 7/10.

Brawlhalla is great, ive sunken 533 hours on this account and 200+ more on my smurf. I've been with this game for over 2.5 years now and I've seen it change alot.
Alot of people like to compare this game to Smash but the two play very, vey differently. While there is no health meaning you must knock enemys off stage, simillar to smash. Brawlhalla gives each of its many legends (playable characters) two weapons. These weapons have light attacks which are the same for all characters using the same weapon. Then there are signitures (heavy attacks) or sigs, these are compleatly unique to the legends and hit much, much harder then light attacks making them great for finshing of an enemy.
Initially the game seems weird to play as its quite different from the smash formula/physics. But after some play,the game really opens up. There are the casual game modes like 1v1v1v1 free for all, holiday exclusive gamemodes, and even an unranked 1v1 gamemode ment to test experimental features (called Experimental, amazing ikr).

Then comes the ranked modes... these are for more seasoned players that have a better grasp on the game. If your new be warned, your gonna get your butt kicked. There are ranked 1v1s and 2v2s, the latter of which is quite fun as the 2 person dynamic is hecktic. The ranks go from tin (unranked) > Silver > Gold > Platinum > Diamond (the "pros" ;v)
The game is free, and truely free to play. By that I mean no EA levels of BS. All legends can be unlocked easily by playing the game and logging on daily, and cosmetic items (like skins, colors, etc) can be ocasionally purchased with the (free curency) gold, but ussualy the (premium curency of) Mammoth Coins.

An early access game that shows a lot of promise and still has a lot of deep gameplay mechanics at this stage in lifestyle. Definitely worth the sub-$20 pricetag.
Things I like:
-In depth crew simulation, with over a dozen classes, and their effectiveness is tied to the overall type of captain you're trying to be (trader, pirate, etc), as well as the type and tech level of the ship components you use, In each game, you're managing a handful of officers and literally 2 dozen crew members as they level up and gain talents every 3 levels or so.
-In depth individual class, each class has a unique set of talents which are all gamechangers. Each class has something like 12 unique talents.
-In-depth ship management, with over 75% of ship being modular - you can change out cargo bays, weapons, sensors, crew quarters, brig, armor plating, weapon lockers, fuel bays, for each other and a variety of other components.
-In-depth contact/mission simulation - where a contact is a person who gives you missions, as well as 1-5, out of maybe 20, other things, such as missions, black market access, trading permits, bounty permits, pardons, introductions to others, discounts, special gear and special crew. The missions also vary widely depending on what contact you use, and if you are a trader and going to a military officer for attack contracts, you won't really have to the skills to succeed; similarly, a bounty hunter, unless specially built for non-bounty missions, won't do well on intelligence missions that require a lot of stealth and quickness, and you will fail skill checks and have the agent you were supposed to smuggle onto a planet discovered because you couldn't sneak past the port authorities
-In-depth faction reputation mechanics - each action you take is affects a variety of factions in a logic fashion. Patrol and find an enemy pirate - gain rep with the faction that controls the area. Blockade and intercept a merchant in the same area - lose rept
-Open world with a variety of ways to make money. You aren't forced into missions, and trading is very lucrative. You can also go exploring uninhabitated worlds, go spy and sell intel for income, you can smuggle, you can pirate, you can go bounty hunty, you can mine resources
-The beginnings of a promising story arc. The game's in early access, so the story isn't done yet, but it is filled with interesting decisions.
In short, I love the game. Thank you devs!

One thing that the visual novel Higurashi manages better than the anime is in being immersive. Play this game alone in the dark, with headphones on and it can definitely be really, quite immersive and spooky. While it cannot boast to have the same level of illustration as many other visual novels, the greatest strength of HIgurashi is in its writing. The characters are likeable, and the story (plus the tips system) are genuinely interesting and clever. The UI is simple and effective. The music can be a bit hit-or-miss, ranging from functional to excellent. The story itself can also be a bit too anime from time to time, but the strong points more than make up for it.
One bitter pill to swallow is the fact that I did watch the Higurashi anime before reading the visual novel. As far as I've seen so far, the anime mirrors the VN quite well. The problem with that is I've already got an idea of what is happening (which does impact the spooky level negatively). I have to say, however, that despite this Higurashi manages to be creepy and I'm enjoying it plenty. Although the VN doesn't handle action quite as well as its anime counterpart, it has the benefit of more internal monologue and substantial depth. It's also incredibly long--I've invested two evenings so far and still haven't completed the first arc, Onikakushi.
I recommend you get this game, but do yourself a favor and make it as immersive an experience as possible. It's definitely worth it, especially if you enjoy intrigue or being spooked.

While Iron Sky: Invasion (and its add-ons) is not the end-all be-all of space fighter simulators, it probably doesn't have any right to be as good as it actually is, especially for a video game based on a movie. The whole of the game took a fair portion of the latter half of the film - basically the entire space fight and Earth fleet reinforcement segment - and stretched it out without making it boring. The tone of black comedy and "just run with it" silliness from the movie is preserved, from the mission briefings with Madame President Totally-Not-Sarah-Palin, to the political shenanigans of the various national representatives, to the over-the-top voice acting from the various pilots in the fleet.
The controls are keyboard-and-mouse, primarily mouse oriented. On screen contextual tips do show up from time to time, which can help if you go a long time between having to use a specific feature of the ship. The learning curve for controlling the ships is very short. There are some technical problems - while I haven't noticed any crashes or freezes, it doesn't like my graphics card and the mission briefing videos lag the entire game as often as not. They can be skipped with no penalty and watched later, it's just distracting.
Unfortunately, once the tutorial is over, the difficulty curve spikes pretty hard; it's all but impossible for a new player to know what to do and how to do it. There's a certain amount of flexibility - if a squadron of Nazi ships makes it to earth it just applies a penalty to reputation, which is a score by any other name - but there's no option to turn down or postpone side missions, they get added to your to-do list automatically when you head to a friendly station for resupply and repairs. When you're running all over near earth orbit trying to play space tag with the Fourth Reich, something's gotta give. That said, you can buy yourself time to fight the smaller fighters and do side missions by taking out the engines in the big ships, leaving them adrift - but the only mention of this strategy comes up once during the tutorial on sub-system targets. It's very easy to miss.
Having said all that, if you liked the movie, you'll probably like the game. And even if you didn't like the movie, you might still like the game. After all, it's a game that lets you fight Space Nazis. I'll repeat that: You get to fight Nazis. In Space. And who can honestly say they never wanted to do that?

I've heard good things about this game and really love management sims, so I played the Story mode to learn how to play the game and I have to say the mechanics are certainly one of the best features of this game.
The writing of the story itself is pretty poor, but this game doesn't take itself seriously. The story is done by a scrolling text on the bottom of the screen which sometimes changes too quickly to read, and there is no voice acting in terms you'd expect. Instead they use a technique similar to Simlish so the game can be played in multiple languages. However, story mode is but a tutorial and the game seems well rounded in terms of mechanics and animation.
There are several aspects to the game mechanics and running a successful hospital hinges on being able to provide enough staff and equipment to deal with the influx of patients without going into the red, as well as keeping everyone happy. Happiness is determined by how much decoration is placed and there were times where it felt more like "Interior Design Tycoon". It's fairly easy as management sims go, but still enjoyable.
I especially enjoyed discovering new diseases and putting new systems in place to treat them. The diseases are shown on collectible cards which show info on examination and treatment procedures. They are collected by researching someone with an unknown disease.
Overall this game is great if you're looking for a management sim.

I am stating that I recommend this game with a caveats as a lot of people don't seem to get the point.
- This is a game in only the loosest sense of the word. It IS actually a game, but it requires a great deal of patience(not only to play, but to understand it), and no score is kept.
- This game is NOT about pressing buttons. It's about pressing buttons once, and then not pressing buttons again for as long as possible.
- The tutorial is kinda bad in that it really doesn't explain the game at all, it just tells you how to work the controls, not what they mean. The game part of this is about finding balance. (Sure, you could just keep spawning things, but that gets old fast.)
- The Oxygen content of the water seems to control the algae growth(dace food) and how many creatures you can keep in the pond at any one time. Increase the Oxygen, slow the algae growth, but get more critters.
- The basic stock are the Dace and the clam. At the lowest Oxygen levels, you can spawn 3 dace and 2 clams and have the pond run seemingly indefinitely without any other input. By adjusting the Oxygen levels and initial spawns, you can see how long the ecosystem lasts as you build it.
- If you want something fast paced, this is not your game.
- This is a game for after work where you just want to forget the rest of the world exists and do something mind-numbing without the stupidity of Hollywood. It's simple at the beginning, but harder the more complex you make it.
