These guys have a lot of chutzpah. I guess they didn't get the message that said two brothers shouldn't undertake such an ambitious project that trangresses and remixes many of the traditional genres to create an epic sandbox space trading rpg set in an evolving almost 4X like universe that has a life of it's own far beyond the actions of a single captain. Whether they didn't get the message or just refused to heed it is a very good thing, because they've succeeded amazingly with the initial release of Star Traders Frontiers.
Seriously who hasn't been playing an RPG and just wished that they could quit the story and go for a romp around the world and still have fun and progress and influence the outcomes of various events from a different angle, and then maybe pick up the story again after it's progressed some without you. STF offers that and so many other ways of playing and engaging the with world that it's hard to believe it can all be held together. The game manages to bust the boundaries and yet it still provide an environment that will demand a high-level of focus from the player in order to accomplish whatever goals they're pursuing.
Having played the game considerably in the alpha stage, it's worth saying that this, like other deep games, requires the player to take some time to learn to swim. It's not one that you pick up and immediately know how to play. It is, however, definitely worth the investment to figure it out. Playing in Early Access you've also got the opportunity to help influence the further development of the game and work out this kinks that aren't working for you. These developers are probably the most responsive devs to their community and if something is working, or fully implemented right now, you can be sure that they will get it smoothed out, sometimes in 24 hours, sometimes a bit longer ;).
Either way I can't wait to see what this game will be like when it reaches full maturity. Is it too early to start throwing around words like "a legend" or "epic?"

This game. First its a Trese Brothers game. These guys do WORK. Templar Battleforce, SteelHeroes RPG, Star Traders 4x, etc. etc. We are talking about updates that are FREE, and last about as long as Paradox updating. We are talking YEARS of polishing, free updates, a fantastic community, and a downright amazing developer response time. These guys are up there with Soldak, CD Projekt RED, and Spiderweb software when it comes to amazing post-release support. Templar Battleforce recieved a rediculous amount of content and is to this day one of my favorite Space-Hulk/XCOM type games.
So what are you getting with this title, its current release, and future plans. First, lets discuss what the game is. You are a space trader. Its a 2D top-down strategy game where you fly around, accept missions, trade goods, fight pirates, and generally whatever you want to do. All while maintaining your ship, your crew, and your rep with the various space factions. Escape Velocity Nova, Space Rangers 2 HD, Endless Sky, Oolite, Star Nomad 2, all do similar things. So what ELSE are you getting? ST:F offers a living, breathing galaxy. Not quite X3:Terran Conflict, but far more than Freelancer. You have warring factions, blockades, contacts for missions who you build relationships or play against one another.
Then you have the crew. Your crew consists of regular joes who help on the ship or in combat. Your officers are like the captain and can have 3 jobs, everyone gets levels and talents. Which is good, because space is dangerous. I'm not just talking starship destruction. Crew in-fighting, sickness, mutiny, all kinds of things can go south very quickly, which is manageable with said talents everyone gets. Think Sid Meier's Pirates. You don't leave port without a time limit. Same applies here, fuel, supplies, etc all play a part in day to day life. You are managing a ship and crew. You are a star-captain. Act like it.
In the game's current state its missing some story content, but you've got a big galaxy to roam around in, working faction interactions, and a rediculous amount of things to do. Want to Spy for a faction? ok. Pirate traders? Sure thing. Hunt down bounties? No problem. Explore new planets and get into combat? Absolutely.
Combat in this game is turn based. So your ship moves toward the enemy ship, and you choose what weapons to fire or talents to use. Ground/Boarding Party combat is .... well it reminds me of a Darkest Dungeon-lite. You assign 4 positions and it plays out a bit like an rpg. Talents and weapons play a key role here.
The game is polished and playable right now. However, Trese Brothers is OUTSTANDING when it comes to content addition, and polishing of their game. If their past titles are any indication they will still be tweaking and perfecting this sandbox gem years from now.
Ever watched Firefly? Smugglers V, Endless Sky, and Space Rangers 2 not doing it for you? Give this a try. Its fast becoming my favorite 2d Sid Meier's Pirates clone. So much going on here, and as they add more story and sandbox features I can't imagine it not becoming one of the best of its kind.
It also runs on potatoes. Like an actual potatoe. Out of the ground. With no electricity, and it has an AMAZING price. The fact that you don't own it already hurts me like when you bought Pixel Privateers and Star Nomad 2. Or when you pre-ordered Star Sector. This game rocks. If you like space, crew/ship management and making your own way among a vibrant and living universe with Warhammer 40k esque lore, than you owe it to yourself to own this game.
Sounds like a paid review huh? Well there are some downsides. The UI needs a bit of work, but I prefer it to say Star Nomad 2. The game can feel a little barebones if you are new to this type of game, and have no idea how to make it up from nothing in a crap ship. Its a bit grindy, (granted this genre is much like JRPG's.) and frankly it could use more weapon and ship types. However, again, I have had nothing but great experiences with Trese Brothers.
As someone who freaking adores open ended ship trading/fighting games, from New Horizons mod, to Elite Dangerous, to  Escape Velocity Nova(Endless Sky.), I have been playing this type of game for the last decade or so. Constantly looking for the one that was perfect for me. Space Rangers 2 was close, but it lacked crew. EV: Nova was close, but it again lacked people aboard my ship. (and the combat was tedious.) I only have a few hours after work and family, and I'm playing this game. In a golden age of video games, media, and my other hobbies, I still find myself thinking about my next captain and the strategies it will take to thrive in Hard mode. It already is very good, and with the quality I expect out of Trese Brothers, I expect it to become great.
Christ. You read all that? You must really not be sure. Take it from me. This game is worth your time. Not buggy. Fun, and will have lots of content upon full release. Plus its one of the most polished EA's Ive ever played, and the community actively gets responses from the developer. Get on it.

Simply an amazing game that brings a very complex simulation of a life as a captain of a starship. It reminds me very much of the pen & paper RPG Rogue Trader which I hoped would see a computer adaptation at some point. Now it is here.
You can pursue some very well crafted storylines, explore, trade, fight both in space and on the ground and in the boarding actions (crew combat is done very much like the Darkest Dungeon). A lone engineer goes back to the lab he works at, at night, because he's forgotten his kid's diapers. He boots up his computer, drinks a beverage containing hallucinogens, and then trips out for about 2 hours, thinking he's in outer space with an alien friend that beats up people with the strangest of sounds.
Warm. Good. The improved graphics are a welcomed change to it. Are we in a movie?
One of the best bits of it. It's not complex, but it's dreamy, and unravels with a nice pace and some surprises. I really felt out there for a while, and it's only a pity that it's so short, and it doesn't even have a single word written or spoken.
Some parts are difficult to grasp (more due to the controls than the game's design), like jumping at the right moment, for example, but in general it's simple and well adapted to what it wants to convey. There's basically only basic movement (up down left right jump) and a gun. The gun is one of the better aspects of the game, actually, because it fits in so well with the story. You advance by discovery, there are checkpoints so no fear of dying, but the game doesn't "try to much" to lead you in a given direction as much as others, and there's also a lot of trial and error.
Minimalist but impressive. Rotoscoping, here, like in Prince of Persia, makes for a very smooth atmosphere.
Again minimalist and at times a bit distracting, but the effects (especially the gun and the elevators) are really nice.
Once every couple of years should be fine, but yeah, definitely worth it.

A weak thumbs up.
Pros
- Neat aesthetic and idea.
- Decent length.
- There are three extra ways to solve levels:  Elegant (solve with only one object), Old School (solve without pins), Awesome (you manually mark one of your solutions as Awesome...)
- Can quickly reset levels. Helpful when going for Elegant / Old School solutions
Cons
- The ability to mark solutions as Awesome is good, but forcing people to do it to earn the star is stupid.
- The physics don't always make much sense. Even after playing for hours I'm often surprised by how an object reacts. It will have more/less mass than I expect.
- I wish there was some way to Undo things. It's annoying to have to redraw/redo several things after you mess up drawing a single thing.
-- The game sometimes has trouble distinguishing between when you want to draw a pin vs. a small object.
- Too many puzzles have essentially the same solution.
- Game fails to launch on a retina MacBook Pro if you've set your system resolution to 1920x1200. I had to switch back to the default resolution to get the game to launch.

A free clicker-type game that does not have any microtransaction option whatsoever. That alone is pretty notable, considering what the genre's like these days, though it's not the only reason I'd recommend this. The game keeps track of how quickly you reach and re-reach certain milestones, so you can actually feel a sense of progression as you play. And instead of having long lists of options for what to upgrade and by how much, the User Interface is pretty streamlined.
There are bad points, but they tend to be the same as with every other clicker in existence: default music gets repetitive if you play for more than a few minutes at a time, a limited number of enemy designs (well, block layouts in this case) to click through, and no grand reward other than being able to do things even faster in your next run. Not enough to be a dealbreaker, I think, but maybe playing way too many variants of clicker games has impacted my judgement.

Well, first of all, this is a Klei game. That might tell you something of it's quality (hinthint: it's very good).
Mark of the Ninja is best experienced first-hand, and even a review might suck some of fun out of it, so my best advice is to purchase the game, and have a great time discovering it's charm. If you're still undecided, here's some of my thoughts about the game as a whole, having finished it 4 times.
Mark of the Ninja is a platforming stealth game, and it's mechanics and controls perfectly consolidate the type of gameplay it's trying to do - you can hug and climb walls, sometimes even climb across ceilings if the situation requires it, and it all feels natural, like the Ninja you play as is an extension of you.
There is combat in the game, and it can be the focus, but it's not very encouraged as it's a high risk - variable reward situation at all times. Like a ninja, your best course of action is to move unseen to your objective.
The campaign features a few locations with their own quirks, maybe there are snipers watching the complex, maybe the weather compromises your vision, perhaps the floor is crumbling; these variations add interesting and fun challenges for the player to play around and overcome.
Besides that, the levels are very non-linear, in that, though there are set objectives, there is a multitude of paths to them, and some may be easier or harder depending on your playstyle.
Having fully completed all the it has to offer, I'd say Mark of the Ninja is not a hard game. It may take a few tries in a few scenarios, but with the tools provided, good positioning, a plan of action and a bit of luck here and there, anything is possible to overcome - just have some patience, like a real ninja would. And the game does have a New Game+ mode, but it only changes a few things - it doesn't really make the game harder, it's just a bit more punishing of mistakes.
In conclusion, it's hard to understate how much of a great time I've had with Mark of the Ninja. If you've read this far, and you're convinced to buy this gem, I hope that you have a great time with it as I have. Happy stealthing!

Sit back, relax, and draw with some crayons.  Get the little red ball to touch all the stars and you’ll finish the level.  Crayon Physics Deluxe from Petri Purho is a simple game in premise, and you’ll immediately understand how to play it from the first level.
Each level  is a different drawing from a child’s imagination.  Simply push the red ball into the star in whatever way you can manage.  Your main method of control is to draw objects into the world using your mouse.  While the game is quite fun early on, it quickly becomes devilishly difficult.
Your drawings will start off simple enough: make a box to drop on the ball to knock if forward, draw a line to build a bridge across a gap.  However, soon you will need to aim the ball through small holes, or make it climb up an uneven surface with enough momentum to crest a peak and fall back down at just the right speed to fly into the star.  Trying to do some of these tasks is almost absurd, but finally figuring out a way (or accidentally swiping the star unexpectedly) is a moment full of joy.  The game has seven worlds and one bonus level once you collect 120 stars (out of 150 total), and there are a lot of interesting puzzles to solve.
The soundtrack is a small handful of relaxing lullabies, which mesh nicely with the visuals, and contrast strongly with the amount of mental anguish you will be going through. When objects hit each other, there is a satisfying “thump” and then the ball goes flying off the screen, crap dang it all that work wasted.
The visuals are entirely unique in gaming, and everything really does look like crayons drawn on paper. The different items like trees, boats, houses, and dinosaurs are cute and fun to discover.  The resolution only goes up to 1024x768, so it tends to look a little fuzzy on large HD screens.
In order to “master” each level, you need to find an elegant solution (only one item drawn) and an old-school solution (no pushing the ball, no extra pins drawn), and also specify one of your solutions as an Awesome solution.  Once you do that, you will get a bonus star for that level.  Annoyingly, you will have to manually select an awesome solution for each and every level in order to get that star.  This is a tedious process that keeps you out of the puzzles for far too long.
This game is quite a brain-burner, and it will either give you a few hours of fun or days of frustration; depending on your approach to it.  Luckily it is quite easy to skip levels, and go somewhere else for a while. A lazy Sunday afternoon is a perfect time to spend with some crayons and lovely puzzles.

Gremlins is an online board game where the objective is to score the most points after a set number of rounds. If there is a tie, the Gremlin with the most money wins followed by the least Malice.
The gameplay proceeds according to the class that the player randomly receives at the start of the game. You have a hand of 6 cards that keeps getting replenished after you play a card. On your turn, you have to play a card and move according to the number of dice pips on the card. It ranges from 1 to 6. Your movement follow the arrows on the board and you may not backtrack against an arrow unless it is bi-directional or you have a special ability. To score points, you have to play cards that show a green gear symbol.
Conclusion, while this is a neat game, the sheer randomness turns me off. I was initially very attracted to the design of Gremlins Inc but the huge swings and dependence on luck makes me decide that I would not play this game much. You might as well have rolled dice to determine the winner.

Battlepaths is the best Jon Arbuckle game on steam where you whack and smack people and monsters on their face. In fact, it's the only Jon Arbuckle game where you whack and smack, it would make Garfield puke its guts out.
The game as a rogue-lite sometimes adoringly looks similar to the pen and paper version of Dungeons and Dragons, where you meet your friends, play with basic card cutouts of heroes and villains and battle maps, and in general have a grand ol' time. Other times though, Battlepaths' simplicity of combat and looting serves to a fault filled with frustration and eyes rolling.
Graphics are simple and funnily-cartoonish 2D fare that looks okay and functional overall, with enough color and variety, Animation however, is almost non-existent. You move like a cardboard cutout (meaning you don't move at all, you just spawn to the next spot) and only move a hand up and down in the air, which represents either an attempt to fight or a fist-shaking at the game creators for giving everyone no animations whatsoever,
As for the story, there is none: You play as Jon Arbuckle which for some reason in this game calls himself Rick, a would-be adventurer. You make a character, choose a level of difficulty, you start with the first zone, pick up the most generic quests possible, whack stuff that moves, you level up, and finally as you grow stronger, you unlock new area with more dangerous stuff that needs to be whacked some more.
There is music and sound... which are completely unobtrusive and forgettable, that you'll soon turn a podcast and do some multitasking.
The battle system, which is a bread and butter for all rogue-lite games, in Battlepaths is very simple where you have only one attack until you unlock up to four, very simplistic special combat moves and effects, either passive or active. Which is fine and even kind of a relaxing, until the game decides to put some effort to it, and introduce enemies with gazillion hit points, or ranged units that have a chance to hit you three or four times in a row per your move. Yes you read it right, you move one block at a time, while enemy ranged units stand from several blocks away, happily filling you with arrows and ice/fireballs while you can do squat. Meaning, in later part, the game uses cheap and annoying tricks to increase the difficulty.
You can call upon beasts from the bottle to fight at you side, which is a cool idea, except they are weak and have next to zero intelligence. They are fine if you spawn them right next to your enemy, as they attack them, but if an enemy is a couple of blocks away, chances are your summoned beast is only going to give them a threatening glance as they refuse to move or attack.
Looting system is a bit more complex, with enough variety to satisfy that inner crave to bogart everything. You can also upgrade loot with augmentation stones which give random benefits, as well as cancel upgrades or re-arange upgrades with appropriate magic stones.
Overall, Battlepaths is a solid, if uninspired game that is going to offer you 5-10 hours of average fun. And for a price it's asking, you could do far worse.

Other reviewers have captured the game, as it stands, far more eloquently than I could, so I'll just add bits and pieces here.
The first impression you get of this game is "immense". At first glance, its scope seems similar to - or even larger than - that of Paradox's grand strategy offerings. Whether this proves to be the case in the long run is something I shall no doubt discover and share here.
The second impression: "oldschool". Oldschool in a good way. In a comforting, "I'm at home" type of way. Even though I have little-to-no idea of what I'm actually doing yet. The interface, though bewildering at first (not unlike a Paradox title) is very welcoming (very unlike a Paradox title) and not so daunting that you're inclined to simply give up. Over time, the UI starts to make sense. A lot more sense than it does at the beginning, anyway. Hotkeys are a welcome addition here and, once you've become familiar with them, you can achieve most things with them. Tooltips is another welcome feature which compliments the available hotkeys well.
The third impression: "Just one more turn."

Whether you're already a fan of the anime/manga or you're dipping into the world of Higurashi for the first time, I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys visual novels. The characters are loveable, the mystery is very interesting and the psychological horror aspect is brilliant in my personal opinion. Even as someone who's watched the anime twice and knew what was going to happen, I still found myself quite spooked on multiple occasions. I was also surprised by how engaged I found myself in it, despite again, having already watched the anime twice. The VN definitely has enough to keep those who enjoyed the adaptions interested, while giving those who jump in for the first time an absolutely captivating experience.
I really only have two complaints. The first is that the pacing can be quite slow at points. Though that's more of a nitpick that applies to the genre as a whole for me and it never drags for very long, so don't even worry about that one. More of a personal peeve than anything else and it never truly affected my enjoyment.
The second complaint is not even about the game itself, but rather the marketing. Despite MangaGamer insisting otherwise, this is a novel through and through. No gameplay is present. I could go on about how this is essentially lying to the consumer but I'll hold my tongue. Personally, I don't mind the lack of gameplay as the story itself was more than enough to keep me invested during all of my playtime. But understandably, the lack of any sort of gameplay or choice will turn off some players. Which is part of why the misleading marketing really annoys me, but I digress
All in all though, if you enjoy visual novels I implore you to at least check this one out. It's not exactly expensive either, so do yourself a favor and pick it up if you haven't already.  You won't be disappointed.

Biff Benedict Pocoroba (born July 25, 1953 in Burbank, California) is a former Major League Baseball catcher, who also played a few games at third base. He was drafted by the Atlanta Braves in the 17th round of the 1971 amateur draft.
As a rookie, Pocoroba got attention during spring training in 1975 by throwing out 11 straight would-be base stealers. [1] He made his major-league baseball debut on April 25, 1975, as a defensive replacement in the Braves' 5–3 loss to the San Diego Padres at San Diego.
His best season was in 1977 when he achieved career-highs with 123 games, a Batting average of .290, 8 home runs, 24 doubles, and 44 runs batted in. In 1978, he made the National League All-Star team, finishing the season with a .242 batting average, 6 home runs, and 34 RBI in 92 games. A torn Rotator cuff injury slowed his career [2] and he played his last game on April 20, 1984, at the age of 30.

With the recent influx of 2D fighters on Steam, sometimes the key to getting noticed is to have a different approach.
angle is "Romance of the Three Kingdoms", but almost every character is a girl. Guan Yu? Cao Cao? Sun Shang Xiang!? All girls. Furthermore, this game is a spin-off of
, an adult visual-novel/strategy game about a young man who travels back in time to this Three Kingdoms era. To be honest, I'm a little surprised that
is an awesome fighting game.
In terms of game-design,
is unlike other contemporary 2D fighters. Instead of having its combatants soar into the air and devastate each other with dizzying combos, this game keeps it very grounded. For the most part, combos rarely go beyond two-in-ones, or jump-in > follow-up > special. A lot of matches are determined by fighting-game basics. By that I mean spacing, footsies, pokes, anti-airs, and so on. It's not that these elements aren't present in other fighters, but players mistakenly tend to ignore them as the genre becomes increasingly complicated. If I were to draw comparisons,
could be considered a faster-paced
.
Going further, the moves you perform all have wildly-varying degrees of safetyness. Light attacks are generally a good idea for applying pressure, but they probably won't decide matches. Medium and heavy attacks have their uses, and with proper timing and spacing, you can control the flow of the match. However, when you hold forward, or down/forward and perform a medium or heavy attack, everything changes. Your heroine performs a high-risk attack. It's slow, can be countered in many ways, but it can also dramatically effect the outcome of the fight.
Now I'm not sure what to call it. A critical-counter? A fatal-counter? A romantic-counter? Well, it doesn't really matter. Basically, when the opponent is hit with a certain move, they crumple to the floor. This gives the player still standing an opportunity to land a massive combo. We're talking wall-splats, ground-bounces, the works. Off of a single one of these counters, players can expect to lose anywhere from 30 to 60 or even 100%(!!) of their life. It sounds crazy, but keep in mind that the larger combos will require some rather precise positioning, execution, and a lot of meter. To add to this, you can't get hit by these devastating counters if you aren't caught pressing buttons. Obviously the answer to avoiding these situations isn't "don't try to attack", but you have to be wary.
While I've just discussed what can be considered the x-factor of a Koihime Enbu fight, these occurences are few and far between. If your opponent is well-aware that you're fishing for a crucial-counter, they're going to have no trouble picking you apart. In this game, the simplest combos or even single-attacks can do serious damage. A lot of the time, you'll find that the best strategy is to stick to the basics. Aside from those mythical 75-100% combos, the execution barrier for this game is very low. This allows players to devote their energies towards understanding match-ups, looking for openings, and hopefully, winning matches. While I think that the roster could stand to have a few more entrants, it does strike the right balance between depth and accessibility. Every character is easy to use, but they can also offer some unique moves or interesting tactics. Aside from everyone having good and bad match-ups, there doesn't seem to be any truly ineffective characters.
As far as content goes, it's fair to say that this game is a better buy for competitive players. While this tends to be the expectation when it comes to fighters, a sizable number of these games still include extensive single-player modes. Unfortunately, this isn't the case for
. I'm going to start this portion of the review off by admitting that... well... I got a little curious and did some research. I browsed the Koihime Muso wikia, looked up some other related materials, and now I'm interested in seeing more of the storyline. Unfortunately, the scenario mode in Koihime Enbu is a little disappointing. Each character has their own story, and dialogues with their opponents in-between matches, but the plot isn't there.
I suppose I shouldn't be asking for a storyline that affects the
canon, especially with the omission of a few key characters (such as the male lead and Ryūbi Gentoku aka Liu Bei). Still, as a huge fan of the
novel, I was hoping for something with a little more depth, rather than a handful of gags and sorta-intimate moments. Still, the scenario mode might be worth checking out, since at least it gives some insight on everyone, and will help newcomers get used to how the game works and the franchise that it spawned from.
The training mode in this game is very well-designed. It covers all of the functionality that fighting game fans are accustomed to, such as a multitude of options, the ability to practice against the CPU, and even allowing for two players to spar with each other. Alongside the training mode, there is also a challenge mode where players can attempt several combos, each more convoluted than the last. Training mode can also be accessed while waiting for online matches, which is always welcome.
As far as the online-play is concerned, I believe that it's satisfactory. There have been some instances of lag, most notably when I (an American) was playing against someone from Japan. Speaking of, expect the competition to be extremely stiff and punishing.
has been in Japanese arcades since 2014, and on consoles since the beginning of this year. I've already had a few matches, where I put up as much of a fight as a training dummy. This is partly because some of the strategies I've run into, simply won't occur in the single-player modes.
To give an example, one of my opponents was a Sonshōkō (Sun Shang Xiang) player. The first round was a close win for me, my opponent won the second. After the second round, I noticed that my opponent had a full bar of meter. So what happened in the third round? On my end, everything went to Hell. Each faction in the game has a couple selectable strategists. Summoning help costs meter, but they offer some useful techniques, if you know how to employ them. Anyway, Ryomō (one of the strategists), throws three projectiles at the opponent. While this is happening, Sonshōkō has some freedom to attack or defend at will. I wasn't prepared for this. So needless to say, all of my advances were thwarted, I fell victim to some nasty mix-ups, and I couldn't even land chip-damage on my opponent.
That's not to say that all of your fights will be decided by unfamiliar tech. In every match, there is a measurable level of chaos. To explain it better, I'll post a link to a video:
. Notice how several seconds pass by in the first round without a single hit being registered. As the match progresses, both players start taking risks, and the rounds are decided far more quickly. High-level play can be extremely methodical, so if you don't have the patience for it, you'll get hurt.
Although
is lacking in terms of single-player content, I have every reason to believe that this is one of the better fighting games on Steam. It has its own style, and offers enough playability to challenge gamers of any skill-level.

A worthy successor to the original.  Combat is vastly improved over the first game;  the Creepy Treat cards give you more options than "fight to build up your super meter" and "use your super move", and the costume affinities introduce more strategy into how you select your targets in battle.  As well, there is more variety in enemies. Different types of enemies use different spells and tactics, and feel much less like simple reskins.  Outside of battle, the graphics and the writing have all the charm of the original game.  The only thing that feels lacking is character customization; hopefully, if there's a Costume Quest 3, both the first game's battle stamps and the second game's Creepy Treat cards will be on the menu.  If you loved the first game, you'll love this one too.  If you haven't played the first... well you should, but give this a try anyway.

- Graphics are VERY outdated for a 2012 game, looks like a much older game that hasn't aged well
- UI is pretty clunky (no sort in inventory, etc.)

- Many game design decisions are... well... let's call them old-school (no Town Portal spells or similyr)
May still be considered OK for a low budget production. Without the storyline it would not be recommended at all.

Full Disclosure: TBG Discord Moderator and Alpha Tester here; been playing for the past 6 months.
I can highly recommend this game for fans of endless sky, star nomad 2 and other space trading games.

I realize that it is one of my favourite games on Steam. I didn't play it as much as some other games, but I think they made something timeless. I love the pace, the gameplay, the traps, the fact that every tower is randomly generated. It's the kind of game you could play anytime when you got no idea what to play else. It is very enjoyable to any kind of player I think, as there are 4 difficulty modes (easy is a strall if you just want to play it cool, normal gives you a fluid pace yet asks the player to stay alert, hard adds tension and adrenaline, and nightmare is for masochistics but stays fun despite being unfair sometimes, thanks to the checkpoints). I think what I like the most is that the gameplay is very simple (move, jump, push, use), but as the blocs of the tower are always moving and changing, the playground is modified every couple of seconds and it forces the player to be watchful. This transforms the game into something that is not only a puzzle game, but also an action/platformer game, and if everything is ruled by simple mechanics, all things piled together makes for something complex and satisfactory for the player.

Frankly, I miss tycoon games. I was hoping that this would re-spark the genre, but this game shows literally what is wrong with many new tycoon games:
Hospital Tycoon:
1. Has poor controls. A game like this needs to be playable without moving your hands off the mouse to the keyboard and back again every few seconds. I rarely say this, but this game has an absolutely atrocious control setup. You will be confused before even learning how to play.
2. You don't do much in this game. Now I really love games that engage the player. As a simulation game, the player should be busy and not just sit around waiting for people to die of cancer. After I had build every facility I could, I thought I would get somewhere, but the game just has you watch people walk around. While the game has many management features, it does not force the player to really use them.
3. Has annoying "Sims"-esque voices. The game really tried to be the sims and ended up falling WAY short.
4. On that "Sims" note, this game isn't really about managing a hospital. Instead, it is about sexist relationships between the nurses and doctors presented in a way like "The Sims", but is really just as bad as any soap opera like "Grey's Anatomy".

A lot of focus on art and visuals but not much on gameplay mechanics and balance.
It's fun on a casual, non-competitive level. And I don't mean competitive as in EVO or tryhards, I mean competitive as in "I want to fight my opponent on fair ground in a well balanced arena and win by my own merits and skill."
It's not even a case of character tiers or any particular character just outclassing the others, it's the fact that the universal systems are pretty weak. Things that you expect from other fighting games just aren't here.
The good news is that the skill floor is very low -- you can get by pretty well just mashing buttons, and inputs for specials/supers are absolutely no more difficult than a modern street fighter game.
The bad news is that the skill ceiling isn't particularly high, either.
Before buying this, consider what kind of fighting game fan you are. If you want to train, get better, and feel like you've really accomplished something by doing so... you might not want to get it.
Do I recommend this game to others? Not personally, no. But that doesn't necessarily a bad game.

Now the snark is out the way, I'd argue that playing Inquisitor in the year of our Lord 2015 really
a surprisingly  enjoyfull experience and I'm immersed entirely in the atmosphere and the world.
Yeah, it's... curious to play such a game precisely now. We've got Pillars of Eternity, Divinity - OS and Wasteland 2 that are true heralds of the modern renaissance of the classical text-rich, immersive isometric(-ish) WRPG and still more beautiful games like Tides of Numenara to come, and playing Inquisitor feels extremely similar and evokes the same good pleasure responses like playing any of those games, or reading a great rich fantasy novel.
Sure, graphics show it's age and are nothing to celebrate, but the updated UI and modern resolution support make playing it an enjoyfull enough experience and deep world-building and atmosphere are (so far) top notch and I don't see any truly meaningful differences in playing Inquisitor from reading Wasteland's descriptions, enjoying PoE's diverse dialogue trees, or being delighted by unexpected char perk from making some decision in Divinity.
Yes, I recommend it.
Cause it made me exclaim in tiny sweet delight for obtaining those before mentioned boots and for hearing an interesting story.. erm.. to boot. Cause I leveled up by two levels solely by killing bats around the first hub area. Cause I was then experiencing sweet "agony" of choice - where should I spend the points - in stealth, or in thieving. Cause I got to be the medieval detective and because of it I got to hear at least 10 different ways of different people saying somebody had his

This is a Pay-4-Play game with 50 free tokens, which amounts to a demo period.  After the free tokens are gone, you are paying them or you are done.  Oh, and if they say you lose connection before you even make your first move, those tokens you spent to play that map are gone.  There is no such thing as owning this game.  This is an arcade game where you need to keep pumping in the quarters to pay from now to eternity.  At least Candy Crush lets you come back after a cooloff period if you don't want to pay for immediate continue.
So... play this decent game for 50 tokens.  If you get addicted, start looking for the quarter slot on your computer.  Or if you love it, go buy the board game and get reaquainted with your IRL friends.  It'll be cheaper in the long run than entering your credit card number.
Would I play again?  If I had been able to buy the game instead of rent it, sure I probably would.  Would I pay from now to eternity to rent time on the game?  Not on your life.  Would I buy the table-top game IRL?  Not after the sour taste in my mouth from losing my last 3 tokens trying to Storm Paris and having it say I disconnected.

Ive been a huge fan of the Treses Brothers for a few years now, owning all their games on Android, and a few on Steam as well. Over the years i have seen their talents grow, from the art style to game mechanics, and it feels like it has all built up to this game.
While Templar Battleforce is one of my favourite games of all time (I mainly play it on Android, but bought it on Steam as well), this game has blown me away.
The art is fantastic, and the gameplay phenomenal. Its kind of hard to describe what it is really. Its like a weird cross between Sid Meiers Pirates, Mount & Blade and a turn based RPG. But that still doesnt do it justice.
The sandbox is amazing, and is what im currently loving. You can do what ever you want. Mine planets, be a pirate, buy and sell goods for a prophet, hunt bounties, sway intergalactic politics, and theres even a main story line if you want to follow that.
My only gripe currently is that at first the UI isnt too intuitive (Took me a solid 5 minutes to work out how to accept a mission. EDIT: Less than 24 hours later, and this is fixed) but after a while it becomes second nature.
This will be a game i will play for a long, long time, and at its price, it is so worth it, i would happily pay double for it.

Superb version of a classic boardgame although, as usual, "free to play" means "limited demo" unless you want to pay extra. Games only take about 15 minutes, it's easy to learn, the manual's only a few pages, but gameplay's excellent... the sign of a great game. All you need to know about is movement, terrain restrictions and range modifiers and you're away. The visuals may put some people off (it's hexey, same as the boxed real-life version) but behind that it's a gem. Roll the dice, get symbols that match your target type to hit, destroy units or capture a location to get a victory point medal. Simple but effective.
The only trouble is the pay to play model, imo one of the nastiest money leaching and off-putting things to happen to gaming in the last 20 years. Once the 50 free gold runs out you're stuck with only 2 free maps. It may only work out as pennies to play a match but if  they'd sell it as a complete game, drop the "free" tag and the extra payments, it would've been great (and maybe had a larger number of long term players). It's happened with other boardgame conversions such as Ticket to Ride, Smallworld, Catan, Space Hulk, Talisman, so why not this too?
Use the free bits then buy the boardgame until they come to their senses and release it as a full game where you can play to your heart's content without paying extra for the pleasure.

I didn’t really know what to expect with Diamond Dan. For whatever reason, this game always caught my eye whenever it became discounted during the big steam sales. So I finally picked it up. Lo and behold, the game isn’t terrible. It’s not even half bad. It may be one of the uglier ducklings of the bunch, but underneath a lacking appearance is a surprisingly entertaining puzzle-lite platformer.
Each level is comprised of a cubic tower, itself filled with constantly shifting cubes that you must traverse to reach the bottom. You have the option of two playable characters, the first being able to move nearby blocks, whilst the other can outright destroy them at the expense of losing the ability to double-jump. While the beginning levels contain little challenge, further levels become longer, and introduce new types of traps that become increasingly difficult to avoid, both due to your own incompetence and slow transitioning speed of the screen while you transfer between the different sides of each tower.
The platforming itself is tight, and it’s satisfying leaping between booby trapped walls and floors. There is no time limit to each level, and your performance in each is based on how many jewels and coins you can collect, all of which add to your end score. Activating and narrowly escaping traps goes towards earning a score multiplier, though aside from leaderboard and achievement junkies, there’s no real incentive to pursue higher scores beyond personal gratification. However, there are higher difficulties, and beating each earns you a shinier medal, so that provides some longevity for those who enjoy a challenge.
I’ve actually enjoyed what I’ve played of DD. Visually, it can be pretty unappealing, especially the character models, though the in-game aesthetic looks alright, if a bit dated. One thing I am fond of is the menu; it’s all set up at a desk, with each option being one of a series of items lying on it. Your view follows your cursor, so it’s almost like you’re actually sitting at the desk, and it’s neat to see things added to it after you complete each level. It’s a nice touch, and it adds a bit of charm to the experience.
Diamond Dan is surprisingly alright, given its budget price and lack of fanfare. It may be lacking visually, but the gameplay is tight and even challenging in later levels and on higher difficulties. It’s not terribly long, and can likely be beaten in several short hours, either on a lazy afternoon, or as a break between larger adventures. I wouldn’t call it a diamond in the rough, but after a few strokes from a shirt sleeve, even this jewel shows off a modest gleam.

Diamond Dan is a puzzle platformer based more on quick reflexes than logic.  You must descend towers of ever-shifting blocks to find a map at the bottom and escape.  Sounds simple, but you can be crushed or thrown from the tower, and many of the blocks contain traps such as water or spike pits, projectiles, or enemies living inside the walls who will pull you to your death. Checkpoints are created by opening shortcuts with keys.
Traps can be triggered without harming yourself, if you do it quickly, and doing so rewards you by increasing your multiplier, which adds to the value of any treasure you pick up. Your score at the end of the level is then multiplied based on the difficulty you're playing on.  Difficulty affects density of traps and how quickly the blocks shift (it can get insane) and can be changed at will for any level.
You can play as Dan (pushes blocks) or Ann (shatters blocks) on any level and there are separate leaderboards for each.  Friend and global leaderboards and tons of achievements.

A rich game, which adapts to many different playstyles. You have to manage your crew (its health and morale and its varied attributes, skills, talents, and traits), but your goals are your own. You can play the great game (politics) for all it’s worth, or focus on trade, legal or not, or spy, or prey on merchants, or protect them from pirates, or land and explore.
You don’t have to fight, but if you do, you’ll discover that ship combat and crew combat each are their own game. For crew combat, for instance, you decide which of your fighters join the fray and in which relative positions; then, each turn, you decide which talents they use among those you had them learn (like your captain, your officers and crew improve with experience).
The paths you can take are as numerous as the stars, and no aspect of the game feels half-baked or shallow. Even after the many hours I played during the alpha stage, I was left with plenty to try—and that was before the stories were added!
Sounds overwhelming? It could be. It isn’t. If you try to excel at everything from the get-go, you’ll find it tough, but if you focus on what interests you most, you’ll learn what you need as you go. Plus, the newly added stories will take you by the hand, at first, and make sure you both learn the ropes and discover the lore of the Star Traders universe.
I can hardly wait to have more time to play!

Keep in mind, this review takes into consideration the following: An understanding of the game's state and length as provided above for all to see
; the fact that the release date states December 15, 2016, again for all to see; and the fact that I paid only $.89 for the thing.
First off Near Midnight is more a demo than a full game. Something I don't mind paying $.89 for. As I understand it used to be $3. Something I may not have paid at the time for this. The game has promise, however. That is provided the developer contnues to actually work on it. That stated, I'm not entirely confident this will be in proper early access by December. We shall see though. Now, I'll list the pros and cons and then explain my review status afterwards.
Pros:
Great backstory
Good setting
Decent atmosphere
Partial controller support (quite a pleasant surprise for me)
Cons:
Looping intro sequence
Texture ripping
Poor lighting
Annoying sfx
Noninteractable items, save for one solitary pistol
Summary:
Yes, I'm giving Near Midnight a recommend and a positive review. Why? Simply put, because it has promise if it is worked on.
I did not include the length in the pros/cons because that information was privy to anyone willing to spend more than a second looking at the store page. There is a dev announcement for September 5, 2016 that states they know the game is short and not fully developed. A warning that is ready for the masses right there on the store page. So I will NOT be holding that against the game because I was warned about it before purchasing. I full well knew I would have between 1-10 minutes with this.
I did appreciate what Near Midnight is trying to accomplish here. This game does have promise provided we see these guys continue to develop it and are not trying to nickel and dime us here. And I, personally, felt $.89 wasn't such a bad development "donation" for continued development. I spend more on a candy bar that is quickly digested. I'm not upset about the purchase. I like the backstory. I enjoy the fact that it takes place on a rural farm and that the daughter is seemingly possessed by a spirit or demon. At least, that is the assumpting I made based on the background text. I absolutely love that there is at least a rudimentary native support for controllers already. My Xbox One controller easy accomplished all thing I required for interacting in the game world. It was a very pleasant surprise and I appreciate that it was included. I also like the house itself. There were a few logical fallacies I found with it, but I'll go into detail about that below. The house is a great setting for the game. I just hope there are more rooms in the future or a spooky mechanic that extends the play area later on. The girl is downright creepy and I appreciate that. The actress has done a great job conveying this girl. I like that there is no HUD or UI. It added to the horror factor by not showing us how many bullets were in the gun. Keep the lack of UI present.
Well that was the positive paragraph. On to the gritty stuff.  DEVELOPER, consider this a personal note to you as well.
Right off the bat I noticed something negative. The fact that the intro sequence continually loops itself until you click on "Skip." That needs to be taken out as soon as possible. The intro needs to be voiced over and once played, go directly to gameplay. None of this looping nonsense. As soon as I entered the house I looked to my right and noticed a texture tear between the first and second floors. I could see the light blue of the sky between the two. Throughout play I also spotted quite a few of these texture tears running vertically on a number of the walls. The second thing I noticed about the textures is that the house is way too destitute for what the backstory provides. From my understand we are arriving to inspect noises after a recent double homicide. There is no reason why the house interior should look like it has been left to fall apart for over 20 years in the wilds. I imagine these attentive and caring parents also upkept the house fairly well. Something the dev might want to consider. I get going for atmosphere, but at the cost of immersion is always a bad decision. Some of the sfx are a little....much. The awful bong sound that exists with every spooky change just kills the immersion for me. Just use the laughter or weird sounds that accompany the bong sometimes. Some sfx that is relevant to the room or house at some level. Cut that bonging sound out of the game. It is horrible. Absolutely horrible. There is a point where we hear dripping after coming across a note about a bathroom. It makes no sense. There is no tub anywhere or a bathroom that I found. So that was just poorly done. Expand the house to accompany what you're going for here. The lighting needs to be fixed. As another reviewer stated, it looks nothing like the video on the store page. If the lighting were like that and we had a flashlight, this demo experience would have been a lot better. The abrupt ending would have been a bit more intense if we had a flash of something hitting us or the girl rushing towards us and blacking the screen out. The sudden cutoff and return to the menu screen is disappointing. More so considering we can't restart or close the game because the mouse cursor fails at that point.
Overall, the game has promise but is full of flaws. Keep on developing and see this vision come to light.
TL;DR
PROS
Great backstory
Good atmosphere
Partial controller support
CONS
Looping intro sequence
Texture ripping
Some bad sfx and lighting
Unsatisfying abrupt ending
Considering the pros/cons, I still recommend the game. For $.99 it is worth investing in for the continued development of the title. Something that could genuinely become great as long as the developer continues developing. I'd much rather promote support of a project that could be good than to squelch creativity entirely and shut down an endeavor. Call me an optimist, I suppose.

Inquisitor looks old, plays like and a 90's RPG and will be spewing very long blocks of text at your face. If that doesn't turn your off, keep reading because there's much more to it than that.
You can kind of guess this game is going to take some time to finish from the get go and that impression would be right, I'm only around 20 hours in and there's a lot to do and a lot to see. In the first act, you're helping the local branch of the church to solve several cold cases of mysterious murders and unexplained disappearances, tracking down heretics and allies of the devil. The game takes the form of a really old school isometric RPG, not too dissimilar from Arcanum. You will be wandering into an original world mixing a middle-age central europe setting with medieval-fantastic aspects. Think "The Name of the Rose" meets "Lord of the Rings".
The game will have you speaking to a lot of people to fill your journal with information and clues and to collect evidence, picking and using skill from your character sheet, selecting and equipping spells and managing your inventory. While the mouse driven interface can get a little bit confusing, hiding some vital parts of your character sheet under what looks like very small tabs on a 1080p monitor, you can use (and definitely should learn) the keyboard bindings for most actions.
The variety of items you will come across is just mind numing. From potions and spell scrolls, to weapons and armors, all items have different levels of quality, need to be repaired and maintained in working order, and combined to ensure your survival against the spawn of the devil and the creatures of the wilderness.
The combat, while on par with the 90's tech powering the engine, is nothing really exciting and can get quite frustrating if you're trying to use skills and spells on top of your trusty sword. The special effects (confusion, blindness...) while incredibly creative, can be very off-putting to say the least.
What really sets this title apart from the modern games that pretend to be RPG's today is the writing. Sure there's a lot of it but it's both well written (or should I say translated) but is also engaging an immersive. It's likely that you will want to know more about the world... and the NPC's will be more than happy to tell you all you may want to learn. I found the conversations with certain characters to be rewards in and of themselves.
The music is nothing short of amazing, taking a really classical route with an early baroque feel, far removed from the generic post romantic and modern orchestral music. A choice fitting the universe in many ways.
It should be said that Inquisitor also does a better job at analysing the psyche of its character and reflecting some of the dark parts of the human condition much better than any other hipsterish indie non-game. Most of that exploration flows organically with the gameplay, the setting and the artistic direction of the game. Just for that I think anyone with a passing interest in character development in games should at least take a look at the first act of this game, just to see how to do it right.
I love this game and I would recommend it to anyone loving old-school RPG's, however, remember the introduction of this review, it might not be your thing and that's totally understandable.

Disclaimer: I am a moderator on the Trese Brothers’ Discord Server, and was a closed Alpha playtester. I recived my key from backing the Kickstarter.
Star Traders: Frontiers is primarily a game about a single Captain, their ship, their loyal Officers and their crew. The gameplay is primarily sandbox oriented, with the player being able to freely move from world to world, trading in the Exchanges, exploring the vast untamed Wild Zones, Spying for precious intel, fighting in the silence of the void or chasing down criminals in a gravity well. However, every choice made comes with consequences, be they good or ill. Crew, Officers, and even the Captain can and will die in battle or in unforgiving wilderness. The Factions do not treat lawbreakers kindly, and beware the terror of the Xeno.
The story is still only in its opening stages, but it already has a lot to do. In the interest of avoiding spoilers, I shall only say that many things happen, and you can choose your level of involvement. Do you stay aloof and neutral, fully back your allies, or maybe just go on your way, seeking out another distant star for different opportunities?
The galaxy is full of secrets, potential, allies and enemies. Make no mistake, your first Captain will die. And likely your second and third as well. The difficulty scale in this game is not a joke. Even as an experienced player, I still lose Captains to careless mistakes, falling behind the difficulty curve, or simple bad luck. However, if you prefer a less harrowing experience, the lower difficulty options will make for a more forgiving world, perfect to learn in until you feel that you can move up to the next rung on the ladder.
Finally, the devs, the Trese Brothers, are always looking to improve their games, and have an excellent track record of doing so. In the closed Alpha alone there have been over 60 updates, and if the original Star Traders RPG is anything to go by, there will likely be hundreds more in the pipeline. The devs are almost always on their forum or in their Discord server, and they are always happy to take suggestions, requests for new features, and answer questions.
Now Captain, the Crew are at their stations, the Engines are warming up, and the galaxy awaits you. May the stars welcome you with all their light.

I've been an active  member of the Alpha community for Star Traders: Frontiers since it went live, and I have to say that it's been the most wonderful experience ever spent playing and assisting in the creation/debugging of one of the most satisfying and challenging sandbox universes crafted.
For your $15 you are buying access to one of the most positive and friendly communities, as well as a deep and engaging sandbox game that allows you to gear your ship toward whatever style of play you find most exciting, whether it be trading, spying, fighting, or just exploring.
You get:
-Map Generation that is seeded carefully so as to make every quadrant feel unique and engaging, instead of just giving you extra "random" content.
-A Job System that allows for both extreme focus, and broad protection. The choice on how each of your crew members should select their feats is up to you. Re-assigning their perks is just a click of a button away.
-Ship combat that is both tactical and terrifying, where your prowess as a captain is your best defense, but every torpedo fired may be the last one that you need, or the last one that your opponent does.
-All your actions have consequences. Kill off the opposition to your favorite contacts, or balance their powers and profit off of the blood feud. Your actions will change the world around you, and the impact will only deepen as development continues.
The developers are active every day, and in contact almost 24/7 trying to craft the best gaming experience they can. It is the kind of game they would (and do) play, and they are very proud of that fact. Once you join this community, you will be, too.

This is a difficult game to properly describe, but it's a Space Trade Exploration Adventure RPG with Global Events triggering things throughout the galaxy.  That being said, it can also be played as a sandbox game.
Choose your primary Career, your Faction affiliation, select your initial skill and attributes, hire and train your crew, purchase and upgrade your ship, promote your best crew to Officers, and launch yourself into the void of space.  Whether you play as a merchant, pirate, spy, explorer, military commander (or several other careers), you'll be challenged by faction wars, trade bans, offers of missions to faraway sectors with great risk/reward, hostile ship attacks, and the ever-present risk of Xeno attacks in space or wilderness zones.
As you trade between economic zones on various planets, accept missions for payments, hold pirates ransom, spy on enemy planets, sell intel to your contacts, patrol friendly territory, blockade your enemies and blow hostile ships to smithereens, you and your crew will be gaining valuable experience and learning new jobs and talents. Upgrade your ship, crew weapons, armor and enhancements, deploy specialized gear to maximize your career goals. The contacts you meet will offer missions to enhance your reputation with factions (or turn you into a war criminal with other factions).  Many of the missions lead to story arcs in which you can help shape major events and shake up the galaxy.
The decisions are yours Captain.  You are a Star Trader.
The Trese Brothers have polished the game to a very usable state, hence the release to Early Access.  They are known for constantly updating their games to improve balance, add new features (often from players just like you and I), fix bugs, and provide new content.  See Templar Battleforce and Heroes of Steel for examples of their commitment.
In short, definitely recommend this game.

I have just completed this, and I feel compelled to review it. I originally bought it just to see what it was like. I had seen the show several times, I thought it would just be a lot of text to scroll through. It turned out, to be a bunch of text to scroll through. However, what I never thought would happen, did. I thought that having seen the show so many times, there would be no effect. I have never been so wrong.
First of all, I have to credit the excellent sound design. The music is fantastic, there are energetic and lively tunes, and more sombre slower paced tracks. Not to mention compelling scenes aided by no music at all. The sound effects are crisp, and they all feel like they have actual impact. The cicada cries never become annoying, and they serve as insanely fitting background noise.
This is a visual novel, and I'd be comitting a crime if I didn't applaud the fantastic writing. Not only is it superbly translated, (From what I can tell, my japanese is a little sketchy) The dialogue is witty, and snappy. You'd think I'd be frowning, sad, or scared the whole time. However, the slice of life sections made me smile and laugh more often than the actual show did. All of the characters speak so naturally, and abide by their characters well. The normal sections are hilarious, and the creepy sections have this undeniable weight to them, as if you are completely sucked into the world.
The atmosphere is too good to describe. The game can set any scene and it becomes believeable and almost surrealy life like. The simple fact that there is a static image on screen, with words covering a good portion of it, and I am completely immersed is something to praise. The writing, the art, the sounds, they all come together to make the game really transcend its own medium, to become something far more.
The art, first of all, the characters are absolutely beautifully drawn. From the screenshots, they are far improved from the original versions. They are all far more expressive than I'd think possible. How they can so easily shift from emotion to emotion is incredible. They do reuse the exact same faces and sprites often, however, they never become boring to look at. Also, new ones are occasionally added, the spice things up. Rena in particular has the greatest set of faces in the entire game. Now, the backgrounds are a little disappointing. They all look ok, as I cannot tell if they are photographs with a filter, or water color. Maybe if they were higher resolution, or fitted the characters better, they would be better. However, it is nothign but a minor flaw.
As for content density, the game itself is about 4-5 hours long. If you read all the tips, and do the after party. Now, I did not use auto mode, nor did I skip all of the text. Also, I read at 606 words per minute, at an average of 250, it would probably be closer to 9-10 hours. Overall, I was surprised with the amount of content there was. The tips flesh out the world, the after party is fun, and the story itself is well written.
In the end, I cannot reccomend this enough, even if you have not seen the show, this is absolutely fantastic. If you are ok reading it, then I whole heartedly reccomend purchasing this!

One of the better early access titles on Steam.
Very engaging stealth game.
Should be more popular.

Pros:
+Good Presentation (Graphics, animation quality, sound, etc.) It really looks nice, and I would believe you if you told me this game was made by a big budget studio.
+Great Writing. Despite the lack of voice overs, the sense of humor and amount of character put into the writing is very entertaining and believable.
+Great content to map size ratio. Despite there only being 3 main areas, none of which are that large, the level design, quests, and characters dispersed throughout actually give you a lot to do and explore in each one.
+Intriguing Story, though unfinished. Since its in Early Access, you get kind of blue balled once the content is cut off, but enough was there to get me interested in the main characters.
+Limitless potential if further development continues at a steady pace
Cons:
-Mediocre optimization. Motion blur significantly reduces framerate, and certain areas my framerate was halved. Random huge frame drops for 1-2 seconds on occasion as well. I have a GTX 1060, which is by no means a weak card.
-Barebones main stealth mechanic. For a game designed purely on stealth, the stealth mechanic is a little bland. It uses a simple system where line of sight and your movement near enemies increases their awareness of you, and once the awareness bar reaches full, you're caught. Only, not really, because you can just outrun the guards and hide as soon as you break line of sight, and they make no attempt to search the hiding spots.
-Currently, not enough content. I don't think the amount of game justifies its price. I'm writing this immediately after I beat it (not 100%, but pretty close, 24/26 quests completed) so my time played (4-5 hours) is accurate to around how long it'll take you to finish. If you do decide to purchase it consider it a donation to help move development along, not as a purchase of a full game. Which you should be doing for every EA title, honestly.
Things of Note:
=As of this review, there is absolutely no combat. Purely stealth. There are outfits that provide various bonuses, but they don't affect gameplay significantly enough to really make a huge difference other than aesthetics. This is not the Dark Souls: Prepare to Mice Edition you're looking for.
=Controller STRONGLY recommended. Despite not being DS:PtME, it still needs a controller about as badly. Keyboard controls are pretty wonky, and don't allow to walk, which affects your ability to sneak.
=No voiceovers. It'd be really nice if they could find some really good VA's, but I'd rather them stick to text than get someone to phone it in.
=Occasional bugginess, as should be expected with early access titles.

It’s 3:00 a.m. and you are thinking “Just one more turn”.  Problem is you were thinking the same thing at 9:00 p.m.  Should you try to get a couple hours sleep before work or classes?
The weekend can’t come soon enough, Star Traders Frontiers awaits.
Looking at my small amount of Steam playtime,  masks  the hundreds of hours, I have  played the game during Alpha testing.  Month after month what kept me coming back for more?
If you would like to get a basic  introduction of the game mechanics take a look at the
Wiki pages for Star Traders Frontiers.   As the game, and rules expand.  The Wiki pages are automatically updated.The Wiki pages just scratch the surface, you really need to experience the depth for yourself in realtime play.
I can write four or five pages.  But that wouldn't be a review, and who would have the patience to read it.  When looking for a new game, my eyes glaze over after about a page.  That length belongs in a Steam guide I’ll be putting together later.
There is an Advanced mode button.  This lets you create your Captain, Officers, and crew
to your exact finely detailed specifications. Quick start is like looking at your watch to see what time it is.  Advanced is like building your own watch.  Advanced will offer you all 9 current Captain types to start with instead of 4.  Each Captain and officer will develop up to 3 jobs as you play.
This game is not frozen in carbonite.  Trese Brothers will continue to add content and fix bugs long after purchase. As normal, Steam will update with the new versions as they are released.
Quick Start:
After installing if you want to jump right in without allot of setup, there are 4 pre-made Captain templates for you to choose from. You can start playing in two or three minutes.

Select a Template and Click the Launch button.
Choose game difficulty.
Choose a Map: You can use the default map or create your own.
Choose a Faction:  Which house or Syndicate do you want to join at the beginning.
Customize, Choose from male or  female Captains.  How do you want your Captain to dress
What does the face look like and more.
Click the Launch button
Simple right?  You just started a very long fun journey.  How, when, and the people you interact with in this game determines your fate.  Each of them has enemies and friends, if you perform a service for one contact are you helping or hurting someone else in a distant quadrant?  When you meet them they won’t forget what you did.  If you return from a mission is your contact still alive?
Crew & Officers:  Each of them have their own distinct personalities, and traits.  You can decide to promote them, fire them, or just take a calculated risk.  They can quit or even mutiny.  What makes a crew member tick affects the rest of the crew, and ship performance.  Like everybody else none of them are completely good or bad.  You will not automatically understand who they are, hidden traits will be revealed during game play.
Hot Keys, are increasingly rare in laptop/desktop games.  Saves allot of clicks.  Hover over an icon to reveal the keyboard shortcut.  The Escape key is your best friend to exit cutscenes you have seen a dozen times before, and backing out of other screens quickly.
I’ve done my best to keep the review brief.  If you want to know more, Steam guides are being prepared.  Google “Trese Brothers” to see hundreds of helpful Forum  threads, and as mentioned above take a look at the Wiki pages.   I have played for almost a year.
Buy it, try, it and be immersed.  Leave your everyday life behind for a few hours downtime every day.

The second game of the X-Com series takes matters into dark waters. The alien invaders have returned, but not from the sky. They call the seabed their land and need to be stopped. As the commander of a special unit with international backing, you are chosen to step up to the challenge and show this alien filth what it means to rule the land! Oh, and the ocean.
The story follows the first installment of the series. Set 40 years after the defeat of the aliens, a new threat emerges from the deepest corners of the ocean. X-Com (Extraterrestrial Combat Unit) gets reactivated to combat these new invaders of mans land. The player, being the commander of X-Com, needs to gain the upper hand in the conflict and bring peace to the seas. Failure is not an option.
The gameplay is similar, if not nearly exactly the same, as in "X-Com: UFO Defense". It can be divided into two larger parts: The strategic level, the world map/geoscape, and the tactical level, the missions/battlescape. The geoscape allows the player to lay down the foundation of their strategy. The land and sea aswell bases, submarines and other activities get displayed. Multiple screens and options can help the player to understand the current situation like spending of funds or USO (Unidentified Submerged Object) activity. It runs in real time, but can be paused at any time. The missions on the other hand are round based. Here the aquanauts take a stand against the aliens. Civilians are from time to time caught in the middle of the firefight. Researching new technology and manufacturing new weapons, armour and more aids the boots-on-the-ground and helps battle the alien menace. At the same time an eye needs to overlook the financial situation of the whole X-Com operation. A firm grip is aswell needed on the governments of the world which are driven by greed and will only tolerate a low amount of failure.
The game differs only slightly in the graphics and sound department in comparison to its ancestor. The pixelated style gets reinforced by the bright colour palette, being more intense than its previous installment. The soundtrack sets a dark and creeping contrast to the shining pixels. Lingering in the deepest seas, the atmosphere is based on mystery and the uncomfortable feeling that something is with ones crew in these waters. A 'bug', one could call it a feature, strengthens all of this: Crackling sounds. Both annoying and funny, they can easily distracted the player. A quick fix would be a simple restart of the game.
"X-Com: Terror From The Deep" is a worthy follow-up to the 1994 science fiction game "X-Com: UFO Defense". Refining the already great gameplay and atmosphere, the second part of the X-Com series adds its own little bits and bobs. These are not many, but they create a solid foundation on which the creeping soundtrack and the mysterious setting grasp on. Although the game has its own problems, like finding the last son of a gun on the huge maps which can frustrate the player from time to time, the game has a lot of depth and one can easily sink dozens of hours into it.

I got this game as part of the Humble Bundle.
When the first trailer for this game came out, I was interested in the first few seconds until I saw how PVP focused the game is. I never paid a thought to the game since. Now that it was part of the Humble Bundle, I thought I'd give it a try. Upon starting the game, I immediately went into the customization options as that is a very big component for me in any video game. The customization was very so-so and I understood I would need to progress through the game to unlock more. I used whatever DLC that came with the HB which included the shotguns and weapon attachements for the handguns. I played the Tutorial and immediately lost interest. The gameplay is so unrealistically fast and the camera angle is too awkward of a 3rd person view.
I am a very big COOP focused person and I like to play with my friends. We generally enjoy PVE games. This game is not one of those. It is very PVP focused and the NPC enemies in this game are just fodder that gets in your way. I guess that was the point.
All in all, I never had any high expectations for this game. This game was a game that was never meant to be created. It almost seems as though it was some experimental Resident Evil multiplayer component that was never attached to a larger franchise piece. It feels as though the game was rushed and thrown out into the wild to fend for itself and to be forgoten by it's creators. Wasted man hours went into this game that didn't look like it would make a return on all the investments made by the company. Seems like Capcom had some spare cash laying around before RE7 came out and just wanted to make a quick and crap game.
COOP PVE like a horde mode, though a tired but true gamemode, would have done this game wonders. Yes Horde mode has popped up in a lot of games these days but it is also a game mode that works and you generally can't get wrong.

While it may be an 'Anime' Fighting game it plays more like your traditional 2D Capcom or SNK fighter. Moves have huge recovery and not everything is cancellable, on block you’ll always be minus, meaning you have to be smart with your button choice. Frame traps are non-existent because of this outside of chaining jabs together. The lack of air dash, air blocking and constant pressure separates this from the ‘anime’ style of game. Don’t worry though you have massive supers that do 40% and show the ladies in all their glory.
The game is a counterhit paradise; if you’ve played SFV it’s similar to crush counters except this whole game revolves around it. Without counter hit you might be doing 15%-20% damage, on CH we’re talking 40-75% damage depending on your resources.
Overall it’s very easy to pick up and play, you can freestyle for the most part and a lot of the characters have universal systems. Training mode is solid and with a large cast size with vary archetypes that all feel awesome to play. The input system is incredibly easy also; each character has 3 special moves, 1 super and another super that can only be done during the CH/CrushCounter state. There’s universal overheads, launchers and sweeps, allowing you to jump between characters and have an understanding with no problem.
The major problem is this game has been out for some time on the JPN PSN and even longer in arcades, you might have a hard time finding games outside of launch. There are also not many resources, so unless you’re ready to create your own combos or scour YouTube to find them you’ll be in trouble. With SFV being the mess that it is it’s not a bad time to try and explore other fighting games, in saying that you might be better off trying popular anime games such as Guilty Gear or BlazBlue.

I will review all my humble bundle games and see which is worth playing and which is not! Like a lot of people i buy H.B. games as a pack because i want some of the games, but not all. I will play for 5 minutes (or a little bit more) and give you my opinion on it. Sometimes the game will surprise me, sometimes it will be a total disappointment. Just keep in mind this is my opinion only and is not an objective view of the game. You might actually like it!
The review will be constructed into 5 parts:
1. Game description (from what I’ve seen in the time I’ve played).
2. Did i finish the game (YES/NO/Maybe in the future) and why.
3. Pros/Cons.
4. Final thoughts.
5. Rating
So let's begin...
1. Game description:
A small game with a lot of puzzles. The premise is the same in every puzzle, get the sleeper to bed. The visuals and artwork is fantastic, I always loved the M.C. Escher style of drawings, combine that with a little of Dali surrealism and you get a fantastic looking game. The problem is that the puzzles are time based. I would have liked a little more time to set-up and think the whole puzzle before you start.
2. Did i finish the game? NO/ Maybe in the future
The fact that you have a small time until the puzzle starts and you don’t have time t think made me uninstall this game after I repeated the same level about 5 times. Maybe in the future I wil finish it but not very sure about this.
3. Pros/Cons.
PROS:
-Great colors and visuals
- superb artwork and music
CONS:
- Got to think very fast to solve it.
4. Final thoughts:
I love puzzle games and this one looks fantastic. Although the fact that you don’t have enough time too think and have to act fast makes me not recommend this game. If the speed of the game doesn’t bother you, go ahead buy it, otherwise wait for a sale or go to other puzzle games
5. Rating
5/10
