If you don't play these kinds of games don't expect it to be easy even on the lowest difficulty and this is by no means the hardest bullet hell game out there.
There is much more offical Touhou work including Manga, fighting games, various spin off gimmick shooters, stand alone music, and source books. Pretty much all of it has been translated into english and great place to find it all is
of course you can jump through some hoops to get your hands on physical copies of all this stuff too. The Touhou wiki is also a great resource to help you get into the series.
Outside of the offical stuff lies a dedicated community with talented artists, muscians and writers who have really made Touhou come alive and kept it going for so long, I personally have made many great friends thanks to this series and my experience with the fans has been mostly good, of course you still have to look in the right places to find the good as with everything.
All in all I am happy to see any Touhou on steam as I want a way to repay ZUN for all the great experiences his creations have given me for nothing even if this game isn't my favourite. I hope to see more of his work come to steam and I look forward to seeing how this entry does on steam.

What's with the number 9? Who is ZUN and why are there this many beer jokes about him or her?
If you're new to bullet hell games, take your time. Don't listen to any of that. The overwhelming culture surrounding Touhou is hiding an actually very simple game - and Hidden Star in Four Seasons in particular is one of the most simple installments, even. All you have to do is to pick a character, pick a shot type and be on your way. You'll die lots until you start understanding how to play bullet hell games in general and Touhou in particular.
Listen to the music. It will guide you through the stages.

I've played a lot of tycoon games in my childhood and it's saddening to see this genre die. After playing this game, I can see why. The concepts are great but the execution is terrible.
Gameplay in a nutshell:
1. Pause game
2. Place tables and decorations in your restaurant
3. Hire staff
4. Add recipes to the menu
5. Save game
6. Fast forward time
7. ???
8. Profit!
My biggest complaint with this game is that whenever you get access to a higher quality ingredient supplier, you need to go into EACH recipe to change your supplier. Once you've done that, you have to adjust the price of that recipe in EACH restaurant. If you don't do these steps, your food ratings and/or your profit margins will drop. I guess the developers wanted to allow more micromanagement but it's annoying when you just want to update all of your restaurants.
Other things to consider:
- There's no 16:9 support
- The textures/models are dated (this game was released in 2009)
- The auto save for the campaign doesn't work for me
- You have a finite number of chefs in the campaign so don't fire them
Overall, I still think it's a decent tycoon game. If you're bored with the other popular tycoon games (e.g. SimCity, Game Dev Tycoon), give this game a shot if it's on sale.

Great concept, for one programmer this is an impressive achievement. BUT the game is VERY early access. I bought this game after it'd already been in EA almost 9 months. It's still very much pre-alpha. There are lots of bugs and many tweaks need to be made before this game will show its true potential. Several bugs require re-loading a previously saved game, so save often!  I think this guy needs to bring a few more programmers on if he wants to finish it within a couple years. Although graphics are dated (not bad, just dated), this game has a pretty ambitious scope and if it's done by one guy only it'll take 5 more years to finish.
The tutorial mission moves slowly. It's really more of an extended prologue mission with tutorial elements. The story starts out very cliche but then gets interesting. It shows promise. Your characters have stats out the wazoo to raise by either using the skills or leveling. It's defintely a hardcore RPG, which I really like.
The turn-based combat system is decent albeit a bit basic. It can be hard to spot enemies, there's no real cover system, although you can crouch or stand, and there should be an "overwatch" mode (a la modern X-COM) or at least an option to delay taking your turn until your enemies go first. Also there should be a feature to center the screen on an enemy, and scroll through enemies this way, which would take the frustration out of searching for an enemy that is sometimes off screen and hard to spot in darker environments.
Although individual environments can feel repetitive, there's a lot of variety between different locations. I've seen 5 so far and they all have their own unique atmosphere.
Once you get a spaceship, you can fly to various spaceports and then take missions planetside, on various planets. There''s also rudimentary mining and trading. In addition, you can travel between star systems. Ship combat will be included in the future. This very much feels like Wasteland 2 but in a sci-fi setting with open world space travel. Very cool. It's too bad so many of these features are so bare-bones right now.
I can tell this is a diamond in the rough, but it's maybe too early for anyone who actually wants a semi-polished early access game. My guess is this will be in development at least two more years, perhaps much longer. If the developer sticks with it, he'll have a great game. I hope this game realizes its potential, but I think I should've let this bake another year or two before purchasing.

Some pretty nice danmaku that's worth the low price for fans of the genre - and it's fairly easy, so it might actually also be good for newcomers? Grazing is important here (see NineByNine's review for details), so as someone who enjoys grazing so much that I often end up doing it even in games where there's zero reward, I'm very pleased.
I've got one major complaint, though - the point items are way too big! Visual distraction is a given in danmaku, but when the point items are bright blue and bigger than most of the bullets, it feels like nothing but a cheap way to increase difficulty. Sometimes it makes deaths feel like they weren't your fault and didn't have much to do with your actual skill level, and it really messes up the whole "if you die it's your fault, just keep trying and learn the pattern and then it'll feel amazing once you beat it" thing that makes danmaku so fun and rewarding... There's a fine line between fair and unfair when it comes to this visual distraction trickery stuff, and this goes too far imo.
All that said, it's still one of the better bullet hell games I've played on Steam and it's cheap, so recommended.

The kingdom of Rughzenhaide is under attack by an unknown army. To save the life of princess Selphine, her royal bodyguard Ritona casts a teleportation manakravte (a magic spell pretty much) to escape the fallen kingdom. However, something goes wrong and they end up being transported to the other side of the world. From there, Selphine and Ritona begin their journey back home, meeting and interacting with people along the way.
That's pretty much the plot of the Fault series. And yes, I'm going to be briefly talking about the series as a whole rather than this visual novel by itself. While I do feel that Fault Milestone One is a great visual novel and could be enjoyed by itself as a stand-alone visual novel, the rest of the series is absolutely worth checking out after you've finished reading this one.
The first time I read Fault was around 2015, when Milestone 2 Side: Above wasn't even out yet. First time I read it, I liked it. I definitely wasn't blown away by it, but I enjoyed it well enough. Then the second visual novel came out and I'd say that would be the point where I really started getting into the series. I started seeing the potential of Fault being an amazing visual novel series and how much worldbuilding can be done with it. It caught my interest, and to this day I want to see this series grow bigger and better... And that's exactly what it's been doing these past few years.
Fault - Silence the Pedant is going to be released in 2018 (assuming there aren't any major delays anymore), which tells a story about Ritona 5 years before the events of the first Fault. The demo to that is already out and is looking like the contender for best in the series by far. Then Milestone 2 Side: Below will continue the main story. There's also the comic series
which expands the universe of Fault and makes it feel more alive, "
" (a children's book in the Fault universe) is going to be released on Steam soonish, and even more things to come! It's mind-blowing! I haven't seen this much effort and detail put into a world or setting in most higher budget or better known visual novel titles or series. It's what I think makes Fault stand out as one of the best visual novel series that I've ever read, and I wish more people would read it.
In closing, Fault is a precious gem that's buried under a bunch of other less obscure titles. So far all the visual novels are short and don't really last longer than 10 hours or so, but with all the worldbuilding and small details put into it, it's one of the most beautiful and amazing universes I've seen in fiction. If you're willing to wait a while for the next entry in the series to come out, Fault is definitely worth a read.

Finally got around to playing the "old" PoP trilogy games for the first time and started with this one. If you are looking to buy this, keep in mind the following things:
This game is from an era, when going 3D with every franchise was the new cool thing to do. Everybody was experimenting, people didn't really know yet what are good/bad things to do with 3D graphics. As such, you'll notice this game often forces you into some weird camera angles and the camera controls (wtih kb/m at least) are pretty terrible.
Next, this game actually has a wonderful combat system, very advanced for its time. I'd say its on par with modern Dark Souls combat, you just don't quite have that many special moves. Parrying is a thing however, so is vaulting over enemies, using walls to lounge and do a powerful stab etc. There's a lot of things you can do, ABOUT WHICH THE GAME DOESN'T TELL YOU MUCH! There are hints, but this old game expects you to sometimes take a look at the player manual. Luckily, it's available on Steam! Just right-click your game in the Library -> "View Player Manual".
The movement is pretty much the one that's in Assassins Creed now. After playing this game you'll see how AC sadly pretty much took the PoP franchise over. That being said, I'm not a fan of this movement system, simply because there's minimal skill involved. The game does everything for you. You rarely need to "time" jumps right like in other platformers, like in sidescrollers or more famously, the Crash Bandicoot games. Sometimes you'll have to time a wallrun right to avoid sawblades, but that's it. It's all about the looks. You can watch your character do cool acrobatic movements - certainly captivating in 2004, where precise and cool animations like these were unheard of in games other than Tomb Raider. You'll sometimes be confused as to what you're supposed to do, or where you're supposed to go. Camera angles don't make it obvious, BUT you do get to watch your "future" in visions, which are supposed to tell you where and how to go.
Last but not least, graphics is something you'll have to bear with, but its really not that bad. Not too blocky anymore, actually utilezes physics based objects (hair, courtains...), so pretty advanced for its time. You will want to download the unofficial HD patch, to be able to play in higher resolutions in 16:9 aspect ration.

Time Clickers is a clicker game.
However, unlike other games in the same genre, the player has to shoot things to level up.
That's the major difference with this production, so far as clicker games are concerned.
Each level has a randomised structure, or structures, of blocks in the middle of the screen.
You shoot them to gain points; the more points you get, the more effective you can make your weapon.
And you can get more weapons as the game goes on.
Every few levels there is a boss level; the difference being that you have to destroy all of the blocks by a set time.
If you fail, you can try again - or go back a level and destroy more blocks until you have the points available to make your weapons stronger, to try again.
You can also get time-limited bonuses for your weapons, which can be very helpful in overcoming the harder boss levels (or just for finishing the standard levels faster).
You keep on levelling up, until it gets too hard, then you reset the game, getting some bonuses as a result, which makes it easier to level up when you start again.
And so on, ad infinitum.
I can recommend it as just another clicker game, but on that basis alone.
If you're not into clicker games, then don't bother.

Having missed out on playing Grandia 2 originally, I jumped at the chance to do so on my PC. I have played Grandia way back when, and although the sequel does not share any of the characters or the world, the art style and vibrant characters and environment do seem familiar - in a good way!
So, what is it about this game that makes it so that months after putting it down, it is a game I look back on with misty eyes and a headful of fun memories and wish there were more out there like it?

You play as Ryudo, a bounty-hunter of a sell sword who will lend his blade for some coin (or free food, at times!). Now this guy, for me, he single-handedly raised the game from a pleasant experience to a hilarious one! Unlike your typical helpful hero, Ryudo always had a sarcastic remark waiting to be sprung and was more than happy to tell you what was on his mind! Whilst, this could have created a rather annoyingly obnoxious character, it did the opposite. I appreciated the honesty in his amusing quips, he did not care if you were the Pope or the princess, he was going to tell you exactly what he thought of you! He seemed to have little patience for children too, but let's be honest, who does? I'll come to some quotes from him a little later, it is best seen for yourself!
A few other things worth mentioning:
It was easy on the eyes. Unlike some games I have played, whereby the blandness and greyscale worlds are literally seeping out my soul, Grandia 2 was vibrant, it was alive, it had locations where I was happy to prance about and look for things to kill. Granted, I always spent a little too long in the towns looking for people to annoy/houses to loot! So many pots to overturn!
The characters were interesting, well written and brought to life with some great voice acting. The ever- changing expressions on their dialogue reels were a nice touch too, Ryudo could go from looking very annoyed, to being dumbfounded, with the expressive imagery. A nice little touch taken from the original game.
The combat, in my opinion is what most players will remember the game for. It does away with the random monster encounters, with the enemies visible in the world around you, giving you the option to sneak behind them for a surprise attack or... sneak by them entirely if you were not feeling the need to bloody your sword! When you are wanting to battle, you will have the ability to move your characters around the battlefield, set up attacks and abilities in such a way that you are able to interrupt or counter-attack foes – this is incredibly satisfying! To control the combat in such a way, meant you were almost always able to render some enemies useless! There is also no end of abilities, magic and special moves that you can unlock through experience gain.
In short, I cannot recommend Grandia 2 highly enough. It has everything I love in a game and then some. The combat system and memorable cast of characters alone is a good enough reason for me to buy you all a copy! But I can't! Because, money and stuff! No word of a lie, this may very well be the best bullet hell since Ikaruga. You can change your weapons, hits and continues to suit your preferred playstyle, the difficulty scales perfectly, and the soundtrack is utterly phenomenal. Recommended without hesitation to both shmup lovers and newcomers alike, it's simply one of the best games in the genre, and is ridiculously good value too.

This game still manages to maintain its charm even so long after its release. The first of a great 3D platforming trilogy, this one arguably holds up better than the other two in its overall appeal and longevity. This game introduced a more realistic approach to platforming that worked fluidly, brought about a charming story to go with, and also managed to work "time control" into a platforming game in a way that didn't feel cheap or badly implemented. It's also got a neat soundtrack that fits the theme of the game quite well, though it doesn't hold itself too tight to Persian/Arabian styled music.
However, being that this is a port of an old Xbox game, this does present issues. WHile strange glitches can occur, they are not the main source of problems, as they are not frequent enough to be. The main issue is controller compatibility. Finding a controller that the game responds to with full control is hard for one, glaring reason: the analog stick sensitivity. Most modern gaming controllers have to be specially calibrated for this game in order to work well enough that platforming isn't gimped or otherwise impossible due to the prince not moving the correct speed at all points of the analog stick. This results in the keyboard being used for the game, or painstaking calibration of a controller for one specific game. Other issues beside this one are minor, such as fog not working right with modern PC builds or other such things.
I would still recommend this game for 3D platforming enthusiasts. Just keep in mind that controlling this game can be problematic at best, crippling at worst...if you can look past that glaring fault for this port, definitely give this a try. It's easier to obtain nowadays than an Xbox game.

Before Ubisoft was churning out broken, annual Assassin's Creed titles, they actually made some incredible action/adventure masterpieces. This is one of them.
Just a disclaimer: I'm not the kind of person that finds fixing old games up problematic, but be warned that as-is, the Steam version does not feature widescreen and full controller support. There are easy ways to fix this, however - turn to the guides and off you go.
Now then, what have we here, presentation-wise? A stellar art style with 2003 appropriate graphics in the visual department. This game looks pretty amazing considering its age because of the superb blending of great lighting effects, texturework and achitecture. Granted, the character models aren't that pretty, but even though graphics have evolved a lot since 2003, games that create such a choerent visual style are rare nowadays. The controls are... not there for the controller and done well enough, I played it with an X360 controller this time, but I remember the controls being fine on the KB+M as well, save some questionable camera angles. Sound design is also excellent although not as abundant in the music department (even though the quality is A+) and there are occasional voice acting cringe-moments. However, the tone and mood of this game are portrayed so well that you'd really miss the corniness if it were suddenly removed.
This brings me to the story. It's essentially a story within a narrative, which is pretty cool because if you do manage to die, the narrator (i.e. the Prince, and no, his name isn't Dastan) just wriggles his way out with a "no, that's not what happened). This game features a time rewind ability which you can upgrade gaining more uses, and it serves as the main "you done f*ked up" saving mechanic. But back to the story: you're a Prince that ransacked a vault, found a magic dagger, then plunged it into a giant magic hourglass, unleashing all sandy Hell in the process, so you are left to clean up the mess and get the girl. While not as good a love story as the 2008 PoP, it's still fairly enjoyable and compared to the follow-up Warrior Within, it has a lot more charm and likeable characters.
But where this game really stands out is the gameplay. First off, controlling the Prince is an absolute blast - the smoothness of movement and animations that were later perfected in Assassin's Creed have their roots here (I could swear Altair and co. have some reused animations from this game). The platforming is absolutely stellar, just challenging enough. The combat is... ok, but some fight sequences seemed a bit tacked on and unnecessary. A rather unique mechanic is having to "consume" enemies after they're down - if you don't stab them with the Dagger of Time (TM), they just come back up again. This adds tension to the combat, but can sometimes be annoying. The combo tree isn't nearly as advanced as in PoP:WW, but it's satisfying enough.
There is really nothing more I can say here, it's a very good first installment to a fairly successful trilogy and it deserves to be played and appreciated for it's polished gameplay, compact visual style and unique mechanics. A classic in every sense of the word.

In Between is developed by Gentlymad and published by Headup Games. It was quite the train trip, metaphorically speaking. Took me a while to review it since “happiness” isn’t on this game’s shortlist of emotions it expresses.

It is not a story without hope. I played games that were truly nihilistic, but In Between walks a thin line from which it never derails. I’m not going to talk of the plotline a lot but to give you an impression, once our protagonist discovers that he is terminally ill, life itself and his thoughts take on a new meaning. What really drew me to this title, is the rarity it exhibits. A story driven puzzle-platformer that can bring a tear to most players is not common at all. From a gameplay perspective, we have 60 levels structured into several chapters, each of them an allegory to the Kübler-Ross model. Known colloquially as the five stages of grief (denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance). Not an easy theme to digest which is exactly why I believe this game is not for everyone. And this is not an elitist interpretation, merely an observation. A large percentage of gamers desire direct means of entertainment. An even more in-depth explanation would be that comedies will always be more popular than tragedies. It is ultimately up to you to decide.
While certain levels do require some trial & error, the graphical and sound assets provide a smooth experience. Voice acting, a feature that is absent from a vast majority of platform games I played lately, is making a triumphant return and adds another fine layer over the storyline. The 2D sprites, especially those within the dream sequences, are very detailed and offer substantial insight upon the protagonist’s happier moments in life. A game with very few flaws and no technical issues.

+ Emotional story
+ Mix of puzzle and platforming sections
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards
- Unbalanced difficulty
After playing for the last few months quite a few 2D platformers, I thought I’d seen everything this genre has to offer on Steam. In Between proved me wrong and even though I had a certain degree of anxiety while playing it, I don’t regret giving it a chance to unravel its tragic tale. It is a break from conformity and I appreciate it for that reason alone.

Restaurant Empire II is the sequel to Trevor Chan’s Restaurant Empire which was released back in 2003 and although I have not played the original fans of both games give you the distinct impression that Restaurant Empire II is really just a glorified expansion to the original. Taken on it's own merits however, it's a decent enough management game that unfortunately gets bogged down in minutia and micromanagement rather quickly.
The game starts you off with the campaign from the original game, a new campaign based more around Desert House's and Coffee Shops and a sandbox mode. The sandbox mode however is pretty barebones and many of the staples from the campaigns, such as the minigames, chef reputation, cooking contests etc are removed. Add that to the fact that in Sandbox you start with pretty much everything already unlocked it becomes a rather futile experience.
The campaigns start you off as a small restaurant owner and slowly unlocks content and areas as you progress through various scenarios with pre-set goals. A small dash of storyline is thrown in but it can be safely ignored. Your goals throughout the campaign vary rather wildly in difficulty and it's often best to delay winning the easier scenarios until the very last moment so that you can use the extra time for your chefs and staff to get more skilled and more money to flow into your bank account.
The game at it's core is simple enough, you start a restaurant, place a kitchen, some bathrooms, furnish the seating area, hire some staff, pick a menu and off you go. However once you get going the game becomes anything but simple. The game will often tell you that you have trouble serving meals on time but doesn't give you any information as to why that is. Should you hire more servers? Hire more chefs? Move the tables closer to the kitchen? Solving problems with your restaurants quickly becomes purely trial and error until you get that perfect setup that you will never have to change. It doesn't help that the AI path-finding is nothing short of atrocious.
And that brings us to the menu. As you progress through the game you will start to unlock specialty ingredient suppliers which allows you to increase the quality of your meals at a cost, however using these new high quality ingredient's have to be done individually for each recipe in each restaurant and likewise for changing the price making it an incredibly frustrating experience.
All in all Restaurant Empire II is a game with a few good ideas that are unfortunately marred by it's many design flaws and it's not really a game I'd recommend to anyone but extreme fans of management simulations. If you have a burning desire to play a game that lets you build and manage a chain of eateries I suppose this is really your only choice but if not, then you can find better entertainment elsewhere.

Grim Legends 3: The Dark City is not a sequel of any previous Grim Legends as you may think. That’s another grim legend which is totally independent from the others.
You’re Sylvia, an apprentice and acolyte of an order which hunt down every demon from the world to make it safer. You’ve lost your memories in an accident that occurred some time ago and now you need to defeat a demon which have been located near a cathedral with the help of your mentor. Then will begin a chain of events that will lead to a very bad omen. The Incarceri Stone (a powerful artifact that binds Koshmaar, a horrifying creature from another world) will be stolen and the city of Lichtenheim as well as the world will be compromised.
The bonus story let you play after the consequences of the main story. You’ll play as a male member of the order to save himself from the evil.
As every Artifex Mundi game you can move freely in different area (a Cathedral in the prologue and after in the Lichtenheim city) and need to solve some puzzles and find all objects in hidden objects scenes. The game has 3 difficulties and a guest feature: every one of the family can play an independent save and resume the game where they left it. When you first play the game you’ll have a notebook where you have all your objectives. Adding to that you’ll have a hint button that will help you in many ways but be warned that you may not use it in any puzzle or hidden object scene (HOS). Hints can be used to know where you need to go, where is the next interaction or to show an object in an HOS or to skip a puzzle. About the Hidden Objects Scenes, there are 3 different types: The one where you need to find objects with their name or with their shape or several items of the same kind. But in any of them you may encounter some blue text or red shaded shape that mean you’ll need to interact with the scene using or not an additional item of the scenery.
To conclude this part, you’ll also have an inventory to store useful items through your journey.
As some Artifex Mundi game, you’ll have some collectibles to find hidden through the sceneries: 30 skeleton dolls.
One of the very good thing of this game is that there are 7 unique features you won’t find in any other Artifex Mundi game:
⦁	Rune Battle mini-games
⦁	Memory Mirror mini-games
⦁	A smart combine or interact feature for some specific items
⦁	A “fake” 3D for some specific objects which you can interact and rotate the view to another side.
⦁	A few shooting parts (2 or 3 in total) when you need to shoot at the right time.
⦁	A few conversation parts (where you need to talk every topics)
⦁	A notebook free of notes! Only objectives, no notes about the story or events. (maybe because you are in a hurry so you can’t make a personal diary?)
When you’ll play through the main story you’ll need to fight possessed people: to fight them you’ll play a rune mini-game. The runes in the red circle represents your enemy’s runes and the blue yours. Runes come in a set of two runes: you need to select the set of runes which your opponent haven’t got in order to hurt him/her. You’ll need to make 3 successful attempts in order to make him/her pass out. But these mini-games aren’t that challenging as you have all the time you want to select the right set.
After he/she passed out, you’ll need to look at the attached mirror and “fix” their memories. Each Memory Mirror game have 3 progressive steps and each Memory Mirror have their own rules. One is rotating some circles, another is swapping tiles, another is sliding tiles… When you succeeded to go through their memory you’ll be able to lift the curse on them and take away their cursed mask.
As I said earlier you’ll find several items where you’ll be able to interact with in your inventory. They are marked with a white plus in a green circle. When you click at them you zoom in the item. Some items need only to be combined with another or several items to have the final item.  And some other items can be interacted with in order to solve them. These last items are most likely in a fake 3D, meaning that you can rotate them in another view.
Finally the game has a few shooting parts where you need to shoot at the right time:  the cross will move around the target and you’ll need to shoot when you’re in range with it.
(*) :
In addition to no skip or use any hint while playing every puzzles and Hidden objects scenes, there are more missable achievements. I won’t list them all but I’ll talk about some of the main one.
There are collectibles or interactions achievements : skeleton dolls and reading texts.
There are at least two achievements that ask you to no skip any cut scene.
There are achievements that requires a perfect without any limit of time : “False Positive” and most of the Rune Battle mini-games.
There are the Memory Mirror achievements that need you to finish each of them within 3 minutes.
So I strongly suggest you to follow a guide on steam especially if you don’t really wish to make a second playthrough.
Finally if you missed anything while finishing your first playthrough, you’ll need to play the game again with or without the same profile. The good thing is you only need to succeed where you failed to get the achievements left. This is true for the skeleton dolls if you restart a new game with your same profile and it also may be true for some others too !

This game just just as good as I remember it.
The battle system ensures that even easy fights are engaging. Often times there are 6 or more enemies to face in a single fight, and the starting "turn" order is randomized, which means that the same fight can play out in many different ways. While you're not really threatened with death outside of a boss battle, the distance between save points can be kind of long. This means you don't want enemy damage to add up, so you'll want to end fights as quickly and safely as possible. This means you'll make interesting decisions between canceling the opponents turn or spending MP or SP to use more powerful attacks. When you time your cancel after the opponent has chosen their next attack, but before the attack comes out, you cancel the entire attack completely, which is increadibly satisfying.
(spoilers, obviously)
Some people might find the plot to be sort of generic for a JRPG, but the characters are memorable and feel grounded and realistic. Without spoiling much, it has a similar vibe to Super Mario RPG, as a "roadtrip plot" where you meet interesting characters and learn about the world along the way to a distant destination. The best part, in my opinion, is when your characters sit around a dinner table and somewhat-organically discuss their thoughts on recent events. This gives the characters a chance to "respond" to the plot in a way so many Japanese games/anime lack (outside of mid-battle sermons and internal monologues) and it builds a believable friendship among the cast.
Works good. Some UI elements like the Save menu that's been adapted for PC look a bit simple, but function perfectly. The textures are clear, and despite it's age, the stylized and colorful art design has aged gracefully, for the most part. The addition of a "hard mode" is greatly appreciated, though it's still not very challenging outside of boss battles. I haven't done any A/B comparisons to see what's changed in the Hard Mode, if anyone knows, please let me know. All-in-all If you are going to buy this game, this is the version I recommend buying.

TL;DR: A short puzzle game about guiding a sleepwalker to their bed.
The action happens in a dream world with non-Euclidean topologies and art inspired by Salvador Dali's work. You control a benevolent dream cat or dog creature that tries to guide Bob the sleepwalker to his bed within dream. Bob obeys three big rules: He continuously walks forward and turns right in front of obstacles. Letting him wake up loses the game.
You can influence his movement by blocking his way with big dream apples and let him walk over crevasses using bridges made of fish. These are the only tools you get. Also some monsters and environmental objects can and have to be affected by these tools. It's very nice that you can see where Bob is going by footsteps that appear in front of him, making it easy to see what's going to happen next.
Puzzles are usually simple and easy and often have several solutions. They consist of two parts: get the apples and the fish and then use them to navigate Bob through the maze. Usually you have plenty of time to act, but at later levels you have to be fast as well. Still, the only times during the 30 levels of the game I got stuck were because of the non-Euclidean graphics tricking me into thinking I can't do something. I consider this a flaw because it was merely confusing and served only as deliberate confusion, a distraction from the puzzle.
It takes less than hour to complete the game for the first time and the subsequent speed-run achievement is not difficult to earn after you've completed the game once. After beating the game once it presents you with a more difficult "Nightmare mode". It adds to the basic levels several keys that Bob has to grab before the bedroom opens. These levels can be quirky but nevertheless not difficult.
Graphics are quite nice except for the occasional confusion they induced as mentioned above. Music consists of hazy and forgettable tunes appropriate to the dreamworld. But the voice acting! I disliked the voices that sounded like a drunken person struggling to speak with throat noises. They probably mean to create atmosphere, but to me, they were mostly annoying in their derpiness.
I should mention that I experienced problems running the game: my desktop powerhorse could not run it because of an unknown error, but I finally managed to play it on a laptop. I used mouse for the whole game despite it suggesting a controller. Mouse controls were fine but they did require a bit of getting used to. Basically, the dream cat walks towards the cursor when pressing left mouse button but then it could get stuck in the way to an obstacle - there's no pathfinding to work around this.
There is little to no story unless you consider the few cutscenes in the dreamworld a story. Basically, Bob (who apparently is a narcoleptic sleepwalker if that's a thing) falls asleep and needs to get to bed. So really the puzzles are the only thing to experience here. They can last you for three playthroughs, each one taking from 45 minutes to one hour. As it costs only 5 € I think it's worth it if you like puzzle games. Remember though it's only a short experience and there's basically no replay value afterwards. If you're merely intrigued, get it on sale.

A light-hearted and dream-like inspiration of David Lynch's perspective on the dreamscape,
is a simple and quick puzzler. There's a significant level of polish here for a freshman title, however the 30 levels lack the depth of other mature puzzle platforming games. Once the player has learned the basic verbs for solving these challenges, the rest of the game can be completed in a breeze and the Nightmare Mode doesn’t offer enough variety to keep hardcore puzzle solvers interested.
However, while
may be a slumber start for Bedtime Digital Games, it shows some promise and a high understanding of its theme that provides a pleasant and relaxing interlude between the far more difficult and obtuse puzzle games from the indie scene. This will be a developer to look for on future releases.

Another World/ Out Of This World is a truly incredible game. One stormy day a young scientist named Lester Knight Chaykin decides to go to his lab to work on his particle acceleration experiment. As he sits back and grabs a cold drink he is unaware that a bolt of lightning has struck his lab. It interferes with his experiment and before he knows whats happening he is sent to another world. It is from this point that the game truly starts. This game is a cinematic platformer like Prince Of Persia and Flashback. You must observe your environment and plan your actions ahead of time in order to survive.\ This game can be really challenging, especially to the first time player, as there are many puzzles and a lot of trial and error. Once you have beaten the game a few times you can complete it in a fairly short amount of time but thanks to the difficulty levels and graphics/ sound options avaliable (you can toggle between the original graphics and sound or the new hd ones) you'll probably want to replay this game quite a few times. If that isn't enough for you this 20th anniversary edition has other cool bonuses like a making of video and the soundtrack. If your not a fan of cinematic platformers this game probably wont change your mind but if you do this game is a must play. Not relating to the game I'm using \ to represent a new paragraph because the tab key doesnt seem to work properly for me. If anyone knows the issue please let me know. I hope you get many exiting hours out of this masterpiece of a game.

I am a fan of the TBT and RTT games like XCOM, the UFO series, JA and JA 2, and so on. This game is a worthy and playable successor to JA and XCOM, even in it's current Alpha state, and the promised sandbox / open world features make me look forward to much more. If you're in to TBT's or want to be, I heartily recommend it as well worth the $20. If this developer manages to deliver half of what he's planning, I'd pay 3x that, so I'm glad I got in early.
That being said, this is pre-alpha. There are some things in the pre-alpha you should be aware of:
There is little quest guidance as to where to head next or find quest objectives, and this makes the beginning/tutorial phase on the Dauntless colony ship slow. I spent most of my time combing the vessel for my next quest objective rather than really playing and enjoying it. So if you know TBT's pretty well already and are willing to learn the hard way, I'd say give the tutorial a miss and dive right in. I wound up googling my way through much of the Dauntless quest progression when I did do it.
Currently content gets repetitive between the 12 and 20 hour mark for me. However, I'm only 1/10th to 1/20th of the way through character progression, leaving plenty of room for when the developer adds new content or I return for another fix.
It's somewhat unclear from the documentation which features are available and which are planned. If you find yourself confused from time to time, join the club. Just bear in mind that it's a pre-alpha and carry on.

It's really hard for me to do an unbiased review of this game, so I would rather speak about my
personal experience.
When I was about 11 years old, I played the first X-COM: UFO Defense through and through.
As a kid I thought it was the most challenging, well-put togheter game I'd ever played.
Time passed by, and, one fateful day, I read the review of X-COM: Terror From the Deep in a french
magazine. There was only one thing left to do: BUY. IT. NOW.
And, thanks to my parents (and me being a good boy around xmas ;)) I got my hands on a copy of this
game. I still own the original box, floppy disc edition.
I played this game at least one week per month for about a year and a half.
It's now 2014, and I still haven't found a game so compelling since. Everything in this game pulled me
in, and would never let me go. The music. The atmosphere. This always present feeling of dread. The pressure put on your shoulders when trying to save as many civilians as possible during a Terror mission without sacrificing your favorite soldiers.
And, above all else, the incredible depth of the tactical options that were offered to you throughout the game. Both in combat situation and on the Geosphere's more laid-back, strategical planning.
This is the kind of game that involves you so much that you start to create your own stories about your pixelated soldiers. I knew their names.I knew what they were capable, or uncapable of doing while on a mission. I knew them, and losing any of them had some kind of impact on me. "They were my soldiers. my mates. They were good soldiers, and I'll never forget them."
To me, X-COM: Terror From the Deep defines the word "classic" when it comes to Strategic planning and Tactical
Combat.

The game drops u off in the midle of a scene were the first ep left off, ur main protagonist is aparently unconsious while the princess is kidnaped, so the main objective is set from the very begining as u try to save the princess throughout the game.
That beeing said the story is not very convoluted and theres not much to it, i guess the point is to drag the story along the various ep's and focus more on the gameplay.
The game had a slow start to let  the player feel confrtable with the different control mechanics wich felt ok,
it could have tryed to introduce a couple more to not make the player feel so strained but the core movements felt fine.
While some of the early sections relyed on patience and carefull timing i felt that the absence of a soundtrack to be
boring and it didnt really complemented the atmosphere, but to compensate the boss fights have bit more energy to it.
There a some parts in the game were i felt that the main mechanic didnt really fit that task as if the dash didnt seem
to overcome the obstacle with ease making it a bumer and more a situation of trial and error. Wich brings me to my next point
were in the last level u have to rely a bit to much on your mistakes, as the checkpoints seemed a bit to harsh giving the player too much of a punishement for dyng,
it felt like a tedious experience that is not coesive with the rest of the game.
I felt the need of more sections like the mirror in the cave wich is a very interesting mechanic,
but overall Vox Populi Vox Dei 2 feels like a decent sidescroller for the price and quality
even doe i didnt found any gamebraking experience such as bugs or errors,
i just felt it lacked a bit more content and polish in some levels.

Don’t go in to Higurashi When They Cry: Chapter 1 expecting any definitive answers to much of anything. The first instalment of the cult favourite visual novel which made developers 7th Expansion’s name, Onikakushi is a prologue first and foremost, designed to get fans clamoring for more. It’s purely linear; there are no choices of any kind. It also trades in anime cliches far too often in lieu of real character development, the writing is painfully overdone (as in, multiple paragraphs when one would do), the ending is fairly predictable and the protagonist takes forever to realize things are going badly wrong.
That said, this is still an engaging and surprisingly disturbing little story. For all the amateur presentation drags it down, and the way it blatantly shills the next chapter (”Buy it or you’ll never find out what’s actually going on!”), it’s not hard to feel hooked. Keiichi, the young protagonist, has moved to the village of Hinamizawa with his parents, a tiny rural idyll where his bohemian father can pursue his painting career. But for all the village kids seem welcoming enough, Keiichi still hasn’t quite adapted to country living, and when he starts asking questions about the area’s tangled history, he swiftly begins to regret it.
A gruesome murder case, and a fabled curse that strikes down any outsider the village’s guardian deity doesn’t care for… why do his friends seem to know more than they’re letting on? Is he in danger? Not that it’s that difficult to guess; there wouldn’t be that much to get excited about, otherwise. Again, Onikakushi’s biggest weakness is it’s plainly not interested in explicitly detailing “why”, favoring atmosphere over anything too cerebral. The scene-setting is fairly thin, too; it reads like an anime fan’s idea of how kids bicker among themselves.
Even so, when the villagers finally drop their masks, it’s scarier than one might expect - for all the gore and blank-eyed cartoon sociopathy, a couple of the scares are subtle enough to be genuinely unnerving, even playing in broad daylight. And though it’s not hard to guess the ending, the journey there and the questions it raises are evocative enough to stick with you, for all the game’s flaws. Whether Higurashi actually goes anywhere worthwhile from here is another matter entirely, but as prologues go, this is fairly effective stuff.

I'm glad that the Touhou Project series is finally available on Steam. It means more fans of the series can directly support the creator by purchasing the game. It also marks the beginning of more Touhou games (official or fan-made) on Steam. I hope that eventually all Windows Touhou games will be available on Steam.
To celebrate the release of the first Touhou game on Steam, I'll share the story of how I got into Touhou and why I love it.
The year was 2013, I was attending my math tuition class in a classroom at my high school when my friend who sat next to me showed me a gameplay video of Touhou 12.8 (Fairy Wars) on his phone. That was the first time I saw the gameplay of a Touhou game. During that time, all I thought was: "Wow, this game looks so difficult." After the class ended that day, I totally forgot about it.
Fast forward to 2015, I was in my first year at university. I discovered that the popular video on YouTube - Bad Apple, is from the Touhou Project series. This made me grew curious about the series, because each character in that music video was so unique, distinct, and beautiful. So, I began to do research on the series. I found out that the latest game at that time was Touhou 15 (Touhou Kanjuden ~ Legacy of Lunatic Kingdom), which was only released a few weeks ago at that time. I downloaded the game to try it. Unfortunately, I played the game with no sound because I was at the Cafeteria of my university and I didn't bring an earphone with me. I reached stage 5 after dying many times, then I was stuck at Clownpiece's fight. I got frustrated by it so badly I uninstalled the game immediately.
A few months had passed as I continue my busy university life. I started my 3-month internship at a government agency. During my internship, I spend a lot of time making web forms and fixing bugs. So I would open up YouTube and play some music through my earphone while I work.
One day, I decided to play Bad Apple again. Listening to it reminds me of how beautiful and enlightening the song is. When the song is finished playing, I switched to YouTube and I saw another Touhou music recommended to me. I clicked on it and found out it belongs to a playlist called "All Touhou Music (1/2)". I decided to give it a try because I was running out of music to listen to after a few weeks since my internship started. Immediately, the first music (EOSD title screen - Scarlet Beyond a Crimson Dream) already caught my attention when the melody at 0.25
seconds of the music started playing. I thought: "Wow, this is so different from what I usually listen to."Even though that was the first time I listen to it, I gained the feeling of familiarity, acceptance, and cherish from it. The following songs in the playlist also gave me the same feeling.
Then, I saw the picture in the 8th video in the playlist. "Who is that girl?" I thought. "She looks so cute." I saw elegance, confidence, and wisdom eminating from the character. The music of that video only reinforced what I thought. I found out her name is "Koakuma" from the comment section. Wanting to know more about the character, I searched "Touhou Koakuma" on Google. That was the first time I visited the Touhou wiki website.
I was a bit sad when I discovered that the character was insignificant in the game and even her name was given by the fans. But I quickly got over that when I discovered more and more interesting characters by reading the wiki. "A bird youkai that has the power of nuclear fusion?" "A youkai that has something to do with subconscious?" "A sword-wielding girl who is half-human, half-phantom?" "And a vampire that can destroy anything by crushing the 'eye' of it?" My interest for the series started to grow again like a spark before it turned into a wildfire.
I discovered that the first Windows game of the series is Touhou 6. Coincidentally, my internship was nearing its end at that time so I had more free time. I downloaded the game and try to play it but immediately, I was stopped by an issue. My PC that''s running Windows 10 couldn't run the game properly. The fps of the game was not limited and everything was sped up to the point where it cannot be played anymore. But, being an IT student, I quickly identified the problem, found the solution, and implemented the solution by downloading a vsync patch for the game. After solving the issue, I started playing the game.
I was hooked the moment the game starts. The sometimes-cheeky but meaningful dialogue. The easy-to-get-into story. The mesmerizing background pattern when enemy uses a spellcard. The beautiful yet deadly bullet patterns
. And the already great soundtrack becomes perfect when they're in-sync with the game's flow. I know immediately that this will be one of my favourite game of all time. I was determined to beat the game without using continues under normal difficulty to get a good ending. After a few weeks of practice, I finally did it, and I will never forget the feeling of accomplishment and satisfaction I get during that moment.
At the same time, I discovered the works of the Touhou fandom on YouTube. The weird but great IOSYS music videos always put a smile inside me. The 4-koma by Colonel Aki left me feeling warm-and-fuzzy. The 3D battle video by minusT always make me feels hyped and gives me goosebumps. And the countless doujin arts, music, and memes make me realize how great it is to be in a community where everyone from different backgrounds share their love for one common thing, where they can get together no matter how different they are between each other. As someone who is coming from a multicultural country, where sometimes misunderstood and lack of symphaty can cause confliction. Touhou to me is more than just a game, it is a community that unites people, eliminates conflicts, and it is where peace can be built upon.
Touhou has changed my life - in a good way. I find myself having more patience through teaching new Touhou players the mechanics of the game, I become more fond of compromise rather than conflict after learning about Gensokyo and the Spellcard rule. I picked up my drawing hobby again that I stopped after highschool. The official Touhou printworks made me start to read books regularly again. I started learning Japanese so I can know more about the series. And I started learning piano so I can play Touhou music. Knowing that something as wonderful as Touhou exists, it gave me more will than ever to continue living.
There is still a long journey awaiting me. I've yet to play (or get good at) some of the newer Touhou games. I haven't got the time to get into the fighting games yet. And I still dream for the day when I can clear an Extra stage easily. I'm glad that ZUN had decided to make international fans of the series easier to purchase the game by releasing the game on Steam. When I first heard the news, I was a bit worried about its effect on the community. But, I believe everyone who loves Touhou will continue to love it, and will warmly welcome any new fans into this big family by respecting each other.
Thank you for what you're doing, ZUN. I will always love Touhou. And I'm proud to call myself a fan of Touhou Project.

In Between is essentially a VVVVVV clone, but what sets it apart is its story-driven narrative, art design, improved graphics & presentation, and and clever, more succinct puzzles. In addition to the gravity rotating phsyics and visuals being much more refined, you play as a man dying from cancer, and each of the five sets of levels symbolically deal with the five stages of grief in intriguing ways. They manifest themselves as environmental elements you must avoid or work with to advance; for instance, anger is represented as red balls which fluctuate in size and haunt you by moving toward you unless you bring them to a standstill by facing them. As you progress through the levels, you relive key memories and gain insight into the player character's backstory and state of mind during his struggle with terminal illness. It is a unique approach to the indie 2D platforming genre with more intimacy & pathos than you'd typically find in it, and it's an excellent PC port that greatly improves on the original Android release. Those who enjoy games such as Limbo, Braid, and The Bridge (as well as VVVVVV, naturally) should check this out; its length doesn't justify the full price, though on sale it's worth every penny.

It may not look like much compared to any games in the Might&Magic series, however there is more than this game than it's cover lets on. While staying impressively true to the Might&Magic universe, it brings a lighter mood to the usually serious Might&Magic games. Even in it's "combat" you can see many similarities to past games of the series. Though don't be confused, this game is much different. It is more strategic than anything, and often requires you to think about your moves rather than just throwing units at the enemy. It is probably one of the most relaxed, fun, and challenging strategy games I have ever played. Not to mention the availability of co-op online gameplay, which brings in even more strategy than with just one-on-one gameplay.
There aren't many cons I can think of off the top of my head. If anything, it would be the role luck plays in many of the games. Sometimes you just get delt a bad hand, and that can ruin the whole game. Even with the Relics you get from playing the campagin, they often aren't enough to save you from a bad start. Or sometimes the enemy start is just so good, you can't come back from his initial moves.
Even so, this game is great. Whether you're into hardcore strategy or just enjoy a relaxed strategy, this game might be for you. While you can play hardcore and think 5 billion moves ahead of the other player(s) you can also just think one or two moves ahead,and still have fun, maybe even win! This is a great game, no matter what side of gaming you come from!

Anyway, I'd strongly recommend this game, you'll definitely get your money's worth out of it, at the very least. Just don't expect anything related to any other Might & Magic game from buying it.

Crayon Physics is a really unique puzzle game that inspires players to create silly and unique solutions, but doesn't always mechanically work properly (which is important for what this game is).
Crayon Physics has you creating contraptions from the top of your head to move a ball from one location to another. Draw a box in the sky, let it fall onto one side of the ball, and thanks to physics, the ball will be pushed in the opposite direction. Draw a bigger box and it'll be heavier. Or maybe attach a rectangle to a pivot point, and let it swing down to knock the ball like a golf club. And then watch as the ball runs up ramps that you've set up beforehand, or crosses your drawn bridge, or busts through obstacles to reach the goal.
Except the "Physics" in Crayon Physics don't always work the way you anticipate. And a lot of times, you are setting up weird contraptions in such a limited space that you feel like you are cheating your way to a real solution when it works just slightly differently than the 19 previous tries in the way you wanted. Like other physics-based puzzle games, there is oftentimes just frequent reconstruction of a valid approach because physics decided not to be kind.
Crayon Physics is a fun game, but download the demo first to see how much you'll be fighting the physics engine. When it works, it's pretty fun and makes you feel smart. When it doesn't... well... it just feels cheap. Only recommended if you can get it for relatively cheap.

This is a remarkable piece of work done by a game developer striking out on his own that demonstrates that sometimes a single holistic vision beats the burdensome bureaucracies, stultifying politics and stifling committees found in larger development team efforts.
There is no single piece of this game I could point to as a design error, which is a remarkable feat for anyone but especially someone shouldering the whole effort.
I highly recommend it.  It plays very much like a passible JA2 / Fallout tactics type shooter but without the pitfalls of either and done in a very promising backdrop of open world with all manner of divergent and emergent gameplay potential.
The game has a very strong Firefly vibe, and the gameplay really reflects that.  You have a crew, and in the final vision as I understand it you'll be flying that ship around in the natty fringe of the galaxy doing whatever people do to get by.
Worth every second of your life.

tl;dr - though I marked this a "Yes", consider it a "mixed" review. the first 1/3 of it is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the second is alright, and the end is good. also, no player interaction.
Although many people may prefer to go into games blind, I think there are a few things you should know before delving into Higurashi (many people who are familiar with the franchise may know this already. but hey, I didn't).
First, the beginning is long, slow-paced and stupid. But once things finally kick off, it's pretty good.
Second, in case you're a fan of visual novels: don't expect any interaction in this like most VNs out there. In case you are not familiar with the genre: expect to read a lot. In fact, reading is what makes the largest part of this game. There are sprites and sound, sure, but in the end you're still in for hours of reading.
This novel has many downsides, of course. The beginning is
. Narration is really infantile and there are lenghty descriptions of completely irrelevant things. I get what they're trying to go for by setting that extremely cliché anime mood and then revealing, little by little, that life in Hinamizawa isn't all that relaxing and fun, until it gets to a point when it's taken a 180º curve and turned into the creepy mystery story that people are actually here for. But it still would've been better had they cut some of that snooze-inducing crap at the start and inserted something else, like extra material content or CGs.
Anyway, I still recommend it since the story does turn out to be interesting and somewhat creepy. The writing style near the second half of the game, particularly when describing Keiichi's paranoia, is enticing and has just the right amount of detail. However, especially in case you're a fan of horror/mystery and not in for the kyute moe animu grls and school shenanigans, you'll need to be really patient for the first 2~3 hours or so.

The trailer for this game is exactly what you get, so if you enjoyed it, you will enjoy this game. It is a combat-based action RPG in the style of an older Diablo game with a focus on straightforwardness, simplicity, and an absurd, lovable, and cartoonish style. The main character, Rick, is a melee fighter that you can augment by choosing different stats and items to wear.
Like Diablo, the fun of the game is in beating things up and finding items.  Rick accomplishes both of these by slamming his knife into enemies until they die in Rogue-like fashion. The strategy comes how you plan ahead by choosing what to wear, what to carry, where to stand, etc. rather than the actual combat, which is mostly just your stats comparing with the monsters and deciding how to use your consumable items. You also have a special meter that can be used to give yourself a boost for a short time. It's easy to understand and enjoyable.
Once you finish the game, you can try again with a different character and a stat focus. There are 9 or 10 special abilities you can pick as you level, some of which are passive. You can have up to 4, but some of them won't be relevant for the way you're playing. For example, I wouldn't choose a power like Flash (which uses your special meter to teleport you) on a character focused on Strength and Speed because I would never have enough Willpower to use it consistently. Or similiarly, I wouldn't choose Eagle Eye (which raises your attack rating and critical hit rate) on a character with a high Dexterity because I would already be hitting everything accurately and it would be redundant. You can choose a special ability to focus on one path, use in an emergency, or to balance out a weakness. There are enough different combinations and achievements to play through the game several times if you want.
If the store page appeals to you and you're looking for a light, enjoyable game, I recommend this. It's exactly what it looks like and it has enough depth for me to enjoy 90+ hours.

In short: it's turn-based casual simplified Diablo.
No,really, quests that are "kill them all", respawning monsters/loot, suffix-prefix loot system, magic drop boosts, two-three meaningful parameters (DPS, attack/defence (chance to hit/be hit), three resistances). And that's all.
If you are fond of err... flash-like rogie-lite games, it can be your game. Otherwise - too cheap and simply. Worth to spend one-two coffee-breaks in my opinion, but no more. 60/100.

The visual novel of the first anime series i ever experienced from start to finish, naturally i'm a bit biased towards the series but I know an unbelievable amount of people can back me up when I say Higurashi is a masterpiece of story telling, suspense, mystery, and friendship. It makes me happy that the series is now available to a fresh audience here on steam, and I will no doubt buy every chapter for myself, and chapters for my friends as well. If you ever only play one visual novel in your life, you cannot possibly go wrong with Higurashi.

You’re in a small village, Hinamizawa where an event takes place every year during June; and each event will always have a mysterious death, with someone going missing along with it. No one knows why this is…but it only happens each year after the event. Will you be able to find out who or what lead these tragic events?
With its improved and updated graphics, it sure looks better than before and it stands up with today’s standard of anime drawings. They didn’t attempt anything new here and its nothing impressive. Also, most of the background art are just real life pictures with filters over them; this is fine but it looks kinda weird in some places especially when it’s used many times over and over again.
A very slow start, but it eventually gets to the point halfway through the novel. They’ll start telling you about ‘the curse’, past events that happened before you moved in and more about the characters themselves. This eventually leads you to start wondering if the mysterious deaths were done by humans…or by the curse, or maybe both…you wonder…
It could’ve been better really, some of the music tracks are the same and are played repeatedly in many of the scenes which was kinda annoying to hear after a while. But that’s not to say the music is bad, they’re ‘okay’ for the most part; just not the best.

Playing
was a very interesting experience. This is the third installment in the
series, but none of the three games are connected. It’s actually very far removed from the other two, which were set in worlds of fantasy, like out of a storybook while this game has a more gothic feel and could easily be set in the real world. That aside, it’s a great game filled with lots of hidden object scenes and puzzles to keep players busy.
You take the role of a demon hunter named Sylvia who is apart of a secret organization called The Order. The game is filled with its own vocabulary as the different monsters have strange names and history behind them. The basics aren’t hard to grasp, The Order keeps magical stones with evil spirits locked inside of them but one ends up being stolen. Sylvia and her mentor go to find it but discover that it’s already been used and a town has been dragged into demonic chaos. The story revolves around saving those possessed by demons, finding the stone and sealing away the evil once more. There are some interesting twists and turns, a love story, and a mystery to solve as Sylvia lost her memory a year ago and works to recover it. There are a lot of different elements at play but the story is woven together very well.
As with most games in this genre, you use your mouse to control things; clicking on people and objects to interact with them as well as solving puzzles. The game has amazing hidden object scenes that offer a decent level of challenge as do the puzzles. It’s a good game for beginners and veterans of this genre alike. One thing I enjoyed were the items in the game that required further examination, you get to zoom on an item and figure how it works or what it needs, like unscrewing a rocket to get the gun powder out. Another fun feature are the magic battles you have to win in order to help return a possessed person back to their human state. They require finding a rune that doesn’t match any on the enemy’s side and as the game progresses they become more challenging. There are also hidden collectables in the game.
The artwork in this game is top notch, to the point where you might not even suspect it was a hidden object game. The setting, the cutscenes, and character models all feel like they’re out of an adventure game. I dare say this game reminded me of an
title. All of the hidden object scenes are beautiful and don’t strain the eyes, the characters move very smoothly and every cutscene is gorgeous. Audio-wise the voice acting is also well done and of high quality. I can’t complain about the background music and sound effects.
is amazing and I can’t really say anything negative about it other than the fact that this could have easily been a standalone title instead of part of the
series. This game offers a great challenge, it’s beautiful and, most importantly, fun. There are Steam achievements and trading cards to collect plus a bonus chapter that adds completion to the story. If you’re a fan of hidden object games you need this game in your library, if you’re not a fan this game could very well change your mind.

AMD FX 8370 Eight-Core 4.0GHz

So, seeing as how I can make almost ultra settings in the new Doom, it should've fully worked for a game several years old. I heard Windows 10 started it. EDIT: Still crashes. Not every few minutes or anything, but I think it may have something to do with autosaves.
IMPORTANT EDIT: While inconvienent, there is a way to stop the game's crashing. Just disable it's cloud saving within it's properties in Steam. Never crashed again. How to fix the frames? Don't get cocky with your computer. I know, the game should be high-end friendly, but it isn't. Lower the shadow resolution (4K works decent for me). 8K can actually be a bit too crisp with shadows, so like PC Gamer mentioned, use 2K - 4K. As much as some complain about the graphics altogether, deal with it. Games are supposed to be fun, not just pretty. That's why I hate mentioning graphic quality when it's not necessary.
The other problem with it's porting would be the interface/messages. Myself, and I'm sure many others, use the 360 controller. It works great. Feels just like the console. The problem is, the game doesn't care. It has a controller layout screen in the title's settings, but every in-game message will tell you commands for the keyboard. You'll have to realize that the in game controller showing setting will need to be changed, as well as the title (at least, that's the only way it worked for me). The keyboard controls look like crap too, so I fully recommend controller.

As others have said, the game is very unpolished and clunky, the graphics dated, and the UI not always intuitive. That said, the ambition of including so many different styles of gameplay into one game is impressive, and the game has a strange charm to it that kept me coming back for more.
The story is at times interesting, at times baffling, and it is very linear, with two paths to explore. But it has a slight System Shock 2 vibe to it with a dominant AI manipulating people.
I found it sometimes very obvious what was needed, and other times I wished there was a little more information. The voiced audio is mumbled and can be challenging to understand, especially for the parts without subtitles, but you can understand enough to get by.
The biggest let down for me was how money doesn't mean anything. The game refers to it multiple times, and even gives you 1,000 credits at one point, but you can never see how much you have, and the couple of merchants don't show prices because you can take their entire inventory for free.
There are lots of systems, with lots of planets to explore, and the mining aspect could have been more engaging, but you quickly realise there is no point at all in mining anything other than what is required for the current mission.
So, this all sounds like I didn't like the game, right? That's the confusing part... because I enjoyed playing the game and working around the quirks.
Also worth noting, the one time I was stuck and couldn't understand how to do what the game wanted me to do, based on the information given, I posted on the discussion group and the dev was quick to reply with a hint to get me going again.
While I do not think this game is worth full price, there is enough enjoyment to be had here for a sale price to be worthwhile. If you see it reduced, or find it in a bundle, give it a try.

When I first got a copy of the game back in 2009, it was pretty much what I expected out of a game that had been developed by a rather small group. Don't get me wrong though, I really did enjoy the game! Now, after coming back to it 6 years later, I must admit, the amount of time and effort this group has put into remastering this game really did pay off (from my PoV). At first, the mechanics of the game was a bit complicated to understand, and at the time, being a gamer whom wasn’t really one, I just enjoyed skipping and getting into it only to have been met with confusion, lack of understanding, etc.
Now, with that being said and with the reconstruction of this game, I must admit, I found it to be very understanding. What I mean with that statement is that I can skip (or accidentally skip) information and still be able to know what I am supposed to do and which keys to do it from. I believe this to be an excellent aspect of the game, considering the developers have put a huge effort and time into reconstructing it, specially taking into account notes given by the testers.
Regarding the storyline, having seen the game gone from the main game and it’s episodes into one solid game, I believe this to be another key point. I believe it has helped with understanding what’s going on and even for some players to really get into the role of being the protagonist. This is also really reflected in regards to the gameplay as it takes true to the previous aspect I mentioned. Keep that in mind, having played the game back in 2009, this newer version has really impressed me. Of course, all that glitter’s isn’t gold; the AI is a bit predictable and buggy, and I had a bit of trouble with the shooting (Crosshairs on the enemy, fired, but no death. I believe it was because I was on an inclination so probably there was a piece of the world blocking me or I just really bloody suck at it). There was also issues with the AI generally just rushing you and you having an excess of items such as ammo. I believe that the developers can fix this and even make it harder depending on the difficulty level.
Considering all this, from my subjective opinion, I would recommend this game. I consider not only the price to be a huge factor when it comes to getting your bang for your buck, but also just in general. In all honesty, with such a small development group and considering the game is from 2009 but remastered for 2015, I believe this group did a fine job with the resources and time they had. Even if it’s just to fart around and have some small fun, I still would recommend this game.
At the end of the day, the proof is in the pudding. You'll get bad reviews; you'll get good reviews. I think considering what such a small team put together + Price, it's a fun, humorous, action game.

I completed Incognito, on both branches if there was a choice. It works more like an interactive movie than a game, or rather a mashup of games that are so easy that they don't really provide a challenge.
There is an adventure part with voiced dialog and characters and some HHGTG references (if you know why a framed map of Norway would be one, you're a fan), but it is completely linear, and has all of two branches; the first branching unites seemlessly a short while later, the second branching has no effect other than the obvious one of playing the same section as either a wolf or a fox. There is a storyline, but all you get to do is fetch items.
There is a RTS part where you harvest minerals with 4 tanks and a probe and there maybe some enemies, but the enemy AI is dumb (all they know to do is to rush at you) and your own AI is no better (the weak probe always wants to repair the tanks and gets shot in the process). There are different building types, but no gameplay to use them.
There is an fps part where you have different guns (the railgun one-shots pretty much everyone, including closed doors), plenty of ammo, weak enemies (shoot them once, they die, they shoot you, you lose 5% health if that), and dumb AI: all they know is to rush at you, provided they notice you at all - simply shoot them down at range, done. You have lots of ammo, lots of food, it's as if the difficulty was set to "child's play", but the game has no other difficulty settings. There's a shop system in parts of this, but since there is no money, you can just use the shop as you would any crate.
There is a vehicle combat part where you drive a tank, but the enemies are weak and their AI is dumb: all they know is to rush at you, and they wont if you shoot them at range. Since the camera is above and behind the tank, you can see terrain where the tank can't see, and the reticule skips over that when you try to move it there, which is very annoying.
There's also space flight,and while you have been gathering material for shields and weapons, there is no opportunity to use them - it's stricly travel only, and the game is not quite aware that there's a difference between "star system" and "galaxy". Also, it's pretty much 2D, though you can do 3D if you tilt the camera, but then you have to accept that the ship isn't going to be pointing where you're thrusting.
Oh, and then there are 3 minigames that you can play from your inventory. Just don't. There's also an anagram game that you need to play to hack doors that has stats for "score" and "words found", but every door opened on the first word I found, so they weren't actually used.
This is a dedicated amateur effort alledgedly 6 years in the making that tries to do five different things, but does all of them badly. Sure, if you like amateur productions, feel free to have a go if it ends up in your Steam library (e.g. via bundlestars), but you (and I) would be better off spending your time on a game that's actually good: I recommed
if you want to play with/against an insane  AI, or
(if you can still get it and get it to run) which was actually designed by Douglas Adams himself and has talking bots with 10000 lines of text.
But maybe it's not meant to be a  game: maybe the "game" sequences are actually easy by intent, and the "game" is actually an ugly interactive movie. In which case, watch a real movie instead. Even
is much better than this.

From the game title, I thought it was like Taikou Risshiden (太閤立志伝) which was an old game series featuring Toyotomi Hideyoshi's way of progression to ruler of Japan (天下人). That's a training simulation RPG instead of strategic game. Even though I was surprised from the very beginning, it's still a very nice game.
The major selling point is that I can use other generals instead of Daimyo to play the game. I can make him my own story. Some very famous one such as Sanada Yukimura (真田幸村), there are numerous events relevant to them such as Siege of Osaka (大阪冬/夏の陣) which can change the tide of history. I think most of the Sengoku history lovers like me want to change the history, and this game is definitely for us.
Apart from that, the game graphics is wonderful that it shows us beautiful Japanese castles, villages and troops. In battle mode, the horse insignia (馬印) and flags (旗印) display according to the clan I use, I truly appreciate this realistic feature which shows serious gaming design down to very little detail.
Despite so many good features to praise, one thing that I want to comment is the price of the game. The current price in Steam is HKD 468 (around USD 60), which is acceptable. When I ordered the physical box set in early this year, it was around JPY 15000 (around HKD 1000 / USD 130) (the shipping cost was NOT included). That was so expensive ... however, as a long time fans of KOEI historical game series, I have to accept that if I wanna get the game asap. I hope that price of KOEI games in the future can be more reasonable like Steam now.
