Definitely a step in the right direction from FF13, but there is still room for improvement...
We are not completely free from corridors, character limitations (which goes step further actually, by giving you only
characters to play with (AND NONE OF THEM IS LIGHTNING?! Seriously, screw you SE...) and that's it! You can tame hundreds of monsters to fill up that third slot, sure, but it's not complete freedom, you know) or no-think combat, but the game is just too short to make these things unbearable.
Which is not a bad thing; you can rush through main story in 30 or so hours and it won't be even that difficult to do it, but you can also choose to mess around, do side quests and explore areas and times  you won't get to in the main line (FF13-2 chose not to use areas from previous game, or at least not at main stage, but rather introduced time travel, so you can explore the same areas in different eras or even in alternate timelines. Which is kind of lazy, if you ask me, as you are at the exactly same spot like three times but once there is sun, other there's night and last it's snowy. And it counts as three different areas...). For that reason most of the encounters are pretty easy because you can literally trigger them at any point of the game.
So uh, story... How should I put it... FF13 had story but it took a long time to get through it. 13-2 is in story part kind of shallow... At the beginning you are introduced to your goal (and also a minor point that the ending you've seen in 13 is a lie, lol. What a way to build a sequel!), but when you ask anyone how to get there, they're all like; "Oh I don't know... Try going through this Time Gate and see if something happens..." So you go and wait until something actually happens (that doesn't take long, mind you) and you kill something that somehow prevents another Gate from being used and you go on. And when you finally somehow made it to your destination, you are told you're late and whole world is being destroyed because of it. And that's it! That's the whole story! No plot twists, just few minor bumps here and there that didn't even matter in the end...
And don't even get me started on the conversations... I wanted to say it in FF13 review, but I reconsidered, however FF13-2 did it in so much bigger scale... Absolute most of the conversations are completely pointless, just to fill up awkward silence while you're waiting for something to happen! And what better thing to talk about than the reasons why you're on this journey?! I mean, first few times it's kind of bearable as those are new lore bits for the player. But I was sick of hearing the same; "For Lightning!", "For Hope!", "For the future!", "For the world!" and "You must not give up now!" over and over and over through the whole game!
One point I criticized about FF13 is having no way to replay the story with your maxed out characters. In 13-2, areas are not connected in the game-world but only through Historia Crux (Crossroad of Time and Space), that means you can from there reset time in each particular location back to the point before you entered it for the first time! (I guess it might not be so big of a deal for most people but I really enjoy having the option to brutally kick asses of the first bosses)
Which kind of leads me to another plus of this game; you get dialogue options! You can choose how your characters will respond, what they will ask about, what approach they'll take to a problem. And the time reset I mentioned allows you to go back and try out the other options you did not pick the first time and experience other challenges or even endings. Although it doesn't always cause much of a difference, it's still much better than the FF13 the Movie...
Combat is pretty much similar, but it gets some depth in form of the monster partners as each one of them has some unique abilities but you can consume that monster and give that ability to another one and create super-killing machine (FEED ON YOUR FRIENDS AND GROW STRONGER MY MINIONS!).
As I said in the beginning, this is definitely improved version of FF13. So much improved that it even might be worth paying for, how about that?! Just one thing to mention, the game expects you to know the events of FF13 and lore behind the world as it builds upon that. You have the option to read a summarized version of it's story in-game, but it's not too explaining about most of the side stuff and lore, so you might want to go through 13 first...
Oh, and for those wondering; I played it on the same machine as FF13 and 13-2 had much better performance than that. I even sometimes hit 30 fps in small areas :P

The Touhou Project (東方Project), also 東方プロジェクト (Touhou Purojekuto) or Project Shrine Maiden, is a Japanese doujin game series that specialises in shoot 'em ups by sole Team Shanghai Alice member ZUN. Generally, it's a series of 2D (with 3D background) vertically-scrolling danmaku shooting games, that also creates related print works and music CDs. There are also five fighting game spinoffs co-produced with Twilight Frontier, called "danmaku action games." The works of Touhou Project are sometimes called the Touhou Series (東方シリーズ Tōhō shirīzu) for convenience.
The setting of the Touhou Project lies in a haunted region of Japan called Gensokyo (幻想郷 Gensōkyō, lit. "Land of Illusions" or "Land of Fantasy"), sealed away from the outside world by the Great Hakurei Barrier. Reimu Hakurei is the protagonist of the project, who lives at the Hakurei Shrine that lies on the said barrier. She, along with the secondary character Marisa Kirisame, set out to solve various incidents that happen throughout the land, mostly cause by youkai. With this, they're both youkai exterminators.
The land is mainly inhabited by humans and youkai alike, who live in their own regions. Humans mostly settle in the Human Village, whilst youkai can be found mostly anywhere, such as the Youkai Mountain, the Forest of Magic and Makai. Some species include magicians, beasts, vampires, ghosts, tengu, mermaids, and kappa. There are others species that could be youkai depending on definition, such as fairies, spirits, phantoms, vengeful spirits, poltergeists, hermits, oni and gods.
Originally in the PC-98 canon, it was simply called "The Eastern Country". Long before the Touhou Project '​s story begins, there lived many youkai as well as some humans in the area. After a few humans lost their way into Gensokyo, humans became afraid of approaching this area, although others settled here for the sake of youkai extermination. However, as time went on, humans developed civilisation and multiplied in number, and thus the youkai became distressed about how this would affect the balance between humans and youkai. Thus, 500 years before the events of the Embodiment of Scarlet Devil, Yukari Yakumo developed the "boundary of phantasm and substance", which was favoured by the youkai and protected the balance. This was called the "Youkai Expansion Project" and made Gensokyo a phantasmal world that automatically called out to the weakened youkai of the outside world. Other things that disappear from the outside world, like extinct animals, lost tools and architecture, also became abundant in Gensokyo. Since Gensokyo was a plot of land in Japan that was separated by a barrier, it is Japan that is immediately outside of this barrier.
As a result of the seal, Gensokyo became inaccessible from the outside world, and similarly, those in Gensokyo were unable to leave. Gensokyo's existence could not be confirmed from the outside world, nor could the outside world be confirmed within Gensokyo. As a result, the isolated community developed its own civilisation, different from that of the outside world. Although separated by a barrier, it is a bordering world to its outside, as opposed to being in a parallel universe. There are no seas in Gensokyo, since it is an inland mountain.
In present Gensokyo in all Touhou games since EoSD, as opposed to the outside world where unscientific phenomena were dismissed as "superstition" by the time of the Meiji era, magical and spiritual qualities prevail. The only known gateway from the outside world into Gensokyo is the Hakurei Shrine. The spell card rules were also established to keep up the relationship between humans and youkai, which is necessary for the preservation of the balance of Gensokyo. The Great Hakurei Barrier, managed by Reimu, was constructed in the year 1885, which is described as a "barrier of common sense" and is thus a strong logical barrier that not even youkai can pass through. The youkai were at first against its construction, but then gradually understood its usefulness.
In Gensokyo, incidents occur once in a while, where there's an event that affects all of Gensokyo with an unknown cause at the time it occurs.[2] Touhou games mainly focuses on incidents in its stories, but there are also works such as Mountain of Faith that are about events other than incidents.
Frequently, incidents are due to a youkai's whim or curiosity, and usually Reimu (and on some cases others imitators such as Marisa) would go to investigate it to then find and punish the perpetrator. When a major incident occurs, the spirits and fairies are affected by the circumstances, the incident, and the perpetrator, and experience an increase in power for the duration incident, so there are also cases where a mere fairy can defeat Reimu. It has additionally been stated that people of the village also go out to resolve incidents.[3]
The Touhou Project does use the Gregorian calendar, but since the moon is more important to youkai, there exists the "Youkai Lunisolar Calendar" in Gensokyo, and although it's not used except for some youkai, it features prominently in works that have dates, such as Bohemian Archive in Japanese Red. This calendar doesn't merely take into account the waxing and waning of the moon, but also its colour and the cycles of its edge, and has a 13th intercalary month called Uruu. The smallest unit of this calendar is the month, and the calendar era, called "~th season", goes through a sexagenary cycle. the Embodiment of Scarlet Devil occurred in the 118th season, Immaterial and Missing Power and Perfect Cherry Blossom in the 119th, and Phantasmagoria of Flower View in the 120th. The opening of the "Gensokyo Chronicles" to the public was on the 121st season. This calendar is set such that the end of World War II is on the 60th season.
Touhou (東方) means "Eastern" and can refer to some or all of the areas, cultures or histories within East Asia. Historically, the term "the Orient" was widely used to refer to trade goods, artwork, literature, other items or topics related to countries in East Asia such as China, Japan, Korea or Vietnam. Officially, "Project Shrine Maiden" is the term for referring the series in English, but the English-speaking community regardlessly calls it the "Touhou Project" like the Japanese do. According to the Music Room Special in Mystic Square, the naming scheme of 東方ＯＯＯ originally came from one of the first songs he composed for Highly Responsive to Prayers, called Touhou Kaikidan (東方怪奇談)

"Experience what it’s like to be Batman and face off against Gotham's greatest villians. Explore every inch of Arkham Asylum and roam freely on the infamous island." - Steam store page description
Batman: Arkham Asylum is a 2009 action-adventure video game based on the DC Comics hero, Batman. Developed by Rocksteady Studios, the game was published by Eidos Interactive alongside Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment for the Xbox 360, PlayStation 3 and PC. Arkham Asylum is based off the long-running comic book serious and was written by Paul Dini, who also went on to help with writing Arkham City.
The story involves Batman and his archenemy the Joker pitting themselves against each other inside Arkham Asylum after the Joker takes over the place. Batman becomes trapped inside and is forced to fight through Arkham Asylum in order to stop the Joker.  Alongside this, many of the people in the game are voiced by voice actors from the DC Animated Universe such as Batman by Kevin Conroy, the Joker by Mark Hamill and Harley Quinn by Arleen Sorkin.
In terms of gameplay, the gameplay is presented with a third-person perspective view in which the player can use Batman's combat, stealth, detective skills and gadgets in order to fight through the inmates of Arkham Asylum and even use gadgets to traverse certain areas of the Arkham Asylum.
GOTY version of this game includes all of the DLC except the Play as the Joker DLC and Prey in the Darkness DLC. Though these are possible to get on PC if you know how to.
If you're having some issues with the game, visit my guide!
Overall, this is a fantastic Batman: Arkham game and a fantastic Batman game in general. I highly suggest purchasing this if you like Batman and want a good Batman game to play!

I cannot recommend this game. The idea is nice, but it has too many technical flaws. I'm always puzzled, how Capcom manages to damage their PC ports with such a high precision.
- Why is there still a "press start" screen in 2016, especially considering the loading times of this game? This screen does nothing but add an interaction during the load screen.
- This might be a "problem" with my machines, but after the "press start" screen, I don't have sound at all. I tested the onboard sound, an external USB sound device and a bluetooth device, but no sound was played.

- Switching to aim view warps your character and zooms a little. Considering how RE4 is said to have been the first game with modern shoulder-view mechanics, this is almost a bit disturbing.

Hidden Star in Four Seasons is the 16th and currently latest instalment in the mainline touhou games, and an otherwise pretty good release from the current era (2nd Modern Windows Era). The game is designed to be a breath of fresh air compared to the last game, Legacy of Lunatic Kingdom, and it does feel like the difficulty takes part of a more beginner friendly path, which makes this a good game to start from.
HSiFS introduces a mechanic into the series called “Sub-Seasons”, where on the character screen, you can choose a secondary season along with the character and can level up its power on the bottom left by collecting season items. Each season sub-shot has different power and mechanics reminiscent to the season’s representing character’s shot. (i.e. Summer gives spread-out ice bullets similar Cirno’s shot)
You can also release your season by pressing C, this drains your season level back to zero (ex. Summer) and activates a “mini-bomb” where the power of it depends on the gauge’s level, with a cap of 6. Like before, what the release does depends on the selected sub-season.
General gameplay is what you’d mostly expect from an average touhou game, plenty of enemies shooting bullets, collecting points and power items, dodging all the pretty patterns from bosses. You gain lives through scores and bombs by beating bosses. The bosses in HSiFS are pretty good for the most part, the final boss is great, and the stage 5 boss is a bit crazy compared to the usual difficulty for 5th stage bosses. (although not Clownpiece-tier)
The music is amazing, and it always has been when composed by ZUN. I always notice myself unconsciously banging my head at certain points while dodging bullets at the same time.
My personal favourite songs from this game are:
(2nd Stage) and
(4th Stage)
And the characters are mostly good, but this is being said from a fan. As a new player, you won’t exactly be taking notice on anything but the design and maybe personality, since the games for the most part have always been vague in character backstory. That’s why written works exist. I’m sure fans, while focusing on design and personality, also enjoy potential lore and relations with other existing characters as well.
Aunn is as pure as a cinnamon roll and deserves all the cuddles.
There is however a big flaw myself and some others have found with this game, the visibility of the bullets is very weak at an amount of points. Now this has almost never been a problem with touhou, but with this game you'll be finding a lot of the season items and backgrounds lacking much contrast between the bullets, which is something really important in a
game.
What's strange is the bugs from the Comiket release still exist, thankfully the most notable one (crashing from clearing certain 5th boss spellcard practices) can be fixed with the same patcher mentioned at the top.
Hidden Star in Four Seasons stands as an enjoyable experience for both newcomers and experienced players alike (but not as enjoyable compared to the early windows games) and a potentially decent entrypoint for those willing to get into the touhou fandom. Hopefully ZUN does release more of his games onto steam making it simple for foreigners to play without needing to pirate them.

The game drew me in with its theme and promise of elegant mechanics. I'm just going to jump right to it. I give this game a 3 out of 10.
Some people will like this game, and I can see why. It has a fun theme, has an interesting board (despite being static), and presents a challenge in trying to find out the optimal line of play.
These are the biggest 3 issues I have with the game.
1 - It just doesn't look/feel cleany designed. It has blatant kingmaking issues, and far too much "take that". The board is hard to read. The twisted roads and direction symbols required close scrutiny to discern which paths were available to take in trying to reach a destination. The cards have the effects listed in strange places on them that doens't flow well. I had a hard time discerning what most of the cards did, and what conditions were required for effects to resolve. I figured out most of it by the end of my first game, but there were still times where I would play a card on the space I was supposed to and the effect I thought would go off just didn't happen. A mix of too much information in your hand, board, and the inability to easily understand what was going on in both make this game inaccessible to put it mildly. There’s something to be said about the doujin shmup scene, especially when it comes to accessibility and difficulty curves. Indeed, the sheer size of the challenge laid out before would-be bullet hell players often proves itself to be the greatest obstacle that separates those who develop a fondness for games of the genre and those who don’t. While the sub-genre has always possessed a high entry-barrier that no doubt contributed to its limited appeal outside of Japan in the past, those games that hail from the doujin variety tend to stand out in particular. With Danmaku Unlimited 2 Doragon Entertainment seeks to recreate that iconic doujin experience. For the most part, they succeed.
If Danmaku Unlimited 2 has an in-depth story, it isn’t presented in the game. Like most shmups, Danmaku Unlimited 2 puts narrative to one side and gives its full, undivided attention to the gameplay experience alone. While each of the game’s five stages provides some degree of context for the action, it’s clearly the case that this isn’t a story-driven game.
The driving force behind Danmaku Unlimited 2 stems from its well-polished, highly-refined core gameplay. A typical scenario begins with the player gunning down countless enemies as they appear at the top of the screen, all the while avoiding the beautiful but deadly hail of bullets sent the player’s way. Defeating enemies causes scoring items to appear and fall towards the bottom of the screen. The final phase of each level is indicated by a boss, who throws a series of different bullet patterns at the player in sequence, switching to the next pattern each time the player inflicts a certain amount of damage upon the boss. Dealing with such heavy densities of enemy fire can prove troublesome, but that’s where ‘Trance’ comes in. Destroying one’s opponents charges the Trance Gauge. When the gauge is full, Trance can be activated, converting bullets in the player’s immediate vicinity into scoring items and also enabling the player to unleash more powerful attacks than before.
The enemy placement within each level has been well-thought through. Weaker enemies are often clumped together, prompting the player to mow them down in quick succession to boost their score, while stronger enemies like to hide at the top of the screen, peppering the player with bullets and forcing them to take evasive action. However the bullet count consistently remains quite low, particularly for a game seeking to emulate a doujin shmup. It isn’t made any more challenging by the fact that the bullets also tend to move rather slowly. Those two factors lead to the game feeling somewhat easier than what one might initially expect, which could be a good or bad thing, depending on one’s past experience with bullet hell games. Players who are no strangers to the conventions of the genre are more than likely to find themselves underwhelmed even on higher difficulties, which is a shame, considering that those are the people most likely to possess the strongest appreciation for the doujin shmup.
Before setting off to battle; either from the start of the game or from any stage of the player’s choosing via ‘Free Play’; one may choose from one of two modes. ‘Burst Mode’ provides the player with a potent beam attack which can be used for going on the offensive, or for clearing a path through enemy bullets. The advantages afforded to the player by having such a tool at their disposal are offset by their inability to generate scoring items by killing enemies through the use of normal fire: accurate, efficient use of the beam attack and Trance become the only means of guaranteeing a high score. ‘Classic Mode’ offers up more a traditional bullet hell experience that those already acquainted with the genre should feel right at home with, in which attacks of any sort are adequate for creating scoring items.
The beam attack and Trance are both well-conceived mechanics. They can double up as additional defensive measures for those getting to grips with the action, while also serving as means for securing additional points, for individuals already on top of things.
Players operate the Senko fighter, a versatile craft capable of undergoing numerous upgrades to suit the situation as necessary. Playing the game in any mode earns the player experience. Accumulating experience will gradually allow the player to progress in rank until they hit the top and become an Ace. As rank increases so too do the player’s options to outfit the Senko with the capabilities of their choosing. Players can opt for three different forms of attack for their fighter, in addition to the beam attack. It’s possible to take multiple forms of attack for the sake of versatility, or to focus on upgrading one in order to support a specific playstyle. Those willing to forego the luxury of having extra lives and credits at their disposal will find themselves able to maximize their offensive capabilities. This upgrade system gives players a chance to experiment and find a playstyle that works for them, while also lending the game additional replayability. It’s a nice touch, and one that feels original but still has its place in a bullet hell game.
Danmaku Unlimited 2 is a visually stunning 2D piece – the graphics are easily some of the best seen in a bullet hell game in recent times. The cyan/purple colour palette gives the game’s environments an ‘otherworldly’ look, but not one that feels too far-fetched. Ships have a bold, coloured outline that makes them stand out, even when the screen is literally filled with explosions and scoring items. The centralized HUD also makes a difference: it’s nice not having to take yours eyes too far from the action to glance at some game-critical info. A cyan-coloured dot marks the player ship’s hitbox, which still remains easy to spot in the midst of a heated battle, thanks to the trail it gives off. Unfortunately the same can’t be said about the game’s audio. Most; if not all; of the music quickly gets repetitive. The sound effects themselves are surprisingly weak, and don’t have any real impact, with some explosions being barely even audible even at higher volume levels.
Overall Danmaku Unlimited 2 is a fairly enjoyable game that’s likely to find the most favour with those caught in the middle-ground. Long-time veterans of the genre might find the experience a little too light, but for the uninitiated and anyone with only a moderate degree of bullet hell experience, Doragon Entertainment’s love letter to fans of the doujin shmup delivers an entertaining package that; generally speaking; knows and understands at least part of its audience.

Given the high praise this game received, particularly as a smart phone game, I was curious to check it out on the PC. Sadly, I fell rather disappointed by this game, and consider it to be severely lacking. Even among independently developed games it can’t measure up.
The game itself seems okay at first sight. You get a modifiable fighter plane with weapons — straight shot, homing shot, wide shot — that you can mix and match. There are two scoring modes, Burst and Classic, and four difficulties each. Following STG convention, the game has five stages, with mid and end bosses, and if you finish the game on one credit on at least hard’, you’ll face a ‘true last boss’ as well. As a bonus, there is a boss rush mode, and a free play mode for those who like to credit feed through the game.
While Danmaku Unlimited 2 follows the STG formula in broad strokes, it sadly goes awry in many, many areas. Let me describe some of the problems I’ve had with it one by one:
1) The music is incredibly bland and does not synchronise with the action on screen at all.
2) There are very few sound effects, not even for basic actions like shooting.
3) The shield system is poorly thought out. If effectively acts as a life bar, meaning that you can take several hits. However, if you slip, you lose the ship. This seems needlessly punishing. As I'll describe later on, there are situations where it's easy to trip up due to design flaws of the game.
4) Bullet visibility is pretty poor. While you can tell bullets from the background, there is not enough contrast. Have you ever wondered why in Cave games the bullets have garish colours, while the backgrounds may even seem a bit washed out? Here, bullets and background are often in similar colors. This problem might have been prevented had there been actual background images instead of mostly static colors.
5) Further, I am not fond at all of how some of the bullets overlap. There are instances where smaller bullets move underneath larger ones, so while you focus on avoiding the larger ones, you may get hit by a small bullet that just emerged underneath it.
6) In many STGs, there is a dead zone around turrets, meaning that if you’re getting close, they won’t fire. In Danmaku Unlimited 2, this is not the case, which means that as you move past a large space ship, you may just get hit without expecting it.
7) What I also find very unfortunate is that smaller enemies don’t get invincibility frames. Particularly in stage 5 it may happen that you get hit because you didn’t memorise yet that you entered a part of the stage where a swarm of small enemies enters from the side. Those deaths through collision punish players who have not yet memorised a stage, and are a sign of poor game design, in my opinion. A good counter example on Steam is Crimzon Clover, by the way, where enemies that fly into the screen can’t hit you for a few frames.
8) Overall, the difficulty is really uneven. Some boss patterns in later levels are laughably easy, just to be followed by much trickier ones. In a carefully balanced STG I expect something different.
9) I strongly dislike that I have to unlock game features. This means that you start out with an underpowered fighter, and have to earn in-game currency (thankfully no IAP), to unlock more lives, continues, or more powerful weapons.
10) There seems to be a bug: When you 1cc the game, you end up at the title screen, but you don’t unlock any achievements, or get any of your in-game currency. However, if you then enter a new mode, and exit prematurely, then the game records your progress.
11) Minor quibble: I would have appreciated if the game let me skip the credits.
12) The high score boards are hacked, which is always unfortunate, as it shows a lack of support of the developer.
13) The scoring system is poorly thought out, since a few successful actions completely negate the entire rest of the game. Some people are upset because in Cave games it is often the case that you score more in stage 5 than in the entire rest of the game, even though stage 5 normally is a lot longer and has a lot more enemies, so it’s pretty much justified. In Danmaku Unlimited 2, though, your score depends on something like a minute or two of play time in total.
*** added ***
14) The achievements with point values seem broken. I just reached 1 billion in total,  but it didn't activate.
15) Some bullets, like the hexagons, are incredibly poorly designed. Those only harm you if you get hit by the center, meaning that the hitbox of your ship can safely sit on a large part of the area of those bullets. Another example are the large bullets in the last phase of the stage 5 boss. However, those have no demarcated center. Just like with the other bullets, if you don't know this, then you think those boss patterns are a lot more difficult than they are.
16) The transition from iPhone to PC should have led to changes in the control setup. On the phone, the speed of the ship is relative to the speed of your finger. In this version the ship has a relatively high default speed, and to slow it down, you have to use the burst shot. This is fine in Classic mode, since that shot is available without limit. However, in Burst mode, you can only slow down by activating a burst shot with a separate gauge that has to be filled. If the gauge isn't high enough, the ship does nothing at all. This means that some boss fights, where you have to weave though tight patterns, are incredibly tedious, and take a lot longer than they otherwise would.
Considering all those issues, some minor, some large, I simply cannot recommend Danmaku Unlimited 2. There are other STGs of much higher quality available on Steam, or on consoles. My personal recommendation on Steam is Crimzon Clover: World Ignition, which is also independently produced, and one of if not the best STG around.
I'd recommend this game to people who think that touch screens are a superior input alternative for STGs, those who think that superplayers can dodge rain, and those who consider Touhou to be the pinnacle of this genre. Danmaku Unlimited 2 is not the bullet hell you need, but the one you deserve.

Almost at its 8th anniversary, Arkham Asylum still holds up. It boasts an impressive voice cast including Kevin Conroy as The Dark Knight, Mark Hamill as the Joker, and Arleen Sorkin as Harley Quinn, all reprising their respective roles from the animated series.
Gameplay-wise it is mainly split up between combat and predator sections. The combat is easy to pick up, but hard to master. The predator sections require you to be more stealthy as you pick off armed thugs one-by-one. Both of these sections have their own set of upgrades to counter specific enemies. There are also small detective-esque segments where you analyze a crime scene, (though it is pretty straight forward in this game as opposed to the sequels).
In the main storyline, Batman's archenemy, the Joker, instigates an elaborate scheme to take over Arkham Asylum, pitting Batman against many of his well-known incarcerated villains. This game was a significant milestone in the superhero game genre and deservedly won game of the year.

I pretty much never recommend games on steam because I simply don't care, but I can't resist writing a review for Another World. I remember playing it a lot when I was a kid and loving it, but I never beat it because of the brutal difficulty. I recently picked it up on a whim during the steam winter sale for only a few bucks, and it was probably one of the best games I've bought in my entire life. Without sounding like a sales pitch, Another World really isn't just a game, it's an experience. It truly is one of the most gorgeous and captivating games I've ever played, and I don't plan on forgetting it any time soon. A must-play for anyone who can appreciate a great classic retro game; not for something simple like pick-up-and-play capabilities, but for amazingly stunning visuals to tell an engaging and immersive story.

If you're looking for a game where you're immersed in a truly alien landscape, I can't recommend this game enough.
There's no obvious mission or narrative to begin with, besides 'staying alive somehow': you are literally the only human being in this game. The player and the protagonist, Lester, are equally isolated from the game's surroundings - there's no HUD, there's no explanatory text besides the menus and closing credits, and you're left to discover how things work by yourself. Unless you're a savant or playing from a walkthough, you WILL die - many, many times - and you WILL be frustrated when you can't get that water jumping sequence just right - but the payoff when things go -just right-, trust me, is incredible.
Another World balances reflex action sequences with methodical environmental puzzles perfectly, backed up by a checkpoint system. The soundtrack is mostly background environmental material, and the utterly beautiful flat-shaded polygon graphics are stunning: if I were to sum the game up in a sentence, I'd say it's strange, it's alien, and it has a compelling narrative that's entirely told through 'showing' and not 'telling'.

Higurashi Onikakushi chapter may not have a long story, but it does have an interesting one that you'll want to finish. It is a horror/mystery, so there are dark themes in this game - YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED!
-
The story has a slow start (kind of) but definitely speeds up before the halfway mark.
It focuses on Keiichi Maebara, a 16-year old student who has moved to the rural village of Hinamizawa with his parents due to his father's work as an artist. After living there for about a month, Keiichi has gotten used to the life there with his new friends: Rena Ryuugu, Mion Sonozaki, Satoko Houjou, and Rika Furude. While everything appears normal with the village at first, Keiichi learns from a visiting photographer, Tomitake, about some mysterious murders which occur each year. What makes it even stranger is that Rena and Mion, when asked about it, deny the existance of them. Days pass and the anual Cotton Drifting (Watanagashi) festival approaches, and Keiichi finds out from Tomitake and and a friend of his that the murders are supposedly tied to a curse from the village's god, Oyashiro-sama.
Following the festival, Keiichi is visited by a police detective, Ooishi, who alerts to him about
. Keiichi is told that this is a result of the curse, and is warned by Ooishi that he could be next. Although skeptical at first, Keiichi begins to become paranoid about his surroundings, and begins to become suspicious of Rena and Mion, who begin acting strangely.
What will happen to Keiichi? Are Rena and Mion up to something? Is the curse real? Will I stop asking all these questions? Find out the answer to all of them (except the last one) in this chapter!
It is worth mentioning that all the character sprites that appear in the game have been redesigned by MangaGamer, however you can switch between the original and new sprites if you wish. The sprites from the Playstation versions can be used through use of mods, although I personally don't see anything wrong with botht he old and new sprites. All of the backgrounds and music remain the same as the original, and that I find is good, as it helps preserve the feel that the sound novel is supposed to give.
One part I am disappointed with is that there are no CG images used, unlike most visual novels. Some parts of the game would be better with CG images in my opinion, and it confuses me as to why MangaGamer didn't include any, considering they went through the effort to redesign the character models. If you wish to view CG images, I believe there is a patch that adds in the ones from the Playstation versions, although the game is still good without them.
The story takes roughly 10 hours or so to finish, which is short compared to many visual novels. This is due to that this is only chapter 1 of the game. For the complete story, there are 8 chapters, 4 question arcs and 4 answer arcs. At the time of writing this review, only the first two chapters are released (Onikakushi and Watanagashi), with chapter 3 currently being translated. More games are on their way, although they don't affect the main story.
Buy and Play. 9.5/10

The Touhou series is one of my favorite series of all time, and now that it has an official Steam release, I highly reccomend this game.
Now, this isn't a game that's for everyone. It's a very challenging series that requires a good amount of practice and dedication, as most bullet hell do. Gladly, this entry in the series isn't by any means the hardest, making it a pretty good game to start on in my opinion.
I could probably write for a while as to what I like and don't like about the game, but I'll just turn it into a simple pro and con list.
Pros:
-Great Soundtrack.
-Very simple controls.
-Challenging Gameplay.
-(Mostly) Memorable Characters.
-Challenging, yet somehow memorable patterns.
-Visually nice/interesting to look at.
-You can play as Alolan form Cirno.
Cons:
-Some characters are kinda boring and easy to forget.
-Takes a good chunk of time to get good enough to complete the game. (This could also be a Pro if it's what you're looking for)
-Sparratic difficulty spikes, only really with a few specifically difficult spellcards amongst many easy spellcards.
I'm not going to add it not having English as a Con, however, as that can be easily patched through the various ways the Touhou community has been able to do so.

Regardless of what the RE Loyalists or the CS Trolls say, the game is merely average. It's not the next best thing nor is it the bane of human existence, as many would have you believe. It's merely 'okay'. As it stands it feels like an unpolished alpha that has promise to be a much better game than what it is. The animations feel unfinished, the hit-detection is all over the place and the matchmaking is awful. But it's still hardly the worst game on steam. It would benefit from a few more months of development and perhaps a free-to-play model. One thing i can say for certain is that it isn't worth the money, at the very least it should be $15 but even then i feel that's too much considering CSGO has more content. Despite all this, there's something about the fast-paced third-person multiplayer gameplay that feels greatly satisfying. I can't quite put my finger on it. Perhaps it's because it's uncommon amidst so many similar first person offerings.
+ Fun when you have enough players
+ Encourages teamwork
+ Actually tries to be competitive
+ Concept is pretty cool
- Awful hit detection
- Bad Matchmaking [No Match Browser]
- Feels like an alpha at best
- Matches are way too short [Sometimes only a few seconds]
- Not enough content/maps/modes to warrant purchase
* Filled with leavers/ragequitters
* Is better off being free-to-play
* The multiplayer is more-or-less dead
* Obnoxious/Annoying Music/Voiceovers
Simply put, it could be better but it feels unfinished. Even already for the fact the bandwagon haters got to the game so fast, the game just isn't ready yet. It's better off being free-to-play so they have more time to work on it plus people might actually play it if it's entirely free. Capcom got too ambitious too fast with this, they screwed up. Only time would tell if they could fix it. I just hope they don't let it die, it's something rather different in a swamp of tactical FPS games.

I did enjoy the VN. The art is only about average for the talking portraits, but really quite good for the CG images. The story pulls you in and gets you interested at first. The music suits the events on screen.
Why the not recommended?
There's a section about 2/3's of the way in where the exact same information is repeated around a half dozen times in a row in different stories between different people which feels like the grind padding you get in a lot of RPG's, the kind that's there only to increase the total amount of time played. The twists, aside from the not-so-exciting cliffhanger ending, are so heavily talked about and foreshadowed that only the specifics are kept hidden from the player. And even then the specifics of those specifics, like how did "he" know about this process and specifically how did "he" recreate it other than a Frankenstein's monster type of effect, are never explained well enough at least to my satisfaction, and considering how in-depth the writing goes to ensure the player has a firm enough grasp on the mechanics of mana in this world this is more a little troubling in terms of consistency.
In fact my biggest complaint with this VN is how short it is, and how slowly the story moves.
Maybe this is just the current state of VN's? I don't dislike the game, I did enjoy playing it, but if I hadn't acquired it in a bundle I know for certain I couldn't have brought myself to buy it. I remember playing games like this 10, 20 years ago with multiple CG's, stories, endings, choices, characters, etc. which could easily last someone a good 10, 20 hours or more, even with a skip option. This game had 1 choice only, and it was pretty obvious what the right answer was, though it seems like the choice doesn't matter.
At the pace the story unfolded for this, the first entry, I'm starting to think the developers have no intention of this game series having a real ending after 2, 3, or 4 games, I could easily see them trying to make 10 or more. This is based purely on my experience playing this game.
If you absolutely love VN's and really don't like games otherwise, this might be for you. But to me it's too slow, too short, too limited, and far too expensive considering all of those things. Could easily make a pretty good animated series one day; the entire first VN could be summed up in one to three episodes easily, considering internal monologue, seemingly the bulk of the writing, doesn't normally exist in anime.
Thanks for reading and have a nice day.

Really enjoyed this game when it was ported to the PS2, and it's still one of my favorite cult hit JRPGs, alongside Xenosaga and .hack.  Story is fairly generic and predictable, but the environments and dungeons are pretty diverse, character interactions and development is respectable to good, and the dialogue, while cringe at times, reminds me of a time when anime dubs were enjoyable for sounding cartoony and campy.
The biggest draw to this game, however, is the combat, which is a unique mix of turnbased and real time battle.  Character movement before or after an attack can lead to an attack  missing, and there are ways of coordinating your party's attacks to do extra damage through combos or to delay an enemy's use of a powerful skill or spell.  Boss battles are satisfying in difficulty, and you can gain extra items by killing parts of them before killing the main body (you should anyway, because many times these parts are buffing the boss or throwing extra attacks and debuffs/ailments on your party, so taking those parts out quickly helps you out).
For those who enjoy waifus, Millenia is bae.  Ryudo is also husbando material for you ladies out there.  And Mareg is a bro.
The anniversary edition has enhanced visual and audio (essentially, it's cleaned up), but don't expect a remaster like the FFX Collection.  But if you can look past the dated graphics and the occasionally cringe dialogue/voice acting, and you're looking for a JRPG fix in between FF15 and Personal 5, give this a try.  It's a flawed gem, but a gem nonetheless.

first Steam release
First things first:
Now that that's out of the way, I'm just going to focus on this game in particular, the 16th in the main Touhou series, and how it compares to the rest.
You have 4 playable characters / main shot options: Reimu (homing shots), Marisa (lasers), Cirno with a tan (spread shots) and Aya (narrow piercing shot).
In addition to these, you can choose a subweapon that adds some extra shots and a "release" ability (more on that later), there are 4 and they're named after the four seasons: Spring adds homing shots, Summer adds spread shots, Autumn adds side shots, and Winter adds a single laser that shoots directly in front of you.
You can couple all characters with whatever season you want, so that makes for a total of 16 total unique shot types, which is a lot if you think about it... some combinations are better than others of course, but they're all pretty viable.
The release ability is something unique to this game: by collecting "season items", you charge your season meter, which you can bring up to level 6; each level adds an additional subweapon option, which generally means you'll be killing stuff slightly faster.
By pressing the release button, you "release" all the season power you have accumulated, and you'll be surrounded for a few moments by a small circle that cancels all bullets within it, converting them to season items and automatically collecting them. That means exactly what you think it means: if you cancel enough bullets to fill at least 1 level of the season bar with a single release, you can release again immediately.
Even though their basic function is the same, each season release works differently, thus changing the way you play, and the game will give you plenty of chances to use them in clever ways.
That's it about the new gameplay features, there's not much to say about the rest since it's pretty much the usual.
There's spell practice (thank
ZUN) so you don't have to waste entire runs just to have a chance to get gud at a certain spellcard.
The soundtrack, while being of standard ZUN quality (it's good of course) doesn't really stand out from his other works, but maybe that's just me.
If I have to say one problem this game has though, it's visibility, which is something important in a bullet hell game. There are sections in the game where large amounts of killed enemies or grazed bullets will leave behind a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of season items, and they're just not trasparent enough, making a mess with all the bullets and enemies flying around. The final boss non-spell attacks also consistently have the bullets of the same color as the background, making them quite harder to see.
There's also something to say about the difficulty balance, the first half of the game feels very easy as opposed to the second half which is much harder in comparison. In other games it is usually a more steady increase.

It worked fine on my Windows 10 computer.
Pretty good difficulty curve - playing on normal difficulty there were only a couple of later boss battles where I had to go into double figures of replays to master.
Won't spoil the story for you - much better to play through without spoilers since there's a definite plot and a couple of decent twists. Killer Croc here is a far darker villain than the one who appears in "Suicide Squad".
The game definitely plays better with a controller.
So the game breaks down into: -
1) Massed minion battles - where Batman must fight half a dozen upwards henchmen armed with hand to hand weapons.  Batman can't take much damage so you have to chain attacks and use dodges to win.
2) Navigating the environment.  Batman starts with a line which can be used to ascend (and can effectively drop any distance where there is a floor) and later adds spray on explosive to blow up walls, a grappling hook to pull down weak walls, and a line to cross chasms.
3) Battles with firearm armed minions.  Guns do huge amounts of damage to Batman so sneaking up behind firearm armed enemy and taking them out silently is the only effective way to deal with them.  Can be tricky in larger groups.
4) Boss battles.  Similar to minion battles except Batman relies far more on his Batarang to disorient foes and use the environment against them since he can't win slugging toe to toe.
5) Finding hidden items.  These unlock histories of the Asylum's residents, the story of the Asylum, and a series of collectibles.  Irrelevant to main story line except to boost experience.
6)  A few pure stealth sections.
Criticisms ?  2010 game so graphics are no longer state of the art.  For "The World's Greatest Detective" there is literally no detective work for the player.  There are no options on conversations, there are no puzzles for the player to solve (other than getting in or out of awkward to access locations which occur frequently).  The game play I've described above is pretty much the game.  There isn't a huge degree of variety of enemy and tasks.  I completed the main game in about 16 hours so not the longest campaign.
But these are quibbles.  Film adaptations have a deserved reputation of producing some of the worst games in video gaming history.  But this is a solid gold achievement.  Strong plot, well chosen cast of characters, and the Asylum itself is a dark, intimidating environment.  Both the story and the kit are true to the character and you really get to play as "The Dark Knight".  This is an exceptionally well designed and superbly implemented game and at sale price should be an essential for any Batman fan or fan of the gaming styles described above.  Far better than the first Chris Nolan movie.

Other than that there's not much else to point out, you either like the story or you do not.
The story at first may feel like it's throwing too much information and getting nowhere but it does get a lot more interesting as it goes on. The characters have very distinct personalities and are very likable and relatable. The story gets very dramatic at some parts but it does leave you feeling that it made sense and perhaps think about the concept itself. There is nothing annoyingly unrealistic. The end will leave wanting more but at that point you can buy Milestone Two. Without spoiling, all I can say is that in my opinion the story is very interesting and worth your time.

This review contains some spoilers. They will be marked with the spoiler tag.
Let me level with you: I hate most visual novels. The conventions, the storytelling, the characters, the dialogue -- they're usually all usually pretty awful. Most visual novels, quite frankly, are garbage.
fault: milestone one, however, is not.
This visual novel is what you might call a diamond in the rough. It has some visual novel-isms, as I like to call them -- ear-grating conventions of visual novel storytelling -- but once the story starts rolling, it proceeds with a logic and purpose that is as undeniable as it is robust.
This review will be broken down into two sections focusing on the writing and on the technical elements.
fault stumbles with its first steps by suddenly thrusting upon the viewer a lot -- and I do mean a lot -- of rushed exposition and a swift introduction to some unlikable characters. I admittedly found myself at first wondering why I should care what happens to any of them. The game at first seemed to me like someone's fanfiction -- or a replay of a tabletop roleplaying game.
However, after the weaker introductory portion, fault quickly finds its footing with some strong characterization, an engaging and thoughtful narrative, and some mercifully concise, meaningful dialogue. Thank Christ. If I ever again have to read even a single line of rambling internal monologue from yet another bland, gutless protagonist who does little more than point out the obvious, I am going to break something. (Looking at
, World End Economica.)
I cannot emphasize this enough: fault is written by writers who care not only about the lore in their world -- I would strongly advise you to read through fault's encyclopedia before playing -- but also about the characters who have to live in it. The writers care enough to ask questions -- the right questions -- about the existential and ethical implications of their story and assume that the audience is smart enough to not only follow the thread of those questions but be interested in their answers. All of this is precisely what thoughtful writers ought to be doing, and I am, quite frankly, amazed to see it here in a visual novel -- when you rarely see it in any works at all.
Ultimately, fault's strengths rest on two things: interesting, complex, and likable characters as well as interesting, complex, and far-reaching ideas.
Let's move on to some of the more technical aspects.
The art and character designs are fine. I'm not sure whether or not any of it is particularly remarkable -- the zoom effect is nice, at least -- but it gets the job done, and that's what matters. The narrative alone is strong enough to carry the visual novel, not to mention the mostly well-written dialogue and compelling characterization.
I have a lot of praise for the background music. The opening theme is lackluster, but the background music is the real backbone of scenes, reinforcing with ease whatever emotions or ideas lie behind characters or locations.
fault: milestone one is a kinetic novel. As far as I can tell, the single choice you make in it has no tangible effect on how the story proceeds. That's fine; I have no real problem with that. I'm letting other readers know this, however, in the interest of a useful review.
There are some problems with the user interface. It isn't well-designed, and it was distressing to me that I was unable to change the speed at which some specially-scripted text appears on the screen. (In fact, I was unable to bring up the settings at all during the prologue, which also annoyed me.) Thankfully, I believe this only happens during the prologue. There's always at least one fly in the ointment, isn't there?
Scene transitions are a little clumsy and add unnecessary bulk to the game, and there are some questionable translation choices when it comes to names -- but these are, I feel, minor issues, all things considered. As I said at the beginning, fault: milestone one isn't perfect by any means -- it's a diamond in the rough.
Overall, I would recommend this visual novel to anyone who is looking for one that strives to live up to the novel part.

**SPOILER-FREE REVIEW**
As the first game of Batman Arkham series, Asylum succeeds in every way in my point of view. I will be honest from the start and confess that I played all these series in no particular order  leaving Asylum the last. You ask why? Well because compared to its successors I find that this game doesn't have too much of an unexpected plot. So yeah Batman finally caught Joker and he's bringing him to the Arkham Asylum, a place built on an island by Amadeus Arkham in hopes to cure the craziness in the villains of Gotham, to me even in comics this place resembles the prison Alcatraz due to it's location. In the Asylum Batman wishes to follow and take part in the incarceration of Joker mainly because he feels that something is wrong, our crazy clown would never let our caped vigilante catch him so easily and with new goons coming from Blackgate, we can say that B-man had his reasons. He was right, oh boy he was. So Joker frees himself while his inside "friends", Harley Quinn, take control over the whole building leaving the world's greatest detective fight goons and old powerful enemies who escaped in time after the outbreak while trying to get to the bottom of the case where Joker's true intentions on breaking the Asylum are discovered. Yes, the plot is exhilarating but I personally don't find it so unpredictable, still a very good narrative which I believed got an award and funny dialogues. Now that I think about it this game presents more humor than any other Arkham game. Many times I found myself laughing or grinning at Joker's stupid jokes and the interactions between characters.
Gosh... Where to begin. The game is played from a third-person perspective, occasionally first-person in some cut-scenes or ventilation walking. It has a bit for everybody: stealth, parkour, fighting, crime scene scanning and following tracks, the whole game thrives in this category.
As you are playing Batman you have at your disposal a variation of gadgets who you will unlock as you advance in the game but the first one you will have at the beginning will be the Batarang. I am sure you are all too familiar with this "ninja-star" like gadget use in disorienting enemies, stunning them, disabling stuff etc. The second one will have to be the Explosive Gel. It's basically what the name says, you spray it down on a weak surface and it goes K-Boom, helping you in taking down criminals and advance in the game. The third one and my favourite is the Bat Claw, initially the grapple that you use to climb on buildings or escape bad situations, after some progress you will be able to break down fragile walls, stun enemies bringing them to you and help you win the big boss fight. There are many others gadgets in the game, some unlocked only by upgrades but I find these the main and most iconic ones that will get you interested, others will help you open up gates, disable gas bombs, distract enemies etc.
Now let's talk about the combat. Batman Arkham has one of the best and satisfying combat systems ever made. Mainly involving 3 things: attacking, dodging/countering and stunning. But you can always spice it up using some gadgets. Compared with the other games in the series this one is more complicated in my opinion. The counter attacks are a bit late and work when work only with perfect timing while there is no knife escape and all these I found them annoying even tough it might not sound like a big deal. After experiencing this I clearly saw the foundation that the developers used in improving the game and combat, and creating the future masterpieces after this monumental achievement.
OK so we covered up the main stuff but I wanna talk about the upgrades who I remained fairly disappointed of how less they are, mainly consisting in armor upgrading and combos. The other ones are just gadgets.
Riddles. Oh riddles... I am ashamed to say that I never gathered all Enigma's trophies but that's probably because of my laziness because the Asylum is not a big map so for who is patient enough and has the ambition to find them all and solve all the riddles you will find yourselves succeeding in no time.
This game's graphics are amazing and it was released in 2009. The graphics engine belongs to Unreal Engine 3 supporting DirectX 9, frame rate did not drop lower then 60 in my experience.  They all have a comic book 3D look about it which only makes them more suiting for this game. The team said that they used a series of saturated colors in order to transform the place  into a grim looking asylum, bleeding with desperation and insanity. The architecture presents a Gothic look and the sewers and underground structures resemble the Victorian industry. Everything is made to look over-the-top and extravagant and it brought me many times thinking about the comic itself and I confess that Arkham Asylum has the best design compared to the others even in the menu section and character's bios the comic look still stands strong. The originality struck me and I couldn't love it more. As for the details, I advice anybody who wants to enjoy this game at it's best, to use a good graphic card. The details that this place has are INSANE. To files that are scattered around showing familiar names to the smallest pictures on the ground. Jesus at the beginning I couldn't even believe that somebody would take his time for this but the effort was well used.
As for the music I absolutely loved it. Eerie, strange, Gothic instrumentals that created this amazing experience through out the game. Don't have much to say about it though just that it was fitting for this whole place.
Batman Arkham Asylum is the daddy. The entire game was well created. It was creepy, funny, action paced, just a bit of everything and in good measures. The voice actors brought life to the characters, beautiful design helped immersing in this "wonderland" of insanity and the combat system and stealth approaches makes everything fun and challenging. A masterpiece of a game hands down.
Great narrative. Amazing and original design, very detailed. Good graphics. A lot of collectibles.
Not many upgrades to choose from. Batman felt more "normal" so to speak, everytime he would climb or get hit he would show his pain, not saying it's bad but for me I didn't like to see Batman other that stone cold at work.

The game is just pure fun, exploring through locations and flying through the timeline. The combat system is fairly lax, with you essentially swithing strategies throughout a fight instead of picking individual moves to use (though you do that sometimes as well, especially for boss fights). The game also features a Pokemon esque monster capturing and leveling system, with less emphasis on catch em all and more emphasis on get the strongest.
This isn't a game for the hardcore, meticulously plan and grind rpg fans, but it is a great game to chill out and kill giant monsters through the timeline with a typically wierd JRPG story. And I love it.

I'm awful at doing in depth reviews, so I'll give some of my quick thoughts.
I've was introduced to Higurashi through the anime.  While the anime was an amazing adaptation of an intricate story, the source material still stands head and shoulders above.  All of the characters are more fleshed out, and given more attention.  There are jokes and club activity scenes that didn't make it into the anime at all.  The story and backstory of Hinamizawa is given way more detail.
If you've seen the show, or have read the VNs before, on reread, you'll notice so many hints and minor details that clue in at what's actually going on, and it's really satisfying.
If you're completely new to the series, you'll probably be confused about what's actually going on by the end of the game, but let me assure you that Higurashi is one of the few works I've seen where absolutely every loose-end is tied up by the end of the adventure.
The translation is really good, way better than the original localization MG put out years ago, and I'm glad they redid it.  The new sprites are also really pretty, and I actually prefer them to the PS3 versions.  The photo-filtered backgrounds don't bug me, but from what I understand, it's easy enough to patch in the PS3 backgrounds with a little googling.
When I first saw that MangaGamer was going to charge $5-10 per part, I was a little skeptical, but since picking up and playing parts 1 and 2, I'm eager to throw my money at them for the rest.

Another World is a classic title that still holds up today. It's visual style remains unique and still looks good, and the gameplay is great.
It is a pretty linear sidescroller, with lots of puzzle-type sequences and gunplay. There is only one weapon, but it has multiple functions that you will discover as you play. The game has no understandable dialogue, so everything is learned by example or trial and error. You will die, a lot, but checkpoints are common.
The only drawbacks are that the controls can be a little tricky, and that the game is very short. You will be able to beat it in a couple of hours pretty easily, but the length is about right, and there is a lot of variety.
Definitely pick this up, especially if it's on sale for a few dollars. I loved it back when it came out, and it's still great today.

Stellar Tactics:
~~~~~~~~~~~
The “Phase virus” is bringing mankind to its knees! But that was not the worst of it; a meteor homing for earth was the last straw.  The fight for survival was intense and the best of humankind (not infected) worked day and night to build four massive spaceships to send the remaining healthy humans to space to find new worlds to colonize. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP . . .  you’re just being woken up! BEEP.BEEP.BEEP. . . You and your team are on one of these spaceships! Welcome to Stellar Tactics!
Stellar Tactics is an adventure / action / turned-based combat game set in a space environment.
First, it’s customization time! Yes, you will have to create your four men’s or women’s (mixed if you like) squad. You will be able to mix and match faces, hair, complexity and voices for each of your characters - plenty of fun there. Add some points to your attributes (strength, dexterity, agility and more) as well as your skills in weaponry, hand-to-hand combat and specialities (hacking, crafting and others).
When you are done, your four-person squad will be awoken from their deep sleep capsules.  You will be greeted by Dr Rhamus, a top scientist on board your spaceship. You quickly find out that your squad is a special elite force and the reason for your sudden wake-up call is that the “Phage Virus” contaminated personnel on your giant spacecraft. The “Phague Virus” attaches itself to the neurological system and destroys the brain host; in short, you become a zombie if you are affected!
Upon this great introduction, you will be sent to accomplish quests. As you go through the spaceship, your squad will be able to search boxes, cabinets, wardrobes for items (ammunition, money and other things). It will be very easy to spot by using the LCTRL key. As soon as your squad encounters one or more enemies, the turn-based combat will automatically take over.
I hope you have found enough ammunition, because you will need it! Each of you characters will have movement and action points. So, the trick is to be able to see your foe and be able to target and shoot them. Long-range weapons will help you shoot from a distance and depending on what you are using, you can set up your gun to shoot just one or a burst of bullets. The enemies are fast and not easy to defeat, to be honest with you. Some will fight bare-handed but others will shoot projectiles from their hands, or even use metal objects to inflict personal injury. During the battle, one or several of your personel might obtain skill upgrades or even level up. If that’s the case, make sure to open your character page and distribute points to your characters attributes.
Very nice graphics with a good story so far. The commands need to be much smoother in my opinion, sometimes it can take a couple of clicks to get your squad to move, which can be annoying. A mini map would be helpful too.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Interesting story
-	Great character customization
-	Good turn-based combat
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls need to be smoother
-	No achievements or trading cards (at this stage)
This is a very impressive early access game – I am glad to have Stellar Tactics in my game library.
8/10

Danmaku Unlimited 2 is a great japanese bullet hell game for fans of the genre and newcomers. Yes, you read it right: newcomers. If you're new to these kind of games, don't be afraid of all this barrage of bullets you saw on the screenshots; there's an easy mode to start and you can use continues. Between each playthrough you'll rank up and will be able to buy more lifes, upgrade your weapons, etc.
You can choose to play two full-featured modes ("Classic" and "Burst" - the latter is score oriented) and two extra modes ("Boss Rush" and "Free Play"). DU2 has only five levels, but they have good replayability.
This game works well with keyboard, Xbox 360 controller and generic joysticks (it even has DirectInput as an option). The soundtrack is top-notch will keep you on the edge of your chair during your playthroughs.
If you always wanted to try a bullet hell game but don't want to spend much money on something you might not like, I suggest you to try Danmaku Unlimited 2. You'll probably enjoy it. Also, It's cheap enough at the full price and an absolute steal when it's on sale.

It looks nice and plays fairly well, but the gameplay is lacking. Mechanics are basic and depthless. Though clean, responsive and of a fair variety, they just aren't fun and boil down to look, run jump and interact. Doing anything at all, from walking back and forth, to collecting money bags, fighting with quick time events or 'flying' in a circular motion while shooting a cthulhu like monster, really feels like a slog. The different points of view idea is novel, though let down by a rather cut and dry, linear delivery. The story, aimed to be relatable en mass and good intentioned, is boring, uninspired and cliche; made worse by a lack of voice acting in favour of shallow, robotic, text delivered internal thoughts. As a result, there is little reason to be emotionally invested in any of the characters or events as they unfold, or rather do not unfold, as levels are self contained and void of interconnection.
To me it feels like a museum piece. Though interactive, there is no weight to your actions and the tangents, intended to deliver from various points of view and offer the illusion of choice, instead feel linear and contrarily, predetermined. Though you could, in theory, spend a good few hours playing through each level, exploring every alternative decision or method of completion, the lack of qualities mentioned above leaves me with no motivation to do so.
It is free and it is indy, so maybe I'm being too harsh, but I just can't enjoy it. Too often indy games are all style and no substance, or their promises are too ambitious to deliver. I'd love to see more creative liberty from indy devs beyond graphics. Rethink game mechanics and the notion of what a game is and can achieve and most importantly, focus on quality and ingenuity, not quantity and the status quo.

It finally happened, ZUN finally put a game on Steam. He actually did it, the absolute madman.
Touhou 16 but now on Steam. It's pretty much the same as 16, but now you don't have to feel guilty about pirating the game or spend $50+ on importing a CD. You get to choose from 4 playable characters, each with their own play styles and level of difficulty. The game is short but offers a ton of replayability.
Even though Touhou 16 is 16+ games into the series, it's a great starting point for new players. It's the most accessible game since it's on Steam, it's the most recent game so it's the most functionally stable one, and you don't need to play previous games to play or understand this one. Not to mention it offers a practice mode and an easy difficulty option for players to improve.
It's a great game with a nice community and a near endless supply of fan content. Half the fun that comes from this series is all the art and music people create.
If you're interested in the game, consider getting an English patch. You can play without it (fly around and shoot, don't need language for that), but you miss out on the story since you can't read anything. Touhou Community Reliant Automatic Patcher (thcrap) is your friend, and free too!

I passed over Grandia II when I was growing up, but I remember it being highly regarded at the time.  I went into this PC version with high expectations based on that and I was pretty underwhelmed.
First the good parts:
- The translation is pretty decent
- The PC port seems alright
- Being a Grandia game, the battles can at times be engaging
- Being a Grandia game, there's lots of dialogue and character interaction if you want it.
But now for the bad parts...
- The story is mostly generic and stupid in a very JRPG way.  It's typical of JRPGs of its era.  It's the sort of plot that I might have thought was good when I was a 12-year-old, but most adults would be embarrassed by it. The characters are mostly annoying most of the time.  Their behavior is juvenile and tedious, which makes it hard to care about them.  The dialog is good when the characters are just chatting, but awful when they're talking about anything related to the plot, especially towards the end.  I've heard enough JRPG monologues about how the power of the heart will overcome any obstacle, thanks.
- The battle system had potential, but throws away nearly all of that potential by 1) making battles take too long by using any strategy except unleashing powerful AOE attacks over and over, and 2) making all the AOE attacks consist of 20-second-long low-budget CGI animations.  Because there are save points where you can heal all over the place, the most rational course of action is to just use Sky Dragon Slash or "Zap All" or whatever every single battle.  This means you spend 80% of the time in battles watching the same crappy 320x240 animations over and over again. There's no option to skip these animations. Not fun. This is not a game that respects the value of its players' time.
To be honest, I'm a little confused by other reviews seeming to praise the story.  Maybe I'm just getting to old to enjoy this sort of thing.
They should have taken their CGI budget and spent it on writing instead.

It's not hard to figure out what Danmaku Unlimited 2 is, I mean it says it right on the "box". This is a bullet-hell 2D shooter, the kind where your screen gets flooded by death and you're expected to survive and get a high-score. While lacking in style, DU2 has the fundamentals down pat, is sufficiently challenging, and can be quite entertaining.
I forgot the plot to this game. It was probably too dramatic and complicated for me to understand.
To start with, DU2 has an upgrade system. It's a little unique in that while you eventually get more points to distribute, you never get enough to max out anything. Your options include increasing your firepower, your ADS (shield), and additional lives & continues. Extra survival sounds nice, but taking damage will severely penalize your score. Unless beating the true boss reveals the best ending since -insert your favorite videogame ending here- I'd consider investing elsewhere. Most of your "upgrades" are going to come the old-fashioned way, playing through the game again and again until you figure it all out.
There are two modes of play, burst and arcade. I'm going to refrain from speaking too much on the scoring systems. If I understood anything at all I'd have scored trillions of points. If I had to guess, I'd say getting a high-score involves lots of staying close to bullets, knowing when to trigger the hyper ability, and keeping that multiplier high. Burst mode is probably a bit easier to figure out, since you can use a wicked laser to build up the multiplier. Arcade mode is easier though, mainly because holding down the fire button provides a homing shot, allowing you to focus almost entirely on dodging stuff.
Honestly, there's not much else to say. Danmaku Unlimited 2 doesn't really throw any curveballs. Once you understand the basics, it's all a matter of dealing with the increasing intensity of enemy fire. Each of the five stages has the standard mid-boss/boss setup, and the bosses themselves are multi-form behemoths with the occasional gimmick. Like I said, this game doesn't do much to stand out in terms of visuals. This can be considered a good thing however. Not everybody wants to play a shooter, where all of the characters are little girls, and they're fighting an army of giant crocodiles over the world's supply of rice cakes.
Danmaku Unlimited 2 delivers exactly what you'd expect out of a quality 2D shooter. It's probably sitting in your Steam library right now, alone and unloved. Take a chance on it sometime.

As for newcomers who may wonder if they want it:
Touhou is a rather challenging bullet-hell game. The story of each part is mostly self-contained, meaning that you can start at Hidden Star in Four Seasons. English-patches will very likely be avaible very soon. (They are getting worked on as I write this review), however, you can play this game without understanding a thing. You shouldn't, but you can. You'll be playing a young lady who's trying to make her way through bullets from all sides, utilizing her own attacks and bombs. Already own the game but decided to buy it again to support ZUN officially releasing these games to the west. The game uses the same score file as a regular instillation of the game for those concerned, it's nice to know I can switch between the steam version and the English patch without any added work. I'll provide some resources and just a little bit of advice for new users below.
New players can read up on the gameplay at the Touhou wiki:
There's a translation of all the dialoge over there too:
The steam version doesn't seem to be working with the English patcher provided by Touhou Patch Center at the time of this review. If you're new it's worth getting familiar with the patcher either way:
My advice to new players is start with normal (difficulties: easy, normal, hard, lunatic) and go down to easy if that's too tough. If you're never clearing the 2nd stage without bombing for your life and using all your continues than take it down a notch, half the fun is just getting better at it over time. Also, there's a really useful mode called spell practice (4th from the top) which I highly recommend using if you find yourself always getting hit by a specific boss pattern (aka Sell Card). Touhou is a bullet hell game so it's not going to be easy but it's still supposed to be fun, so have fun with it. If you are looking for the hardest game around then there are plenty of bullet hells that would leave most of us suicidal, this isn't really one of them though, it's a fun game that offers flashy patterns, cute characters and a great soundtrack.
